=== NOTES 5:3 | R&d Spending in India - Gerd, Innovation Indices, Patents Ecosystem
## SUB 0 | Innovation Rankings – GII, NRI, India Innovation Index
[3:0:0] # Global Innovation Index (GII)
[3:0:1] - Published by **WIPO** (est. **1967**, **Geneva**, UN specialised agency; 1883/1886 Paris/Berne conventions, 1893 = predecessor bureau BIRPI).
[3:0:2] - **7 pillars:** 5 input (institutions, human capital and research, infrastructure, market sophistication, business sophistication) + 2 output (knowledge-technology, creative).
[3:0:3] TABLE head: Year | India's rank
  [3:0:3.0] 2015 | 81
  [3:0:3.1] 2016 | 66
  [3:0:3.2] 2017 | 60
  [3:0:3.3] 2019 | 52
  [3:0:3.4] 2022 | 40
  [3:0:3.5] 2023 | 40 (retained)
  [3:0:3.6] 2024 | 39
  [3:0:3.7] 2025 | 38 of 139
[3:0:4] - **DST report 2022:** India **3rd** in scientific publications (NSF database), in PhDs awarded and in number of start-ups – but **40th** in the GII (TREI-RB 2023).
[3:0:5] # Other indices (APPSC G1 2024 statements – all four correct)
[3:0:6] - **WIPO Report 2022:** India **7th** in **resident** patent filing activity (later **6th** in both resident and non-resident filing, WIPO 2023).
[3:0:7] - **Network Readiness Index 2023:** India **60th**, up from **79th (2019)**; NRI 2024 = **49th**.
[3:0:8] - **International IP Index 2024** (US Chamber, 12th edition): India **42nd of 55**.
[3:0:9] # India Innovation Index (NITI Aayog)
[3:0:10] - Publisher **NITI Aayog** (with Institute for Competitiveness); aim – rank States/UTs to lift the GII rank.
[3:0:11] - **2019 (first edition): Karnataka 1st** among major states (APPSC DAO).
[3:0:12] TABLE head: Category (2021, 3rd edition, released 21 July 2022) | Leader
  [3:0:12.0] Major States | Karnataka
  [3:0:12.1] North-East and Hill States | Manipur
  [3:0:12.2] UTs and City States | Chandigarh
[3:0:13] - **AP:** **9th** among Major States (2021, score 13.32); Telangana 2nd.
[3:0:14] - **State R&D policy:** **Karnataka** released India's first State Research, Development and Innovation Policy (Bengaluru Tech Summit, Nov 2022).
[3:0:15] ~~ Sources: DST Year End Review 2023 (dst.gov.in/node/7484, as quoted in search results); PMF S&T Part 8 (pmf-science-tech-08) p.78 (WIPO 1967, Geneva); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 p.40; app notes 5:3 (sub 3, 4)
## SUB 1 | Patents, Copyright and IPR Law
[3:1:0] TABLE head: Act / policy | Provision
  [3:1:0.0] Patents Act, 1970 (amended 2005 for TRIPS) | Protection 20 years from filing; novel, inventive, industrially applicable
  [3:1:0.1] Copyright Act, 1957 | Published book: lifetime of the author + 60 years
  [3:1:0.2] Trade Marks Act, 1999 | 10 years, renewable
  [3:1:0.3] National IPR Policy, 2016 | "Creative India; Innovative India"
  [3:1:0.4] SIPP 2016 | Free start-up IP filing facilitation
[3:1:1] - **Not patentable in India:** **plants and animals** (except micro-organisms), **plant varieties** and **essentially biological processes** for producing plants or seeds (Sec. 3(j)); plant varieties are protected instead by the **PPV&FR Act, 2001**.
[3:1:2] - **IPAB** (Intellectual Property Appellate Board): set up **15 Sept 2003**; heard patent appeals from 2 April 2007; **abolished in April 2021** (Tribunals Reforms Ordinance/Act 2021) – appeals now go to the **High Courts**.
[3:1:3] - **CSIR** = the Indian institution with the most patents – it has filed more patents than all individual Indian patentees put together (APPSC G2 2003).
[3:1:4] - **Resident vs non-resident filings:** in **January-March 2022**, Indian applicants filed **10,706** applications against **9,090** by foreign applicants – first time in 11 years.
[3:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 8 (pmf-science-tech-08) p.69-74 (patents, copyright, what cannot be patented); NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 p.40 (IPAB set-up); IPAB abolition 2021: general knowledge, not checked; app notes 5:3 (sub 5)
## SUB 2 | Researchers, Publications and Research Institutions
[3:2:0] TABLE head: Indicator | India
  [3:2:0.0] Researchers | 262 FTE per million
  [3:2:0.1] Scientific publications | 3rd globally (nanoscience also 3rd, after China, USA)
  [3:2:0.2] Patent filing | 6th (WIPO 2023)
  [3:2:0.3] PhDs awarded (2021-22) | 32,588 (most in Science 7,408, then Engineering 6,270)
  [3:2:0.4] PhD enrolment (2021-22) | 2.12 lakh (+81.2% from 1.17 lakh in 2014-15)
[3:2:1] - **SCImago Institutions Ranking 2017:** **CSIR 9th** among 1,207 government (public research) institutions of the world; 75th overall (12th in 2016).
[3:2:2] - **ISSN** = **International Standard Serial Number** – an **8-digit** code for serial publications (journals, magazines); books carry the ISBN.
[3:2:3] - **AP:** **IISER Tirupati** 20th among Indian institutions in Nature Index 2026; **IIITDM Kurnool** = Institute of National Importance.
[3:2:4] ~~ Sources: AffairsCloud, "CSIR ranked 9th Public Research Institution of the World" (2 Sept 2017); general knowledge, not checked (ISSN); app notes 5:3 (sub 2)
## SUB 3 | GERD and Who Spends on R&D
[3:3:0] TABLE head: Country | GERD (% of GDP)
  [3:3:0.0] India | 0.84% (FY 2023-24) – 15-year high, ending a decade-long fall
  [3:3:0.1] USA | about 3.5%
  [3:3:0.2] China | about 2.4%
  [3:3:0.3] Israel | about 6.3% (2023) – world's highest (PMF Lens gives ~5%)
  [3:3:0.4] South Korea | about 5% (2023) – 2nd
[3:3:1] - **Earlier:** **0.64-0.65%** (2020-21). National target: **2% of GDP**.
[3:3:2] - **Total R&D funding:** Rs 1.33 lakh crore (FY20) → **Rs 2.45 lakh crore** (FY24).
[3:3:3] - **FY 2023-24:** private industry share **51.8%** – passed public funding **for the first time**; 2020-21 private only **~36%** (USA ~70%, South Korea ~76%).
[3:3:4] - **Agency shares of central R&D (2020-21):** **DOS 18.4%**, ICAR 12.4%, DAE 11.4%, CSIR 8.2%, DST 6.8%; **DRDO** long the largest (31.6% in 2017-18).
[3:3:5] - **Why private R&D lags:** risk aversion, weak lab-industry links, **shortage of deep-tech capital**.
[3:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens Aug 2026 (pmf-lens-2026-08-02) p.88; PMF S&T Part 1 p.43-44; app notes 5:3 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 4 | Start-ups and R&D Funding Reforms
[3:4:0] - **Startup India – 16 January 2016:** Fund of Funds Rs 10,000 crore, **3-year tax exemption**, exit in **90 days** (not 30), self-certification.
[3:4:1] - India = **3rd-largest start-up hub**; **1.59 lakh** DPIIT-recognised start-ups (Sep 2025); unicorns: India **4th with 61** (Hurun Global Unicorn Index, Jun 2026).
[3:4:2] - **Support:** **AIM** (Atal Tinkering Labs, incubators); **iDEX** with India-Korea **KIND-X**; **MANAGE, Hyderabad** – agri-start-up incubation.
[3:4:3] - **ANRF Act 2023:** funds **basic and applied** research; ~80% of funds went to IITs (Aug 2026 critique).
[3:4:4] - **RDI Scheme – 1 July 2025:** **Rs 1 lakh crore**; custodian **ANRF**; private R&D in AI, quantum, biotech, energy.
[3:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:3 (sub 6, 7)

## SUB 1 | Gravitational Waves, LIGO-India and Mega-Science Projects
[5:1:0] # Gravitational waves
[5:1:1] - Predicted by **Einstein (1916)**; ripples in space-time from **merging black holes**, neutron-star collisions.
[5:1:2] - **LIGO** = **Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory** (USA); first detection **14 September 2015** (announced 11 Feb 2016); **Nobel 2017**: Weiss, Barish, Thorne.
[5:1:3] - **Second detection** announced **June 2016**: two **black holes** merging ~**1.4 billion light-years** away (not white dwarfs).
[5:1:4] - **eLISA** (evolved Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) = space mission to **detect gravitational waves** (not neutrinos).
[5:1:5] - Black-hole merger observations (UPSC 2019) = **gravitational waves detected**, not Higgs bosons.
[5:1:6] # LIGO-India
[5:1:7] - At **Aundh, Hingoli**, Maharashtra; **DAE + DST** with US **NSF**.
[5:1:8] - Lead institutions: **IPR Gandhinagar, IUCAA Pune, RRCAT Indore** (not IIST or "Kepler's Observatory").
[5:1:9] - Consortium = **IndIGO** (Indian Initiative in Gravitational-wave Observations) – the APPSC G2 2017 key said "IndLIGO", which is not the name.
[5:1:10] # Other projects and telescopes
[5:1:11] TABLE head: Project | Site | Indian lead
  [5:1:11.0] ITER | Cadarache, France | ITER-India, IPR Gandhinagar (leads both LIGO-India and ITER-India)
  [5:1:11.1] Thirty Meter Telescope | Mauna Kea, Hawaii | DST + DAE; IIA Bengaluru
  [5:1:11.2] Square Kilometre Array | South Africa, Australia | NCRA-TIFR, Pune
  [5:1:11.3] INO (neutrinos) | Bodi West Hills, Theni, Tamil Nadu | TIFR
  [5:1:11.4] MACE | Hanle, Ladakh | BARC with ECIL; highest imaging Cherenkov telescope (opened 4 Oct 2024)
  [5:1:11.5] FAIR | Darmstadt, Germany | Bose Institute; DST:DAE 50:50
[5:1:12] - **Devasthal Optical Telescope** (3.6 m, ARIES, Nainital, 2016) = **India's largest optical telescope**.
[5:1:13] - **Sampurnanand Telescope** (104 cm) at **ARIES, Nainital** (Uttarakhand – **not Ladakh**): **50 years** (1972-2022); comets, star-forming regions, clusters.
[5:1:14] - **IIA Bengaluru**: VELC payload of Aditya-L1, Himalayan Chandra Telescope (2 m, Hanle), Kodaikanal Solar Observatory.
[5:1:15] ~~ Sources: PMF Science and Technology Part 8 p.127-128; app notes 5:5 (sub 7); general knowledge for the 2016 detection and DOT size (not checked)
## SUB 2 | ICAR – Origin, Structure, Heads and News
[5:2:0] - **ICAR** = **Indian Council of Agricultural Research**; set up **16 July 1929** (ICAR Day = **16 July**) as a **society** (Societies Registration Act 1860) on the **Royal Commission on Agriculture** report; HQ New Delhi.
[5:2:1] - Under **DARE** (Dec 1973), Ministry of Agriculture; **113 institutes** (72 research institutes).
[5:2:2] - **Director General** = Secretary DARE: **Dr S. Ayyappan** (2010-16, the answer in 2015) → **Dr Mangi Lal Jat** (as of 2026).
[5:2:3] - **KVKs**: district level, **100% centrally funded**, under **11 ATARIs**; first KVK **Puducherry, 1974** (Mohan Singh Mehta committee, 1973). Sep 2026: skill centres in all KVKs by Dec 2028.
[5:2:4] # In the news
[5:2:5] - **13 Dec 2019**: ICAR–**NABARD** MoU (sustainable agriculture, climate-resilient farming).
[5:2:6] - **Sardar Patel Outstanding ICAR Institution Award 2021** (large institute): **ICAR-NAARM, Hyderabad**.
[5:2:7] - **562** high-yielding field-crop varieties released 2019-2021 (APPSC AE 2022 key).
[5:2:8] - **Lumpi-ProVacInd**: lumpy skin disease vaccine developed by **two ICAR institutes**.
[5:2:9] ~~ Sources: Praveen CA360 Jan 2026 p.36; Daily CA 2 Nov 2026 p.3; app notes 5:5 (subs 0, 4); gktoday.in (ICAR-NABARD MoU); adda247 (NAARM award, search result)

## SUB 4 | DAE, AEC and the Department of Space
[5:4:0] # Atomic energy
[5:4:1] - **Atomic Energy Commission: 1948** (Atomic Energy Act 1948), chaired by Secretary DAE; **DAE: 1954** by Presidential Order; both DAE and DoS are under the **Prime Minister**.
[5:4:2] - **AERB** (1983) = **nuclear and radiation safety regulator** (BARC = research, NPCIL = power plants, TIFR = research).
[5:4:3] TABLE head: Unit (all under DAE) | Function
  [5:4:3.0] BARC, Trombay | Began 1954 as AEET, renamed 1967 after Homi Bhabha
  [5:4:3.1] IGCAR, Kalpakkam | Fast breeder reactor R&D
  [5:4:3.2] NPCIL | PSU (1987); builds and runs nuclear plants (23 reactors, 7,480 MW)
  [5:4:3.3] TIFR (1945, Bombay) | Start of organised nuclear research; NCRA-TIFR runs GMRT near Pune
  [5:4:3.4] Heavy Water Board (Mumbai) | Heavy water – not AMD
  [5:4:3.5] IREL (Mumbai) | Beach-sand minerals, rare earths, zircon
  [5:4:3.6] AMD (Hyderabad) | Atomic minerals exploration
  [5:4:3.7] UCIL | Uranium mining
  [5:4:3.8] HBNI | DAE deemed university (NIRF 2025: 7th research, 20th overall)
[5:4:4] - Research reactors: **APSARA** Asia's first (1956), **Dhruva** largest, **KAMINI** only U-233-fuelled.
[5:4:5] - DAE products: Bhabhatron (cobalt therapy), Nisargruna (biogas), AKRUTI (rural incubator), TAG groundnut varieties.
[5:4:6] # Space and defence
[5:4:7] - **ISRO** 15 Aug 1969 (INCOSPAR 1962, Vikram Sarabhai); **Space Commission + DoS 1972**; **ISRO HQ and DoS secretariat: Antariksh Bhavan, Bengaluru**; Chairman V. Narayanan (2026).
[5:4:8] - Arms: Antrix (Sep 1992), **NSIL (2019)**, **IN-SPACe (2020, Ahmedabad)**; NRSC Hyderabad. LVM3-M6 (24 Dec 2025): BlueBird Block-2, heaviest payload from India.
[5:4:9] - **DRDO** (1958), DRDO Bhawan, New Delhi, under **DDR&D**; Chairman Samir V. Kamat.
[5:4:10] - Mandates: ISRO – space for development; DRDO – defence systems; DAE – nuclear power, radioisotopes; ICAR – agriculture; ICMR – biomedical research. ICMR under DHR, CSIR under DSIR.
[5:4:11] - Other HQs: Indian Bureau of Mines Nagpur; CIMFR Dhanbad; NATMO Kolkata; **MIDHANI Hyderabad**.
[5:4:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Science and Technology Part 4 p.61; PMF Science and Technology Part 5 p.9-12; Daily CA 21 Oct 2026 p.4; app notes 5:5 (subs 0-3)

[6:0:2] - **100th (centenary) session: Kolkata, 3-7 Jan 2013** – books say ISC "completed 100 years" in **2013** (strictly 100 years from Jan 1914 = 2014).

## SUB 2 | Vigyan Prasar, Outreach Bodies and the National Innovation Foundation
[6:2:0] # Science communication
[6:2:1] - **Vigyan Prasar**: autonomous body of **DST**, **1989**, New Delhi (not HRD).
[6:2:2] - **DD Science** (one-hour slot on DD National) + **India Science** (Vigyan Prasar's internet/OTT channel, not NCSM) – launched together **15 January 2019**.
[6:2:3] - **Vigyan Dhara**: DST umbrella scheme merging 3 schemes – capacity building; R&D; innovation and technology deployment (Aug 2024).
[6:2:4] TABLE head: Channel | Run by
  [6:2:4.0] Gyan Darshan | 26 Jan 2000; MHRD with IGNOU and Prasar Bharati
  [6:2:4.1] Gyan Vani / Vyas | FM counterpart / UGC-CEC channel
  [6:2:4.2] SWAYAM Prabha | Free DTH, Ministry of Education, 2017, 32 channels
[6:2:5] # Outreach bodies
[6:2:6] TABLE head: Body | Under | Fact
  [6:2:6.0] NCSTC | DST | National Children's Science Congress; VIGYANOTSAV
  [6:2:6.1] NCSM | Ministry of Culture (not DST) | 1978, HQ Kolkata; nodal for SPoCS
  [6:2:6.2] Vigyan Rail | DST (not CSIR) | 2003-04
  [6:2:6.3] Science Express | DST + Vikram A. Sarabhai Community Science Centre | First flagged off 2007
  [6:2:6.4] Rashtriya Avishkar Abhiyan | Ministry of HRD/Education | 2015
  [6:2:6.5] ICMR-SHINE | ICMR | Classes 9-12
[6:2:7] - **ICSSR** (social science) is **not an S&T body**, unlike DST, CSIR, DAE.
[6:2:8] - India's **first dinosaurium**: **B.M. Birla Science Centre, Hyderabad**.
[6:2:9] # National Innovation Foundation
[6:2:10] - Grew from the **Honey Bee Network** (Prof. **Anil K. Gupta**, SRISTI, IIM Ahmedabad); **NIF-India, March 2000**: **autonomous body of DST**, **Gandhinagar**.
[6:2:11] - Mandate: scout, support, spread **grassroots innovations** and traditional knowledge – **not** advanced research with foreign institutes (UPSC 2015: "a only").
[6:2:12] - IGNITE, Biennial Grassroots Innovation Awards, **Festival of Innovation (FOIN)** at **Rashtrapati Bhavan**.

=== NOTES 5:7 | Programmes Promoting S&t and Innovation – Inspire, Fellowships, Atal Innovation Mission
## SUB 0 | INSPIRE – DST Flagship (2008)
[7:0:0] # Basics
[7:0:1] - **INSPIRE** = **Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research**; flagship scheme of the **Department of Science and Technology (DST)**, launched **2008**, to draw young talent into science.
[7:0:2] - **Not** a Ministry of Education scheme and **not** a residential programme for Classes VI–X (the residential part is the INSPIRE science camp; MANAK is an award, not a course).
[7:0:3] # Components
[7:0:4] TABLE head: Component | Full form | Target
  [7:0:4.0] SEATS | Scheme for Early Attraction of Talents for Science | School students (MANAK awards, INSPIRE camps)
  [7:0:4.1] MANAK | Million Minds Augmenting National Aspiration and Knowledge | Classes VI–X, aged 10–15; ₹10,000 each
  [7:0:4.2] SHE | Scholarship for Higher Education | Top-ranked UG/PG students in natural and basic sciences
  [7:0:4.3] AORC | Assured Opportunity for Research Careers – INSPIRE Fellowship (PhD) + INSPIRE Faculty | Doctoral and post-doctoral researchers
[7:0:5] - **2025 data:** MANAK **8.54 lakh** ideas, **46,926** students given ₹10,000; INSPIRE Fellowship **653** doctoral fellowships, **65% women**.
[7:0:6] > ⚠ Trap: SHE = **Scholarship for Higher Education**, NOT "Support for Her Education" – it is not a women's scheme (APPSC FRO 2022). Statement angle: "separate components SEATS, SHE, AORC" ✓ and "DST flagship" ✓; "residential for VI–X" ✗ and "launched by Ministry of Education" ✗ → **B & C only** (TREI-RB 2023).
[7:0:7] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.40 (DST key initiatives: INSPIRE); app notes 5:7 sub 0; online-inspire.gov.in (general knowledge, not checked: camps)
## SUB 1 | Women in STEM – KIRAN, WIDUSHI, WEST
[7:1:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Body | Target group
  [7:1:0.0] WISE-KIRAN (Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement through Nurturing; WISE = Women in Science and Engineering) | DST | Women scientists, esp. after a career break; WISE-PhD, WISE-PDF, WIDUSHI
  [7:1:0.1] WIDUSHI | DST (under WISE-KIRAN) | Senior women scientists, interdisciplinary S&T
  [7:1:0.2] Vigyan Jyoti | DST, with Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti | Meritorious girls, Classes IX–XII
  [7:1:0.3] CURIE | DST | 22 women PG colleges – research facilities
  [7:1:0.4] GATI (Gender Advancement for Transforming Institutions) | DST | Institutions – gender-equity charter, modelled on UK's Athena SWAN
  [7:1:0.5] SERB-POWER | SERB (now ANRF) | Women researchers in academic/R&D institutions
  [7:1:0.6] BioCARe | DBT | Women biotech scientists after a career break
  [7:1:0.7] SEED | DST | 52 STI Hubs for SC/ST communities
[7:1:1] - **KIRAN** is the GoI initiative for innovation and research **especially among women** – not Jan Dhan, Digital India or Make in India (TSPSC 2023).
[7:1:2] - **WEST (Women in Engineering, Science & Technology):** launched **September 2022** by the **Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser** as a new initiative **of I-STEM**; helps women with STEM backgrounds, including after a career break.
[7:1:3] - **I-STEM** (Indian Science, Technology and Engineering facilities Map) = a **national** web portal for sharing R&D facilities (PM-STIAC mission) – **not international**.
[7:1:4] > ⚠ Trap: senior women + interdisciplinary = **WIDUSHI**; GATI targets institutions, not individuals; SERB-POWER is SERB, not DST.
[7:1:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:7 sub 2; pib.gov.in PRID=1857175 (WEST, 6 Sep 2022)
## SUB 2 | Fellowships and Brain-gain Schemes
[7:2:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Awarding body | Target
  [7:2:0.0] VAJRA (Visiting Advanced Joint Research Faculty) | SERB (now ANRF) | Overseas scientists incl. NRIs/OCIs, short spells in India
  [7:2:0.1] Ramanujan Fellowship | SERB, now ANRF | Indian scientists abroad who return
  [7:2:0.2] Ramalingaswami Re-entry | DBT (not DST) | Life-science/biotech returnees only
  [7:2:0.3] J.C. Bose Fellowship (now JC Bose Grant) | SERB/ANRF | Active senior scientists
  [7:2:0.4] Swarnajayanti | DST, 1997 (50 years of Independence) | Young scientists with a proven record
  [7:2:0.5] PMRF | Ministry of Education (2018) | PhD scholars in IITs, IISc, IISERs
[7:2:1] - **Brain drain → brain gain:** **VAJRA, Ramanujan Fellowship and INSPIRE** (Group 1); the ASEAN-India Research Training Fellowship is for ASEAN researchers coming to India – not a brain-gain scheme.
[7:2:2] - ANRF schemes: PMECRG (PM Early Career Research Grant), Prime Minister Professorship, National Science Chair, N-PDF.
[7:2:3] > ⚠ Trap: PMRF is Ministry of Education and not a career-break scheme; Ramalingaswami and BioCARe are the only DBT schemes here.
[7:2:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:7 sub 1; PMF S&T Part 1 p.40 (SERB integrated into ANRF)
## SUB 3 | Atal Innovation Mission (AIM)
[7:3:0] - **AIM** = flagship of **NITI Aayog**, set up **2016** (announced Budget 2015) to promote innovation and entrepreneurship across the country – not DST, Labour or Skill Development (UPSC 2019; APPSC Polytechnic Lecturers 2018).
[7:3:1] TABLE head: Component | Focus
  [7:3:1.0] Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs) | Schools, grades 6–12: IoT, 3D printing, robotics; 10,000 ATLs in 700+ districts
  [7:3:1.1] Atal Incubation Centres (AICs) | Start-ups in universities/institutions
  [7:3:1.2] Atal Community Innovation Centres (ACICs) | Rural and under-served areas
  [7:3:1.3] ARISE | MSMEs
  [7:3:1.4] Atal New India Challenges | Product innovation for national challenges
[7:3:2] - **AIM 2.0 (2024):** **₹2,750 crore** till **March 2028**; **LIPI** – vernacular innovation centres in the 22 scheduled languages.
[7:3:3] - **Budget 2026-27:** ATL funding **₹500 crore → ₹3,200 crore**. **Jun 2026:** **Tripura** first State Innovation Mission under AIM 2.0; **India-France ATL Bridge** launched at **Nice**.
[7:3:4] > ⚠ Trap: "Sardar Patel / Mahatma Innovation Mission" do not exist; Kaushal Navin Lakshay is a distractor.
[7:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.41 (NITI Aayog – AIM); app notes 5:7 sub 7
## SUB 4 | DST Facility and Start-up Programmes – SATHI, FIST, NIDHI
[7:4:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Full form | Purpose
  [7:4:0.0] SATHI | Sophisticated Analytical & Technical Help Institutes | Shared, professionally run instrument centres – tackle accessibility, maintenance, redundancy and duplication of costly equipment and foster collaboration across institutions and disciplines
  [7:4:0.1] FIST | Fund for Improvement of S&T Infrastructure | Upgrade S&T infrastructure in universities
  [7:4:0.2] PURSE | Promotion of University Research and Scientific Excellence | University-only research support (2009)
  [7:4:0.3] SAIF | Sophisticated Analytical Instrument Facilities | Access to costly analytical instruments
[7:4:1] - **SATHI statement-conclusion (FRO 2023):** both conclusions (access/duplication; collaboration) follow → **both i and ii**.
[7:4:2] - **NIDHI** (**National Initiative for Developing and Harnessing Innovations**, DST, 2016): covers the chain from scouting to scaling – **PRAYAS**, Entrepreneur-in-Residence, Seed Support System, Technology Business Incubators, Accelerators, Centres of Excellence; a NIDHI **research park** at **IIT Gandhinagar** (FRO 2022).
[7:4:3] TABLE head: Other start-up support | Body | Fact
  [7:4:3.0] TIDE 2.0 | MeitY, 2019 | ICT start-ups via incubators
  [7:4:3.1] Fund of Funds for Startups | SIDBI | ₹10,000 crore
  [7:4:3.2] Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups | NCGTC | NOT a NIDHI component
[7:4:4] - **RDI Scheme** (Cabinet 1 July 2025): **₹1 lakh crore over six years** for private-sector research, development and innovation.
[7:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:7 sub 3-4; dst.gov.in SATHI (general knowledge, not checked)
## SUB 5 | Student–Scientist Connect and Research e-Platforms
[7:5:0] TABLE head: Programme | Partners | Objective
  [7:5:0.0] JIGYASA (Student-Scientist Connect) | CSIR + Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (2017) | KV students into CSIR labs
  [7:5:0.1] Smart India Hackathon | Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell + AICTE | Students solve problems of ministries and industry
  [7:5:0.2] VIPNET | Vigyan Prasar | Network of science clubs
[7:5:1] - **Shodhganga:** the **national repository of doctoral theses and dissertations** of Indian universities, run by **INFLIBNET** (UGC) – not a Ganga research project.
[7:5:2] - **e-PG Pathshala:** MoE/UGC portal of PG e-content, hosted by the **INFLIBNET Centre, Gandhinagar** (Gujarat; the centre was earlier at Ahmedabad).
[7:5:3] > ⚠ Trap: JIGYASA = CSIR + **KVS**, not CBSE, Navodaya or Army schools; Vigyan Jyoti = Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti.
[7:5:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:7 sub 5; inflibnet.ac.in (general knowledge, not checked)
## SUB 6 | Andhra Pradesh Innovation Ecosystem
[7:6:0] - **Andhra Pradesh Innovation Society (APIS):** set up **2015**; nodal agency for start-ups under the **ITE&C Department**, headed by a CEO; began at **Sunrise Towers, Innovation Valley, Rushikonda, Visakhapatnam** (exam answer for "headquarters"); its office is now at **Mangalagiri** (Amaravati region).
[7:6:1] - AP was the **first State** with an **Innovation and Startup Policy (2014-2020)**; AP has **590 ATLs** (2024-25).
[7:6:2] - **Ratan Tata Innovation Hub (RTIH):** set up by APIS as a Section-8 company; inaugurated **20 Aug 2025**; central hub at **Mangalagiri** with spokes at Visakhapatnam, Rajahmundry, Vijayawada-Guntur, Tirupati, Anantapur.
[7:6:3] - **IIDT (International Institute of Digital Technologies):** **Tirupati**.
[7:6:4] > ⚠ Outdated angle: "APIS HQ = Visakhapatnam" is the old answer; current office Mangalagiri.
[7:6:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:7 sub 8; web search (startupgrantsindia.com, thehansindia.com 2017: APIS est. 2015, Rushikonda/Mangalagiri)

=== NOTES 5:8 | National S&t Missions – Quantum, Supercomputing, Deep Ocean, BIO-E3, Anrf
## SUB 0 | Indian Supercomputers and Computing Firsts
[8:0:0] - India's supercomputer family is **PARAM**, designed and assembled by **C-DAC, Pune** (C-DAC set up 1988) – not Shubham, SX-2, Tejas or EKA.
[8:0:1] - **PARAM 8000 (1991)** = India's **first** (first indigenously developed) supercomputer; C-DAC under **Vijay Bhatkar**, the **father of Indian supercomputing**.
[8:0:2] TABLE head: Machine | Developer / site
  [8:0:2.0] PARAM 8000 | C-DAC (1991)
  [8:0:2.1] Anupam | BARC – from 1991, parallel processing
  [8:0:2.2] Flosolver | NAL Bengaluru
  [8:0:2.3] PARAM Padma | C-DAC (2003) – first Indian system on the TOP500 list (June 2003, rank 171)
  [8:0:2.4] SAGA-220 | ISRO (2011) – about 220 TFLOPS
  [8:0:2.5] SahasraT (Cray XC40) | SERC, IISc – India's fastest in 2015-16 (ahead of Aaditya, IITM Pune)
  [8:0:2.6] PARAM Siddhi-AI | C-DAC (2020) – ranked 62nd/63rd on TOP500 (Nov 2020), India's highest then
  [8:0:2.7] Pratyush / Mihir (weather) | IITM Pune / NCMRWF Noida
[8:0:3] - **Computing firsts:** first analog computer in India designed by **Samarendra Kumar Mitra** (ISI Kolkata, 1953); **TIFRAC** (1960) = first indigenous digital computer; exam keys name **"Siddharth"** as "the first computer made in India".
[8:0:4] > ⚠ Trap: PARAM 8000 is the first; PARAM Shivay is only the first NSM machine; PARAM Padma, not Siddhi-AI, was the first in the TOP500.
[8:0:5] ~~ Sources: Praveen CA360 Aug 2026 p.59 ("the first, PARAM 8000, was launched in 1991"); app notes 5:8 sub 0; web: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercomputing_in_India (PARAM Padma TOP500 2003; SahasraT), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TIFRAC
## SUB 1 | National Supercomputing Mission (NSM, 2015) – Systems and Hosts
[8:1:0] - Run jointly by **DST and MeitY** (2015); implemented by **C-DAC Pune + IISc Bengaluru**; machines linked as the **National Supercomputing Grid** over the **National Knowledge Network**; **40 systems** planned.
[8:1:1] - Indigenous stack: **Rudra** server board + **Trinetra** interconnect + open-source (AlmaLinux) software.
[8:1:2] TABLE head: System | Host
  [8:1:2.0] PARAM Shivay (2019) | IIT (BHU) Varanasi – first NSM machine
  [8:1:2.1] PARAM Brahma | IISER Pune
  [8:1:2.2] PARAM Ganga | IIT Roorkee (March 2022; built by C-DAC)
  [8:1:2.3] PARAM Porul | NIT Tiruchirappalli (May 2022)
  [8:1:2.4] PARAM Pravega | IISc Bengaluru
  [8:1:2.5] PARAM Ananta | IIT Gandhinagar
  [8:1:2.6] PARAM Kamrupa | IIT Guwahati – opened by President Droupadi Murmu, Oct 2022
  [8:1:2.7] PARAM Shakti | IIT Kharagpur; 3.1 PF Rudra-based system at IIT Madras (Jan 2026)
  [8:1:2.8] PARAM Rudra | GMRT Pune, IUAC Delhi, S.N. Bose Centre Kolkata
  [8:1:2.9] PARAM Pragya | IIT Delhi (Sonipat), AI system, Aug 2026
  [8:1:2.10] AIRAWAT (AI supercomputer) | C-DAC Pune, under the national AI programme – 75th in TOP500 at ISC 2023 (Germany, May 2023)
[8:1:3] > ⚠ Pairs trap (AEE): PARAM Shivay ≠ IIT Guwahati; Pravega ≠ IIT Kanpur; Ananta ≠ IIT Mandi → correct pair **AIRAWAT – C-DAC Pune**.
[8:1:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens Jan 2026 (2) p.6 (PARAM Shakti, NSM 2015 by MeitY and DST); Praveen CA360 Jan 2026 p.75; Rocket CA Feb 2026 p.102-103 (AIRAWAT, PARAM Pragya); app notes 5:8 sub 1
## SUB 2 | National Quantum Mission (NQM)
[8:2:0] - **Qubit** = basic unit of **quantum information**; by **superposition** it can be 0 and 1 together (bit/byte are classical).
[8:2:1] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [8:2:1.0] Approved | Union Cabinet, 19 April 2023
  [8:2:1.1] Outlay | ₹6,003.65 crore
  [8:2:1.2] Period | 2023-24 to 2030-31 (8 years)
  [8:2:1.3] Nodal | DST
[8:2:2] - Targets: computers of **50–1000 physical qubits**; satellite QKD over **2000 km**; magnetometers and atomic clocks.
[8:2:3] TABLE head: T-Hub | Host
  [8:2:3.0] Quantum Computing | IISc Bengaluru
  [8:2:3.1] Quantum Communication | IIT Madras (with C-DOT)
  [8:2:3.2] Quantum Sensing and Metrology | IIT Bombay
  [8:2:3.3] Quantum Materials and Devices | IIT Delhi
[8:2:4] - Start-ups backed: **QNu Labs** (QKD), QpiAI. **14 April = World Quantum Day**.
[8:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.75-76 (NQM); daily CA 3 Nov 2026 p.6 and Praveen CA360 Aug 2026 p.32 (₹6,003.65 crore, 2023-24 to 2030-31); app notes 5:8 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Deep Ocean Mission
[8:3:0] - Nodal **Ministry of Earth Sciences**; Cabinet **June 2021**, **₹4,077 crore** for five years; six components.
[8:3:1] - **Samudrayaan** = sub-project (India's first crewed deep-ocean mission); **Matsya 6000** = crewed submersible built by **NIOT Chennai**, **3 people to 6,000 m**; **Varaha** = deep-sea mining machine trialled at 5,270 m.
[8:3:2] - **Components:** deep-sea mining and manned submersible; ocean climate change advisory services; deep-sea biodiversity; deep ocean survey; **energy and freshwater from the ocean** (OTEC-powered desalination); **Advanced Marine Station for Ocean Biology**.
[8:3:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:8 sub 3
## SUB 4 | BIO-E3, ANRF and Other Missions
[8:4:0] - **Bio-E3 = Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment**; Cabinet **24 Aug 2024**; steered by **DBT**; six sectors – bio-based chemicals and enzymes, **smart proteins**, precision biotherapeutics, **climate-resilient agriculture**, carbon capture, **marine and space research**; infrastructure = **biomanufacturing hubs, Bio-AI hubs, biofoundries** (not Technology Innovation Hubs); bioeconomy **over US$165 billion** (2024); Budget 2026-27 **Biopharma SHAKTI** ₹10,000 crore over 5 years.
[8:4:1] - **ANRF:** created by the **ANRF Act, 2023**; **subsumed SERB**; **Prime Minister** = ex officio President of its Governing Board; custodian of the **₹1 lakh crore RDI Fund** via a **two-tier Special Purpose Fund**.
[8:4:2] TABLE head: Mission | Ministry | Year | Outlay / fact
  [8:4:2.0] IndiaAI Mission | MeitY | 2024 | ₹10,371.92 crore; 10,000+ GPUs
  [8:4:2.1] Semicon India | MeitY | – | ₹76,000 crore
  [8:4:2.2] NM-ICPS | DST | Cabinet 6 Dec 2018 | ₹3,660 crore; 25 Technology Innovation Hubs (Section-8 cos.); IISER Tirupati TIH = Positioning and Precision Technologies
  [8:4:2.3] NQM | DST | 2023 | ₹6,003.65 crore
  [8:4:2.4] National Geospatial Mission | DST (Survey of India) | Budget 2025-26 | –
[8:4:3] > ⚠ Trap: NQM is DST, not MeitY; Bio-E3's third E is Employment, not Energy.
[8:4:4] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.40 (DBT – BioE3; SERB integrated into ANRF Act 2023); app notes 5:8 sub 4-6, 5:7 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Andhra Pradesh Quantum Push – Amaravati Quantum Valley
[8:5:0] - **Andhra Pradesh** = **first State** with its own **quantum computing policy**; foundation stone at **Uddandarayunipalem**.
[8:5:1] - Incentive: **100% exemption from stamp duty and registration fees** for tech firms; plan to train 4.5 million people in AI and quantum.
[8:5:2] - **14 April 2026** (World Quantum Day): India's first **Quantum Reference Facility** test beds – **1S at SRM University-AP**, **1Q at Medha Towers, Gannavaram**.
[8:5:3] - MoUs (Feb 2026): **IBM to train 1 lakh youth**; **NIELIT Quantum and AI campus** classes from Sept 2026 at **Acharya Nagarjuna University, Guntur**.
[8:5:4] - PMF: AP announced India's first **133-qubit** quantum computer at Amaravati (April 2026).
[8:5:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.76; app notes 5:8 sub 7

=== NOTES 5:10 | Prominent Indian Scientists – Sarabhai, Kalam, Swaminathan, Khorana, Ramakrishnan, C.n.r. Rao
## SUB 0 | Vikram Sarabhai and the Space Pioneers
[10:0:0] # Vikram Sarabhai (1919-1971)
[10:0:1] - **Title:** **Father of the Indian Space Programme** (Jharkhand PCS 2021; IAS 2007 match).
[10:0:2] - **Institutions:** **PRL Ahmedabad (1947)**; **INCOSPAR (1962)** → **ISRO (1969)**; **TERLS, Thumba (1962)**; **Community Science Centre (1965)**.
[10:0:3] - **Posts:** **first ISRO Chairman** till his death (**1971**); **AEC Chairman 1966** (after Bhabha).
[10:0:4] - **Awards:** Bhatnagar 1962, Padma Bhushan 1966, **Padma Vibhushan (posthumous) 1972**.
[10:0:5] - **Named after him:** **Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC)** = TERLS renamed, **Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala** (asked ×2); Chandrayaan-2 lander **"Vikram"**; **COSPAR Vikram Sarabhai Medal** (1990, COSPAR + ISRO, space scientists of **developing countries**).
[10:0:6] - **2026:** **Annapurni Subramaniam** won the COSPAR Sarabhai Medal at the 46th COSPAR Assembly, Florence – **first Indian woman**, fourth Indian (she had the RVP Vigyan Shri 2024).
[10:0:7] # Other space pioneers
[10:0:8] TABLE head: Person | Organisation | Remember
  [10:0:8.0] Satish Dhawan | ISRO Chairman | Aryabhata; SHAR (Sriharikota) named after him
  [10:0:8.1] U.R. Rao | ISRO (1984-94) | First Indian in Satellite Hall of Fame; Padma Vibhushan 2017 – Science and Engineering
  [10:0:8.2] K. Kasturirangan | ISRO (1994-2003) | INSAT-3B (21 Mar 2000, Ariane 5, Kourou); NEP 2020 drafting
  [10:0:8.3] Kalpana Chawla | NASA | "I am a citizen of the Milky Way"; died on STS-107 Columbia re-entry (2003)
  [10:0:8.4] Tessy Thomas | DRDO | "Missile Woman"; Agni-IV, Agni-V
  [10:0:8.5] K. Sivan / Ritu Karidhal | ISRO | "Rocket Man" (Chairman 2018-22) / "Rocket Woman" (Mangalyaan, Chandrayaan-2)
[10:0:9] > Match angle (IAS 2007): Sarabhai – space programme; M.F. Husain – Picasso of India; Amjad Ali Khan – sarod.
[10:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.37, p.39; PMF LENS Aug 2026 Part 2 p.43 (COSPAR medal 2026); app notes 5:10 sub 0, 5
## SUB 1 | A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
[10:1:0] - **Title:** **"Missile Man of India"**; **11th President (2002-07)**.
[10:1:1] - **Space:** project director of **SLV-3**, which put **Rohini** in orbit (**1980**).
[10:1:2] - **Missiles:** chief of **IGMDP (1983)** – Agni, Prithvi, Akash, Nag, Trishul.
[10:1:3] - **Nuclear:** **Pokhran-II (1998)** with Anil Kakodkar. **Bharat Ratna 1997**.
[10:1:4] - **Fighter flight:** **Sukhoi-30 MKI**, **8 June 2006**, Pune (co-pilot Wg Cdr Ajay Rathore) – first Indian Head of State in a fighter. **Pratibha Patil** flew a Sukhoi-30 on 25 Nov 2009 – first Indian woman in a fighter.
[10:1:5] - **Ideas and books:** **PURA** – Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas (APPSC G2 Mains 2017); **Wings of Fire (1999**, with Arun Tiwari), **Ignited Minds**, **Indomitable Spirit**.
[10:1:6] # Pairs angle (TSPSC G1 2023)

  [10:1:7.2] First Indian in space – Sunita Williams | Wrong – Rakesh Sharma (1984)
  [10:1:7.3] First Indian remote-sensing satellite – APPLE | Wrong – APPLE (1981) was an experimental communication satellite; Bhaskara-I / IRS-1A were remote sensing

## SUB 5 | Swaminathan and C.N.R. Rao
[10:5:0] # M.S. Swaminathan (1925-2023)
[10:5:1] - **Title:** **Father of India's Green Revolution** – HYV dwarf **wheat and rice**, with **Norman Borlaug**; later the **"Evergreen Revolution"**.
[10:5:2] - **UNEP:** **"Father of Economic Ecology"** (UPPSC 2007).
[10:5:3] - **Honours:** **first World Food Prize (1987)**; Ramon Magsaysay 1971; **Bharat Ratna 2024 (posthumous)**.
[10:5:4] - **Chaired:** **National Commission on Farmers** (18 Nov **2004**) – "Swaminathan report"; President, **Pugwash Conferences (2002-07)**.
[10:5:5] # C.N.R. Rao
[10:5:6] - **Field:** foremost **solid-state and materials chemist**; headed the **Scientific Advisory Council to the PM**.
[10:5:7] - **Bharat Ratna:** named **Nov 2013** with Sachin Tendulkar, conferred **2014** (asked as "for the year 2013").

  [10:5:8.1] C.N.R. Rao | 2014 (announced 2013)
  [10:5:8.2] M.S. Swaminathan | 2024, posthumous

=== NOTES 5:11 | Science Awards – Bhatnagar Prize, Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar, Indian-origin Nobel Laureates
## SUB 0 | Indian and Indian-origin Nobel Laureates
[11:0:0] TABLE head: Laureate | Year / prize | For
  [11:0:0.0] Ronald Ross (born Almora) | 1902 Medicine | Malaria – showed the parasite develops in the female Anopheles mosquito (1897)
  [11:0:0.1] Rabindranath Tagore | 1913 Literature | Gitanjali – first Indian and first Asian laureate; knighted 1915
  [11:0:0.2] C.V. Raman | 1930 Physics (alone) | Raman Effect (1928) – first Indian scientist, first Asian in science
  [11:0:0.3] Har Gobind Khorana | 1968 Medicine (shared) | Genetic code; then a US citizen
  [11:0:0.4] Mother Teresa | 1979 Peace | Indian citizen
  [11:0:0.5] S. Chandrasekhar | 1983 Physics | Structure and evolution of stars (astrophysics); US citizen from 1953
  [11:0:0.6] Amartya Sen | 1998 Economics | Welfare economics
  [11:0:0.7] V. Ramakrishnan | 2009 Chemistry (shared) | Ribosome
  [11:0:0.8] Kailash Satyarthi | 2014 Peace | Child rights; his Nobel replica was stolen (Feb 2017) and recovered by Delhi Police
  [11:0:0.9] Abhijit Banerjee | 2019 Economics (with Duflo, Kremer) | Experimental approach to alleviating global poverty
[11:0:1] - **Never won a Nobel:** **J.C. Bose**, **Homi Bhabha**, Vikram Sarabhai, Kalam.
[11:0:2] - **First Indian Nobel = Literature (Tagore)**; first Indian **scientist** = **Raman (1930)**.
[11:0:3] # S. Chandrasekhar
[11:0:4] - **Chandrasekhar limit:** max mass of a stable **white dwarf ≈ 1.44 solar masses**; heavier stars → **neutron star or black hole** – hence exam books' "**principle of the black hole**".
[11:0:5] - Nephew of **Raman**; **Chandra X-ray Observatory** (NASA, launched **23 July 1999**) is named after him.
[11:0:6] > ⚠ Trap: malaria parasite itself was found by Laveran (1880); Ross proved mosquito transmission – but where only Ross is offered, key Ross.
[11:0:7] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.36-39; PMF General Science Part 7 p.84; Rocket Biology p.16, p.22; app notes 5:11 sub 1-2
## SUB 1 | Einstein and Physics Laureates
[11:1:0] - **Einstein: Nobel 1921 for the photoelectric effect – NOT relativity**, Brownian motion, specific heat, mass-energy or Bose-Einstein statistics (asked ×8).
[11:1:1] - **General Relativity (1915):** gravity = **curvature of space-time** by matter; predicts **light bending by gravity** and a **dynamic, expanding universe** (IAS 2018: all three).
[11:1:2] TABLE head: Laureate | Fact
  [11:1:2.0] Wilhelm Röntgen | First Physics Nobel, 1901 – X-rays
  [11:1:2.1] J.J. Thomson | 1906 – electron
  [11:1:2.2] W.H. + W.L. Bragg | 1915, father and son (X-ray crystals); W.L. Bragg (25) = youngest laureate before Malala
  [11:1:2.3] Planck / Einstein / Bohr | 1918 / 1921 / 1922
  [11:1:2.4] Heisenberg / Chadwick | 1932 / 1935 – neutron (discovered 1932)
  [11:1:2.5] John Bardeen | Only person with two Physics Nobels: 1956 (transistor), 1972 (BCS superconductivity)
  [11:1:2.6] Marie Curie | Physics 1903 + Chemistry 1911 – only person with Nobels in two sciences
  [11:1:2.7] Weiss, Barish, Thorne | 2017 – LIGO, gravitational waves
  [11:1:2.8] James Peebles | 2019 – physical cosmology (Mayor and Queloz: exoplanet)
  [11:1:2.9] Agostini, Krausz, L'Huillier | 2023 – attosecond pulses of light

## SUB 2 | Nobel Prize Basics
[11:2:0] - **Alfred Nobel** (Swedish chemist) invented **dynamite (1867)** – not cosmic rays (Victor Hess), dynamo, penicillin, typewriter or gramophone.
[11:2:1] - **Will 1895**; Nobel Foundation **1900**; **first prizes 1901**; instituted by **Sweden** (Peace Prize given in Norway).
[11:2:2] - **Original five:** Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace. **No Nobel for mathematics.**
[11:2:3] - **Economics:** set up by **Sveriges Riksbank (Sweden's central bank)** in **1968**, first given **1969** – not in the will.
[11:2:4] - **How many each year:** **six** (books and keys); strictly five Nobel Prizes + the Riksbank memorial prize.
[11:2:5] - Laureate status cannot be transferred, shared or withdrawn; only the medal can change hands.
[11:2:6] - **RDX** (cyclonite, patented **1898**) – **Georg Friedrich Henning**, Germany, not Nobel.
[11:2:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:11 sub 0; web search (Nobel count: nobelprize.org tasks page, Boston Globe 5 Oct 2026)

## SUB 6 | Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize and Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar
[11:6:0] # Bhatnagar Prize
[11:6:1] - **S.S. Bhatnagar:** "Father of Research Laboratories"; **founder-director and first DG of CSIR**.
[11:6:2] - **Prize:** by **CSIR since 1958** – India's best-known **science and technology** prize; age limit **45**; **7 disciplines** (biology, chemistry, earth/atmosphere/ocean/planetary, engineering, mathematics, medicine, physics – **not political science**).
[11:6:3] - **2010 awardees:** included **Sanjeev Galande**. **Madhav Gadgil** (died Jan 2026) – People's Biodiversity Registers, **Gadgil Commission 2010** (Western Ghats).
[11:6:4] # Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar (RVP)
[11:6:5] - **Instituted 2023**, **first awarded Aug 2024** (exam key: **2024**); highest S&T honour; **13 domains**; replaced 300-odd ministry awards; medal + citation, no cash.
[11:6:6] TABLE head: Category | Recognises
  [11:6:6.0] Vigyan Ratna | Lifetime – first G. Padmanabhan (2024); J.V. Narlikar (posthumous, 2026 list)
  [11:6:6.1] Vigyan Shri | Distinguished contribution
  [11:6:6.2] Vigyan Yuva-SSB | Young scientists up to 45 (Bhatnagar Prize absorbed)
  [11:6:6.3] Vigyan Team | 3 or more researchers (first: Chandrayaan-3 team)
[11:6:7] - **IYBA (DBT, 2005):** Innovative Young Biotechnologist Award – young researchers in frontier biotechnology.
[11:6:8] - **Padma 2025:** 139 – 7 Vibhushan, 19 Bhushan, 113 Shri; **Vinod Dham** ("Father of the Pentium Chip") Padma Bhushan 2025.

=== NOTES 5:12 | Nature and Scope of Ict; Hardware, Software, Memory and Operating Systems
## SUB 0 | Memory and Storage – Units, Primary and Secondary Memory
[12:0:0] # Units in order
[12:0:1] - **Bit** (binary digit) = the **smallest unit** of data/information; **nibble = 4 bits**; **byte = 8 bits** (APPSC 2025; asked 6 times).
[12:0:2] - **Order:** bit < nibble < byte < **KB** < MB < GB < TB < PB < EB < ZB < YB.
[12:0:3] TABLE head: Unit | Equals
  [12:0:3.0] 1 byte | 8 bits
  [12:0:3.1] 1 KB | 1024 bytes = 8192 bits
  [12:0:3.2] 1 MB | 1024 KB (about a million characters)
  [12:0:3.3] 1 GB | 1024 MB (about one billion characters)
  [12:0:3.4] 1 TB | 1024 GB
[12:0:4] - **Smallest time unit** among those asked: **picosecond** (10⁻¹²) < nanosecond (10⁻⁹) < microsecond (10⁻⁶) < second (APPSC G1 2004).
[12:0:5] # Primary memory
[12:0:6] TABLE head: Memory | Nature
  [12:0:6.0] RAM (Random Access Memory) | Primary, volatile, temporary working store – lost when power goes off; not like hard-disc storage; SRAM = cache (faster), DRAM = main memory; RAM sticks use DDR (Double Data Rate)
  [12:0:6.1] ROM (Read-Only Memory) | Non-volatile, permanent memory built into the computer; holds firmware/BIOS (Basic Input-Output System); PROM, EPROM, EEPROM
  [12:0:6.2] Cache | Small, extremely fast memory between CPU and main memory; a portion the processor reaches faster than regular RAM; shortest access time; speeds up processing; made of SRAM
  [12:0:6.3] Registers | Fastest memory, embedded on the CPU chip (electronic memory)
  [12:0:6.4] Memory | Erased by
  [12:0:6.5] EPROM | Ultraviolet light
  [12:0:6.6] EEPROM | Electrically
[12:0:7] - **Speed order:** registers > cache > RAM > SSD > HDD > optical disc > magnetic tape.
[12:0:8] - **Static RAM is faster than dynamic RAM**; **primary storage is faster than secondary** (a statement saying the reverse is wrong).
[12:0:9] - **Memory types:** **semiconductor** (primary), **magnetic** and **optical** (secondary) – "server" is not a memory type.
[12:0:10] - **Virtual memory:** its size (virtual address space) depends on the CPU's **address lines** (32 lines → 2³² bytes).
[12:0:11] - **ROM is a memory, not a computer language.** **DIMM = Dual In-line Memory Module** (RAM stick; older SIMM; laptops SO-DIMM).
[12:0:12] # Secondary storage
[12:0:13] TABLE head: Storage | Fact
  [12:0:13.0] HDD | Magnetic disk, non-volatile; first commercial hard disk drive by IBM (RAMAC 350, 1956); SATA hard disk = magnetic, not capacitive memory
  [12:0:13.1] SSD | Flash memory, no moving parts, faster
  [12:0:13.2] Magnetic tape | Sequential access, slowest; backup and archival
  [12:0:13.3] Flash drive / pen drive | EEPROM-based flash; keeps data without power; low power; costlier, not cheaper, than mechanical disk drives
  [12:0:13.4] CD-ROM (Compact Disc Read Only Memory) | about 700 MB
  [12:0:13.5] DVD (Digital Versatile Disc) | 4.7 GB single layer; 8.5 GB dual layer
  [12:0:13.6] Blu-ray | 25 GB single layer; 50 GB dual layer – stores more than a DVD
[12:0:14] - **Capacity order (decreasing):** Blu-ray > **DVD > CD-ROM > floppy disk**.
[12:0:15] - **RAM is NOT secondary memory**; SSD, hard disk, optical disk, flash drive, floppy and USB pen drive are.
[12:0:16] > Statement angle: "RAM is non-volatile" ✗; "primary is slower than secondary" ✗; "SRAM faster than DRAM" ✓; "Von Neumann = stored-program digital computer" ✓ → answer C and D.
[12:0:17] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:12 sub 5 (old-notes.txt); PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.27-28 (hardware, storage); unit values and memory hierarchy: general knowledge, not checked
[12:0:18] - **Bulk storage:** both **magnetic tape** and **magnetic disk** store very large quantities of data.
[12:0:19] - **1024 bits = 128 bytes** (÷ 8).
[12:0:20] - **Human memory (psychology):** MCQs use **recognition**; essay/fill-in answers use **recall**.
[12:0:21] - **Blu-ray vs DVD:** both **1.2 mm** thick; BD carries HD video and about 5x the capacity (25 vs 4.7 GB).
## SUB 1 | CPU and Hardware Components
[12:1:0] # CPU – the brain
[12:1:1] - **CPU = Central Processing Unit** (NOT "Control Processing Unit") – the **brain**, the **controlling unit** and the **most important part** of the computer; most processing happens here (asked 9 times).
[12:1:2] - **CPU is hardware**, not software – a statement "the CPU is the software that carries out instructions" is false.
[12:1:3] - **Processor parts:** **Control Unit + ALU** (with registers); main memory and storage are **not** parts of the processor.
[12:1:4] TABLE head: Component | Function
  [12:1:4.0] ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) | Arithmetic and logical operations – performs calculations and makes decisions
  [12:1:4.1] CU (Control Unit) | Fetches and decodes program instructions, makes control signals, directs the other units
  [12:1:4.2] Registers | Fastest storage inside the CPU (address, data, instruction registers)
  [12:1:4.3] PSU | Only supplies power
[12:1:5] - **Main components of a computer:** input unit, output unit, processing unit, memory unit, secondary storage – **"basic unit" is not a component**.
[12:1:6] - **After a double-click** of the mouse, information goes to the **CPU**.
[12:1:7] # Buses, chips and processors
[12:1:8] - **Buses:** the wire pathways that **connect the different parts** of a computer (data, address and control buses).
[12:1:9] - **IC chips are made of silicon** (a semiconductor) – not silica (SiO₂), gold, chromium or iron oxide.
[12:1:10] - **Celeron, Pentium, Core** = series of Intel **processors**; **Intel Core i9** = high-end processor with **8 to 24 cores**.
[12:1:11] - **Clock speed** of a processor is measured in **hertz – gigahertz (GHz)**.
[12:1:12] - **IBM = International Business Machine(s)**.
[12:1:13] - **Modem = modulator-demodulator**: converts digital data into analog signals and back – "all of the above".
[12:1:14] - **UPS = Uninterrupted Power Supply** (keeps the computer running briefly when power fails); **SMPS = Switched Mode Power Supply** (rectified AC to low-voltage DC).
[12:1:15] - **Peripheral device:** equipment added to a computer to enhance its functionality (printer, scanner, webcam).
[12:1:16] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:12 sub 3 (old-notes.txt); PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.27-28 (hardware incl. peripheral devices, modems); CPU parts and processor series: general knowledge, not checked
[12:1:17] - **Microcomputer hardware (3 categories):** **system unit, input/output, secondary storage**.
## SUB 2 | Input, Output Devices and Printers
[12:2:0] # Input vs output
[12:2:1] TABLE head: Input | Output
  [12:2:1.0] Keyboard (most common; QWERTY layout) | Monitor (CRT, LCD, OLED)
  [12:2:1.1] Mouse (standard pointing device in a GUI) | Printer
  [12:2:1.2] Microphone | Speaker, earphones, headphones
  [12:2:1.3] Scanner | Projector
  [12:2:1.4] Joystick (lever moving in several directions) | Plotter (drum pen plotter)
  [12:2:1.5] Trackball, light pen, touchpad | Visual Display Unit
  [12:2:1.6] Webcam (compulsory for video conferencing) | –
  [12:2:1.7] Digital camera (input, NOT output) | –
  [12:2:1.8] Barcode reader, OCR, MICR (cheques), OMR (answer sheets), badge reader | –
[12:2:2] - **Touch screen** = both input and output, so it is "not an output device" in exam keys.
[12:2:3] - **Only input:** mouse, keyboard, scanner. **Only output:** plotter, printer, monitor.
[12:2:4] - **Scanner:** light-sensitive device that turns drawings, printed data and images into digital form.
[12:2:5] - **Digitizer:** converts analogue information (drawings, maps) into digital form.
[12:2:6] - **Badge reader:** reads data encoded in a small plastic card.
[12:2:7] - **Barcode:** machine-readable code of **vertical bars of varying widths** (APPSC 2019). **OCR = Optical Character Recognition**.
[12:2:8] - **Caps Lock is a toggle key:** its function goes back and forth each time it is pressed.
[12:2:9] - **Telefax (fax):** sends text and pictures over telephone lines (exam answer for "dialled on the telephone and read on a screen").
[12:2:10] # Printers and displays
[12:2:11] TABLE head: Impact | Non-impact
  [12:2:11.0] Dot-matrix, daisy-wheel, line, drum, serial | Inkjet, laser, thermal
[12:2:12] - **Laser printer:** the fastest of the common printers, the standard **non-impact** printer and the one used for **desktop printing (DTP)**; it uses a **semiconductor laser** (also in CD/DVD players). **Excimer (exciplex) laser**: ultraviolet; used to make microelectronic devices.
[12:2:13] - **OLED advantages over LCD:** can be made on **flexible plastic substrates**, allow **roll-up displays in clothing** and **transparent displays** – all three (UPSC 2017).
[12:2:14] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:12 sub 4 (old-notes.txt); PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.27 (peripherals: printers, scanners, webcams); device roles: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 3 | History, Generations and Inventors
[12:3:0] # Generations → core technology
[12:3:1] TABLE head: Generation | Basis | Example
  [12:3:1.0] First (1940s-56) | Vacuum tubes | ENIAC, UNIVAC
  [12:3:1.1] Second (1956-63) | Transistors | –
  [12:3:1.2] Third (1964-71) | Integrated circuits | –
  [12:3:1.3] Fourth | VLSI and microprocessors | Intel 4004 era
  [12:3:1.4] Fifth | Artificial intelligence, ULSI, parallel processing | –
[12:3:2] - **Miniaturisation** of computers came from **IC chips** (invented **1958**, replaced transistors).
[12:3:3] - **ICs are classified by the number of transistors per chip:** **SSI 3–30, MSI 30–300, LSI 300–3,000**, then VLSI, ULSI.
[12:3:4] # Firsts
[12:3:5] TABLE head: First | Fact
  [12:3:5.0] Word "computer" | From Latin computare (to calculate)
  [12:3:5.1] Pascaline (1642) | First mechanical calculating machine – Blaise Pascal
  [12:3:5.2] Punched cards (1890 US census) | Herman Hollerith – father of punched-card processing
  [12:3:5.3] ENIAC (1946) | Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer – first general-purpose electronic computer, Eckert and Mauchly
  [12:3:5.4] BESK (1953) | Binary Electronic Sequence Calculator – Sweden's first electronic computer
  [12:3:5.5] Osborne 1 (1981) | First commercial portable computer – Adam Osborne (died at Kodaikanal, 18 March 2003)
  [12:3:5.6] Intel 4004 (1971) | First commercial microprocessor
  [12:3:5.7] TIFRAC | India's first indigenous computer
  [12:3:5.8] PARAM 8000 (1991) | India's first supercomputer
  [12:3:5.9] Mobilis (2005) | Bangalore's Encore Software "anytime, anywhere" low-cost mobile computer (Encore also made the Simputer)
[12:3:6] # Persons → contribution
[12:3:7] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [12:3:7.0] Charles Babbage | Father of Computers (inventor of the computer in exam keys); Analytical Engine; conceptual foundations 1833-1871
  [12:3:7.1] Alan Turing | Exam answer for "invented the electronic computer" (Turing machine; wartime code-breaking computers)
  [12:3:7.2] George Stibitz | Recognised as a father of the modern digital computer (relay binary calculator, Bell Labs 1937)
  [12:3:7.3] Ada Lovelace | First programmer
  [12:3:7.4] George Boole | Boolean algebra – devised the logical operators AND, OR, NOT
  [12:3:7.5] Douglas Engelbart | Mouse
  [12:3:7.6] Larry Tesler | Cut, copy and paste
  [12:3:7.7] Tim Berners-Lee | WWW (1989-91)
  [12:3:7.8] Richard Stallman | GNU project (1983), GPL licence
  [12:3:7.9] Linus Torvalds | Linux kernel (1991)
  [12:3:7.10] Dennis Ritchie / James Gosling / Guido van Rossum / Bjarne Stroustrup | C / Java (1991-95) / Python / C++
  [12:3:7.11] Tim Paterson | MS-DOS (from 86-DOS)
  [12:3:7.12] David S. Lee | Daisy-wheel printer (1969, Diablo Data Systems)
  [12:3:7.13] Alexander Bain (Scottish) | Fax (1842)
  [12:3:7.14] Peter Shor | Shor's algorithm (1994)
[12:3:8] > Trap: "Father of the Computer" = **Babbage** (not Hollerith, Pascal or von Neumann); **Berners-Lee** = WWW, not computers.
[12:3:9] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.29 (ENIAC, UNIVAC; Babbage 1833-1871; Berners-Lee WWW 1991); app notes 5:12 sub 1 (old-notes.txt); Encore Mobilis: engadget.com/2005/05/11/the-mobilis-encores-inexpensive-mobile-pc/ (via web search); other firsts: general knowledge, not checked
[12:3:10] - **Richard Stallman** founded the **Free Software Foundation** (1985).
## SUB 4 | Computer Types and Supercomputers
[12:4:0] TABLE head: Type | Feature / example
  [12:4:0.0] Analog | Continuous quantities – car speedometer, thermometer
  [12:4:0.1] Digital | Discrete (binary) data – PCs; works on the logical principle (Boolean 0/1)
  [12:4:0.2] Hybrid | Analog + digital features; converts analog output into digital form – ICU monitors, ECG
  [12:4:0.3] Micro / personal | Most widely used – desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, wearables
  [12:4:0.4] Embedded | Dedicated function inside a larger system – digital watch
  [12:4:0.5] Supercomputer | Largest, fastest and costliest; speed in FLOPS
  [12:4:0.6] Quantum computer | Uses qubits (superposition, entanglement); exam answer for the "smallest and fastest computer imitating brain working"
[12:4:1] - **Teacube:** a **2-inch cube-shaped computer** (APPSC G1 2004).
[12:4:2] - **Q-Day:** when quantum computers may break **RSA-2048** encryption with **Shor's algorithm (1994)**. Oxford researchers made **10 billion quantum entanglements** in silicon.
[12:4:3] # Supercomputers – dated
[12:4:4] - **PARAM Padma** (C-DAC, 2002-03): an Indian **supercomputer** (UPSC 2004).
[12:4:5] - **Tianhe** (Tianhe-1A 2010, Tianhe-2 fastest in TOP500 June 2014): developed by **China** (NUDT) ⚠ an APPSC key gave Japan.
[12:4:6] - **2007:** **IBM Blue Gene/L** fastest; India's **Eka** (CRL, Tata) ranked **4th** (Nov 2007).
[12:4:7] - **ISC 2026:** **LineShine** (China) fastest, replacing El Capitan.
[12:4:8] - **Jan 2026:** **Param Shakti** – 3.1 petaflops, launched by **MeitY** at **IIT Madras** on RUDRA servers, under the **National Supercomputing Mission**.
[12:4:9] TABLE head: Term | Meaning / unit
  [12:4:9.0] Word length | Bits the CPU handles at once (32-bit, 64-bit)
  [12:4:9.1] Clock speed | Hertz (GHz)
  [12:4:9.2] Bandwidth | Data-transfer rate in bits per second (bps)
  [12:4:9.3] MIPS | Million Instructions Per Second
  [12:4:9.4] FLOPS | Floating-point Operations Per Second – supercomputer speed
  [12:4:9.5] Linpack (HPL) | Floating-point benchmark on large dense linear systems – basis of world rankings
[12:4:10] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:12 sub 2 and sub 10 (old-notes.txt); PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.29 (quantum computing); Param Padma, Tianhe, Teacube: general knowledge, not checked
[12:4:11] - **Gauges of computer power:** **bandwidth** (APPSC G1 2004 key), word length (data width), clock speed, MIPS.
[12:4:12] - **Parallel computing:** a large problem is split into smaller parts solved **simultaneously** on many processors.
[12:4:13] - **India's supercomputing:** programme from late 1980s (C-DAC 1988), **PARAM 8000** (1991), **Pratyush** at IITM Pune (2018).
## SUB 5 | Software, Office Tools and Operating Systems
[12:5:0] # Software types
[12:5:1] - **Software** = programs that let the user and the **hardware communicate**/work; two major types: **system** and **application**.
[12:5:2] TABLE head: Type | Examples
  [12:5:2.0] System software | OS (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS), device drivers, utilities, firmware, translators
  [12:5:2.1] Utility software | Antivirus, disk cleanup, backup, compression
  [12:5:2.2] Application software | Word processors (MS Word, WordStar by MicroPro), spreadsheets ("what if" analysis), presentation, DTP, browsers; graphics (Photoshop, CorelDRAW); multimedia (players, editors, Final Cut Pro – video production); database (Oracle, MySQL, MS Access); MS Outlook (e-mail)
  [12:5:2.3] Security software | Firewalls, antivirus, encryption, IDS
[12:5:3] - **Device driver** = system software. **Compiler** and **assembler** are programs, not hardware.
[12:5:4] - **MS Office** = office suite (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Access) – **not an OS**; **Media Player is not an Office component**.
[12:5:5] - **Open source:** source code free to view, modify and share; **GNU = "GNU's Not Unix"**; **Internet Explorer** = closed source.
[12:5:6] - A Word document, video or MP3 is a **file**; the **extension** shows its type (.doc = Word).
[12:5:7] # Office shortcuts asked
[12:5:8] TABLE head: Task | Answer
  [12:5:8.0] MS Word: break column, start new one | Ctrl + Shift + Enter
  [12:5:8.1] Windows logo key + D | Display and hide the desktop
  [12:5:8.2] Excel: Format as Table | Home tab
  [12:5:8.3] Excel: pop-up comment on a selected cell | Cell Tip
  [12:5:8.4] PowerPoint chart for a timeline | Line chart (printed key)
[12:5:9] # Operating systems
[12:5:10] - **Functions:** manages hardware, memory, processes, files, devices, security and I/O; gives the user interface (not line-by-line translation).
[12:5:11] TABLE head: OS type | Feature / example
  [12:5:11.0] Time-sharing / multi-user | Many users share CPU time – UNIX (AT&T, 1969; kernel = main part)
  [12:5:11.1] Real-time | Fixed response deadlines – missile guidance, air-traffic control
  [12:5:11.2] Batch | Groups jobs and runs them without user interaction
  [12:5:11.3] Mobile | Android (Linux-based, Google), iOS, BharOS (IIT Madras)
  [12:5:11.4] Interface | Example
  [12:5:11.5] CLI (command-line) | MS-DOS (Microsoft, Aug 1981, Tim Paterson), UNIX shell
  [12:5:11.6] GUI (icons, windows, mouse) | Windows (Windows 3 – 1990; Windows 11 – Oct 2021), macOS
[12:5:12] - **Linux, Windows, UNIX, Android, MS-DOS** = OSs; **Java, COBOL, MS Office** are not.
[12:5:13] - **Android 6.0 = Marshmallow** (2015).
[12:5:14] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.28 (system, application, enterprise, security software); app notes 5:12 sub 6-7 (old-notes.txt); shortcuts and FCP: general knowledge, not checked
[12:5:15] - **Booting** loads the OS after **POST** checks the hardware; no OS = no boot; **warm (soft) reboot** = restart under software control without cutting power.
[12:5:16] - **Windows** = GUI **multi-tasking** OS; **multiprogramming** = several programs in memory sharing one CPU.
[12:5:17] - **Office shortcuts:** Ctrl+S save, **Ctrl+W close**, **Ctrl+U underline**, **F7 spelling & grammar**, **Ctrl+F2 print preview**.
[12:5:18] - **Spooler:** queues print jobs so the CPU runs user programs while the printer prints.
[12:5:19] - **FAT = File Allocation Table** – the DOS/Windows file system table that tracks where files sit on the disk.
[12:5:20] - **UNIX tools:** **lint** = C program-checking tool; kernel = core; C shell = command interpreter.
[12:5:21] - **Not OSs:** Firefox (browser), MS Office, MS Word; **IBM AIX, Sun Solaris** are UNIX OSs.
[12:5:22] - **CADD** (Computer-Aided Design & Drafting): creates, modifies and analyses designs; also photo-simulations for Environmental Impact Reports.
[12:5:23] - **Apple's OSs:** **iOS** and macOS; Red Hat, Fedora, Ubuntu are Linux distributions.
[12:5:24] - **MS Excel** is a spreadsheet, not a DBMS; MS Access, MySQL, Oracle, IBM DB2 are DBMSs.
[12:5:25] - **UNIX** typically runs **web/internet servers**, workstations and mainframes.
[12:5:26] - **Beerware:** licence letting users do anything with the code (buy the author a beer); term by **John Bristow** (1987).
[12:5:27] - **PageMaker** = desktop publishing; **MS Word, WordStar** = word processors.
[12:5:28] - **Excel:** a workbook is a set of **worksheets**; the **cell** is the basic unit where data is entered.
[12:5:29] - **Word Count** shows pages, words, characters (with and without spaces), paragraphs and lines.
[12:5:30] - **Daemon:** a background program in multitasking OSs; term coined by MIT's **Project MAC** (1963).
[12:5:31] - **Database:** **field** = one category of information (column); record = a set of related fields; table = related records.
[12:5:32] - **GNU** is **Unix-compatible** but contains no Unix code.
[12:5:33] - **Windows** is made by **Microsoft** (not IBM, Apple or AT&T).
[12:5:34] - **Web browser:** fetches webpages and displays them on screen (Chrome, Firefox, Edge).
[12:5:35] - **UNIX:** multitasking, multi-user; rewritten in **C** (1973) – mostly C with a little assembly.
[12:5:36] - **Copy–paste** leaves the original file unchanged and creates a new copy (**cut–paste** moves it).
[12:5:37] - **MS PowerPoint** = audio-visual presentations (slides).
[12:5:38] - **Ctrl + X = Cut** (copy to clipboard and delete); Ctrl + C copy, Ctrl + V paste, Ctrl + Z undo.
[12:5:39] - **Software applications** are characterised by their information **content and determinacy** (Pressman).
[12:5:40] - **Cold boot** (start from power-off) needs a **system disk** holding the OS boot files.
## SUB 6 | Programming Languages, Number Systems and Logic
[12:6:0] # Language levels
[12:6:1] TABLE head: Level | Fact
  [12:6:1.0] 1GL machine language | Only 0 and 1; the only language run directly
  [12:6:1.1] 2GL assembly | Mnemonics; converted by an assembler (not a compiler)
  [12:6:1.2] 3GL high-level | FORTRAN (Formula Translation, IBM 1957, first HLL, scientific), COBOL (business), BASIC (Beginner's All Purpose Symbolic Instruction Code), PASCAL, C, C++, Java, Python
  [12:6:1.3] AI languages | PROLOG and LISP
[12:6:2] - **Cobra, Python, Squirrel, Java** are computer languages; **Linux** and **Paint brush** are not.
[12:6:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [12:6:3.0] Compiler | Translates the whole program at once
  [12:6:3.1] Interpreter | Translates and runs line by line
  [12:6:3.2] Algorithm / Flowchart / Pseudocode | Step-by-step procedure / its pictorial form / English-like outline
[12:6:4] - **Flowchart symbols:** oval = start/end, **parallelogram = input/output**, rectangle = process, **diamond = decision**.
[12:6:5] # Number systems and logic
[12:6:6] - Binary (2), octal (8), decimal (10), **hexadecimal (16; 0–9 and A–F)**; (1010)₂ = 10; **(FF)₁₆ = 255**.
[12:6:7] - **Universal gates: NAND and NOR**; **XOR** = 1 when inputs differ.
[12:6:8] - **Boolean:** A + A = A; A·A′ = 0; **De Morgan: (A + B)′ = A′·B′**.
[12:6:9] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:12 sub 8 (old-notes.txt); PROLOG for AI: general knowledge, not checked
[12:6:10] - **Language uses:** FORTRAN – scientific/HPC; COBOL – business (not OO, not numeric); C – system software; BASIC – education.
[12:6:11] - **Not languages:** Lotus (1-2-3 spreadsheet), FAST, ROM.
[12:6:12] - **C++** (Stroustrup): **object-oriented**, backward compatible with C, widely available.
[12:6:13] - **C++:** ternary = **conditional (?:)** operator; function overloading resolved at **compile time**; 16-bit int = **−32768 to +32767**.
[12:6:14] - **7 in binary = 111** (0111 in 4 bits).
[12:6:15] - **Language generations:** assembly (2GL) → problem-oriented HLL (3GL) → query, application generators (4GL) → natural language (5GL).
[12:6:16] - **BASIC** = Beginner's **All-purpose** Symbolic Instruction Code (**Kemeny & Kurtz**, 1964) – general-purpose, **procedural**.
[12:6:17] - **Program** = an algorithm written in a programming language with its syntax.
[12:6:18] - **BCD = Binary Coded Decimal** – each decimal digit as 4 bits.
[12:6:19] - **Coding** = writing instructions in a language; **bug** = program error giving wrong results.
[12:6:20] - **Machine language** (0/1) rests on **Boolean algebra**.
[12:6:21] - **JavaScript:** 1995 (Brendan Eich, Netscape).
[12:6:22] - **DFD = Data Flow Diagram**.
[12:6:23] - **Turbo C++** (Borland) = compiler/IDE; Windows 98 = OS; Java, BASIC = languages.
[12:6:24] - **OR gate:** output 1 if **any** input is 1; AND needs all inputs 1; NOR is the inverse of OR.
[12:6:25] - **Embedded systems** are mostly programmed in **C**.
[12:6:26] - **Mode (statistics):** the value with the **maximum frequency**; mean = average, median = middle value.
[12:6:27] - **BASIC** is usually run by an **interpreter**; assembly language uses an **assembler**.
[12:6:28] - **First computers** were programmed in **machine language** (0/1).
## SUB 7 | ICT – Nature, Scope and Terms
[12:7:0] - **ICT = Information and Communication Technology**: devices and applications used to **access, store, transmit and manipulate digital information** – hardware, software, networks, data, people, services and infrastructure.
[12:7:1] - **Aim:** smooth **human-human, human-machine and machine-machine (M2M)** communication.
[12:7:2] - **Information Technology** = **connectivity + hardware** in the printed key (JPSC 2016); also taught as computers + communication.
[12:7:3] - **Concerns:** privacy, **digital divide**, job insecurity, over-reliance. **Positive impact of the internet:** best source of knowledge at a click.
[12:7:4] - **Cybernetics:** study of **automation and communication between human and machine** – term by **Norbert Wiener**.
[12:7:5] - **Artificial Intelligence** makes machines intelligent and mimics human actions.
[12:7:6] - **Technology preservation** = **computer museum** (APPSC 2019).
[12:7:7] - **IT terms:** cyberspace, upload, modem ✓ – **"light storage" is not an IT term**.
[12:7:8] - **Smart card:** plastic card with an **embedded microchip**; **digital technology** works with satellite and fibre-optic transmission; a **digital library is NOT only on the internet** (UPSC 2002 → I and II).
[12:7:9] - **Aarogya Setu, CoWIN, DigiLocker, DIKSHA** – all on **open-source digital platforms**.
[12:7:10] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T 05 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-05.txt) p.27-28 (ICT features and components); app notes 5:12 sub 0 (old-notes.txt); IT definition: testbook.com question 60475258aabf2ed433e87984 (via web search)
[12:7:11] - **A computer** only follows the instructions given to it; with no intelligence of its own it does **not replace the human brain**.
## SUB 8 | File Formats, Acronyms and Transmission Modes

  [12:8:0.0] PDF | Portable Document Format (Adobe) | Document

  [12:8:0.3] JPEG | Joint Photographic Experts Group | Image
  [12:8:0.4] GIF / PNG | Graphics Interchange Format / Portable Network Graphics | Image
  [12:8:0.5] ASCII | American Standard Code for Information Interchange | 7-bit, 128 characters; Unicode extends it

  [12:8:2.1] Half duplex | Walkie-talkie
  [12:8:2.2] Full duplex | Telephone

[12:8:7] - **Fax** goes as an analog signal over phone lines, **e-mail** as digital – both forms.
[12:8:8] - **LCD = Liquid Crystal Display**.

  Which secondary storage is sequential-access and mainly used for backup and archival?
  Solid-state drive | Hard disk drive | *Magnetic tape | Pen drive
  x: Magnetic tape is sequential-access, the slowest in the speed order, and used for backup and archival; an SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts.

  x: A nibble is a group of four bits.

  Which type of RAM is used as cache memory?
  ROM | DRAM | *SRAM | EPROM
  x: SRAM is used as cache, while DRAM is used as main memory.
[ned6a0a04375] sub0
  Which one of the following is correctly matched?
  ROM — volatile working memory | PROM — electrically erasable memory | *EPROM — ultraviolet-light erasable memory | EEPROM — erasable only by ultraviolet light
  x: EPROM is erased using ultraviolet light. EEPROM is electrically erasable, while ROM is non-volatile.

  x: EEPROM is erased electrically and BIOS resides in ROM; cache is SRAM, while DRAM is main memory.

  x: ICT aims at efficient human-human, human-machine and machine-to-machine communication.

  P2P | *M2M | B2B | G2C

  Which one of the following is correctly matched with its file type?
  MP3 — Video | *MP4 — Video | PDF — Audio | MOV — Image
  x: MP4 stands for MPEG-4 Part 14 and is a video file format. MP3 is audio, PDF is a document format and MOV is a video format.
[n2699a037f91] sub8
  How many bits does ASCII, the character-encoding scheme for 128 characters, use?
  *7 | 8 | 16 | 32
  x: ASCII is a 7-bit code (2^7 = 128 characters); Unicode extends its range.
[ne260a4432e6] sub8
  The communication from a computer mouse to the computer is an example of which transmission mode?
  Half duplex | Full duplex | *Simplex | Multiplex
  x: A mouse only sends signals to the computer, so the communication is one-way, or simplex (APPSC 2019). Half duplex is two-way but one direction at a time, as in a walkie-talkie. Full duplex is two-way at once, as in a telephone. Multiplexing combines several signals on one channel; it is not a direction mode.
[n2a826613c22] sub8

  GIF — Graphics Interchange Format | AVI — Audio Video Interleave | MOV — QuickTime Movie | *PNG — Portable Network Graphics Interface
  x: PNG stands for Portable Network Graphics, not Portable Network Graphics Interface. AVI, MOV and GIF are correctly matched.

  x: PDF is Adobe's Portable Document Format.

  Apple | *Microsoft | Adobe | CompuServe
  x: AVI is Microsoft's; MOV is Apple's, PDF Adobe's and GIF CompuServe's.
[f6c4316b2b374] sub8
  A telephone call is an example of which transmission mode?
  Simplex | Half duplex | *Full duplex | Multiplexing
  x: A telephone is full duplex; television is simplex and a walkie-talkie half duplex.
[f11f581f60a00] sub8
  For which type of content is MP3 a file format?
  Video | Images | Documents | *Audio
  x: MP3 (MPEG-1 Audio Layer 3) is an audio format; MP4, MOV and AVI are video formats.

  What is the full form of JPEG?

  x: JPEG = Joint Photographic Experts Group; it is a lossy image format.

  Which of the following is an example of half-duplex communication?

  x: In half duplex, data flows both ways but one at a time, as in a walkie-talkie; television is simplex and telephone full duplex.
