=== NOTES 5:39 | Earth Observation – Irs, Cartosat, Resourcesat, Oceansat, Risat, Eos
## SUB 0 | Remote Sensing – Definition, Components and Platforms
[39:0:0] - **Remote sensing:** gathering information about an object **without physical contact**, by measuring **reflected and emitted electromagnetic radiation** from a distance (satellite, aircraft, drone); it uses **electromagnetic waves**, not sonar or electric waves.
[39:0:1] # Components (stages)
[39:0:2] - 1. Energy source / illumination → 2. Radiation through the atmosphere → 3. **Interaction with the target** → 4. Recording by the sensor → 5. **Transmission, reception and processing** → 6. Interpretation and analysis → 7. Application.
[39:0:3] - "Interaction of Energy with **Minimisation**" is **not** a component (APPSC 2022).
[39:0:4] # Disaster uses and platforms
[39:0:5] - Disaster applications: **glacial lakes**, **wildfires**, **wind/cyclone tracking**, floods, landslides – "hills management" is not one.
[39:0:6] - **UAV (drone)** is best for **detailed, localised** damage assessment; satellites for wide areas.
[39:0:7] - **Infrared (thermal) cameras** detect people trapped under **rubble** after an earthquake by their body heat.
[39:0:8] - **GEOSS = Global Earth Observation System of Systems** (built by the Group on Earth Observations, GEO).
[39:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.5; PMF S&T Part 1 p.80-81; app notes 5:39 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Electromagnetic Spectrum, Sensors and Bands
[39:1:0] # Spectrum order
[39:1:1] - Wavelength falls: **radio (incl. microwave) → infrared → visible (red … violet) → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays**.
[39:1:2] - **Colour** of light is set by its **wavelength**; in visible light **red** is longest and **violet** shortest.
[39:1:3] - **Infrared** is longer than red; gamma rays shortest of all.
[39:1:4] - **X-rays** strongly darken (expose) **photographic plates and film** – the basis of radiography.
[39:1:5] # Passive vs active sensors
[39:1:6] TABLE head: Type | Energy | Examples
  [39:1:6.0] Passive | Reflected sunlight or emitted heat | Cameras (visible, infrared, multispectral), radiometers, MODIS
  [39:1:6.1] Active | Sends its own pulse, reads the echo | Radar/SAR (microwave), laser / LiDAR, altimeters
[39:1:7] - **Laser** is the active sensor in a list of cameras (APPSC 2023).
[39:1:8] - **LiDAR = Light Detection And Ranging**: pulsed laser measures distances → elevation, 3D terrain, canopy height. **Airborne Laser Terrain Mapping (ALTM)** is airborne LiDAR: a fast, accurate, cost-effective 3D picture of the ground, used mainly for mapping and survey.
[39:1:9] - Laser uses: LASIK, LiDAR, holography – **MRI is not** a laser use (it uses magnets and radio waves).
[39:1:10] # Which band for what
[39:1:11] TABLE head: Band | Use
  [39:1:11.0] Optical (visible/NIR) | Reflected light; needs daylight and clear sky
  [39:1:11.1] Thermal infrared | Emitted heat → volcanic eruptions, forest fires, urban heat
  [39:1:11.2] Microwave (radio region) – SAR | Penetrates clouds and darkness → all-weather imaging of cloud-covered disaster areas
  [39:1:11.3] Hyperspectral | Hundreds of narrow bands → materials and chemicals
[39:1:12] > ⚠ Cloud-covered disaster area: the answer is the **radio/microwave** band; visible light cannot pass through cloud (the APPSC 2021 key "Visible" is a factual error).
[39:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.5; PMF S&T Part 1 p.80-81, 94 (RISAT all-weather), p.69 (active sensors)
## SUB 2 | Resolution and Remote-sensing Techniques
[39:2:0] - Four resolutions: **spatial** (smallest object seen), **spectral** (number and width of bands), **temporal** (**how often** a satellite revisits the same place), **radiometric** (sensitivity to small energy differences). "**Chemical**" resolution does not exist (APPSC 2025).
[39:2:1] TABLE head: Technique | Maps
  [39:2:1.0] InSAR | Ground deformation – subsidence, earthquake/volcano uplift
  [39:2:1.1] LiDAR | Elevation, 3D terrain, canopy height
  [39:2:1.2] NDVI | Vegetation health (chlorophyll) from red vs near-infrared reflectance
  [39:2:1.3] Thermal infrared | Land surface temperature, fires, volcanic heat
  [39:2:1.4] Hyperspectral | Materials and chemicals
[39:2:2] - Satellite data estimate **chlorophyll**, **greenhouse-gas emissions from rice paddies** and **land surface temperature** – all three (UPSC 2019).
[39:2:3] - **MODIS = Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectro-radiometer** (NASA Terra/Aqua): **52,785 forest fires** detected Nov 2020 – Jun 2021.
[39:2:4] - **Tectonic plate movement** is monitored by **VLBI, SLR and GPS** – not flood or cyclone mapping.
[39:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.106-110; UPSC 2019 key; app notes 5:39 sub 1-2
## SUB 3 | Orbits for Earth Observation and Communication
[39:3:0] TABLE head: Orbit | Altitude | Use
  [39:3:0.0] LEO (Low Earth Orbit) | 200–2,000 km | Earth observation, ISS
  [39:3:0.1] SSPO (sun-synchronous polar) | ~500–900 km | Most EO satellites (IRS, Cartosat, NISAR)
  [39:3:0.2] MEO | 2,000–35,786 km | Navigation (GPS)
  [39:3:0.3] GEO (geostationary) | 35,786 km (22,236 miles) over the equator | Communication, weather; appears fixed
  [39:3:0.4] GSO (geosynchronous, inclined) | Same height | Figure-8 track; NavIC's 4 inclined satellites
[39:3:1] - **Geostationary** = geosynchronous + **circular** + in the **plane of the equator**; also **Clarke's orbit**; period one sidereal day, **23 h 56 min 4 s**. The "22,236 km" statement is wrong (that figure is in miles) → UPSC 2011 key **1, 2 and 3 only**.
[39:3:2] - **Sun-synchronous:** passes each place at the **same local solar time** → even lighting.
[39:3:3] - A satellite does not fall because Earth's gravity **provides the centripetal acceleration** for its orbit (UPSC 2011).
[39:3:4] - LEO imagers = finer detail, periodic revisit; geosynchronous imagers = coarser detail, near-continuous viewing.
[39:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.65-66 (UPSC 2011 explanation); app notes 5:39 sub 3
## SUB 4 | IRS Programme – Origins and Firsts
[39:4:0] - IRS began **17 Mar 1988** with **IRS-1A**: India's **first operational remote-sensing satellite**, launched from **Baikonur** (USSR, Kazakhstan) on a Soviet **Vostok** rocket – not Sriharikota.
[39:4:1] - One of the **world's largest civilian remote-sensing constellations**; data via NRSC and **Bhuvan**.
[39:4:2] TABLE head: Satellite | Year | Fact
  [39:4:2.0] Bhaskara I | 1979 | First experimental EO satellite
  [39:4:2.1] Rohini RS-1 / RS-D1 | 1980 / 31 May 1981 | Satellites launched by SLV-3 (SLV-3 is a launch vehicle, not a satellite)
  [39:4:2.2] IRS-1A | 1988 | Baikonur, Vostok
  [39:4:2.3] IRS-1B / 1C | 1991 / 1995 | Baikonur, Soviet/Russian rockets
  [39:4:2.4] IRS-P2 | 1994 | First IRS launched successfully by PSLV (PSLV-D2)
  [39:4:2.5] IRS-1D | 1997 | PSLV-C1 – first operational PSLV
[39:4:3] - **IRS uses:** crop productivity, **groundwater**, **mineral exploration**, land use, forests, floods, drought – **not telecommunications or traffic studies** (UPSC 2015: 1, 2 and 3 only).
[39:4:4] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.106-108, 112 (UPSC 2015 explanation); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.4, 6-7
## SUB 5 | EO Satellite Series and Their Functions
[39:5:0] TABLE head: Series / satellite | Function
  [39:5:0.0] Resourcesat (2003, 2011, 2016) | Crops, watershed, precision farming (LISS-III/IV, AWiFS)
  [39:5:0.1] Cartosat | Mapping (cartography), city mapping, surveillance
  [39:5:0.2] Oceansat-1 (1999, PSLV-C2), Oceansat-2 (2009, PSLV-C14), Oceansat-3 = EOS-06 (2022, PSLV-C54) | Ocean colour, SST, winds; PFZ fishing advisories
  [39:5:0.3] RISAT | Microwave SAR – all-weather, day-night imaging
  [39:5:0.4] SCATSAT-1 (2016) | Scatterometer – ocean winds → weather forecasting, cyclones
  [39:5:0.5] HySIS | Hyperspectral imaging (not DTH)
  [39:5:0.6] SARAL | ISRO–CNES (France) AltiKa Ka-band altimeter (sea-surface height) – no thermometer
  [39:5:0.7] IMS-1 (2008) | Small satellite with multispectral and hyperspectral cameras – no scatterometer
[39:5:1] - **Match (TSPSC 2018):** GAGAN – navigation; GSAT – communication; **Cartosat – Earth observation**; Mangalyaan – traces of methane.
[39:5:2] - **CNES** is the space agency of **France**; ISRO-CNES **maritime surveillance** pact, March 2019.
[39:5:3] # EOS renamings
[39:5:4] TABLE head: EOS name | Earlier name | Note
  [39:5:4.0] EOS-03 | GISAT-1 | Geo-imaging for near-real-time flood/cyclone watch (announced July 2021); lost on GSLV-F10, Aug 2021 (cryogenic stage)
  [39:5:4.1] EOS-04 | RISAT-1A | SAR; used in NRSC CROP wheat estimates
  [39:5:4.2] EOS-05 | GISAT-1A | GSLV-F17, 4 Sep 2026 – first geosynchronous land imager
  [39:5:4.3] EOS-06 | Oceansat-3 | PFZ advisories
[39:5:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.107-112; TSPSC 2018 key; app notes 5:39 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Cartosat Series
[39:6:0] TABLE head: Satellite | Launch | Feature
  [39:6:0.0] Cartosat-1 | 2005, PSLV-C6 | India's first mapping satellite; stereo images for 3D maps
  [39:6:0.1] Cartosat-2 series | 2007-2018, PSLV | Sub-metre; Cartosat-2E (land survey) on PSLV-C38, June 2017; Cartosat-2 + 30 co-passengers (31 satellites) on PSLV-C40, 12 Jan 2018
  [39:6:0.2] Cartosat-3 | 27 Nov 2019, PSLV-C47 (not C40) | Third-generation agile satellite, ~25 cm, with 13 US nanosatellites
[39:6:1] - Cartosat-2 series (714 kg): PSLV-C37, 15 Feb 2017, record **104** satellites into a 506 km SSO.
[39:6:2] - **Cartosat-2S** images showed **Joshimath** subsidence (NRSC, Jan 2023).
[39:6:3] - Cartosat-3 imagery: Gati Shakti, borders, KASTURI and Bharat Darshan heritage apps.
[39:6:4] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.108-109; app notes 5:39 sub 6
## SUB 7 | NISAR and Recent EO Missions
[39:7:0] - **NISAR** (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar): joint **Earth-observation** mission, partnership signed **2014**; **NASA L-band + ISRO S-band** – world's first dual-frequency radar satellite; **12 m** reflector.
[39:7:1] - Launched **30 July 2025** on **GSLV-F16** from Sriharikota into a **sun-synchronous LEO** (about 747 km) – not a High Earth Orbit; now operational.
[39:7:2] > ⚠ Outdated stems: "to be launched in January 2024" / "set to launch in June 2025" – NISAR flew on 30 July 2025.
[39:7:3] - **EOS-05** (GISAT-1A): GSLV-F17, **4 Sep 2026**, 2,367 kg; visible to long-wave IR; floods, cyclones, fires, crops.
[39:7:4] TABLE head: Lost satellite | Vehicle / date
  [39:7:4.0] EOS-03 (GISAT-1) | GSLV-F10, Aug 2021
  [39:7:4.1] EOS-09 (RISAT-1B, C-band SAR) | PSLV-C61, May 2025
  [39:7:4.2] DRDO EOS-N1 "Anvesha" | PSLV-C62, Jan 2026
[39:7:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 2 p.55-56; app notes 5:39 sub 7
## SUB 8 | NRSC, Bhuvan and EO in the News; Andhra Pradesh
[39:8:0] - Data chain: ground station → processing at **NRSC, Hyderabad** (nodal) → users. Training: **IIRS** and **CSSTEAP**, both **Dehradun**.
[39:8:1] - **Bhuvan:** ISRO's (**NRSC**'s) web-based **geoportal** with **3-D imaging**, open to the public (UPSC 2010) – not a satellite or telescope. Other NRSC/ISRO platforms: **Bhoonidhi, MOSDAC, VEDAS**.
[39:8:2] - Uses: groundwater prospects, wastelands, **FASAL** crop forecasting, drought, NUIS, SIS-DP, **INFFRAS** (Indian Forest Fire Response and Assessment System).
[39:8:3] TABLE head: In news | Agency / satellite
  [39:8:3.0] Joshimath subsidence (Jan 2023) | NRSC with Cartosat-2S
  [39:8:3.1] Landslide Atlas of India | NRSC (2023)
  [39:8:3.2] CROP crop-progress framework | NRSC with EOS-04 SAR
  [39:8:3.3] Glacial lakes | CWC since 2011 with NRSC imagery; Glacial Lake Atlas 2023: 7,570 lakes; Himalayan lake area up ~9% 2011-2025
[39:8:4] - **AP:** **APSAC** (AP Space Applications Centre) is the state remote-sensing agency; **SDSC-SHAR** (Tirupati district) gives Bay of Bengal cyclone data to **APSDMA**.
[39:8:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.4, 9, 13; app notes 5:39 sub 10

  x: Remote sensing obtains information about the Earth without physical contact by detecting reflected or emitted electromagnetic radiation.

  In a remote sensing system, which stage comes right after recording by the sensor?
  Radiation through the atmosphere | *Transmission, reception and processing | Interpretation and analysis | Interaction with the target
  x: The stages run: energy source, atmosphere, interaction with target, recording, then transmission, reception and processing, interpretation, application.
[ndb8a5683f99] sub0
  Remote sensing gathers information about a target without which of the following?
  Electromagnetic radiation | *Physical contact | Transmission and processing of data | A sensor
  x: Remote sensing works from a distance without physical contact, so physical sampling is not one of its stages.

  Consider the following statements about SAR sensors:

  x: Both are correct: SAR sends its own microwave signal instead of relying on sunlight, so it works through clouds and in darkness.
[n8099481514f] sub1

  x: Hyperspectral sensing uses hundreds of narrow spectral bands, enabling identification of materials and their chemical characteristics.
[fb19b4fa27754] sub1
  Which of the following is a passive remote-sensing instrument?
  LiDAR | *Infrared radiometer | Laser ranging sensor | RISAT SAR
  x: Infrared radiometers record emitted heat and are passive; SAR and laser/LiDAR send their own pulse and are active.
[fdacc6421096f] sub1
  What does optical (visible/near-infrared) imaging need?
  Cloud cover | Its own microwave pulse | A laser echo | *Daylight and a clear sky
  x: Optical sensors use reflected light, so they need daylight and a clear sky, unlike SAR.
[ne4c45deaa38] sub1
  Which one of the following is an example of an active remote-sensing system?
  Multispectral camera on Resourcesat | Infrared radiometer recording emitted heat | *Laser-based LiDAR | Visible-band camera on Oceansat
  x: LiDAR sends its own laser pulse and reads the echo, so it is active (APPSC 2023: laser is active). Multispectral cameras, infrared radiometers and visible cameras record sunlight reflected or heat emitted by the target, so they are passive.
[ge24bbd1dbc06] sub1
  Which of the following has the shortest wavelength?
  Infrared rays | Visible light | Ultraviolet rays | *Gamma rays
  x: In the electromagnetic spectrum, wavelength falls from infrared to visible to ultraviolet to gamma rays, so gamma rays have the shortest wavelength.
[nfa3d37506cc] sub1
  Which technique is most directly suited to detecting heat from volcanic eruptions, forest fires and urban heat?
  NDVI | LiDAR | InSAR | *Thermal infrared sensing
  x: Thermal infrared sensing records emitted heat and is therefore useful for volcanic eruptions, forest fires and urban heat mapping.
[n1970791ad86] sub2
  How many types of resolution are there in remote sensing?
  Five | Three | Six | *Four
  x: The four types are spatial, spectral, temporal and radiometric; 'chemical resolution' does not exist.
[g92689ade4962] sub2
  In remote sensing, what does temporal resolution refer to?
  The smallest object a sensor can see | The number and width of spectral bands | *How often a satellite revisits the same place | The sensitivity to small differences in energy
  x: Temporal resolution is the revisit time of a satellite over one place; the other three describe spatial, spectral and radiometric resolution.
[n82eb64ecfe3] sub2
  Which of the following remote-sensing technique pairs is correctly matched?
  InSAR – Elevation and canopy height by laser ranging | LiDAR – Ground deformation such as subsidence | *NDVI – Vegetation health from red vs near-infrared reflectance | LiDAR – Vegetation health from red vs near-infrared reflectance
  x: NDVI gauges vegetation health from red vs NIR reflectance; InSAR maps ground deformation and LiDAR uses laser ranging for elevation and canopy height.
[f720ed72e926f] sub2
  Which remote-sensing technique maps ground deformation such as land subsidence?

  35,786 km | 20,200 km | *500-900 km | 2,000-5,000 km
  x: SSOs are near-polar at about 500-900 km, passing a place at the same local solar time for uniform lighting.

  *23 h 56 min | 24 h 0 min | 23 h 30 min | 12 h 0 min

[n29c71115eb7] sub3
  Compared with geosynchronous imagers, what do LEO imaging satellites generally provide?

  x: LEO gives finer detail but revisits periodically; geosynchronous imagers give coarser detail but observe priority targets very frequently.
[nd62c303f4b4] sub3
  Which orbit is correctly matched with its typical use?
  MEO – Communication | GEO – Navigation | *LEO (200–2,000 km) – Earth observation | SSPO – Satellite appears fixed over the Equator
  x: LEO extends from about 200 to 2,000 km and is widely used for Earth observation. MEO is used for navigation, GEO for communication and weather, and SSPO for polar imaging.
[f323b4ca4625c] sub3
  In satellite orbits, what is the full form of LEO?

  x: LEO is Low Earth Orbit (200-2,000 km), used for Earth observation.
[f21c4d78760a9] sub3
  Why do most Earth-observation satellites use a sun-synchronous orbit?
  *Passes each place at the same local solar time | Traces a figure-8 ground track | Lies in the plane of the equator | Keeps the satellite fixed over one longitude
  x: A sun-synchronous orbit crosses each place at the same local solar time, giving even lighting.
[f4e3bf19b1894] sub3

[f874b4e1fe3c4] sub3

  x: A geostationary orbit is circular, equatorial and has zero inclination; the figure-8 is traced by inclined geosynchronous orbits.

## SUB 1 | Mission Firsts and Records
[40:1:0] # SpaDeX
[40:1:1] - **Space Docking Experiment**: two small spacecraft on **PSLV-C60, 30 Dec 2024**; **docked 16 Jan 2025** → India the **4th** country to dock in space, after the **US, Russia, China**.
[40:1:2] - Docking is needed for **Bharatiya Antariksh Station** and Chandrayaan-4.
[40:1:3] - **Axiom-4, SpaDeX and Gaganyaan** all support **microgravity research** (UPSC 2025: all three).
[40:1:4] # Records

  [40:1:5.0] Most satellites in one launch | PSLV-C37, 104 satellites (15 Feb 2017)
  [40:1:5.1] PSLV-C40, 12 Jan 2018 | 31 satellites (Cartosat-2 series + 30)
  [40:1:5.2] Heaviest payload by an Indian rocket | BlueBird Block-2, 6,100 kg, LVM3-M6, 24 Dec 2025 – direct-to-smartphone broadband
  [40:1:5.3] First dedicated commercial LVM3 flight | OneWeb, 36 satellites (2022)
  [40:1:5.4] First exclusive weather satellite | Kalpana-1, PSLV, 2002

[41:0:0] TABLE head: Mission / object | Agency, year | Fact asked
  [41:0:0.0] Voyager 1 and 2 | NASA, 1977 | Explore the outer solar system; Voyager 2 the only craft to visit Uranus and Neptune

[41:0:6] - **Jupiter:** atmosphere mainly **hydrogen and helium**, with traces of methane, ammonia and water.

## SUB 1 | Foreign Lunar Missions and Moon Firsts

[41:1:3] - **ILRS:** International Lunar Research Station, led by **Russia and China** – rival to the US-led Artemis Accords; Roscosmos said Luna-25 would ensure Russia's **guaranteed access to the Moon**.

## SUB 2 | Chandrayaan-3 (2023)
[41:2:0] - **Launch:** **14 July 2023**, **LVM3-M4** from SDSC SHAR, Sriharikota; follow-on to Ch-2 to show end-to-end **safe landing and roving**.
[41:2:1] - **Modules:** **Propulsion Module** + lander **Vikram** + rover **Pragyan** (names kept from Ch-2) – **no orbiter** (the Ch-2 orbiter relays).
[41:2:2] - **Mass:** **3,900 kg** (lander 1,752 kg incl. **26 kg** rover); life **one lunar day (~14 Earth days)**.
[41:2:3] - **Landing:** **23 Aug 2023** at **Shiv Shakti Point**, near the **south pole** (~69°S) → **National Space Day, 23 August**.
[41:2:4] - **Rank:** India the **4th** to soft-land (after **USA, USSR/Russia, China**) and the **1st near the lunar south pole**; Japan's SLIM later 5th.
[41:2:5] TABLE head: Payload | On | Function
  [41:2:5.0] ChaSTE | Lander | Surface thermal profile
  [41:2:5.1] ILSA | Lander | Moonquakes (seismic activity)
  [41:2:5.2] RAMBHA-LP (Langmuir probe) | Lander | Plasma density
  [41:2:5.3] LRA (NASA) | Lander | Passive laser retroreflector
  [41:2:5.4] APXS | Rover | Elemental composition (Mg, Al, Si, K, Ca, Ti, Fe) of soil and rocks
  [41:2:5.5] LIBS | Rover | Confirmed sulphur (in-situ, Aug 2023); also Al, Ca, Fe, Cr, Ti, Mn, Si, O
  [41:2:5.6] SHAPE | Propulsion Module | Studies Earth from lunar orbit
[41:2:6] - APXS found the soil rich in **iron and magnesium**, poor in aluminium.
[41:2:7] > Asked 12 times: sulphur (×3), launch date, south pole, names, payload → function, "4th country".

## SUB 3 | Mangalyaan (MOM) and Mars
[41:3:0] - **Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) = Mangalyaan**: India's **first interplanetary mission**; **PSLV-C25**, **5 Nov 2013**; Mars orbit **24 Sep 2014** (highly elliptical).
[41:3:1] - **Firsts:** **first country to reach Mars orbit on its maiden attempt**; **first Asian nation**; ISRO the **4th** to reach Mars after **NASA, USSR/Roscosmos, ESA** (not "second after USA"); lowest-cost Mars mission (~Rs 450 crore).
[41:3:2] - **5 payloads** incl. **Methane Sensor for Mars**, **Lyman Alpha Photometer**, Mars Colour Camera, MENCA, TIS; designed for **6 months**, worked ~**8 years** (contact lost **2022**).
[41:3:3] - Route: Earth orbit-raising, then Trans-Mars Injection – a **Hohmann transfer** (elliptical transfer orbit, two burns).
[41:3:4] - Film **Mission Mangal** (2019) on the MOM women scientists: **Vidya Balan** the leading lady (with Akshay Kumar).
[41:3:5] - **Methane on Mars:** first measured by **ESA's Mars Express**, also by NASA's **Curiosity**; with **water and gypsum** cited as evidence for possible life – Mars the planet that **may suit life**. (Jupiter's air also has trace methane – UPPCS 2016 accepted both.)
[41:3:6] - **Next:** Mangalyaan-2 (Mars landing, targeted ~2030); TSPSC 2023 key names **Japan** as ISRO's partner for a new Mars effort (not confirmed: ISRO-JAXA's joint mission is the lunar LUPEX).
[41:3:7] > Angle: launch vehicle and year, "first attempt" statements (UPSC 2016: I and III only).
[41:3:8] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 2 p.18-21, p.38-39; NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.40 (OCR); daily CA 21 Oct 2026 p.4; app notes 5:41 sub 4

## SUB 5 | Chandrayaan-2 (2019)
[41:5:0] - **Launch:** **22 Jul 2019**, **GSLV Mk III-M1** (LVM3) from **Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh**; Cabinet approval **2008** (PM Manmohan Singh).
[41:5:1] - **Orbiter + lander Vikram** (after Vikram Sarabhai) **+ rover Pragyan**; target the **lunar south polar region** – **not the North Pole**. No Moon Impact Probe (that was Ch-1).
[41:5:2] - **Originally with Russia:** Roscosmos was to supply the lander; it withdrew, so ISRO built Vikram.
[41:5:3] - **Result:** partial success – Vikram **hard-landed** (Sep 2019, **Tiranga Point**); the **orbiter still works**, highest-resolution lunar images (~0.25 m).
[41:5:4] - **Orbiter's CLASS** X-ray spectrometer mapped **sodium** abundance on the Moon for the first time (Oct 2022); also mapped chromium and water/hydroxyl.
[41:5:5] - **People:** M. Annadurai – Chandrayaan-1 project director and programme director in early Ch-2 (book key); at launch **M. Vanitha** was Project Director and **Ritu Karidhal** Mission Director.
[41:5:6] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 2 p.14-15; PMF S&T Part 1 p.39 (Ritu Karidhal); app notes 5:41 sub 2; web: theweek.in Chandrayaan-2 sodium (8 Oct 2022)
## SUB 6 | Aditya-L1 and Solar Missions
[41:6:0] - **Aditya-L1:** India's **first solar mission / space-based solar observatory**; launched **2 Sep 2023**, **PSLV-C57**, from the **Second Launch Pad**, SDSC SHAR (NextGen's "25 Jan 2024" is the magnetometer-boom date, not the launch).
[41:6:1] - **Halo orbit** around **Sun-Earth L1**, ~**1.5 million km** from Earth; inserted **6 Jan 2024**; continuous view, no eclipse; life 5 years.
[41:6:2] TABLE head: Type | Payload | Studies
  [41:6:2.0] Remote | VELC (Visible Emission Line Coronagraph, IIA) | Corona
  [41:6:2.1] Remote | SUIT (Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope, IUCAA) | Photosphere, chromosphere (near-UV)
  [41:6:2.2] Remote | SoLEXS | Soft X-ray
  [41:6:2.3] Remote | HEL1OS | Hard X-ray
  [41:6:2.4] In-situ | ASPEX | Solar-wind protons, ions
  [41:6:2.5] In-situ | PAPA (Plasma Analyser Package for Aditya) | Solar-wind electrons, ions
  [41:6:2.6] In-situ | Magnetometer | Magnetic field
[41:6:3] - **7 payloads** = 4 remote sensing + 3 in-situ.
[41:6:4] - **Earth's magnetic field** diverts charged solar particles towards the **poles** → aurora.
[41:6:5] - **Parker Solar Probe** (NASA, **12 Aug 2018**, on a **Delta IV Heavy** – not "Delta VI"): first craft through the Sun's outer corona; traces energy flow heating the corona and accelerating the solar wind. Solar Orbiter (NASA-ESA, 2020), SOHO (L1, 1995).
[41:6:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.46 (OCR); PMF S&T Part 2 p.22-23, p.39-40; Praveen CA360 June 2026 p.76; web: ulalaunch.com Parker Solar Probe launch (12 Aug 2018)
[41:6:7] - **LIBS** is a Chandrayaan-3 rover payload, not an Aditya-L1 one.

## SUB 8 | Chandrayaan-1 (2008)
[41:8:0] - India's **first Moon mission** – a **lunar probe** (orbiter + **Moon Impact Probe**), not manned; launched **22 Oct 2008** on **PSLV-C11** from **SDSC SHAR, Sriharikota (Andhra Pradesh)**; 1,380 kg; 100 km polar orbit.
[41:8:1] - **11 instruments** (5 Indian, 6 from USA, UK, Germany, Sweden, Bulgaria): TMC, HySI, LLRI, HEX, MIP, **CIXS**, SIR-2, SARA, **Mini-SAR**, **M3**, RADOM. (Lyman Alpha Photometer was on Mangalyaan.)
[41:8:2] - NASA's **M3** detected **water molecules** on the surface.
[41:8:3] - **MIP** hit the south polar region on **14 Nov 2008** → **Jawahar Point**; India the **4th** to reach the Moon's surface by impact probe, after **USSR, USA and Japan** (Japan's Hiten, 1993, before India).
[41:8:4] - 3,400+ orbits; contact lost **29 Aug 2009** (~10 months of 2 planned years).
[41:8:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.19-20 (OCR); PMF S&T Part 2 p.12; PMF S&T Part 1 p.100; app notes 5:41 sub 1

## SUB 10 | Space Physics – Escape Velocity, Re-entry, Lagrange Points
[41:10:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [41:10:0.0] Escape velocity | Minimum speed to escape a body's gravity; Earth 11.2 km/s
  [41:10:0.1] Orbital velocity | ~7.8-7.9 km/s in low Earth orbit
  [41:10:0.2] Lagrange points | Five points (L1-L5) where a small object stays balanced; Sun-Earth L1 ~1.5 million km
  [41:10:0.3] Soft landing | Controlled low-speed touchdown
  [41:10:0.4] Hohmann transfer | Fuel-saving elliptical transfer with two burns (used by MOM)
[41:10:1] - An object thrown at **8 km/s** (below 11.2 km/s) **returns to Earth** (book key; strictly a horizontal 8 km/s above the air would orbit).
[41:10:2] - **No atmosphere on the Moon:** low gravity, so its escape velocity is **less than the RMS speed** of gas molecules, which escape.
[41:10:3] - **Re-entry blackout:** a returning shuttle heats up and **ionises the surrounding air**, so radio contact is lost for a while – A and R both true, R explains A.
[41:10:4] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 1 p.49-50; app notes 5:41 sub 10

=== NOTES 5:42 | Human Spaceflight – Gaganyaan and Bharatiya Antariksh Station
## SUB 0 | Human Spaceflight Firsts and Records
[42:0:0] # World firsts
[42:0:1] TABLE head: First | Who / what | When
  [42:0:1.0] Artificial satellite | Sputnik-1, USSR (NASA was set up in 1958 in response) | 4 Oct 1957
  [42:0:1.1] Human in space | Yuri Gagarin, Vostok 1 (~108 min orbit) – first successful human spaceflight | 12 Apr 1961
  [42:0:1.2] American in space | Alan Shepard (Mercury, suborbital); John Glenn first American to orbit | 1961 / 1962
  [42:0:1.3] Woman in space | Valentina Tereshkova, Vostok-6 (USSR) | 16 Jun 1963
  [42:0:1.4] Dog in orbit | Laika (Sputnik-2) | 1957
  [42:0:1.5] Human on the Moon | Neil Armstrong (with Buzz Aldrin), Apollo 11 – USA; the USSR never landed a human | 1969
  [42:0:1.6] China's first crewed flight | Yang Liwei, Shenzhou-5, launcher Chang Zheng-2F; project code 921; China the 3rd nation (not 5th) | 15 Oct 2003
[42:0:2] - **Own crewed launch so far:** **USSR/Russia, USA, China** only – India (Gaganyaan) would be the **4th**.
[42:0:3] - Distractors: Bachendri Pal and Junko Tabei are Everest climbers; Sally Ride = first American woman in space; Magellan = navigator.
[42:0:4] # Records
[42:0:5] TABLE head: Person | Record
  [42:0:5.0] Oleg Kononenko (Russia) | Most cumulative days in space – 1,110.6 days; record broken 4 Feb 2024 (from Gennady Padalka)
  [42:0:5.1] Mark Vande Hei | Longest single NASA flight, 355 days on the ISS (2021-22); now Frank Rubio, 371 days (2023)
  [42:0:5.2] Peggy Whitson | Most spacewalks by a woman (10); US record for cumulative days; commanded Axiom-4
  [42:0:5.3] Christina Koch | Longest single flight by a woman, 328 days (2019-20); named to Artemis II in April 2023; flew around the Moon in Orion, April 2026 – first woman to do so
  [42:0:5.4] Sunita Williams | Then-record 195 days for a woman (from Dec 2006); 286-day stay ended Mar 2025
  [42:0:5.5] Tim Peake | British ESA astronaut, ISS crew
[42:0:6] # Indians and Indian-origin astronauts
[42:0:7] TABLE head: Person | Fact
  [42:0:7.0] Rakesh Sharma | First Indian in space, Apr 1984, Soyuz T-11 (USSR); he and Ravish Malhotra (back-up) were IAF test pilots trained in the USSR
  [42:0:7.1] Kalpana Chawla | First Indian-origin woman in space (NASA, 1997); died in Columbia (2003)
  [42:0:7.2] Sunita Williams | Second Indian-origin woman flown by NASA; daughter of Deepak Pandya and Ursuline Bonnie; an experienced US Navy test pilot (so "no flying experience" is false)
  [42:0:7.3] Shubhanshu Shukla | First Indian on the ISS; second Indian in space
  [42:0:7.4] Anil Menon | Indian-origin NASA astronaut; Soyuz MS-29 (Jul 2026), 8 months
[42:0:8] # Axiom-4
[42:0:9] - **Axiom-4:** **25 Jun 2025**, **SpaceX Dragon on Falcon 9**; NASA, Axiom Space, ESA; **18 days** on the ISS; returned 15 Jul 2025.
[42:0:10] - Crew: **Peggy Whitson** (commander), Shukla (pilot), Uznanski (**Poland**), Kapu (**Hungary**).
[42:0:11] - **7 Indian microgravity experiments** (under HSFC): muscle regeneration, algae, **moong and methi**, microbes, **tardigrades**, cognition, cyanobacteria (not lunar soil mining).
[42:0:12] > Most-asked angle: "first" questions – Gagarin/Vostok 1, Tereshkova, Armstrong, Sputnik/USSR, Rakesh Sharma (Soyuz T-11).

## SUB 1 | Gaganyaan – Programme, Spacecraft and Flights
[42:1:0] - India's **first human spaceflight programme**; approved **2018**; **crew of 3** to a **~400 km LEO** for **3 days**; splashdown in Indian waters, recovery by the **Indian Navy**.
[42:1:1] - Vehicle: **HLVM3** (human-rated LVM3) from **Sriharikota** – not GSLV Mk II; GSLV Mk-III structures redesigned; **Vikas** engine for the L110 stage qualified in **3 tests**.
[42:1:2] - Partners: **Russia and France** cooperate; **DRDO** gives human-centric systems (parachutes, life support, crew recovery).
[42:1:3] # Spacecraft
[42:1:4] TABLE head: Part | Role
  [42:1:4.0] Orbital Module | Crew Module + Service Module; put into orbit by HLVM3
  [42:1:4.1] Crew Module | Pressurised habitat for 3; survives re-entry; parachutes, sea splashdown
  [42:1:4.2] Service Module | Propulsion, power on orbit; fires thrusters to de-orbit, then burns up
  [42:1:4.3] Crew Escape System | Solid motors pull the Crew Module away if the rocket fails
[42:1:5] - Gaganyaan = **two** parts; Russia's **Soyuz** and China's **Shenzhou** = **three** modules (orbital, descent, service).
[42:1:6] # Flights and timeline
[42:1:7] - Sequence: uncrewed **G1 → G2 → G3 → crewed H1**; programme revised to 8 missions (6 uncrewed, 2 crewed); H1 now targeted **Q1 2027**.
[42:1:8] - Original target: **December 2021** (stated in 2018) → repeatedly revised; quote with the statement date.
[42:1:9] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 2 p.3-5, p.25-28; app notes 5:42 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Test Missions, Vyommitra and Gaganyatris
[42:2:0] TABLE head: Test | Date | What it proved
  [42:2:0.0] CARE | 18 Dec 2014 (LVM3-X) | Crew-module re-entry
  [42:2:0.1] TV-D1 | 18 Oct 2023, Sriharikota | Crew Escape System abort at Mach 1.2; sea recovery
  [42:2:0.2] IADT-01 | 24 Aug 2025 | 4.8 t module dropped from 3 km by IAF Chinook, at SDSC-SHAR
  [42:2:0.3] IADT-02 | 10 Apr 2026 | 5.7 t module; 10 parachutes of 4 types; Navy recovery
  [42:2:0.4] SOLVE | 3 Jul 2026 | Solid-motor ground test
[42:2:1] - **Vyommitra:** AI-enabled **female** half-humanoid robot; flies on the **uncrewed G1 and G2**; monitors cabin pressure, temperature, oxygen and life support – calling it a "male robot" is false.
[42:2:2] # Gaganyatris (named Feb 2024)
[42:2:3] TABLE head: Astronaut | Rank
  [42:2:3.0] Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair | Group Captain
  [42:2:3.1] Ajit Krishnan | Group Captain
  [42:2:3.2] Angad Pratap | Group Captain
  [42:2:3.3] Shubhanshu Shukla | Wing Commander (later Group Captain)
[42:2:4] - All **IAF test pilots**; **Pankaj M. Sinha is NOT** a Gaganyatri.
[42:2:5] - Selection: IAF's **Institute of Aerospace Medicine (IAM), Bengaluru**.
[42:2:6] - Training: **Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre, Russia** (via Glavkosmos, Roscosmos' arm) → ISRO **Astronaut Training Facility, Bengaluru**; Shukla and Nair trained in the US for Axiom-4; zero-g via aircraft **parabolic flights**.
[42:2:7] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 2 p.27; app notes 5:42 sub 1-2
[42:2:8] - **Gaganyaan statements (APPSC):** first crewed orbital spacecraft of the programme ✓; DRDO supports human-centric systems ✓; Vyommitra "male" ✗; GSLV Mk II ✗ (HLVM3).
[42:2:9] - **HSFC (Human Space Flight Centre):** created within ISRO/DoS to oversee Gaganyaan; Russia's Glavkosmos trained the crew.
## SUB 3 | Space Stations – ISS, Tiangong and BAS
[42:3:0] TABLE head: Feature | ISS | Tiangong
  [42:3:0.0] Owner | NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA, CSA (not ISRO); intergovernmental treaties | China alone
  [42:3:0.1] Modules | Zarya (Russian, first, 1998), Unity (US), Zvezda, Destiny (US lab), Kibo (Japan), Columbus | Tianhe core (2021) + Wentian (Jul 2022) + Mengtian (final, Oct 2022)
  [42:3:0.2] Status | ~400 km; crewed since Nov 2000; retire ~2030 | Completed 2022
[42:3:1] - Strictly, the ISS is no longer the only active modular station in LEO – Tiangong is one too.
[42:3:2] - **BAS (Bharatiya Antariksh Station):** approved **Sep 2024**; **five modules**; base module **BAS-1 by 2028** on LVM3; full station **2035**; Indian on the Moon by **2040**.
[42:3:3] - Precursors: **SpaDeX** (PSLV-C60, docked 16 Jan 2025; India 4th) – a docking demonstrator; Axiom-4, Gaganyaan.
[42:3:4] # Microgravity research (UPSC 2025)
[42:3:5] - **Axiom-4** (ISS experiments) and **Gaganyaan** (crew microgravity experiments) support microgravity research; **SpaDeX** = docking technology → UPSC key "**only two**" (some books say all three, as SpaDeX's POEM-4 flew experiments).
[42:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 2 p.27-28, p.44-47; web: anantamias.com UPSC Prelims 2025 Q93; app notes 5:42 sub 7
## SUB 4 | Microgravity and the Human Body
[42:4:0] - **Weightlessness** = free fall: craft and astronaut fall with the same **g**, so the **normal force is zero** – books call it "**zero gravity**".
[42:4:1] - No gravity → **weight becomes zero but mass stays the same**; an astronaut's mass never becomes zero.
[42:4:2] - No candle flame in space; astronauts cannot stand erect; an apple released moves along with the ship.
[42:4:3] - Moon weight = **1/6** of Earth's; at **Earth's centre**, true g is zero.
[42:4:4] TABLE head: Condition | Effect
  [42:4:4.0] Bone loss | 1–1.5% bone mass a month
  [42:4:4.1] Muscle atrophy | Postural muscles weaken
  [42:4:4.2] Fluid shift | "Puffy face, bird legs"
  [42:4:4.3] Space Adaptation Syndrome | Space motion sickness
  [42:4:4.4] SANS | Optic disc swelling, vision changes
[42:4:5] - **Charlie Brown effect:** fluid-shift **puffy face and thin legs** in microgravity (not Snoopy or Peanuts effect).
[42:4:6] - Space medicine is also studied through ground **analogues**, not only spaceflight.
[42:4:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:42 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Infrastructure, Institutions and Analogue Missions
[42:5:0] TABLE head: Body / facility | Role
  [42:5:0.0] Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC), Bengaluru | New ISRO vertical leading Gaganyaan
  [42:5:0.1] IAM, Bengaluru | Selection, aeromedical tests, MITRA
  [42:5:0.2] ISTRAC, Bengaluru | Tracking network; ESA adds ground stations (Sep 2026)
  [42:5:0.3] Third Launch Pad, Sriharikota | Preparations from Dec 2019; approved Jan 2025, ₹4,000 crore; for NGLV and human spaceflight
  [42:5:0.4] Dhanush, Sriharikota | India's first private launch pad, Agnikul Cosmos
  [42:5:0.5] Kulasekarapattinam (TN) | SSLV complex; foundation 27 Aug 2025
[42:5:1] - **ISRO Human Spaceflight Expo**: **Jawaharlal Nehru Planetarium, Bengaluru**, **22-24 Jul 2022**.
[42:5:2] # Analogue missions
[42:5:3] - **India's first analogue space mission**: **Leh, Ladakh**, **Nov 2024** (with **AAKA**, **IIT Bombay**) – simulates life in an interplanetary habitat; data for selection, **ECLSS**, work-rest schedules.
[42:5:4] - **HOPE** (Himalayan Outpost for Planetary Exploration): **Tso Kar**, Ladakh; early-Mars-like – high UV, low pressure, cold, saline permafrost.
[42:5:5] - **MITRA**: crew **behavioural** study at Leh with **IAM**; hypoxia, cold, isolation.

  *Centre of Earth – Gravitational pull becomes negligible with distance | Freely falling lift – The floor no longer pushes up, so normal force is zero | Orbiting satellite – Satellite and astronaut accelerate towards Earth with the same g | Deep space far from all masses – Gravitational pull becomes negligible with distance
  x: At the Earth's centre true g is zero because the pulls of the surrounding mass cancel; negligible pull with distance is the deep-space case.
[n961a50aef03] sub4

  Radiation-induced swelling of the limbs | Muscle regeneration after treadmill exercise | *Fluid shifting towards the head in microgravity | Loss of bone mass in the legs
  x: Microgravity causes body fluids to shift towards the head, producing a puffy face and comparatively thinner-looking legs.
[nphysics-23-14] sub4
  Which of the following is NOT correct about astronauts in an orbiting satellite?
  They experience apparent weightlessness | The satellite and the astronaut accelerate towards Earth with the same g | *The mass of the astronaut becomes zero | There is no normal force on the astronaut
  x: The satellite and astronaut fall together with the same g, so the normal force is zero and the astronaut feels weightless; the astronaut's mass stays the same.

  x: Space Adaptation Syndrome is space motion sickness; SANS causes optic disc swelling.

=== NOTES 5:45 | Applications of Space Technology – Agriculture, Disaster Management, Telemedicine, Tele-education, Navigation
## SUB 0 | GIS – Concept, Components and Uses
[45:0:0] - **GIS = Geographic Information System**: a computer system to **store, manipulate, analyse and present** all types of geographical (**spatial**) data – the most complete system for modelling spatial data and community vulnerability.
[45:0:1] - **Father of GIS:** **Roger Tomlinson** – coined the term for the Canada GIS (1960s).
[45:0:2] - Each theme is a **layer**; **overlay analysis** combines layers; data = spatial (vector, raster) + attribute tables.
[45:0:3] TABLE head: Component | Examples
  [45:0:3.0] Hardware | Computer, digitizer (tablet/table converting analog data to digital), scanner, GPS receiver, plotter
  [45:0:3.1] Software | QGIS – free, open-source, cross-platform desktop GIS
  [45:0:3.2] Data | Spatial (points, lines, polygons; satellite images) + attributes
[45:0:4] - **Remote sensing + GIS:** maps prepared from satellite data or aerial photos are digitised and stored in GIS; manual maps are slow to prepare and hard to update.
[45:0:5] - **Decision Support System:** data systems for planning.
[45:0:6] - **Survey of India** prepares India's **topographical maps**.
[45:0:7] # GIS in disasters
[45:0:8] - **Situational awareness map:** real-time weather, hospitals and shelters, damage imagery; **pre-disaster population density maps** are least useful in the live response.
[45:0:9] - Real-time sources: satellite imagery, weather data, sensor networks – **not news channels**.
[45:0:10] TABLE head: Remote sensing | GIS
  [45:0:10.0] Rainfall estimation during a cyclone; post-disaster damage | Mapping spread of infectious diseases; landslide hazard zonation
[45:0:11] - Earthquake **magnitude and epicentre** come from **seismographs**, not GIS.
[45:0:12] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:45 sub 1; general knowledge (Tomlinson, Survey of India)
## SUB 1 | Disaster Management from Space
[45:1:0] TABLE head: Can be monitored from space | Cannot
  [45:1:0.0] Floods, cyclones, drought, forest fires, tsunami inundation, landslides, post-quake ground deformation | Spread of a disease among humans, heart attack; earthquake prediction
[45:1:1] - Satellites give **near-real-time images** (remote sensing) for disaster management.
[45:1:2] - Fire hotspots: thermal-infrared **MODIS** (Terra/Aqua) and **VIIRS** (Suomi-NPP), received at **Shadnagar** (NRSC) → **Forest Survey of India** alert system (not IMD) – the modern **fire alert system**.
[45:1:3] - **NRSC activities:** near-real-time flood and cyclone mapping, forest-fire alerts, spatial flood early warning, **rapid damage assessment of landslides**; **Decision Support Centre**; **NDEM** (National Database for Emergency Management).
[45:1:4] - **Bhuvan disaster services:** NDEM, drought monitoring, flood monitoring – no nuclear-hazard warning.
[45:1:5] - **Ganga-Brahmaputra basin** = most flood-prone area (NRSC).
[45:1:6] - **Landslides:** **DInSAR** gives repeat-pass slope-deformation monitoring, before visible failure, without a ground instrument network.
[45:1:7] - **Global Forest Watch (WRI):** custom maps, forest trends, alerts.
[45:1:8] TABLE head: Satellite | Use
  [45:1:8.0] RISAT / SAR | Flood mapping through clouds
  [45:1:8.1] INSAT-3DS | Cyclone tracks
  [45:1:8.2] Cartosat | Damage mapping
[45:1:9] - **DMSP** (ISRO): INSAT and IRS for imaging and communication; States must request data from NRSC.
[45:1:10] - **INSAT Disaster Warning System:** Cyclone Warning Centre **Chennai → C-band uplink → S-band downlink**.
[45:1:11] - **NDMA** uses GIS for planning, decision support, guidelines; **ISRO** led the **International Charter Space and Major Disasters** from **April 2025** (6 months).
[45:1:12] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:45 sub 5
## SUB 2 | Remote Sensing Basics and Spectral Indices
[45:2:0] - **Remote sensing:** gathering **images**/information about Earth **without physical contact**, from reflected or emitted radiation; covers dangerous or inaccessible areas.
[45:2:1] TABLE head: Type | Energy | Example
  [45:2:1.0] Active | Sends its own signal | RISAT radar, LiDAR
  [45:2:1.1] Passive | Natural radiation (sunlight) | Resourcesat, Oceansat
[45:2:2] - **Microwave / SAR** sees through cloud and darkness; **soil moisture** best measured by microwave/SAR.
[45:2:3] - **InSAR:** compares the **phase** of radar images from **orbiting** satellites → **ground deformation** (quakes, subsidence, landslides).
[45:2:4] - **NISAR:** radar, **L-band and S-band**; centimetre-scale ground movement.
[45:2:5] - Applications: land cover, vegetation, forests, **surface and groundwater**, snow, wetlands, **minerals and hydrocarbons**, crop area and **crop yield** – "all of the above".
[45:2:6] - Soil nutrient testing by **chemical analysis is NOT remote sensing**.
[45:2:7] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [45:2:7.0] NDVI | Normalized Difference Vegetation Index = (NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red); healthy vegetation reflects near-infrared; −1 to +1; most used for drought
  [45:2:7.1] VCI | From NDVI; drought declaration
  [45:2:7.2] Ecology index | Vegetation, water content, biological quantity – not cost and production
  [45:2:7.3] NH Green Cover Index 2025-26 | NHAI + NRSC; satellite green cover of national highways
[45:2:8] - **National Carbon Project** (ISRO-GBP): **carbon pools, fluxes and net carbon balance** of the terrestrial biosphere – vegetation pools, soil pools, fluxes.
[45:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.4-5; Rocket Disaster Management p.23; app notes 5:45 sub 0-1, 9

=== NOTES 5:48 | Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme – Prithvi, Agni, Akash, Trishul, Nag
## SUB 0 | Agni Series – Ranges, Tests and Mission Divyastra
[48:0:0] # Agni ("Fire") – India's surface-to-surface ballistic missiles
[48:0:1] - Developed by **DRDO** (not ISRO); **solid-fuelled**; nuclear and conventional warheads; **fully indigenous**; operated by the **Strategic Forces Command**; a **long-range** missile family (~700 km to 5,000+ km).
[48:0:2] - Only **Agni I–III** were developed within IGMDP; Agni-IV, V, P and VI are later projects.
[48:0:3] TABLE head: Missile | Stages / fuel | Range | Key fact
  [48:0:3.0] Agni-I | Single-stage solid | ~700 km (700–1,200 km) | Tested 9 Jan 2003 (Wheeler Island) and 28 Mar 2010 (700 km)
  [48:0:3.1] Agni-II | Two (two-and-a-half) stage solid | ~2,000 km+ (2,000–2,500 km; NextGen 2,500 km) | MRBM, often loosely called an "ICBM" in old keys
  [48:0:3.2] Agni-III | Two-stage solid | ~3,500 km (3,000–3,500 km) | First flight 9 Jul 2006 failed; 2007 and 2008 flights successful; tested Feb 2010
  [48:0:3.3] Agni-IV | Two-stage solid, road-mobile | ~4,000 km (3,500–4,000 km) | Surface-to-surface IRBM (UPSC 2014: not liquid, not 7,500 km)
  [48:0:3.4] Agni-V | Three-stage solid, canister | 5,000+ km | India's ICBM; tested 26 Dec 2016 from Wheeler (now APJ Abdul Kalam) Island; Dr Tessy Thomas
  [48:0:3.5] Agni-P (Prime) | Two-stage solid, canister | 1,000–2,000 km | Rail-based launcher test, 24 Sep 2025
  [48:0:3.6] Agni-VI | – | 8,000–10,000 km | Under development – the longest-range in any list
[48:0:4] - **Mission Divyastra (11 Mar 2024):** first flight test of **Agni-V with MIRV** (Multiple Independently Targetable Re-entry Vehicle) technology.
[48:0:5] - **ICBM threshold 5,500 km** → Agni-V (5,000 km) is formally on the IRBM/ICBM border; Agni-VI = full ICBM.
[48:0:6] > Agni-V "not exclusively indigenous" is the WRONG statement (it is fully indigenous). Agni-II "ICBM with more than 2,000 km" is the old-key wording.
[48:0:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 (src/science-tech/nextgen-st-group2-02.pdf, OCR) p.57; PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.57, p.64, p.66-68; web: armscontrol.org (Agni-I test 9 Jan 2003); app notes 5:48 sub 2
## SUB 1 | The Five IGMDP Missiles – Types
[48:1:0] TABLE head: Missile | Meaning | Type | Range
  [48:1:0.0] Prithvi | Earth | Surface-to-surface SRBM (liquid) | 150–350 km (Prithvi-III 750 km)
  [48:1:0.1] Agni | Fire | Surface-to-surface ballistic (solid) | ~700 to 5,000+ km
  [48:1:0.2] Akash | Sky | Medium-range surface-to-air | ~25–30 km; Mach 2.5; 18 km altitude
  [48:1:0.3] Trishul | Trident | Short-range, low-level surface-to-air | ~9 km (NextGen: 12 km)
  [48:1:0.4] Nag | Cobra | 3rd-generation fire-and-forget anti-tank | 500 m – 4 km (land version)
[48:1:1] - **Not IGMDP:** **BrahMos** (India-Russia), Astra, Shaurya, Nirbhay, Sagarika, Helina, Prahaar, Barak-8.
[48:1:2] - **Not missiles:** **Pinaka** (multi-barrel **rocket** launcher, ARDE), **Arjun** (tank), Vajra (gun), Tejas (aircraft), Lakshya (target drone).
[48:1:3] - **SLBM:** **K-4** (~3,500 km) and K-15 Sagarika – submarine-launched; Agni, Prithvi and Akash are land-based.
[48:1:4] - Nag is the **shortest-range** of the five; **Prithvi** is the formal SRBM.
[48:1:5] > Classic traps: Nag is **not** a SAM; Agni is **not** a sea-launched cruise missile; Trishul and Akash are the SAMs.
[48:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 (src/science-tech/nextgen-st-group2-02.pdf, OCR) p.56-57; PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.57, p.62, p.68-70; app notes 5:48 sub 1, 7
## SUB 2 | IGMDP – Launch, Objectives, Phases and Closure
[48:2:0] - **Launched 1983** by **DRDO** under **Dr APJ Abdul Kalam**; lead lab **DRDL, Hyderabad** (with RCI and ASL).
[48:2:1] - **Objectives:** **self-sufficiency in missile technology**; a **family of strategic and tactical guided missiles**; competence across technologies, production and deployment. Being "the first country with an international missile market" was **not** an aim.
[48:2:2] - **Five missiles:** **Prithvi, Agni, Akash, Trishul, Nag**.
[48:2:3] TABLE head: Phase | Missiles
  [48:2:3.0] 1984–89 | Prithvi, Trishul
  [48:2:3.1] 1989–92 | Nag, Akash
  [48:2:3.2] 1992–2008 | Agni matured
[48:2:4] - **Closed 2008** after self-reliance was achieved; spin-offs: long-range tracking system, composites, **ring laser gyros**, radomes (not a satellite navigation constellation).
[48:2:5] - **Significance:** turned India from a missile importer into a **missile-exporting** power and laid the base for Agni-V MIRV and BMD.
[48:2:6] - **Aug 2026:** ToT of conventional missiles such as **Nag** to private industry; **Agni stays in state production**.
[48:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 (src/science-tech/nextgen-st-group2-02.pdf, OCR) p.56; PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.62; app notes 5:48 sub 0
## SUB 3 | Nag Family – Fire-and-Forget Anti-tank Missiles
[48:3:0] - **Nag:** third-generation **fire-and-forget anti-tank** guided missile; **IIR** (imaging infrared) seeker, night capable; 8 kg tandem **HEAT** warhead; range **500 m – 4 km**.
[48:3:1] - **Fire-and-forget:** the missile guides itself after launch, so the operator can take cover. (Astra = air-to-air, Prahaar = tactical SSM, Akash = SAM.)
[48:3:2] TABLE head: Variant | Role
  [48:3:2.0] NAMICA | Tracked carrier (modified BMP-2) with up to six missiles; NAMIS = Nag Mk-2 "tank killer"
  [48:3:2.1] HELINA / Dhruvastra | Helicopter-launched – Army / IAF
  [48:3:2.2] MPATGM | Man-portable, ~2.5 km; DRDO flight-tested it at the Kurnool range (2019)
  [48:3:2.3] SANT | Stand-off anti-tank, air-launched, 15–20 km; tested 11 Dec 2021 at Pokhran
[48:3:3] - **Top attack:** climbs, then dives onto the tank's thin top armour.
[48:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 (src/science-tech/nextgen-st-group2-02.pdf, OCR) p.57; PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.70; app notes 5:48 sub 5; general knowledge, not checked (SANT 11 Dec 2021 Pokhran; MPATGM Kurnool 2019)
## SUB 4 | Prithvi and Dhanush
[48:4:0] TABLE head: Variant | Service | Range / fact
  [48:4:0.0] Prithvi-I | Army | 150 km, 1,000 kg; India's first indigenous ballistic missile
  [48:4:0.1] Prithvi-II | Air Force | 350 km, 500–1,000 kg; nuclear-capable; first test 27 Jan 1996, Chandipur; inducted 2003
  [48:4:0.2] Prithvi-III / Dhanush | Navy | 350–750 km; ship-launched short-range ballistic missile ("ship to ship / ship to shore")
[48:4:1] - Prithvi = **liquid** fuel (Prithvi-III: solid first stage); three variants, not two.
[48:4:2] - **Nov 2006:** a modified Prithvi (**PAD/Pradyumna**) intercepted a **Prithvi-II** target – India's first BMD interception; Prithvi-II itself is **not** an air-defence missile for metros. **PAD (Pradyumna)** = exo-atmospheric interceptor (50–80 km).
[48:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 (src/science-tech/nextgen-st-group2-02.pdf, OCR) p.56; PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.57, p.62-63; app notes 5:48 sub 3
## SUB 5 | Akash, Trishul and Their Successors
[48:5:0] - **Akash:** medium-range **SAM**, targets up to **30 km**, Mach 2.5, 18 km altitude; Army + IAF; developed by **DRDO** (lead lab DRDL, Hyderabad).
[48:5:1] TABLE head: Variant | Fact
  [48:5:1.0] Akash Mk-I | ~25 km, Rajendra radar
  [48:5:1.1] Akash Prime | Indigenous active RF seeker; first test 27 Sep 2021
  [48:5:1.2] Akash-NG | ~70 km, canister-launched
[48:5:2] - **Trishul:** short-range, low-level **SAM**; **programme shut down 27 Feb 2008** (never inducted) – the "shelved" missile; replaced by Spyder (IAF), Barak-1 (Navy), Akash (Army).
[48:5:3] - **Akashteer** (BEL + Army) is an **air-defence control system**, not a missile.
[48:5:4] - **QRSAM** (Quick Reaction SAM): indigenous successor; test-fired from **Chandipur** (ITR, Odisha) in **June–July 2017**.
[48:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 (src/science-tech/nextgen-st-group2-02.pdf, OCR) p.57; PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.68-70; app notes 5:48 sub 4
## SUB 6 | Persons – Missile Man and Missile Woman
[48:6:0] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [48:6:0.0] Dr APJ Abdul Kalam | "Missile Man", father of India's missile technology, founder of the indigenous missile programme (led IGMDP); Chief Scientific Adviser at Pokhran-II (1998), not Pokhran-I; 11th President
  [48:6:0.1] Dr Tessy Thomas | "Missile Woman" / "Agniputri"; Agni-IV and Agni-V
  [48:6:0.2] V.K. Saraswat | Prithvi; BMD
[48:6:1] - Not missile scientists in these keys: U.R. Rao (space), R. Chidambaram and Homi Bhabha (nuclear), Raja Ramanna (nuclear), M.G.K. Menon.

## SUB 7 | Test Ranges and MTCR
[48:7:0] TABLE head: Range | State
  [48:7:0.0] Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island (ex-Wheeler Island, renamed 2015) | Off Odisha – Agni tests; AD-1 BMD interceptor (Nov 2022)
  [48:7:0.1] ITR Chandipur, Balasore | Odisha – Prithvi-II (1996), QRSAM (2017)
  [48:7:0.2] Pokhran | Rajasthan – SANT, Nag
  [48:7:0.3] Kurnool DRDO range | Andhra Pradesh – MPATGM

=== NOTES 5:49 | Missiles Beyond Igmdp – Brahmos, Nirbhay, Astra, Pralay, Hypersonic Technology, Mission Shakti (asat)
## SUB 0 | BrahMos – India-Russia Supersonic Cruise Missile
[49:0:0] # Partnership and name
[49:0:1] - **Joint venture of India and Russia:** **DRDO 50.5%** + **NPO Mashinostroyeniya (NPOM), Russia 49.5%** = **BrahMos Aerospace**, created by an Inter-Governmental Agreement signed in **Moscow, 1998** (not USA, France, Israel, Japan, China).
[49:0:2] - **Name:** **Brahmaputra** (India) + **Moskva** (Russia) rivers – "BRAHMOS", not Brahmastra.
[49:0:3] - **Production:** missiles are integrated at the **BrahMos Integration Complex, Kanchanbagh, Hyderabad** (first production unit; later Thiruvananthapuram, and **Lucknow** – BrahMos Integration and Testing Facility, inaugurated **11 May 2025**). Not Bangalore, Mumbai, Ludhiana or Dehradun.
[49:0:4] # Type and technical features
[49:0:5] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [49:0:5.0] Type | Supersonic cruise missile (not ballistic, not ICBM); one of the world's fastest cruise missiles
  [49:0:5.1] Speed | Mach 2.8–3.0 (~3,400–3,700 km/h)
  [49:0:5.2] Role | Essentially anti-ship, also land-attack; not anti-aircraft, not anti-tank
  [49:0:5.3] Propulsion | Solid booster → liquid ramjet
  [49:0:5.4] Navigation | Inertial + satellite; fire-and-forget from a Transport Launch Canister
  [49:0:5.5] Range | 290 km originally → 400–450 km after India joined MTCR (2016); BrahMos-ER 450–800 km. Never 1,200 km
  [49:0:5.6] Platforms | Land, ship, submarine and air (Su-30MKI) – not "only submarines"; in service with Army, Navy and Air Force
[49:0:6] - **Variants:** BrahMos-ER (extended range); **BrahMos-NG** – lighter (~1.5 t vs 2.5 t), for Tejas, smaller warships, submarines, ~Mach 3.5; **BrahMos-II** – planned **hypersonic** (above Mach 5, up to Mach 7–8), scramjet.
[49:0:7] # Tests and milestones
[49:0:8] TABLE head: Date | Event
  [49:0:8.0] 12 June 2001 | First successful test, Chandipur, Odisha
  [49:0:8.1] 12 Feb 2003 | Third test flight
  [49:0:8.2] 13 June 2004 | 7th launch from a mobile launcher; can locate an enemy ship 290 km away
  [49:0:8.3] 2005 | First version inducted into the Navy (INS Rajput)
  [49:0:8.4] Jan and 29 March 2009 | Land-attack Block-II tests at Pokhran, Rajasthan (Mobile Autonomous Launcher)
  [49:0:8.5] 21 March 2010 | Fired from moving warship INS Ranvir, Bay of Bengal, off Odisha
  [49:0:8.6] March 2017 | Extended-range (~400 km) test
  [49:0:8.7] 17 Dec 2019 | Test from ITR Chandipur
  [49:0:8.8] May 2025 | First reported combat use – Operation Sindoor
[49:0:9] # Exports
[49:0:10] - **Philippines** – first export customer: **US$375 million** deal (**January 2022**) for **three batteries** of shore-based anti-ship BrahMos; first batch delivered **April 2024**. Export range about **290 km** (so "490 km" is false).
[49:0:11] - **UAE**: BrahMos and Akashteer only in **early-stage talks** (23 Jun 2026) – nothing delivered.
[49:0:12] > Most-asked missile of the topic: partner country (**Russia**) ×7, "supersonic cruise" ×5, NOT-correct statements (range, platforms) ×4, test sites.
[49:0:13] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.52, p.72-73; web: brahmos.com press release 156 (Integration Complex, Hyderabad); app notes 5:49 sub 1, sub 8
## SUB 1 | Astra and Nirbhay
[49:1:0] # Astra (BVRAAM)
[49:1:1] - India's **first indigenous Beyond Visual Range Air-to-Air Missile** (DRDO); all-weather, day-night; **active radar seeker**. So Astra = **air-to-air** (not surface-to-surface, surface-to-air or air-to-surface).
[49:1:2] - BVR = beyond about 20 nautical miles (37 km).
[49:1:3] - First successfully tested **9 May 2003, Balasore**; ballistic flight test at ITR **Chandipur, 20 May 2011**.
[49:1:4] TABLE head: Variant | Facts
  [49:1:4.0] Astra Mk-1 | 80–110 km (max ~110 km head-on), Mach 4.5, up to 20 km altitude; on Su-30MKI, Tejas
  [49:1:4.1] Astra Mk-2 | ~160–200 km, dual-pulse solid motor
  [49:1:4.2] Astra Mk-3 'Gandiva' | Under development, SFDR engine, 300–350+ km
[49:1:5] - **23 August 2023:** LCA **Tejas (LSP-7)** test-fired Astra off **Goa**; **12 March 2025:** fired from an LCA AF Mk1 prototype.
[49:1:6] - **Export:** **Indonesia** – Astra Mk-1 deal Jul 2026, first-ever Astra export.
[49:1:7] # Nirbhay and ITCM
[49:1:8] - **Nirbhay:** India's first indigenous **long-range subsonic cruise missile** (land-attack, LR-LACM) – **not supersonic**.
[49:1:9] - Range **~1,000 km**; **turbojet**; about **Mach 0.8**; conventional or **nuclear** warheads; **terrain-hugging**; surface-to-surface; seen as India's counter to Pakistan's **Babur**.
[49:1:10] - Flight-tested **7 November 2017** from **ITR Chandipur**.
[49:1:11] - **ITCM** (Indigenous Technology Cruise Missile): Nirbhay successor, **'Manik' small turbofan** by **GTRE**; Jun 2026: family now called **LR-LACM**.
[49:1:12] > Astra is asked as "air-to-air / first BVR" ×8; Nirbhay as "subsonic" (the wrong statement is always "supersonic").
[49:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.52, p.61, p.75; app notes 5:49 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Shaurya, Rudram and Other New Indian Missiles
[49:2:0] TABLE head: Missile | Type / role
  [49:2:0.0] Rudram-I | India's first indigenous anti-radiation missile, air-to-surface, from Su-30MKI, ~150–200 km; homes on radar emissions to destroy enemy radars and communication sites
  [49:2:0.1] Shaurya | Canister-launched, hypersonic, nuclear-capable surface-to-surface (quasi-)ballistic missile by DRDO's ASL, Hyderabad; tested 12 Nov 2008 and 24 Sep 2011; ~700–800 km with 1,000 kg (variants up to ~1,900 km); max speed Mach 7.5
  [49:2:0.2] Pralay | Quasi-ballistic short-range SSM, 150–500 km, conventional warhead, manoeuvrable re-entry; salvo of two fired 31 Dec 2025
  [49:2:0.3] Trishul | IGMDP short-range quick-reaction SAM, supersonic (~Mach 2), tested from Chandipur; discontinued
  [49:2:0.4] VSHORADS | DRDO (RCI, Hyderabad) 4th-generation man-portable air-defence system (MANPADS); DAC-approved buy Jul 2026
  [49:2:0.5] VL-SRSAM | Vertical-launch short-range SAM for Navy ships, derived from Astra
  [49:2:0.6] QRSAM | Quick Reaction SAM, Army's mid-range IADWS layer against low-flying threats
  [49:2:0.7] MPATGM | Man-portable, third-generation, fire-and-forget ATGM; DAC approval Jul 2026
  [49:2:0.8] Prahaar | ~150 km tactical ballistic missile
  [49:2:0.9] LRGB 'Gaurav' | 1,000 kg glide bomb, ~100 km, from Su-30MKI (Apr 2025)
  [49:2:0.10] Pinaka LRGR-120 | 120 km guided rocket; first flight 29 Dec 2025
  [49:2:0.11] NASM-SR | First indigenous helicopter-launched anti-ship missile, IIR seeker
  [49:2:0.12] NASM-MR | Anti-ship missile; maiden flight 14 Jun 2026
[49:2:1] - Shaurya traps: range is **not 900 km** and not more than 1,600 km; speed is **not more than Mach 8**.
[49:2:2] - A **ballistic** missile is a trajectory class – the radar-killer is the **anti-radiation** missile.
[49:2:3] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.52, p.57, p.68-69, p.75; app notes 5:49 sub 3

## SUB 4 | Mission Shakti – India's ASAT Test
[49:4:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [49:4:0.0] Date | 27 March 2019
  [49:4:0.1] Conducted by | DRDO (under the BMD programme); target launched by ISRO – often asked as "joint DRDO–ISRO"
  [49:4:0.2] Launch site | Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island, Odisha
  [49:4:0.3] Interceptor | DRDO PDV Mk-II (direct-ascent kinetic kill)
  [49:4:0.4] Target | Live satellite Microsat-R (DRDO; launched by PSLV-C44, Jan 2019)
  [49:4:0.5] Orbit | Low Earth Orbit, ~283 km (282–300 km)
  [49:4:0.6] Rank | 4th ASAT nation, after USA, Russia, China
  [49:4:0.7] Debris | Low LEO chosen so debris decays quickly – there was debris
[49:4:1] - APPSC G1 2022: "destroyed a live satellite in LEO" and "fourth country" are **correct**; "done in the upper atmosphere to ensure no debris" is **wrong**; "hits targets at 50 km/s at 2,000 km" is **not true**.
[49:4:2] - **Mission Shakti (2019 ASAT) ≠ Operation Shakti (1998 Pokhran-II).**

## SUB 5 | Missile Classes, FOBS and Hypersonic Technology
[49:5:0] # Ballistic vs cruise
[49:5:1] TABLE head: Feature | Ballistic missile | Cruise missile
  [49:5:1.0] Power | Rocket-powered only in the boost phase | Air-breathing (jet), powered throughout
  [49:5:1.1] Path | High parabolic (free-fall) arc | Flies low, constant speed, aerodynamic lift
  [49:5:1.2] Examples | Agni, Prithvi, Pralay, Shaurya | BrahMos, Nirbhay
[49:5:2] - UPSC 2023: "ballistic = jet-propelled subsonic; cruise = rocket only at start" and "Agni-V cruise, BrahMos ICBM" are **both wrong** (neither).
[49:5:3] TABLE head: Class | Speed | Indian example
  [49:5:3.0] Subsonic | Below Mach 1 | Nirbhay
  [49:5:3.1] Supersonic | Mach 1–5 | BrahMos (Mach 2.8–3.0)
  [49:5:3.2] Hypersonic | Above Mach 5 | BrahMos-II (planned), LR-AShM, HSTDV
[49:5:4] # Terms
[49:5:5] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [49:5:5.0] FOBS (Fractional Orbital Bombardment System) | Warhead put into a (fractional) low Earth orbit, then de-orbits over the target; can come from any direction (e.g. over the South Pole); Soviet Cold War concept
  [49:5:5.1] HGV (Hypersonic Glide Vehicle) | Rocket-boosted, then glides at Mach 5+ and manoeuvres in the upper atmosphere; hard to intercept
  [49:5:5.2] MIRV | One missile, several warheads, different targets; first Indian test on Agni-V in Mission Divyastra (11 March 2024), not K-4
  [49:5:5.3] Scramjet | Supersonic combustion, no rotating parts; uses air, does not carry its oxidiser
  [49:5:5.4] SFDR (Solid Fuel Ducted Ramjet) | Uses atmospheric air; demonstrated from ITR Chandipur; for long-range air-to-air missiles
[49:5:6] # Indian hypersonic systems
[49:5:7] - **HSTDV:** indigenous **scramjet** demonstrator; flew above **Mach 6**; scramjet combustion and thermal protection above **2,000°C**; combustor run over 12 minutes (Jan 2026). Not a submarine-launched missile.
[49:5:8] - **16 November 2024:** first flight-trial of India's first long-range hypersonic missile.
[49:5:9] - **LR-AShM:** hypersonic **glide anti-ship** missile for Navy coastal batteries; **~1,500 km**; **peak Mach 10**, average Mach 5 via "skipping"; at the 77th Republic Day Parade; **AP coast ranges** used for validation rounds (Jan 2026).
[49:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.54, p.66-67, p.76; PMF S&T Part 7 p.6-7; app notes 5:49 sub 0, sub 4

=== NOTES 5:50 | Missile Defence and Strategic Forces – Bmd Programme, Nuclear Triad, Ssbn, No-first-use Policy
## SUB 0 | Nuclear Tests – Pokhran I and II, and Tests Abroad
[50:0:0] TABLE head: Test | Date | Code name | Details
  [50:0:0.0] Pokhran-I | 18 May 1974 | Smiling Buddha | "Peaceful nuclear explosion"; PM Indira Gandhi; team led by Raja Ramanna; fission device; India the 6th nation to test
  [50:0:0.1] Pokhran-II | 11 and 13 May 1998 | Operation Shakti (Shakti-98) | Five tests, fission + fusion; PM A.B. Vajpayee; led by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (DRDO) and R. Chidambaram (DAE); India declared a nuclear-weapon state
[50:0:1] - Site: **Pokhran Test Range, Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan** (Thar Desert) – not Sriharikota, Bangalore or Kanchipuram.
[50:0:2] - **11 May = National Technology Day** (marks the Pokhran-II tests).
[50:0:3] - **Operation Shakti** (1998 nuclear test) ≠ **Mission Shakti** (2019 ASAT test).
[50:0:4] TABLE head: Country | Test / site
  [50:0:4.0] Pakistan | Chagai-I, 28 May 1998 (Chagai Hills, Balochistan), soon after Pokhran-II
  [50:0:4.1] China | Lop Nor (Lop Nur) – dried salt lake in the Tarim Basin, Xinjiang; first test 1964
  [50:0:4.2] North Korea | Punggye-ri; claimed hydrogen bomb test 6 Jan 2016; fifth test Sept 2016
[50:0:5] - TSPSC 2023 statements: A (Technology Day = Pokhran) is right; Agni-III is not the "latest" missile of 2018 (that was **Agni-V**); **Mangalyaan** (5 Nov 2013) went to **Mars**, not the Moon; at Aryabhata's launch (1975) ISRO's chairman was **Satish Dhawan** – U.R. Rao led the project.
[50:0:6] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.59-61; PMF S&T Part 6 p.136-137; app notes 5:50 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Nuclear Submarines – INS Chakra, Arihant Class and K-series
[50:1:0] # Leased SSNs
[50:1:1] TABLE head: Boat | Type / origin
  [50:1:1.0] INS Chakra (I), 1988–1991 | Leased Soviet Charlie-class nuclear submarine – first nuclear submarine India operated
  [50:1:1.1] INS Chakra II | Leased Russian Akula-II nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN) (ex-K-152 Nerpa), 8,140 t; commissioned 4 April 2012; returned to Russia 2021
  [50:1:1.2] INS Chakra III | Akula-class SSN, lease awaited (mid/late 2020s)
  [50:1:1.3] INS Shalki, INS Shishumar | Diesel-electric, German Type 209
  [50:1:1.4] INS Sindhuvir, Sindhughosh | Diesel-electric, Russian Kilo class
[50:1:2] - Project 75 Alpha: six indigenous SSNs planned (none in service yet).
[50:1:3] # ATV project and Arihant class (SSBNs)
[50:1:4] - **ATV (Advanced Technology Vessel)** project: DRDO + private firms, with **Russian help** (reactor), built at Ship Building Centre, **Visakhapatnam**, to build **SSBNs**.
[50:1:5] TABLE head: Submarine | Commissioned | Features
  [50:1:5.0] INS Arihant (S2) | 2016 | First indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN), ~6,000 t, 4 VLS (12 K-15 or 4 K-4)
  [50:1:5.1] INS Arighaat (S3) | 29 Aug 2024 | Same size, 4 tubes; first K-4 launch from it, 27 Nov 2024 (Bay of Bengal)
  [50:1:5.2] INS Aridhaman (S4) | 3 Apr 2026, Visakhapatnam | ~7,000 t, 8 VLS (24 K-15 or 8 K-4/K-5)
[50:1:6] - AP angle: SSBNs based at **Visakhapatnam**; **Rambilli** naval base nearby.
[50:1:7] - Arihant is an SSBN, not an "attack" submarine; asked loosely as India's "first indigenous nuclear-powered (attack) submarine" – answer **Arihant**.
[50:1:8] # SLBMs (K-series, named after Dr Kalam)
[50:1:9] TABLE head: SLBM | Range
  [50:1:9.0] K-15 Sagarika | ~750 km; first underwater test-fire 26 Feb 2008 (proved underwater launch); deployed on INS Arihant
  [50:1:9.1] K-4 | ~3,500 km
  [50:1:9.2] K-5 / K-6 | Longer range, under development
[50:1:10] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.73, p.125-126; app notes 5:49 sub 7, 5:50 sub 4
## SUB 2 | Air and Missile Defence – BMD, S-400, Israeli Systems, Sudarshan Chakra
[50:2:0] # Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD)
[50:2:1] TABLE head: Interceptor | Phase and layer
  [50:2:1.0] PAD / Pradyumna (Prithvi Air Defence) | Phase I, exo-atmospheric, higher altitude (50–80 km)
  [50:2:1.1] AAD / Ashwin (Advanced Air Defence) | Phase I, endo-atmospheric, lower altitude (15–30 km)
  [50:2:1.2] AD-1, AD-2 | Phase II, against ~5,000 km-class threats (ICBMs, HGVs)
[50:2:2] - **Swordfish** Long-Range Tracking Radar (based on Israel's Green Pine): tracks missiles and space objects at **1,500+ km**.
[50:2:3] - Jun 2026: DRDO showed multi-layered BMD; same series saw maiden test of NASM-MR (14 Jun 2026).
[50:2:4] # Air-defence systems
[50:2:5] TABLE head: System | Origin / type | Notes
  [50:2:5.0] S-400 Triumf | Russia (Almaz-Antey) | Long-range surface-to-air (anti-aircraft / anti-missile) system, ~400 km; deal 2018; operators Russia, China (first foreign buyer), Turkey, India, Belarus; IAF calls it "Sudarshan Chakra"
  [50:2:5.1] Barak-1 | Israel | Ship-based point-defence SAM
  [50:2:5.2] MRSAM / Barak-8 | DRDO + Israel Aerospace Industries | Army version tested Apr 2025; DAC approved buy Jul 2026
  [50:2:5.3] Phalcon | Israel | Airborne radar on IL-76 = IAF AWACS
  [50:2:5.4] Iron Dome | Israel | Lower (short-range) layer of Israel's air defence; Rafael and IAI; mobile, all-weather
  [50:2:5.5] IADWS | Indigenous (DRDO) | QRSAM + VSHORADS + high-power laser DEW; maiden test Aug 2025
  [50:2:5.6] Akashteer | BEL with the Army | Automated air-defence control network
  [50:2:5.7] Akash Tarang | Indigenous | Anti-drone soft-kill EW system
[50:2:6] # Mission Sudarshan Chakra
[50:2:7] - Announced **Independence Day 2025**; networked national shield (air defence, cybersecurity, surveillance), **Vision 2035**.
[50:2:8] - UPSC 2026: aims at **air defence, BMD and aerial offensive capability**; **rapid, precise, powerful responses** (strategic autonomy); cover **all important public places** by a nationwide shield **by 2035** – **all three correct**.
[50:2:9] - Building blocks: Akash Tarang, MRSAM, VSHORADS; core = **Project Kusha** – DRDO **long-range** (not short-range) air defence, interceptors **M1/M2/M3 ≈ 150 / 250 / 350–400 km**.
[50:2:10] - "Sudarshan Chakra" = IAF's name for the S-400 **and** the Vision 2035 mission.
[50:2:11] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.101-103, p.109-111; PMF LENS Jan 2026 Part 2 p.11, p.20; app notes 5:49 sub 5, 5:50 sub 5-6
## SUB 3 | Nuclear Doctrine, No First Use and Command
[50:3:0] # Timeline
[50:3:1] - **Draft doctrine:** **National Security Advisory Board (NSAB)**, **August 1999**.
[50:3:2] - **No First Use** came from the **Vajpayee government after Pokhran-II** (not Indira Gandhi after Pokhran-I).
[50:3:3] - Formally adopted by the **CCS** on **4 January 2003**.
[50:3:4] # Key tenets
[50:3:5] - **Credible minimum deterrence** backed by an assured **second-strike capability** (survivable SSBNs) – not a bigger arsenal or first use.
[50:3:6] - **No First Use:** only in **retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or Indian forces**.
[50:3:7] - **Massive retaliation** causing unacceptable damage.
[50:3:8] - **No use against non-nuclear-weapon states**; nuclear option kept against a **major biological or chemical attack**.
[50:3:9] - **Unilateral moratorium** on nuclear tests (since 1998) – so a doctrine question "NFU, moratorium, minimum credible deterrence" = **all of the above**.
[50:3:10] - India kept the bomb option open and would **not open its strategic nuclear plants to inspection** (UPPCS 1994: A true, R "India will not produce any bomb" false).
[50:3:11] # Nuclear Command Authority
[50:3:12] TABLE head: Body | Chaired by | Role
  [50:3:12.0] Political Council | Prime Minister | Only body that can authorise use
  [50:3:12.1] Executive Council | National Security Advisor | Advises; carries out directions
  [50:3:12.2] Strategic Forces Command | Tri-service (set up 2003) | Manages and operates the nuclear arsenal
[50:3:13] - **CCS** oversees civilian political control; it does not manage the forces. Aug 2026: Agni user trials held "under the aegis of SFC".
[50:3:14] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.134-137; PMF S&T Part 7 p.1, p.8; app notes 5:50 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Non-proliferation Regimes – India's Status
[50:4:0] TABLE head: Regime | India's status
  [50:4:0.0] NPT (1968, in force 1970) | Not signed – discriminatory: only the five states that tested before 1967 are nuclear-weapon states
  [50:4:0.1] CTBT | Not signed (voluntary test moratorium since 1998; wants time-bound global disarmament)
  [50:4:0.2] NSG | Not a member (blocked by China); got 2008 waiver, follows guidelines
  [50:4:0.3] MTCR | Member 27 June 2016 (35th)
  [50:4:0.4] Hague Code of Conduct (HCoC) | Joined 1–2 June 2016 (against ballistic missile proliferation)
  [50:4:0.5] Wassenaar | Member Dec 2017
  [50:4:0.6] Australia Group | Member Jan 2018
[50:4:1] - India follows the guidelines through the **WMD Act** and the **SCOMET** list.
[50:4:2] - **FMCT:** supports a universal, verifiable treaty that does **not cap the existing stockpile**.
[50:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.8; WebSearch results: armscontrol.org (India joins HCoC, Jul 2016); app notes 5:50 sub 7
## SUB 5 | Nuclear Triad – Land, Air, Sea
[50:5:0] TABLE head: Leg | Platforms
  [50:5:0.0] Land | Prithvi and Agni series (canisterised, road- and rail-mobile); Agni-V (5,000+ km, solid, three-stage; first test 19 April 2012)
  [50:5:0.1] Air | Jaguar and Mirage 2000 (free-fall bombs)
  [50:5:0.2] Sea | K-15 / K-4 SLBMs from Arihant-class SSBNs; earlier Dhanush from ships (INS Subhadra, INS Rajput)
[50:5:1] - **SSBN = most survivable leg** – concealment gives sure **second-strike** capability, which backs NFU. Next step: **continuous at-sea deterrence**.
[50:5:2] - India has a fully operational triad, with **USA, Russia, China** (Apr 2026). US triad = **Minuteman III** ICBMs + bombers + Ohio/Columbia-class SSBNs.
[50:5:3] - Agni-4 user trial 6 Aug 2026: 4,000 km, two-stage solid, road-mobile. SIPRI (Jun 2026): **12** Indian warheads "operationally deployed", linked to **SSBN patrols and canisterised Agni**.
[50:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.57; PMF S&T Part 7 p.3-5; app notes 5:50 sub 3; Agni-V first-test date: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 6 | Nuclear Weapon Technology
[50:6:0] TABLE head: Fission (atomic) weapon | Fusion (thermonuclear / hydrogen) weapon
  [50:6:0.0] Heavy nucleus (U-235 / Pu-239) splits in a neutron chain reaction | Light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) fuse
  [50:6:0.1] Example: Pokhran-I | A fission "primary" triggers the fusion; tested in Pokhran-II
[50:6:1] - **Krytron** = high-speed gas-filled switch that fires a nuclear bomb's detonators (the "trigger"; not a MOSFET, solid-state relay or solenoid).
[50:6:2] TABLE head: Grade | U-235 share
  [50:6:2.0] Natural uranium | ~0.7%
  [50:6:2.1] Reactor-grade LEU | 3–5%
  [50:6:2.2] HEU | 20%+
  [50:6:2.3] Weapons-grade | ~90%
[50:6:3] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.28; app notes 5:50 sub 1

=== NOTES 5:51 | Defence Platforms and Systems – Tejas Lca, Arjun Mbt, Radar and Ew Systems, Naval Platforms
## SUB 0 | Tejas and Other Indigenous Aircraft
[51:0:0] # Tejas LCA
[51:0:1] - **What:** India's indigenous **Light Combat Aircraft (LCA)**, a single-engine, **compound delta-wing, tailless** multirole **supersonic** fighter (Mach 1.6+); smallest and lightest supersonic multirole fighter of its class; digital **fly-by-wire** – India's **first indigenous fly-by-wire aircraft**; over 40% composites.
[51:0:2] - **Who:** **designed by ADA** (Aeronautical Development Agency, DRDO framework), **built by HAL**; named by **Atal Bihari Vajpayee**; HAL handed the first two to the IAF in 2016 (No. 45 Sqn "Flying Daggers").
[51:0:3] - **Variants:** Mk-1 (4th gen) → **Mk-1A** (4.5 gen; **Uttam AESA**, EW suite, air-to-air refuelling) → **Mk-2** (**GE F414** engine, canards); naval LCA and trainer.
[51:0:4] - **Orders:** **25 Sep 2025** HAL contract for **97 Mk-1A** (68 fighters + 29 twin-seaters), Rs 62,370 crore, 64%+ indigenous; earlier order of **83**.
[51:0:5] - **"First indigenous fighter":** exam keys say **Tejas**; strictly Tejas is India's **second** indigenous jet fighter – the first was **HAL HF-24 Marut** (1961).
[51:0:6] - **Distractors:** Akash = missile, Vikrant = carrier, Arjun = tank, Garud/Surya Kiran (aerobatic team)/Sukhoi are not the LCA.
[51:0:7] # Other indigenous aircraft and helicopters
[51:0:8] TABLE head: Platform | Maker | Role
  [51:0:8.0] Dhruv | HAL | Advanced Light Helicopter, twin-engine; all three services + Coast Guard (not a ship, submarine or missile)
  [51:0:8.1] Rudra | HAL | Armed Dhruv (ALH-WSI)
  [51:0:8.2] LCH Prachand | HAL | Light combat helicopter for high altitude; inducted 3 Oct 2022
  [51:0:8.3] HTT-40 | HAL | Basic turboprop trainer
  [51:0:8.4] Hansa | NAL | Light trainer aircraft (Hansa-2 prototype)
  [51:0:8.5] Chetak, Cheetah | HAL (French licence) | Old light helicopters, being replaced by LUH
[51:0:9] - **ADE (Aeronautical Development Establishment, DRDO, Bengaluru):** **UAVs**, cruise missiles, flight simulators, mission computers. **ADRDE** = parachutes and heavy-drop systems; **ASL** = stealth structures, brake discs for Mirage-2000.
[51:0:10] - **C-295:** **medium tactical transport** by Airbus (Spain) with **Tata**; first Made-in-India C-295 rolls out in 2026.
[51:0:11] > Tejas is asked about ten times: "indigenous LCA", "built by HAL", "attained supersonic speed".
[51:0:12] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.85-86 (Tejas, HF-24 Marut), p.90-91 (HAL helicopters); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 2 p.50 (ADE, ADRDE, ASL); app notes 5:51 sub 1
## SUB 1 | Imported Aircraft – Fighters, Tankers and Transports
[51:1:0] TABLE head: Aircraft | Origin / maker | Role in India
  [51:1:0.0] Rafale | Dassault Aviation, France | 4.5-gen multirole; 36 for IAF (IGA Sep 2016; 36th delivered Dec 2022); 26 Rafale-M for Navy
  [51:1:0.1] Su-30MKI | Russia (Sukhoi); licence-built by HAL Nashik | Twin-engine heavy multirole; avionics from Russia, India, France and Israel
  [51:1:0.2] Mirage-2000, Jaguar, MiG-29 | France; UK-France; Russia | Fighters (they receive fuel, they do not refuel others)
  [51:1:0.3] Il-78 (MKI) | Ilyushin, Russia | Mid-air refuelling tanker ("MARS", No. 78 Sqn), inducted 2003
  [51:1:0.4] Il-76 | Ilyushin, Russia | Heavy transport (not combat); platform of the Phalcon AWACS
  [51:1:0.5] C-17 Globemaster III | Boeing, USA | Strategic heavy-lift transport
  [51:1:0.6] C-130J Super Hercules | Lockheed Martin, USA (~$1.1 bn, 2008) | Tactical transport, STOL
  [51:1:0.7] Dornier Do-228 | Germany; licence-built by HAL Kanpur | Maritime patrol / light transport (Navy, Coast Guard)
  [51:1:0.8] BAE Hawk Mk 132 | UK | Advanced Jet Trainer, inducted 2008
  [51:1:0.9] P-8I Poseidon | Boeing, USA | Long-range maritime patrol, ASW
[51:1:1] - **Phalcon:** Israeli **AWACS** radar on the Il-76 – the AWACS of the IAF (Phoenix, Eagle, Kite are distractors).
[51:1:2] - **Rafale deal (Sep 2016):** **36** jets (the older MMRCA plan was 126); Dassault's offset partner was **Reliance**, not HAL – so "126 jets" and "partnership with HAL" are the wrong statements.
[51:1:3] - **Su-30MKI bases:** Pune, Bareilly, Tezpur, Jodhpur and others – **not Jamnagar** (Jaguar/MiG-29 base).
[51:1:4] - **Sukhoi avionics:** the weapon and navigation suite of India's Sukhoi-30 jets came largely from **Israel** (also France, India).
[51:1:5] - **Fifth generation:** **none** of Rafale, MiG-29, Tejas Mk-1 is 5th-gen; India's 5th-gen project = **AMCA** (ADA).
[51:1:6] - **C-5M Super Galaxy:** large **US military transport aircraft** (Lockheed Martin). **F/A-18 Super Hornet:** US (Boeing) carrier fighter; the Hornet family flies with about 8 air forces.
[51:1:7] > Pairs PYQ (UPSC 2025, repeated): Do-228 = maritime patrol (correct), Il-76 = "supersonic combat" (wrong), C-17 = transport (correct) – **only two**.

  [51:2:6.5] Rajput class | Rajput, Rana, Ranjit (decommissioned May 2019) – first guided-missile destroyers | USSR
[51:2:7] - P15B = destroyers; **P17A = frigates** (not destroyers); P28 = corvettes; P75 = submarines.
[51:2:8] - **Decommissioned 12 Jan 2024 at Port Blair:** INS **Cheetah, Guldar, Kumbhir** (not "Magar", not Lakshadweep).
[51:2:9] - **INS Sarvekshak:** hydrographic survey ship – **first Indian warship fitted with solar panels**.
