## SUB 3 | Military Explosives and Their Chemistry
[51:3:0] TABLE head: Explosive | Other names | Note
  [51:3:0.0] TNT | Trinitrotoluene | C₇H₅N₃O₆; shells, bombs
  [51:3:0.1] TNG | Nitroglycerine, Nobel's oil, glyceryl (glycerol) trinitrate | C₃H₅(ONO₂)₃ – a nitrate ester of glycerol, oily liquid
  [51:3:0.2] TNP | Picric acid (trinitrophenol) | (O₂N)₃C₆H₂OH
  [51:3:0.3] RDX | Cyclonite, Hexogen, T-4 | Cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine, (O₂NNCH₂)₃; core of C-4
  [51:3:0.4] HMX | Octogen, High Melting Explosive | TBRL
  [51:3:0.5] CL-20 | HNIW | Most powerful non-nuclear explosive; HEMRL Pune
  [51:3:0.6] LLM-105 | – | Insensitive high explosive
[51:3:1] - **CL-20, HMX, LLM-105** = **explosives in military weapons** (UPSC 2025), not refrigerants or fuels.
[51:3:2] - **Not explosives:** **nitrochloroform** (chloropicrin, a toxic fumigant), phosphorus trichloride, mercuric oxide, graphite; DDT = insecticide, LSD = hallucinogen.
[51:3:3] TABLE head: Mixture | Composition
  [51:3:3.0] Dynamite | Nitroglycerine absorbed in kieselguhr / sawdust
  [51:3:3.1] Gun cotton | Cellulose nitrate – cotton or wood fibre treated with HNO₃ + H₂SO₄; also inks, leather finish, celluloid
  [51:3:3.2] Cordite | NG + nitrocellulose; a propellant
  [51:3:3.3] Blasting gelatin | NG 91–93% + nitrocellulose
  [51:3:3.4] Amatol | TNT + ammonium nitrate – no nitroglycerine
  [51:3:3.5] C-4 | RDX (not HMX) in a plastic matrix
[51:3:4] > 13 PYQs: other name of RDX (×2), nitroglycerine as explosive (×2), not-an-explosive (×2), Amatol, Nobel oil, dynamite, gun cotton.

## SUB 4 | Radar, Doppler Effect and Stealth
[51:4:0] # RADAR and the Doppler effect
[51:4:1] - **RADAR** (Radio Detection And Ranging): **detects and fixes the position** (range, direction, speed) of objects with radio waves.
[51:4:2] - **Doppler effect:** apparent change in frequency from relative motion – source **approaching → higher** pitch; **receding → lower** (a train moving away sounds lower).
[51:4:3] - **Uses:** **police speed radar guns**, **satellite tracking**, medical ultrasound (blood-flow velocity), **Doppler Weather Radar** (cyclones, **heavy rainfall and thunderstorms**), **expanding universe** (red shift = moving away, Hubble).
[51:4:4] TABLE head: Radar type | Principle / use
  [51:4:4.0] Doppler | Speed from frequency shift
  [51:4:4.1] SAR | Imaging at night and through clouds
  [51:4:4.2] AESA | T/R module on every element; electronic beam, no moving antenna; tracks multiple targets – Uttam, MF-STAR
  [51:4:4.3] VHF anti-stealth | Long waves pick up stealth aircraft
  [51:4:4.4] Over-the-horizon | HF waves bounced off the ionosphere
[51:4:5] - **Uttam AESA** (LRDE): solid-state active phased-array fire-control radar, wide-band RF front end, adaptable to fighters (Tejas Mk-1A); "**not capable of tracking multiple targets**" is the false statement.
[51:4:6] # Indigenous radars
[51:4:7] TABLE head: Radar | Role
  [51:4:7.0] Swathi | Weapon-locating radar (guns, mortars, rockets); BEL; exported to Armenia
  [51:4:7.1] Surya | VHF radar that tracks stealth aircraft
  [51:4:7.2] Swordfish | BMD long-range tracking (Green Pine based)
  [51:4:7.3] Arudhra | IAF medium-power 4D surveillance radar
  [51:4:7.4] Ashwini | Low-level lightweight AESA radar (cruise missiles, drones)
  [51:4:7.5] Rajendra | Fire-control radar of Akash
  [51:4:7.6] INDRA | Low-level surveillance (Indian Doppler Radar)
[51:4:8] # AWACS vs AEW&C
[51:4:9] TABLE head: AWACS | AEW&C (Netra)
  [51:4:9.0] Large aircraft (Il-76 Phalcon), long range, full battle management | Smaller jet (Embraer EMB-145), early warning + limited control; DRDO-CABS Bengaluru
[51:4:10] # Stealth
[51:4:11] - **Stealth technology:** **absorbing / deflecting radar waves** – very small **radar cross-section (RCS)** + **Radar Absorbing Material**; not "invisible to the eye".
[51:4:12] - Stealth objects **can** be detected at specific (low, VHF/UHF) frequencies; metamaterials are used to **reduce**, not increase, scattering (UPSC 2026: **1 and 2 only**).
[51:4:13] - **IIT Kharagpur:** low-cost **radar-absorbing metamaterial** to cloak soldiers and equipment from enemy radar.
[51:4:14] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 6 p.99-101 (radar types, AESA, Swathi, AWACS vs AEW&C); app notes 5:51 sub 7, 8, 10

## SUB 1 | iDEX, ADITI, TDF and Indigenisation Lists
[52:1:0] # iDEX ecosystem
[52:1:1] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [52:1:1.0] iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) | Launched by the PM, April 2018; ecosystem for innovation in defence and aerospace (not "industry and trade"), engaging MSMEs, start-ups, individual innovators, R&D institutes and academia
  [52:1:1.1] DIO (Defence Innovation Organisation) | Funds and manages iDEX; a not-for-profit (Sec. 8) company set up by HAL and BEL (not DRDO)
  [52:1:1.2] ADITI | Launched Mar 2024 under iDEX to fund innovation in critical and strategic (deep-tech) defence technology: AI, quantum, hypersonics, directed energy
  [52:1:1.3] DISC (Defence India Startup Challenge) | Problem statements set by the Services
[52:1:2] > APPSC FRO 2022 "NOT correct": iDEX for "industry and trade" – it is for **defence**.
[52:1:3] # TDF, lists and portal
[52:1:4] - **TDF (Technology Development Fund):** MoD programme **executed by DRDO**; grants **up to Rs 50 crore per project**, esp. MSMEs and start-ups.
[52:1:5] - TDF project: **green propulsion** thruster by Bengaluru start-up **Bellatrix Aerospace**, proved in orbit on **PSLV-C58** (Feb 2024).
[52:1:6] - **Five Positive Indigenisation Lists:** bar imports of listed items after set dates. **SRIJAN:** indigenisation portal.
[52:1:7] - **VIMARSH 2026** (Sep): DRDO–industry meet; funding, incubation, test facilities, source-code sharing for **MSMEs and start-ups**.
[52:1:8] ~~ Sources: Daily CA 20 Oct 2026 p.1 (iDEX 2018); PMF LENS Mar 2026 Part 2 p.13 (ADITI under iDEX); app notes 5:52 sub 2

=== NOTES 5:53 | India's Energy Needs and Deficit – Primary Energy Demand, Per-capita Consumption, Peak Deficit
## SUB 0 | Energy Units and Basic Terms
[53:0:0] # Units – the most-asked angle
[53:0:1] TABLE head: Quantity | Unit | Note
  [53:0:1.0] Energy (work) | joule (J) – SI unit | kWh is a commercial unit of energy, not power
  [53:0:1.1] Power | watt (W) | rate of using energy; kilowatt, HP are power units
  [53:0:1.2] 1 unit of electricity | 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J | = 1,000 W × 3,600 s
  [53:0:1.3] Current / voltage / charge | ampere / volt / coulomb | distractors for "unit of power"
[53:0:2] - **Formula:** units (kWh) = watts × hours ÷ 1,000.
[53:0:3]   - 100 W × 4 h = 400 Wh = **0.4 unit**; 5 bulbs × 100 W × 20 h = **10 units**; 100 W × 10 h = 1 unit; 60 W × 5 h × 30 days = 9 units.
[53:0:4] - **Energy crisis:** the danger that fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum run out.
[53:0:5] # Grid and energy terms
[53:0:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [53:0:6.0] Energy intensity | Energy used per unit of GDP; a falling value = growth decoupling from energy use
  [53:0:6.1] Peak demand | Highest power drawn in a 15-minute interval
  [53:0:6.2] Energy shortage / peak shortage | Unmet energy in MU / unmet peak in MW
  [53:0:6.3] Energy security | Four A's: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability (not accumulation)
  [53:0:6.4] Primary vs final energy | Coal, petroleum and natural gas are primary sources that are also used directly as final energy
[53:0:7] > Units PYQs (UPPCS 2017, UP Lower 2009, NDA 2018, SSC 2017, BPSC): always convert W × h → kWh; "kWh is a unit of energy".
[53:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Physics p.52; app notes 5:53 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Demand, Mix, Per-capita Use and HDI
[53:1:0] # Demand and mix
[53:1:1] - India = **third-largest energy consumer** and **second-largest coal consumer**; demand to **triple by 2047**.
[53:1:2] - **Coal/thermal** gives the **largest share of power generation**: ~**55% of the energy mix**, **74%+ of generation** (APPSC EO: "maximum share" = **thermal power**).
[53:1:3] - After fossil fuels, the second source of supply is **solar** (UPPSC 2021).
[53:1:4] - **Non-fossil capacity:** 32% (2014) → **51% (2025)**; the 50% target was crossed five years early.
[53:1:5] - **Sustainable choice:** of coal, oil/gas, hydro and atomic energy, **hydroelectricity** is the renewable option that does not use up its resource (UPPCS 2012).
[53:1:6] # Per-capita consumption and HDI
[53:1:7] - **Per-capita electricity:** **957 kWh (FY14) → 1,460 kWh (FY25)**; about **one-fifth of China's**, one-ninth of the USA's – lower than China's.
[53:1:8] - **Per-capita energy:** about **one-third of the world average**; low, with a large **urban-rural** gap.
[53:1:9] - **HDI link** (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2017): a **certain minimum per-capita energy consumption is needed for a minimally acceptable level of well-being** – hence the strong correlation.
[53:1:10] # Sectors and drivers
[53:1:11] - **Industry** uses ~**50%** of electricity and stays the largest consumer by 2040; **cooking** energy demand falls.
[53:1:12] - Household electrification ~**99%**; **Saubhagya** connected ~**26 million** households.
[53:1:13] - Drivers of peak: **EVs, farm pumps, appliances, cooling, data centres, telecom**; peak **183 GW (Dec 2020) → 250+ GW (Apr 2026)**, ~37% rise.
[53:1:14] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:53 sub 2-3; PMF Human & Economic Geography Part 3 p.18
## SUB 2 | Peak Demand and Deficit
[53:2:0] - **Shortage trend:** **10–15%** earlier → **4.2% (FY14)** → **0.03% (2025)** → **zero by Nov 2025** (first zero-shortage month).
[53:2:1] - **Record peak:** **270.8 GW (May 2026)**, about **90 GW** above 2019.
[53:2:2] - **25 Apr 2026:** no shortage in solar hours; about **2% deficit in non-solar hours** → the **evening peak (6–11 p.m.)** drives the **storage** push.
[53:2:3] - **Delhi's response** to the evening peak: **Time-of-Day tariffs and smart meters**.
[53:2:4] - **Regional imbalances:** poor **storage** and slow **transmission** strand renewable power; heatwaves stress grids.
[53:2:5] - **AT&C losses:** **22.62% (FY14) → 15.04% (FY25)**.
[53:2:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:53 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Reports and Publishers
[53:3:0] TABLE head: Report | Publisher | Key fact
  [53:3:0.0] Energy Statistics (annual) | CSO, now NSO (MoSPI) | Coal, lignite, crude, gas incl. imports/exports, electricity, energy balance
  [53:3:0.1] India Energy Security Scenarios (IESS) 2047 | NITI Aayog | Energy demand 2.7–3.2 times (2012–2040); electricity 4.5-fold
  [53:3:0.2] Electric Power Survey; National Generation Adequacy Plan | CEA | NGAP (May 2026): peak 459 GW by 2035-36; 1,121 GW, 70% non-fossil
  [53:3:0.3] World Energy Outlook; India Energy Outlook | IEA | WEO 2022: coal generation and oil imports peak around 2030
  [53:3:0.4] India Cooling Action Plan (2019) | MoEFCC | By 2037-38: cooling demand −20–25%, refrigerant demand −25–30%
[53:3:1] - **Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero (NITI Aayog, 2026):** renewables about **80% of power generation by 2070**; coal's share falls sharply.
[53:3:2] > Trap: Energy Statistics is not CEA's; IESS is not the IEA's; India Energy Outlook is not NITI's.
[53:3:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:53 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Fuel Gap, NDC Targets and Plans
[53:4:0] # Fuel gap
[53:4:1] TABLE head: Fuel | Position
  [53:4:1.0] Crude oil | ~88% imported
  [53:4:1.1] Natural gas / LNG | ~50% imported; Strait of Hormuz a risk to LPG (2026 gas crisis)
  [53:4:1.2] Share of world reserves | oil 0.4%, gas 0.6%, coal 7% (not oil 7%)
[53:4:2] # NDC targets (versus 2005)
[53:4:3] TABLE head: NDC | Emission-intensity cut | Non-fossil capacity
  [53:4:3.0] First NDC (2015) | 33–35% by 2030 | ~40%
  [53:4:3.1] Updated NDC (Aug 2022) | 45% by 2030 | 50%
  [53:4:3.2] New NDC 2031–35 | 47% by 2035 | 60% (not 50%)
[53:4:4] - Emission intensity already **36% below 2005**.
[53:4:5] - **BEE** and **NMEEE** (a mission of the **NAPCC**) work under the **Energy Conservation Act 2001** through **ESCOs** (Energy Service Companies).
[53:4:6] - **Draft National Electricity Policy 2026** – **Ministry of Power**; replaces the **2005** policy; **100 GW pumped storage by 2047**.
[53:4:7] - **COP31 "35 by 35":** electricity = **35%** of final energy by 2035. **Nuclear:** 24×7 baseload, cuts fossil imports.
[53:4:8] # Andhra Pradesh
[53:4:9] - CEA **Resource Adequacy Plan** (2025-26 to 2035-36): peak **30,927 MW** by 2035-36; ~**5,588 MW** new thermal; **APERC** cleared the first **1,600 MW**.
[53:4:10] - Sep 2026 roadmap: **1,500 MW / 6,000 MWh BESS**; central VGF project with **NHPC 500 MW / 1,000 MWh**; **APGENCO** allowed to import coal.
[53:4:11] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:53 sub 5

=== NOTES 5:54 | India's Energy Resources and Import Dependence – Crude Oil, Coal, Gas Import Share; Energy Security
## SUB 0 | Import Dependence, Suppliers and Oil Challenges
[54:0:0] # Import share by fuel
[54:0:1] TABLE head: Fuel | Import share (newest)
  [54:0:1.0] Crude oil | 88.5% (PPAC provisional, July 2026)
  [54:0:1.1] Natural gas / LNG | ~47–51% (2026); Qatar = key LNG supplier
  [54:0:1.2] Coal | ~26%, although India is the second-largest producer
  [54:0:1.3] Lithium | ~90%
  [54:0:1.4] LPG | Depends mainly on OMC stocks; semi-strategic underground storage only ~0.14 MT
[54:0:2] - India = **3rd-largest energy consumer** and **3rd-largest oil consumer** (2026).
[54:0:3] # Crude suppliers (2025)
[54:0:4] TABLE head: Supplier | Share
  [54:0:4.0] Russia (largest in recent years) | ~35%
  [54:0:4.1] Iraq | ~20%
  [54:0:4.2] Saudi Arabia | ~15%
  [54:0:4.3] USA | ~8%
[54:0:5] - Others: UAE; West Asia + Africa ~65% of supply (Dec 2025).
[54:0:6] - **OPEC** produces ~**40%** of global oil; its share of India's crude imports fell **below 50%** (Aug 2025).
[54:0:7] - **Saudi Arabia:** world's **number one oil exporter** and the usual exam answer for "largest reserves" (strictly, Venezuela has the largest proved reserves; Saudi Arabia second).
[54:0:8] # Core challenge (APPSC G2 2025)
[54:0:9] - Managing oil consumption = **supply-chain disruptions and fluctuating global oil prices** (not low demand, steady prices or abundant reserves).
[54:0:10] TABLE head: Angle | Issue
  [54:0:10.0] Price | Global volatility feeds domestic inflation
  [54:0:10.1] External | Crude imports = biggest driver of trade deficit / CAD
  [54:0:10.2] Route | Chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz
[54:0:11] # The 2026 Hormuz shock
[54:0:12] - **Strait of Hormuz** (between **Iran and Oman**) effectively closed by Iran, early March 2026; it carries ~15 million bbl/day (~**34%**, about **one-third**, of world crude trade) and a fifth of global LNG.
[54:0:13] - India's crude basket **$82.04/bbl** (July 2026) vs $70.95 a year earlier; LPG output raised **35 → 54 TMT/day** under the LPG control order.
[54:0:14] - Response: proposed **41 MT strategic fuel system** (Aug 2026); more domestic coal and gas; LNG/LPG from the US, Oman, Nigeria, Angola.
[54:0:15] # Import bill
[54:0:16] - Crude import bill **FY 2024-25: $137.0 billion**; July 2026: $13.7 billion, up 41% (PPAC).
[54:0:17] - Higher oil prices → wider **trade deficit** and higher **inflation**.
[54:0:18] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:54 sub 2-4
## SUB 1 | Import-substitution Fuels – Methanol, Ethanol, CBG
[54:1:0] # Methanol Economy (NITI Aayog)
[54:1:1] - Driven by **NITI Aayog**. Aims (**APPSC G1: all three correct**): (i) cut the **oil import bill**, (ii) cut **GHG emissions**, (iii) convert **coal reserves and municipal solid waste** into methanol. Increasing LPG imports is not an aim.
[54:1:2] TABLE head: Term | Meaning / use
  [54:1:2.0] Methanol | Low-carbon, hydrogen-carrier fuel from biomass, high-ash coal, agri-residue, CO₂, natural gas; partly replaces LPG and kerosene in cooking
  [54:1:2.1] DME (Di-Methyl Ether) | Two methanol molecules minus one water molecule; replaces propane in LPG and diesel in slow-RPM engines
  [54:1:2.2] M15 | 15% methanol in petrol: at least 15% cut in petrol/crude imports
  [54:1:2.3] 20% DME in LPG | Saves about ₹6,000 crore a year
[54:1:3] # Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP)
[54:1:4] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [54:1:4.0] January 2003 | 5% EBP in 9 sugarcane States + 4 UTs (incl. AP)
  [54:1:4.1] ESY 2025-26 | E20 achieved (target advanced from 2030)
  [54:1:4.2] 1 Apr 2026 | E20 with minimum 95 RON mandated
[54:1:5] # Compressed Biogas Obligation (CBO) in City Gas Distribution
[54:1:6] - Share of CNG/PNG: **1% / 3% / 4%** (FY 2025-26 to 2027-28), **5% from 2028-29**; aim: replace **LNG** imports.
[54:1:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:54 sub 7
## SUB 2 | Hydrocarbon Vision 2025 and Upstream Policy
[54:2:0] - **Hydrocarbon Vision 2025:** long-term hydrocarbon plan **adopted in 2000**; exam keys link it with **storage of petroleum products** (UPPCS 2000) – it calls for adequate strategic storage of crude and products, within a wider aim of energy security.
[54:2:1]   - Focus: **self-reliance** through **indigenous production** and **equity oil abroad**; appraisal of all sedimentary basins; **free market and competition** – it does **not** ban private participation.
[54:2:2] - **HELP:** a **single licence for all hydrocarbons**; **OALP** = **Open Acreage Licensing Policy** – companies choose and bid for blocks.
[54:2:3] - **ONGC Videsh (OVL):** overseas arm of ONGC; acquires **equity oil and gas abroad** (not LPG retail).
[54:2:4] - **One Nation One Gas Grid**; refiners + Shipping Corporation of India JV (2026).
[54:2:5] - **TAPI** (Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India) stalled; **IPI** (Iran–Pakistan–India) dropped by India 2007-08.
[54:2:6] ~~ Sources: web search summaries of Hydrocarbon Vision 2025; app notes 5:54 sub 6
## SUB 3 | Energy Resources and Domestic Reserves
[54:3:0] # Classification
[54:3:1] TABLE head: Basis | Types
  [54:3:1.0] Renewal | Renewable (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, tidal, geothermal) vs non-renewable / fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and nuclear fuels
  [54:3:1.1] Use history | Conventional (fossil fuels, hydro, biomass) vs non-conventional (solar, tidal, geothermal, nuclear, ocean thermal)
  [54:3:1.2] Not from the Sun | Geothermal (Earth's heat), tidal, nuclear
[54:3:2] - "Conventional" ≠ non-renewable: hydro and biomass are **both conventional and renewable**. Alcohol, ether and water gas are not fossil fuels; **natural gas** is.
[54:3:3] # Reserves – number game
[54:3:4] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [54:3:4.0] Share of world | ~17% of population vs 0.4% oil, 0.6% gas, 7% coal reserves
  [54:3:4.1] Coal | World's fifth-largest reserves; second-largest producer
  [54:3:4.2] Sedimentary basins | 26, only 7 producing
  [54:3:4.3] Thorium (monazite) | 11.93 Mt monazite; Andhra Pradesh largest (3.72 Mt), then Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Kerala, West Bengal
  [54:3:4.4] Uranium | Low-grade; large deposit at Tummalapalle (YSR Kadapa, AP)
[54:3:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:54 sub 0-1; PMF Human & Economic Geography Part 3 p.18
## SUB 4 | Strategic Petroleum Reserves
[54:4:0] TABLE head: Phase I site | State | Capacity
  [54:4:0.0] Visakhapatnam | Andhra Pradesh | 1.33 MMT
  [54:4:0.1] Mangaluru | Karnataka | 1.5 MMT
  [54:4:0.2] Padur (largest) | Karnataka | 2.5 MMT
[54:4:1] - Phase I total **5.33 MMT** ≈ **9.5 days** of crude needs when full; actual stock ~3.37 MT → ~5 days. **IEA norm = 90 days** (not 60).
[54:4:2] - **Phase II:** **Chandikhol (Odisha)**, **Padur** (in both phases); proposed **Bikaner (Rajasthan)**, Rajkot (Gujarat).
[54:4:3] - Proposed plan (Aug 2026): **41 MT = 28 MT crude + 9 MT LNG + 4 MT LPG**; no underground gas storage yet.

## SUB 5 | Partnerships, Demand-side Measures and Critical Minerals
[54:5:0] # Partnerships
[54:5:1] - **IEA:** India's **association** status activated in **March 2017** (APPSC: "association status announced in 2017" = IEA, not OECD/IAEA/MTCR); sought full membership (Oct 2023).
[54:5:2] - **Global Biofuels Alliance:** launched 9 Sep 2023 at the **G20 New Delhi** summit; core founders **India, USA, Brazil**; secretariat **New Delhi**.
[54:5:3] - **International Energy Forum:** secretariat **Riyadh**; India hosted the **16th IEF Ministerial** in **New Delhi** (April 2018).
[54:5:4] # Demand side
[54:5:5] - **PM E-DRIVE:** from **1 Oct 2024**, outlay **₹10,900 crore**, **replaced FAME-II**; extended to March 2028. NITI's **India Electric Mobility Index** (Aug 2025).

=== NOTES 5:57 | Coal Sector – Reserves, Production, Washing, Commercial Mining, Gasification
## SUB 0 | Coal Types, Carbon Content and Fuel Quality
[57:0:0] TABLE head: Type | Carbon (NextGen/PMF) | Notes
  [57:0:0.0] Anthracite | 80–95% | Highest carbon, best quality; hardest, little smoke, highest calorific value; J&K (Kalakot), small quantity
  [57:0:0.1] Bituminous | 40–80% | Most widely used; includes the coking grade; Jharkhand, Odisha, WB, Chhattisgarh, MP
  [57:0:0.2] Sub-bituminous | – | Between bituminous and lignite; used in power plants
  [57:0:0.3] Lignite (brown coal) | 40–55% | High moisture; Neyveli (TN), Palana (Rajasthan), Lakhimpur (Assam)
  [57:0:0.4] Peat | below 40% | First stage of wood turning into coal
[57:0:1] - Order of carbon: **anthracite > bituminous > sub-bituminous > lignite > peat**.
[57:0:2] - International (ASTM-style) tables give lignite **25–35%**, sub-bituminous 35–45%, bituminous 45–86%, anthracite 86–97% – use these when the options are on that scale.
[57:0:3] - **Calorific value** depends mainly on the **carbon content** (moisture and ash lower it).
[57:0:4] - A good fuel has a **high** calorific value, low moisture, harmless combustion products and controllable burning – "low calorific value" is not a property of a good fuel.
[57:0:5] - **Coal is a natural (fossil) fuel**; petrol and diesel are refined, charcoal is made from wood. **Lignite** contains carbon (tin, silver, iron are metals).
[57:0:6] # Gondwana vs Tertiary coal
[57:0:7] - **Gondwana** (~250 million years): **98% of reserves**, 99% of production; coking and bituminous coal; Damodar, Mahanadi, Son, Godavari, Wardha valleys – hence Gondwana rocks are India's most important rock system.
[57:0:8] - **Damuda series** (Lower Gondwana): India's **metallurgical (coking) coal** and the most productive fields.
[57:0:9] - **Tertiary** (15–60 million years): younger, **low carbon, high moisture and sulphur**; lignite (chief producer **Tamil Nadu**); **North-East India and J&K** (extra-peninsular), about 2% – not "mainly Peninsular". Bituminous coal is a Gondwana coal.
[57:0:10] - Some coal lies buried under the **Ganga alluvium and the Deccan Trap**.
[57:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Geography Part 7.2 p.4; PMF Human & Economic Geography Part 3 p.13-14, p.19-21; app notes 5:57 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Coalfields, Reserves and Producing States
[57:1:0] TABLE head: Coalfield | State
  [57:1:0.0] Jharia (largest coking-coal field, Damodar Valley), Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura | Jharkhand
  [57:1:0.1] Raniganj (first coal mine, 1774) | West Bengal
  [57:1:0.2] Talcher (Brahmani valley), Deogarh (IB Valley) | Odisha
  [57:1:0.3] Korba (Hasdeo valley), Raigarh | Chhattisgarh
  [57:1:0.4] Singrauli, Umaria | Madhya Pradesh
  [57:1:0.5] Singareni | Telangana
  [57:1:0.6] Makum | Assam
  [57:1:0.7] Mawlong (Tertiary) | Meghalaya
  [57:1:0.8] Barmer (lignite) | Rajasthan
[57:1:1] - **Mosabani** (Jharkhand) is a **copper** mine, not a coalfield.
[57:1:2] - **Damodar Valley = "Ruhr of India"**: about **one-fourth** of India's coal reserves; coal-based iron and steel belt.
[57:1:3] - **Reserves:** India's coal resources **400.715 bn t (1.4.2025)**; earlier GSI **389.421 bn t (1.4.2024)**. Largest total resources: **Odisha (100,976 MT)**, then Jharkhand (93,254 MT), Chhattisgarh; **Jharkhand** still leads in **proved** reserves.
[57:1:4] - **World rank:** India has the **fifth-largest** coal reserves but is the **second-largest producer**.
[57:1:5] - **Largest producing State:** **Odisha** (239.40 MT, ~24% in 2023-24), then Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand (older books: Jharkhand).
[57:1:6] - **Lignite:** **47.37 bn t (1.4.2025)**; **Tamil Nadu** (Neyveli) leads, then Rajasthan, Gujarat; TN is also the chief lignite producer.
[57:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Indian Geography p.24-28; NextGen Indian Geography Part 7.2 p.4; PMF Human & Economic Geography Part 3 p.13, p.18-22; Ministry of Coal Annual Report 2025-26 ch.2 p.28-29
## SUB 2 | Indian Coal Quality, Imports, Washing and Health
[57:2:0] - **Indian coal:** **high ash (35–45%)**, **low calorific value**, **low sulphur (~0.5%)** and a **high ash-fusion temperature (~1500°C)** (UPSC 2013: "1 and 2 only").
[57:2:1] - **Pollution (UPSC 2020, all correct):** coal ash contains **arsenic, lead and mercury**; coal plants emit **SO₂ and NOx**; Indian coal has high ash.
[57:2:2] - **Imports:** **coking coal** mainly from **Australia** (the steel industry imports it, UPSC 2015); non-coking from **Indonesia, South Africa**.
[57:2:3] - **Coal washing (APPSC G1 2024 A–R):** washing raises generation efficiency and cuts costs, but washed-coal use stays limited because it raises the cost of power and hurts plants in **merit-order** dispatch – **A and R true, R explains A**.
[57:2:4] - **Problems:** poor quality, movement bottlenecks, **low washery use**, rising coking-coal imports – not "excess high-quality coking coal".
[57:2:5] - **Pneumoconiosis** (black lung): dust disease of **coal-mine** workers.
[57:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography Part 3 p.15, p.18, p.24; app notes 5:57 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Production and Coal Companies
[57:3:0] - **2024-25: about 1,047.5 MT** (1,047.52 MT, Ministry of Coal) – first year above **1 billion tonnes**; 2025-26 target 1,157 MT.
[57:3:1] - Coal meets about **55%** of commercial energy needs and about 70% of power generation.
[57:3:2] - **Coal India Ltd** (1975, HQ **Kolkata**, not Ranchi): **Maharatna**, world's **largest coal producer**; **7** subsidiaries; **CMPDI** = planning arm.
[57:3:3] - **SCCL:** **51% Telangana, 49% Government of India** (AP Reorganisation Act 2014) – not a CIL subsidiary.
[57:3:4] ~~ Sources: Ministry of Coal Annual Report 2025-26 ch.2 p.29; app notes 5:57 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Commercial Mining and Laws
[57:4:0] - Supreme Court (2014) cancelled **204** coal blocks → **Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015** for their auction.
[57:4:1] - **MMDR** amendment March 2021: **sale of coal from captive mines**; another amendment declared **coking coal a Critical and Strategic Mineral**.
[57:4:2] - **SHAKTI (2017):** replaced the **New Coal Distribution Policy 2007**; linkages by **auction or tariff-based bidding**.
[57:4:3] - **Revenue-sharing commercial auctions** began **2020**; 13th round opened **August 2025**; 14th-round agreements first with **underground coal gasification** clauses.
[57:4:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:57 sub 3
## SUB 5 | Gasification, CBM and UCG
[57:5:0] - **Gasification:** coal + oxygen + steam → **syngas (CO + H₂ + CH₄ + CO₂)**; runs **IGCC** plants.
[57:5:1] - Products: SNG, methanol, **ethanol**, **urea**/ammonia, hydrogen, DME – **not nitroglycerine** (UPSC 2025).
[57:5:2] - **CBM** = "**sweet gas**"; free gas in joints, **adsorbed** in micropores.
[57:5:3] - **UCG:** in-situ; the MoEFCC panel **refused to waive the 300 m** minimum depth.
[57:5:4] - **National Coal Gasification Mission:** **100 MT by 2030**.
[57:5:5] - **Surface Coal/Lignite Gasification scheme** (13 May 2026): **₹37,500 crore**; up to **20%** of plant cost, cap ₹5,000 crore; no bidders yet – bid windows kept open, not withdrawn.
[57:5:6] - Commercial blocks: **50% revenue-share rebate** if at least **10%** output is gasified.
[57:5:7] - **JSPL Angul** (Odisha): only commercial-scale plant; **Talcher**: first gasification fertiliser plant.
[57:5:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:57 sub 5-6

=== NOTES 5:58 | Oil and Natural Gas – Basins, Refineries, Spr, Gas Grid, City Gas Distribution
## SUB 0 | Fuel Gases – LPG, Natural Gas, CNG, LNG and Their Chemistry
[58:0:0] # What each gas is made of
[58:0:1] TABLE head: Fuel | Main constituents | Key facts
  [58:0:1.0] Natural gas | Mostly methane (CH₄), with some ethane, propane, CO₂, N₂ | Cleanest fossil fuel; burnt directly or piped
  [58:0:1.1] CNG – Compressed Natural Gas | Methane (80–90%) | Natural gas compressed to 200–250 kg/cm²; vehicles
  [58:0:1.2] PNG – Piped Natural Gas | 85–95% methane | Supplied to homes through city gas networks
  [58:0:1.3] LNG – Liquefied Natural Gas | Methane | Cooled to about −160°C; volume shrinks about 600 times; carried in special cryogenic tankers; lighter than air
  [58:0:1.4] LPG – Liquefied Petroleum Gas | Propane + butane (roughly 65% butane, 35% propane; a little ethane) | Refinery / gas by-product; liquefied under pressure; heavier than air
[58:0:2] - **LPG is NOT mainly methane** (IAS 2005: A false, R true). When only one gas is asked, **butane** is the chief constituent; the 3-gas option is **ethane, propane and butane**.
[58:0:3] - **LPG is odourless** in its natural state; **ethyl mercaptan (ethanethiol)** is added so that a **leak can be smelt** (the "rotten" stench).
[58:0:4] - **Butane (C₄H₁₀)** is the gas in **cigarette lighters**; it is a **Natural Gas Liquid (NGL)**.
[58:0:5] - **Propane** (an LPG gas) is a clean-burning fuel; coke, petrol and wax are not "clean energy" (NDA 2019).
[58:0:6] - **Methane** is a **greenhouse gas** (ethane, propane, butane are not counted as GHGs); in the air it oxidises to CO₂ in about a decade.
[58:0:7] - **Methane + air** (firedamp, 5–15% methane) causes most **explosions in coal mines**.
[58:0:8] # Other fuel facts asked
[58:0:9] TABLE head: Fuel / term | Fact
  [58:0:9.0] Water gas | CO + H₂ (producer gas = CO + H₂ + N₂)
  [58:0:9.1] Acetylene (ethyne) | Gas welding (oxy-acetylene flame)
  [58:0:9.2] Kerosene | Calorific value about the same as petrol (~45,000 kJ/kg); LPG ~55,000, methane/CNG ~50,000
  [58:0:9.3] Hydrocarbon order by molecular weight | Methane (16) < ethane (30) < propane (44) < butane (58)
  [58:0:9.4] Petroleum | A mixture of many hydrocarbons of different densities; its grade depends on their relative proportion (NDA 2016: both true, II does not explain I)
[58:0:10] - **LNG statements (IAS 2005):** only "LNG is liquefied under extreme cold for storage and transport" is right; India's first LNG terminal is **Dahej** (Gujarat, Petronet LNG, 2004), not Hassan; NGLs (ethane, propane, butane, natural gasoline) are separated from **natural gas**, not from LPG.
[58:0:11] > Exam angle: "main constituent of LPG" is asked a dozen times – butane (with propane); methane is natural gas / CNG.
[58:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Chemistry p.3, 27, 33-34; PMF Human & Economic Geography EG-MR p.45 (LNG, CNG, PNG); PMF Environment Part 7 p.70 (LPG, ethyl mercaptan); app notes 5:58 sub 3
## SUB 1 | Petroleum Geology, Basins and Oil Fields
[58:1:0] # Geology
[58:1:1] - **Coal, petroleum, natural gas** = conventional, **non-renewable** fossil fuels.
[58:1:2] - Oil is found in **Tertiary** sedimentary rocks; petroleum = 90–95% hydrocarbons.
[58:1:3] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [58:1:3.0] Source rock | Organic-rich shale where oil forms
  [58:1:3.1] Reservoir rock | Porous, permeable sandstone or fissured limestone
  [58:1:3.2] Cap rock | Impervious bed that seals the trap
  [58:1:3.3] Traps | Anticlines, faults, salt domes; commercial oil at the crest of an anticline
[58:1:4] - Layers by density from the top: **gas, oil, water**.
[58:1:5] - **Wet gas** = associated with oil; **dry gas** = non-associated; **sour gas** = rich in **H₂S**.
[58:1:6] - Conventional gas: permeable sandstone. Unconventional: impermeable sandstone, shale, coal seams – costly technology.
[58:1:7] # Basins and fields
[58:1:8] TABLE head: Basin | State | Key fields
  [58:1:8.0] Krishna-Godavari (KG) | Andhra Pradesh | Ravva, KG-D6; a peri-cratonic passive-margin basin on the east coast
  [58:1:8.1] Cambay | Gujarat (onshore) | Ankleshwar, Kalol, Khambhat
  [58:1:8.2] Mumbai Offshore | Maharashtra coast | Bombay High (1974), Bassein (South Basin) gas
  [58:1:8.3] Assam Shelf / Assam-Arakan | Assam | Digboi (1889, oldest), Naharkatiya, Moran
  [58:1:8.4] Barmer-Sanchore (Rajasthan) | Rajasthan | Mangala, Bhagyam, Aishwarya – Rajasthan is the largest onshore oil producer
  [58:1:8.5] Tripura fold belt | Tripura | Trishna gas project
  [58:1:8.6] Cauvery | Tamil Nadu | Narimanam, Kovilappal
[58:1:9] - **Category I** basins (commercial production): Cambay, Mumbai Offshore, KG, Cauvery, Assam Shelf, Assam-Arakan, Rajasthan (not Andaman).
[58:1:10] - **26 May 2026:** Oil India struck gas in the **Sanu Formation, Dandewala, Jaisalmer**.
[58:1:11] - **ONGC** headquarters: **Dehradun** (Uttarakhand).
[58:1:12] > Exam angle: AP's petroleum region = **KG basin** (not Araku, Rayalaseema or Nallamala); its gas basin is Krishna–Godavari, not Krishna–Penna.
[58:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography EG-MR p.38-39; NextGen Rocket Sheets Indian Geography p.28; app notes 5:58 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Shale Gas, Coal Bed Methane and Gas Hydrates
[58:2:0] TABLE head: Resource | Where held | India
  [58:2:0.0] Shale gas / oil | Fine-grained, low-permeability shale below 1,500 m; horizontal drilling + hydraulic fracturing (fracking) | Cambay basin largest; also KG, Cauvery, Gondwana (Damodar), Assam-Arakan, Indo-Gangetic; ONGC estimate 187.5 TCF in five basins
  [58:2:0.1] Coal bed methane (CBM) | Adsorbed in coal seams; released by pumping water out | Damodar valley – Raniganj (first commercial output), Jharia, Bokaro
  [58:2:0.2] Gas (methane) hydrates | Methane-water ice crystals under the seafloor and in Arctic tundra / permafrost | KG, Mahanadi, Andaman offshore (not Damodar)
[58:2:1] - **Hydraulic fracturing** is the technology that stimulates the flow of oil or gas and raises the recoverable volume.
[58:2:2] - **Guar gum** from the seeds of the **cluster bean** thickens fracking fluid and carries sand into the cracks – hence guar's new importance (UPSC 2014).
[58:2:3] - **Methane hydrate (UPSC 2019):** warming may release the methane; deposits lie under the seafloor and in Arctic tundra; atmospheric methane oxidises to CO₂ in a decade or two – **all three true**.
[58:2:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Human & Economic Geography EG-MR p.53-57; PMF Environment Part 2 p.25-26 (methane hydrates, UPSC 2019); app notes 5:58 sub 2

## SUB 4 | Exploration Policies – NELP, HELP, OALP
[58:4:0] TABLE head: Policy | Year | Provision
  [58:4:0.0] NELP | 1997-99 | Blocks bid out; production-sharing contracts (profit split after cost recovery)
  [58:4:0.1] Discovered Small Fields | 2015 | Auction of small fields of ONGC and OIL
  [58:4:0.2] HELP | 2016 | One licence for all hydrocarbons; pricing freedom; revenue-sharing contract – firms bid the share of revenue for the Government
  [58:4:0.3] OALP | 2017 | Firms choose blocks and bid year-round using the National Data Repository
  [58:4:0.4] Samudra Manthan | 3 Aug 2026 | ₹84,084 crore to 2030-31; 50% drilling support (cap ₹675 crore/well); open to all OALP block holders
[58:4:1] - **NELP blocks, JV blocks, nomination blocks and CBM blocks** are all **petroleum exploration** blocks (RAS 2010).
[58:4:2] > Exam angle: APPSC G1 2017 – under HELP the Government earns through a **biddable revenue-sharing contract**, not production-sharing.

## SUB 6 | PNGRB and City Gas Distribution
[58:6:0] - **PNGRB** (Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board): statutory, **PNGRB Act 2006**, under the **Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas**.
[58:6:1] - Regulates **refining, processing, storage, transportation, distribution, marketing and sale** – **excludes production of crude oil and natural gas** (UPSC 2025: only two of the four).
[58:6:2] - Authorises entities for **city gas distribution (CGD)** in Geographical Areas and fixes pipeline tariffs.
[58:6:3] - **AP CGD:** **10 GAs**; target **83.61 lakh** PNG connections by **March 2032**.
[58:6:4] ~~ Sources: UPSC 2025 PYQ explanation (PNGRB Act 2006); app notes 5:58 sub 7

=== NOTES 5:59 | Electricity Sector – Capacity Mix, Generation, Transmission, Discom Finances, Electricity Act 2003
## SUB 0 | Electricity Basics – Units, Frequency, Transformers
[59:0:0] - Discoms bill consumption in **kWh ("units")**; India's grid runs at **50 Hz** (not 60 Hz) – MPPSC 2008: A true, R false.
[59:0:1] - **Step-up transformer** raises **voltage** (and lowers current) for long-distance transmission; it does **not** raise power.
[59:0:2] - A **transformer works only on AC** (mutual induction); a **capacitor stores electric charge/energy**; a **generator/dynamo** converts mechanical to electrical energy.
[59:0:3] TABLE head: Transformer / generator fact | Answer
  [59:0:3.0] Protection not provided on small distribution transformers | Buchholz relay (used on oil-filled transformers of about 500 kVA and above)
  [59:0:3.1] Power factor of a transformer | Depends on the power factor of the load
  [59:0:3.2] Maximum efficiency of a distribution transformer | Designed for about 50% of full load (it runs lightly loaded most of the day)
  [59:0:3.3] Low power factor of a DG set | Needs higher excitation current
[59:0:4] - The **integrated national (all-India) power grid** evens out supply-demand mismatches between regions.
[59:0:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Sheets Physics p.31-32 (transformer, generator); app notes 5:59 sub 3; general knowledge, not checked (transformer protection and efficiency)
## SUB 1 | Andhra Pradesh Power Scenario
[59:1:0] - **AP Reorganisation Act 2014, Twelfth Schedule:** power of the **Central Generating Stations** is allotted to AP and Telangana in the ratio of the **actual energy consumption of the last 5 years** of their DISCOMs; APGENCO units divided by location.
[59:1:1] - AP's installed capacity = thermal (coal), hydel, gas, solar, wind – **no nuclear** plant in AP.
[59:1:2] TABLE head: Plant | Location / owner
  [59:1:2.0] Simhadri STPP | Visakhapatnam; NTPC, 2,000 MW
  [59:1:2.1] Hinduja National Power | Visakhapatnam; Hinduja group (private)
  [59:1:2.2] Dr NTTPS | Ibrahimpatnam, Vijayawada; APGENCO, 2,560 MW (Stage V 800 MW, Dec 2023)
  [59:1:2.3] Dr M.V.R. RTPP | Muddanur, Kadapa; 1,650 MW
  [59:1:2.4] Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah TPS | Krishnapatnam, Nellore; 2 × 800 MW
  [59:1:2.5] Vijjeswaram | Gas-based (Godavari)
[59:1:3] - **No coal of its own** – coal from **Singareni and MCL**. Installed + contracted **21,297 MW**; T&D losses **9.25%**.
[59:1:4] - DISCOMs: **APEPDCL Visakhapatnam**; **APSPDCL Tirupati** (not Hyderabad); **APCPDCL** re-formed **2020, Vijayawada**.
[59:1:5] - **Free farm power:** **Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy** (CM from 14 May 2004). **BPL SC/ST** households: free up to **200 units/month**; aqua farmers **₹1.50/unit**.
[59:1:6] - **24,691** tribal households electrified under **PM JANMAN** (not RDSS).
[59:1:7] - APGENCO plans two **3,200 MW** ultra-supercritical plants: **Srikakulam** and pithead **Talcher** (Odisha).
[59:1:8] > Exam angle: Kothagudam is in Telangana; the Visakhapatnam-district plant is **Simhadri**.
[59:1:9] ~~ Sources: AP Reorganisation Act 2014, Twelfth Schedule C(1), C(6) (Gazette p.69); app notes 5:59 sub 10, 5:60 sub 9
## SUB 2 | Transmission – One Nation One Grid
[59:2:0] - **One Nation-One Grid-One Frequency** = world's **largest synchronous grid**; over 5 lakh ckm.
[59:2:1] - **Five regional grids** (N, E, W, NE, S); **Southern** synchronised last, **December 2013**.
[59:2:2] - **POWERGRID (PGCIL)** = Central Transmission Utility.
[59:2:3] - **Green Energy Corridor:** began with a **PGCIL study (2012)**; built from 2015.
[59:2:4] - Record peak **270.82 GW** (21 May 2026); peak shortage **4.2% (2014) → 0.03% (2025)**.
[59:2:5] - **BESS** helps meet the **evening peak** when solar fades.
[59:2:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:59 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Discom Finances – Why the SEBs Went Sick
[59:3:0] - Causes: **below-cost sale** to farm and domestic users, **poor cost recovery**, high T&D losses, **rising commercial losses**, **delays** in commissioning new projects.
[59:3:1] - **Not a cause:** the **autonomy of States** over generation and distribution (APPSC G2 Mains 2017).
[59:3:2] TABLE head: Metric | Meaning | Trend
  [59:3:2.0] AT&C loss | Technical + commercial loss | 22.62% (FY14) → 15.04% (FY25)
  [59:3:2.1] ACS-ARR gap | Average cost of supply minus average revenue realised per unit | ₹0.78 → ₹0.06
[59:3:3] - DISCOMs: loss ₹67,962 crore (2013-14) → **profit ₹2,701 crore** (FY25). States spend about **₹2.4 lakh crore/year** on power subsidies.
[59:3:4] - **PFC Integrated Rating** grades DISCOMs every year.
[59:3:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:59 sub 6; APPSC G2 Mains 2017 key
## SUB 4 | UDAY, RDSS and Smart Meters
[59:4:0] - **UDAY** (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana, Ministry of Power, **Nov 2015**): financial turnaround – States took over **75%** of DISCOM debt.
[59:4:1] TABLE head: Operational / supply side | Demand side
  [59:4:1.0] Feeder and DT metering, smart meters, transformer upgrades, coal swapping, cutting transmission loss, cheaper funds | Energy-efficient LED bulbs (UJALA), efficient pumps, fans, ACs
[59:4:2] - **RDSS (2021):** **₹3.03 lakh crore**; results-linked; to FY 2027-28; nodal **REC and PFC**; smart meters on **TOTEX (PPP)**; **20.33 crore** smart meters sanctioned.
[59:4:3] - **EESL** signed an MoU with **PNGRB** for smart PNG meters.
[59:4:4] > Exam angle: the UDAY "demand-side intervention" is **LED bulbs**; coal swapping and lower transmission loss are supply-side.
[59:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:59 sub 7; APPSC G1 key (UDAY)

=== NOTES 5:61 | Nuclear Energy – Three-stage Programme, Reactor Types, Phwr/fbr/ahwr, Thorium Strategy
## SUB 0 | Fission vs Fusion – Chain Reaction, Reactor vs Bomb, Energy of the Sun
[61:0:0] TABLE head: Point | Fission | Fusion
  [61:0:0.0] Process | Heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + slow neutron → barium + krypton + 2–3 neutrons + energy) | Two light nuclei join (deuterium + tritium → helium + neutron)
  [61:0:0.1] Trigger / condition | Neutron hit on a fissile nucleus; critical mass | Very high temperature (10⁷–10⁸ K) and pressure – "thermonuclear"
  [61:0:0.2] Energy | Large | More per unit mass (3–4 times fission)
  [61:0:0.3] Where | Nuclear reactors (controlled), atom bomb (uncontrolled) | Sun and stars, hydrogen bomb; fusion power still at R&D stage
[61:0:1] - **Breaking apart of a nucleus = fission**, not fusion – the "NOT correct" statement in APPSC/UPPSC items.
[61:0:2] - All present-day nuclear electricity comes from **fission**.
[61:0:3] # Chain reaction and criticality
[61:0:4] - Each fission releases **more neutrons** (2–3), which split more nuclei → **chain reaction**; fast neutrons are **slowed by a moderator (graphite, heavy water)** so that U-235 captures them. Not every neutron causes a fresh fission, and neutrons do not all react "immediately" (UPSC 2001: only statements I and III).
[61:0:5] - **Critical mass** = minimum fissile mass that sustains a chain reaction; **criticality** = self-sustaining chain reaction – every operating reactor is "critical".
[61:0:6] - **Reactor vs atom bomb:** both use a chain reaction; in a **reactor it is controlled** (moderator, control rods), in a **bomb it is uncontrolled**. Reactors do use moderators (CDS 2017: only II and III correct).
[61:0:7] # Atom bomb and hydrogen bomb
[61:0:8] TABLE head: Feature | Atom (fission) bomb | Hydrogen (thermonuclear) bomb
  [61:0:8.0] Principle | Uncontrolled fission of U-235 / Pu-239 | Uncontrolled fusion of deuterium and tritium into helium, triggered by a fission bomb
  [61:0:8.1] Person | Otto Hahn (with F. Strassmann, 1938-39) – discovered nuclear fission | Edward Teller – "father of the hydrogen bomb"; first US test Nov 1952, Eniwetok
  [61:0:8.2] Power | Large | Far more powerful
  [61:0:8.3] Hiroshima, 6 Aug 1945 (first) | Little Boy | U-235
  [61:0:8.4] Nagasaki, 9 Aug 1945 | Fat Man | Plutonium-239
[61:0:9] - Only **Hiroshima and Nagasaki** were atom-bombed (not Tokyo, Sendai, Miyazaki).
[61:0:10] - **North Korea** claimed a successful **hydrogen bomb** test (January 2016; again September 2017).
[61:0:11] - India's **Shakti 1998** (Pokhran-II) series included a thermonuclear device.
[61:0:12] # Energy of the Sun and stars
[61:0:13] - Sun and stars shine by **nuclear fusion** – hydrogen nuclei fuse into **helium** in the core (about 15 million K); not fission, chemical reaction, photoelectric effect or gravity. "Energy generation in stars" is the statement **not** associated with fission.
[61:0:14] > Exam angle: about 35 PYQs – "principle of the atom bomb / hydrogen bomb", "energy of the Sun", "difference between reactor and bomb = controlled chain reaction". Uncontrolled fusion = H-bomb; controlled fission = reactor.
[61:0:15] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.22-28 (fission, chain reaction, bombs, fusion, Sun); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 4 p.19, 23; app notes 5:61 sub 1
## SUB 1 | Atomic Structure – Nucleus, Isotopes, Isobars and Isotones
[61:1:0] TABLE head: Particle | Charge | Mass | Location
  [61:1:0.0] Proton | +1 (equal to the charge of a positron) | ≈ 1 amu | Nucleus
  [61:1:0.1] Neutron | Zero | ≈ 1 amu (slightly more than proton) | Nucleus (does not revolve around it)
  [61:1:0.2] Electron | −1 | ≈ 1/1837 of proton | Shells around the nucleus
[61:1:1] - **Nucleus = protons + neutrons** (nucleons); it holds **almost all the mass** of the atom. Rutherford's **gold-foil (α-scattering)** experiment showed a small, dense, **positively charged nucleus** at the centre.
[61:1:2] - Electrons are held to the nucleus by the **electric (electrostatic)** force; electrons in the outermost (highest) shell are **valence electrons**. Atoms of different elements have **different atomic numbers and different numbers of valence electrons**.
[61:1:3] - Discoverers: electron – J.J. Thomson (1897); nucleus – Rutherford (1911); neutron – **James Chadwick (1932)**.
[61:1:4] # Atomic number, mass number, atomic weight
[61:1:5] - **Atomic number (Z) = number of protons** (= electrons in a neutral atom); fixes the element.
[61:1:6] - **Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons** – a whole number; neutrons = A − Z.
[61:1:7] TABLE head: Example | Working | Answer
  [61:1:7.0] ⁹⁴Pu²⁴² | 242 − 94 | 148 neutrons
  [61:1:7.1] Carbon, 6 protons, A = 12 | 12 − 6 | 6 neutrons
  [61:1:7.2] 18 electrons, 20 neutrons | 18 + 20 | A = 38
  [61:1:7.3] 7 electrons in M-shell, 18 neutrons | 2 + 8 + 7 = 17 protons; 17 + 18 | A = 35
  [61:1:7.4] Atomic weight W, atomic number N | protons = Z | N
[61:1:8] - **Atomic weight** is the average mass of an element's isotopes, so it **can be a fraction** (mass number cannot).
[61:1:9] - **Uranium (Z = 92)** is the **heaviest naturally occurring** element.
[61:1:10] # Isotopes, isobars, isotones
[61:1:11] TABLE head: Term | Same | Different | Example
  [61:1:11.0] Isotope | Atomic number (protons) | Mass number (neutrons) | ¹H, ²H, ³H; ¹⁶O, ¹⁷O, ¹⁸O
  [61:1:11.1] Isobar | Mass number | Atomic number | ³H and ³He
  [61:1:11.2] Isotone (isoneutronic) | Number of neutrons (A − Z) | Atomic and mass numbers | ³H and ⁴He (2 each); ¹⁴C, ¹⁵N, ¹⁶O (8 each)
[61:1:12] - Isotopes have the **same chemical properties** (same electrons) but different physical properties (mass).
[61:1:13] - Hydrogen isotopes: **protium** (no neutron), **deuterium** (1 neutron, "heavy hydrogen"), **tritium** (2 neutrons, radioactive, made by hitting **lithium** with neutrons) – isotopes of **hydrogen**, not carbon.
[61:1:14] - **Heavy water (D₂O):** **deuterium** (an isotope of **hydrogen**) takes the place of ordinary hydrogen; discovered by **H.C. Urey** (Nobel Chemistry 1934).
[61:1:15] - **Helium nucleus** = **2 protons + 2 neutrons** (= the alpha particle).
[61:1:16] > Exam angle: NDA/SSC/state PSC recall items – mass number = p + n, isotope = same Z, isobar = same A, isotone = same neutrons; isotopes/isobars "both reversed" → neither statement correct.
[61:1:17] ~~ Sources: Rocket Chemistry p.39-41 (atomic structure, isotope/isobar/isotone table); PMF S&T Part 4 p.22, 24 (deuterium, tritium); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 4 p.22-24; app notes 5:61 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Nuclear Fuels – Fissile vs Fertile, Enrichment, What Is Not a Fuel
[61:2:0] TABLE head: Isotope | Type | Key fact
  [61:2:0.0] U-235 | Fissile | Only 0.7% of natural uranium; the isotope that powers reactors and fuels bombs
  [61:2:0.1] U-238 | Fertile | 99.3% of natural uranium; absorbs a neutron → Pu-239
  [61:2:0.2] Pu-239 | Fissile | Not natural; bred from U-238 – a "good nuclear fuel"
  [61:2:0.3] Th-232 | Fertile | Th-232 + neutron → fissile U-233
  [61:2:0.4] U-233 | Fissile | Fuel of Stage III and of KAMINI
[61:2:1] - **Uranium** is the main fuel of nuclear reactors (the metal "used for producing electricity"); **thorium** is usable only after breeding into U-233.
[61:2:2] - India's PHWRs burn **natural uranium** (unenriched; mostly U-238 with 0.7% U-235).
[61:2:3] - **Enrichment** = raising the share of **U-235** (not U-238) by **isotope separation**; most common method: **gas centrifuge** (uranium as UF₆; earlier gaseous diffusion).
[61:2:4] TABLE head: Use | U-235 level
  [61:2:4.0] Light-water power reactors | 3–5%
  [61:2:4.1] Research / some naval reactors | Up to 20%
  [61:2:4.2] Weapons-grade | About 90% (far above 20%)
[61:2:5] # Not a nuclear fuel
[61:2:6] - **Moderators, coolants, absorbers:** graphite, heavy water, sodium, **boron, cadmium**, beryllium oxide (moderator).
[61:2:7] - **Zirconium** (alloy cladding of fuel rods – corrosion-resistant, absorbs very few neutrons) is "essential for the construction of reactors"; it is **not radioactive**.
[61:2:8] - Also not fuels: **helium** (inert gas), **lead**, **calcium**, **chromium** (not linked to atomic power), radium (radioactive but not a reactor fuel). **Monazite** (thorium ore), thorium and **beryllium** are linked to atomic power.
[61:2:9] - "Good nuclear fuel" among U-238, Pu-239, neptunium, "thorium-236": **Pu-239** (fissile); U-238 is only fertile (APPSC 2007).
[61:2:10] > Exam angle: "Which is NOT a fuel?" – cadmium, lead, calcium, helium, chromium; "uranium isotope used in power plants" – U-235; "thorium + neutrons" – U-233 (APPSC Group 1 2002, repeated).
[61:2:11] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.24, 38, 41-42 (fissile fuels, enrichment levels, centrifuge, zirconium cladding); PMF S&T Part 5 p.5 (prescribed substances: zirconium alloys, beryllium); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 4 p.24; app notes 5:61 sub 0
[61:2:12] - **Pitchblende (uraninite)** = chief ore of **uranium** (the nuclear-power fuel); **monazite** = thorium ore.
## SUB 3 | Radioactivity – Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Half-life
[61:3:0] - Discovered by **Henri Becquerel (1896)** in uranium; Marie and Pierre Curie found polonium and radium (1898). Radioactivity is a **nuclear** (not chemical) property; a radioactive substance emits **alpha, beta and gamma** rays. Measured by the **Geiger (Geiger–Müller) counter**.
[61:3:1] TABLE head: Emission | Nature | Charge | Stopped by
  [61:3:1.0] Alpha | Helium nucleus (2p + 2n); mass ≈ helium nucleus/atom | +2 (positive) | Paper or skin – least penetrating
  [61:3:1.1] Beta | Electron (β⁻) or positron (β⁺) emitted by the nucleus | −1 (negative) / +1 | Few mm of aluminium
  [61:3:1.2] Gamma | Electromagnetic radiation (photons) | Zero | Lead or concrete – most penetrating
[61:3:2] - Penetrating power (same energy): **α < β < γ**.
[61:3:3] - **β⁻ emission:** a neutron turns into a proton + electron → the atom gains **one proton** (Z rises by 1).
[61:3:4] - **Zero charge:** neutron, **neutrino**, gamma. **Deuteron** (a proton + neutron nucleus) is not a sub-atomic particle in the usual list.
[61:3:5] - **Half-life** = time for half the nuclei to decay; a substance never decays "completely".
[61:3:6] TABLE head: Half-life | After | Remaining | Decayed
  [61:3:6.0] 10 days | 20 days (2 half-lives) | 1/4 | 3/4
  [61:3:6.1] 5 years | 20 years (4 half-lives) | 1/16 | 15/16
[61:3:7] - Natural decay series: **uranium** (U-238 → Pb-206), **thorium** (Th-232 → **Pb-208**), **actinium** (U-235 → Pb-207); **neptunium series = artificial**; there is **no "carbon series"**. Lead is the stable **end product of uranium decay**.
[61:3:8] - Elements above Z = 82–83 are radioactive (plus technetium 43, promethium 61); **astatine, francium, tritium** are radioactive, **zirconium (Z = 40) is not**.
[61:3:9] - **Xenon-135** = "nuclear poison" – a fission product that absorbs neutrons.
[61:3:10] > Exam angle: charge of α/β/γ, half-life arithmetic (RAS 2007 repeated), "not radioactive" (zirconium, IAS 2001 and 2007).
[61:3:11] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.29-31, 37 (types of radiation, Becquerel, half-life); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 4 p.20-21, 23; Rocket Chemistry p.40-41; app notes 5:61 sub 2
## SUB 4 | Reactor Components and Reactor Types
[61:4:0] TABLE head: Part | Function | Substances
  [61:4:0.0] Fuel | Fissile material | U-235, Pu-239, U-233
  [61:4:0.1] Moderator | Slows fast neutrons to thermal speed so U-235 can fission (does not absorb them or stop the reaction) | Heavy water (D₂O), graphite, ordinary (light) water, beryllium oxide
  [61:4:0.2] Control rods | Absorb neutrons, control the rate | Cadmium, boron, hafnium, silver-indium
  [61:4:0.3] Coolant | Transfers heat from the core to make steam | Heavy water, light water, CO₂, helium, liquid sodium
  [61:4:0.4] Reactor core | Where fuel, moderator and control rods are located | –
[61:4:1] - Without control rods the chain reaction goes **out of control**; without a moderator a thermal reactor stops.
[61:4:2] - **Heavy water** is chiefly a **moderator**; in PHWRs it is **both moderator and coolant**. **Ordinary water** is also both in PWRs/BWRs.
[61:4:3] TABLE head: Reactor | Fuel | Moderator | Coolant | Example
  [61:4:3.0] PHWR | Natural uranium | Heavy water | Heavy water | Rajasthan (first), Kaiga, Kakrapar, Narora – Stage I
  [61:4:3.1] BWR | Enriched uranium | Light water | Light water (boils in core) | Tarapur units 1-2 (India's first, 1969)
  [61:4:3.2] PWR / VVER | Low-enriched uranium | Light water | Pressurised light water | Kudankulam
  [61:4:3.3] Gas-cooled (Magnox) | Natural uranium | Graphite | CO₂ | UK
  [61:4:3.4] FBR | MOX (Pu-239 + U-238) | None | Liquid sodium | FBTR, PFBR – Kalpakkam
  [61:4:3.5] AHWR | Th-232 + U-233 / Pu | Heavy water | Boiling light water | BARC design
[61:4:4] - **Light-water reactors** (light water as moderator and coolant) make up **over 85%** of world capacity; PWR alone about 70% of reactors.
[61:4:5] - **May 2017:** Union Cabinet approved **10 indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs** in "fleet mode".
[61:4:6] > Exam angle: "function of heavy water / moderator" (UPSC 2011 ×2, IAS 2011) = slow down neutrons; "if control rods are not used" = chain reaction goes out of control (RAS 1992 ×2).
[61:4:7] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.38-46, 51-52 (components, PWR, BWR, PHWR, FBR, AHWR, reactor tables); app notes 5:61 sub 3; May 2017 PHWR decision: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 5 | Fast Breeder Reactors – FBTR, PFBR, IGCAR and BHAVINI
[61:5:0] - **Breeder reactor:** produces **more fissile material than it burns**; electricity still comes from **fission**. Fast neutrons (no moderator) turn the **U-238 blanket** into **Pu-239** (and Th-232 into U-233); **Pu-239 fissions** to give energy.
[61:5:1] - **No moderator; liquid sodium coolant**; fuel MOX from reprocessed Stage I spent fuel. FBRs are **Stage II** (not Stage I).
[61:5:2] # FBTR (Fast Breeder Test Reactor)
[61:5:3] - At **IGCAR, Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu)**; critical **18 October 1985**; design based on French **Rapsodie**.
[61:5:4] - Coolant **liquid sodium**; fuel indigenous **plutonium-uranium mixed carbide** (plutonium-rich).
[61:5:5] - **2005** milestone: IGCAR reprocessed FBTR's mixed-carbide fuel.
[61:5:6] # PFBR, Kalpakkam
[61:5:7] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [61:5:7.0] Capacity | 500 MWe (1,250 MWt); sodium-cooled, pool type
  [61:5:7.1] Designed by | IGCAR (Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Kalpakkam, est. 1971 as Reactor Research Centre)
  [61:5:7.2] Built and operated by | BHAVINI (Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd, PSU of DAE, 2003, HQ Kalpakkam)
  [61:5:7.3] First criticality | 6 April 2026 → India enters Stage II
  [61:5:7.4] Delay | Cost doubled; about 16 years late
[61:5:8] - PFBR = India's **first indigenous FBR**; India the **2nd country after Russia** to run a commercial-scale fast breeder. Next: FBR-600 / 2 × 500 MWe units at Kalpakkam.
[61:5:9] > ⚠ "Who developed / built PFBR": APPSC keys **BHAVINI** (builder, operator); IGCAR is the designer – read the verb.
[61:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.45-46 (FBR); PMF S&T Part 5 p.2, 12 (BHAVINI, IGCAR); Rocket CA Jan 2026 p.162 (PFBR criticality 6 Apr 2026); PMF Lens Apr 2026 p.8; app notes 5:61 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Three-stage Programme, Thorium and the AHWR
[61:6:0] - **Homi J. Bhabha** – "father of the Indian nuclear programme"; 1950s plan to use **abundant thorium** against **scarce uranium**; aim: self-reliance through a **closed fuel cycle**.
[61:6:1] TABLE head: Stage | Reactor | Fuel | Output
  [61:6:1.0] I | PHWR (D₂O moderator + coolant) | Natural uranium | Power + Pu-239 in spent fuel
  [61:6:1.1] II | FBR (liquid sodium, no moderator) | MOX: Pu-239 + U-238 | Breeds more Pu-239; Th-232 blanket → U-233
  [61:6:1.2] III | AHWR / thorium reactors | Th-232 + U-233 | Large-scale thorium use
[61:6:2] - **Thorium:** India holds about **25%** of world thorium (3rd largest) but only about **2%** of uranium – so thorium is the element with **large reserves in India**.
[61:6:3] - **Thorium over uranium** (UPSC 2012): far **more abundant**, **more energy per unit mass mined**, **less harmful (long-lived) waste** – all three.
[61:6:4] - **Monazite** = principal thorium ore (also rare earths – lanthanum, cerium); resources about **13.15 million tonnes** (DAE); beach sands of **Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh** – not the entire coast; only **IREL** may process and export it.
[61:6:5] # AHWR (Advanced Heavy Water Reactor)
[61:6:6] - **300 MWe**, designed by **BARC**; **heavy-water moderated, boiling light-water cooled**; fuel (Th-U-233) MOX and (Th-Pu) MOX – so it also burns **plutonium-bearing** fuel; **not yet built**.
[61:6:7] - A **bridge from Stage I to Stage III** for large-scale thorium use.
[61:6:8] - **ANEEL fuel** (thorium + **HALEU**, US firm Clean Core Thorium Energy, May 2026) is usable in existing PHWRs.
[61:6:9] - Stage III hurdles: thin fissile inventory, long builds – **not** lack of thorium.
[61:6:10] # Uranium mines
[61:6:11] TABLE head: Mine | Location
  [61:6:11.0] Jaduguda | East Singhbhum, Jharkhand – India's first uranium mine; UCIL seat
  [61:6:11.1] Tummalapalle | YSR Kadapa, AP – UCIL mine and processing plant
[61:6:12] - About **80%** of imported uranium comes from **Kazakhstan** (Dec 2025).
[61:6:13] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 5 p.1-4 (three stages, thorium share, UPSC 2012 explanation); PMF S&T Part 4 p.46-47 (AHWR); PMF Lens Sep 2026 p.7; app notes 5:61 sub 4, 7
[61:6:14] - **KPM** (Kylleng-Pyndengsohiong-Mawthabah, Domiasiat) uranium deposit is in **West Khasi Hills, Meghalaya**; AP's second deposit is **Koppunuru, Palnadu (ex-Guntur)**.
## SUB 7 | Research Reactors, BARC and DAE Institutions
[61:7:0] TABLE head: Reactor | Site | Key facts
  [61:7:0.0] Apsara | BARC, Trombay (not Kalpakkam) | Pool (swimming-pool) type; critical 1956; India's and Asia's first research reactor; Indian-built
  [61:7:0.1] CIRUS | Trombay | 40 MW, natural uranium, heavy water; with Canada; shut 2010
  [61:7:0.2] Dhruva | Trombay | India's largest research reactor (100 MW); isotopes, materials testing
  [61:7:0.3] KAMINI | Kalpakkam (IGCAR) | 30 kW; world's only U-233 reactor
  [61:7:0.4] Purnima I–III | Trombay | Thorium/U-233 research reactors; shut
[61:7:1] - Kaiga, Kudankulam and Narora are **power** stations; **Dhruva** is the research reactor.
[61:7:2] - World's first reactor (**Chicago Pile-1, 1942**) was built by **Enrico Fermi**, an **Italian** physicist (Italy → USA).

[61:7:4] # Acts, mission and SMRs
[61:7:5] - **Atomic Energy Act, 1948** – atomic energy for **peaceful uses**; replaced by the 1962 Act.
[61:7:6] - **SHANTI Act 2025** – repealed the **Atomic Energy Act 1962** and **CLNDA 2010**; licensed private companies/JVs may build and run plants.
[61:7:7] - NPCIL fleet: **25 reactors, 8,880 MW** (incl. one under long shutdown; **24 operating, 8.78 GW**, Sep 2026); target 22.38 GW by 2031-32.
[61:7:8] - **Nuclear Energy Mission** (Budget 2025-26): **100 GW by 2047**; **₹20,000 crore** for SMRs.
[61:7:9] - **SMRs:** up to **300 MWe** per unit, factory-built, refuelled every **3–7 years**; **Bharat Small Reactors** (NPCIL) based on the **220 MW PHWR**; **CODENE** at **IIT Hyderabad** (Jun 2026).

## SUB 8 | Fusion Research – Tokamak, ITER and IPR
[61:8:0] - **Fusion reactors** work on the **fusion of light nuclei** (not fission of heavy nuclei), usually in a **tokamak** design, at **very high temperature** (UPPSC RO/ARO 2016: ii and iii).
[61:8:1] - Plasma confinement: **magnetic** (tokamak) or **inertial** (lasers on fuel pellets).
[61:8:2] - **ITER:** **Cadarache, southern France**; tokamak, world's largest magnetic-confinement experiment; members **EU + India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia, USA** – **Canada is not a member**; India joined **2005** and supplies the **cryostat**; about **500 MW out from 50 MW in**.
[61:8:3] - **Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar** (not BARC): **Aditya** (first Indian tokamak) and **SST-1**.
[61:8:4] - **December 2022:** first fusion ignition with net energy gain – **National Ignition Facility, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, USA**, using lasers.
[61:8:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 4 p.27, 29, 50 (fusion conditions, confinement, ITER); app notes 5:61 sub 8
[61:8:6] - **Aditya** (commissioned **1989**; Aditya-U 2016) is IPR's own medium-size tokamak, **not part of ITER**; **ITER-India** at IPR is India's domestic agency for ITER.
[61:8:7] - **ITER cost:** host **EU pays about 45%**, each other member about 9% (mostly in kind) – not the USA.

## SUB 0 | Nuclear Power Plants – Location, State and Firsts

  [62:0:1.0] Tarapur (TAPS) | Maharashtra (near Bombay) | 2 x 160 MW BWR + 2 x 540 MW PHWR | India's first nuclear power plant (1969); BWRs supplied by the USA ("Atoms for Peace"); TAPS 3-4 = first 540 MW PHWRs
  [62:0:1.1] Rawatbhata (RAPS/RAPP), near Kota | Rajasthan | RAPS 1-6 + RAPP-7 (700 MW), RAPP-8 next | Oldest PHWR site; RAPS-1 (1972-73) = first PHWR, with Canada (CANDU/AECL)
  [62:0:1.2] Kalpakkam (MAPS), near Madras | Tamil Nadu | 2 x 220 MW | First fully indigenous PHWR (MAPS-1 critical 1983); also IGCAR (1971) and the PFBR
  [62:0:1.3] Narora (NAPS) | Uttar Pradesh | 2 x 220 MW | PHWR (not VVER); in Seismic Zone IV
  [62:0:1.4] Kakrapar (KAPS), Surat district | Gujarat | 4 units, 1,840 MW | KAPP-3 = first indigenous 700 MW PHWR, commercial operation 30 June 2023
  [62:0:1.5] Kaiga (KGS), near river Kali, Uttara Kannada | Karnataka | 4 x 220 = 880 MW; Units 5-6 begun 2026 | Capacity factor >90%; Kaiga 1-2 began operating in 1999-2000 (newest then)

[62:0:4] - Seismic zones: **Narora Zone IV**; Kaiga and Tarapur Zone III; Kalpakkam Zone II.

## SUB 1 | Nuclear Accidents and Nuclear Security
[62:1:0] TABLE head: Accident | Country | Year | INES
  [62:1:0.0] SL-1 | USA (Idaho) | 1961 | –
  [62:1:0.1] Three Mile Island | USA (Pennsylvania) | 1979 | 5 (partial meltdown)
  [62:1:0.2] Chernobyl | Ukraine (then USSR) | 26 April 1986 | 7 (worst) – reactor explosion during a test
  [62:1:0.3] Kashiwazaki-Kariwa | Japan | 2007 | Earthquake → radioactive water leak at the world's largest plant
  [62:1:0.4] Mayapuri | Delhi, India | 2010 | Orphan Cobalt-60 source
  [62:1:0.5] Fukushima Daiichi | Japan (earthquake + tsunami) | 2011 | 7
[62:1:1] - Non-nuclear distractors: **Bhopal** (gas leak, 1984), Guadalajara (sewer explosions, 1992), Sayano-Shushenskaya (hydro plant, 2009).
[62:1:2] - **Dirty bomb** (radiological dispersal device): a **conventional explosive** that scatters radioactive material (Cs-137, Co-60); **no** city-flattening atomic blast and it is **cheaper** than a nuclear weapon.
[62:1:3] - **Nuclear Security Summits** (US-led, started by **Obama**, not UN): **Washington 2010 → Seoul 2012 → The Hague 2014 → Washington 2016**; India announced **GCNEP** (now at **Bahadurgarh**) in 2010. The **International Panel on Fissile Materials** is an independent expert group, not an IAEA organ.
[62:1:4] - **ICONS 2024** (IAEA ministerial conference, **Vienna, 20-24 May 2024**): India said it had **reconstituted the inter-ministerial Counter Nuclear Smuggling Team (CNST)**.

## SUB 3 | IAEA, Safeguards, NSG and Treaties
[62:3:0] # IAEA
[62:3:1] - **IAEA:** set up **1957**; HQ **Vienna, Austria**; autonomous body in the UN system; ~180 members; **India a founding member**; reports non-compliance to the **UN Security Council**.
[62:3:2] - **Why only some Indian reactors are under IAEA safeguards:** they use **imported uranium**/technology; strategic reactors use domestic uranium.
[62:3:3] - **2006 separation plan:** civil and military facilities separated; civil reactors under safeguards so NSG members could supply fuel.
[62:3:4] - **India-Specific Safeguards Agreement:** **2 February 2009**. **Additional Protocol:** signed **2009**, in force **2014**; implication = **civilian reactors come under IAEA safeguards** (wider access, declared civilian facilities only).
[62:3:5] # NSG and export controls
[62:3:6] - **NSG:** **1975** ("**London Club**"), response to **Pokhran-I (1974)**; **48 members** (China, New Zealand, Ireland are members; **Iran is not**); consensus; no permanent secretariat.
[62:3:7] - India applied **2016**; blocked mainly by **China**; membership would give **technology access + a say in rule-making**, NOT NPT membership.
[62:3:8] - India's regimes: **MTCR 2016 → Wassenaar 2017 → Australia Group 2018**.
[62:3:9] # Treaties
[62:3:10] TABLE head: Treaty | Year | India
  [62:3:10.0] PTBT (air, space, underwater tests) | 1963 | Signed
  [62:3:10.1] NPT | signed 1968, in force 1970 | Never signed – discriminatory
  [62:3:10.2] Seabed Treaty | 1971, in force 1972 | –
  [62:3:10.3] SALT II (US–USSR) | 1979 (not 1967) | –
  [62:3:10.4] CTBT | 1996 (not in force) | Not signed – no time-bound disarmament
  [62:3:10.5] TPNW | in force 2021 | Not signed
[62:3:11] - Doctrine: **No First Use**.
[62:3:12] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 5 p.13-14 (IAEA 1957 Vienna; UPSC 2020 imported uranium), p.15-22 (NSG 1975, 48 members, India 2016/China; MTCR, WA, AG; NPT, CTBT); app notes 5:62 sub 6-7

[62:4:7] - **Pollution:** a nuclear plant causes **less (air) pollution** than thermal plants, city traffic or aircraft – low-carbon base-load power.
## SUB 5 | Civil Nuclear Agreements and the NSG Waiver
[62:5:0] - **NSG waiver (September 2008):** clean waiver for civilian nuclear trade; ended **34 years** of exclusion.
[62:5:1] - **India–US 123 Agreement (2007 text, signed 2008):** named after **Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954**; **Manmohan Singh** and **George W. Bush**; it gave India an **"advance right to reprocess" US-origin safeguarded spent fuel** and support for a strategic fuel reserve.

  [62:5:2.3] Australia | Signed 2014, in force 2015
  [62:5:2.4] Japan | 2016
  [62:5:2.5] Vietnam | 9 December 2016, New Delhi (Vietnam = 14th country)

## SUB 7 | Nuclear Safety – AERB and Zones
[62:7:0] - **AERB:** set up **15 November 1983** by **executive order** under the Atomic Energy Act 1962; worked under the **DAE**; **SHANTI Act 2025** gave it **statutory** status.
[62:7:1] - Powers: licensing plants and fuel-cycle facilities; inspections; suspend/revoke licences; **radiation safety in medical and industrial uses**; waste; transport of radioactive material.
[62:7:2] - **MDEP:** AERB became the **11th member** of the Multinational Design Evaluation Programme on **4 April 2012**.
[62:7:3] - **Nuclear safety ranking:** **Australia** ranked first (NTI Nuclear Materials Security Index, 2012).
[62:7:4] TABLE head: Zone | Rule
  [62:7:4.0] Exclusion zone | At least 1.5 km radius (AERB siting code; often written "1–1.5 km"); no public habitation
  [62:7:4.1] Sterilised zone | 1.5–5 km; only natural growth of population
  [62:7:4.2] Emergency Planning Zone | 16 km; concentric zones for protective actions
[62:7:5] - **Defence in Depth** (multiple layers); **ALARA** = As Low As Reasonably Achievable.
[62:7:6] - Dose limits: **20 mSv/year** (5-year average); max 30 mSv in a year.
[62:7:7] - **Convention on Nuclear Safety:** adopted 1994, in force **1996**; India a party.
[62:7:8] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 5 p.10 (AERB 1983 executive order, functions); Australia safety rank: general knowledge, not checked; WNN "India joins multinational design group", 5 Apr 2012 (11th member); DAE Saga vol.2 ch.7 and AERB siting monograph via search (exclusion 1.5 km, sterilised 5 km); Rocket Disaster Management p.20; app notes 5:62 sub 9
## SUB 8 | Liability Law – CLNDA 2010 to SHANTI Act 2025
[62:8:0] - **CLNDA 2010:** operator liability **no-fault**, capped at **₹1,500 crore**; **Section 17(b)**: operator's recourse against suppliers; Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool.
[62:8:1] - **SHANTI Act 2025:** assent **20 Dec 2025**; **repealed the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and CLNDA 2010**; private Indian firms and JVs may build and operate; FDI capped at **49%**.
[62:8:2] TABLE head: Facility | Liability cap
  [62:8:2.0] Large | ₹3,000 crore
  [62:8:2.1] Medium | ₹1,500 crore
  [62:8:2.2] SMR | ₹100 crore
[62:8:3] - Total cap **300 million SDR**; appeals to **APTEL**; Government keeps **enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and heavy water**.
[62:8:4] - **Aug 2026:** Supreme Court issued notice on a petition challenging the **liability caps**.
[62:8:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 5 p.9 (SHANTI: supplier clause, graded caps); app notes 5:62 sub 8

=== NOTES 5:64 | Renewable Energy Sources and Installed Capacities in India – Overall Targets
## SUB 0 | Renewable vs Non-renewable, Conventional vs Non-conventional
[64:0:0] # Classification
[64:0:1] TABLE head: Basis | Sources
  [64:0:1.0] Renewable | Solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass, biogas
  [64:0:1.1] Non-renewable | Coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear (uranium); minerals such as iron ore
  [64:0:1.2] Conventional | Coal, petroleum, natural gas, hydel, firewood, cattle-dung cake
  [64:0:1.3] Non-conventional | Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biomass – by definition renewable
[64:0:2] - **Most-asked NOT:** **nuclear is NOT renewable** (asked ×4) and NOT non-conventional – uranium is a finite, non-fossil fuel (Rocket Environment).
[64:0:3] - **Fossil fuels:** coal, petroleum, natural gas – formed from buried organisms; ultimate source the **Sun**; all non-renewable.
[64:0:4] - **Natural gas is NOT green energy**; sunlight, wind and algae (biofuel) are.
[64:0:5] - **Petroleum** is the non-renewable raw material of both **plastics** (e.g. toothbrushes) and **gasoline**.
[64:0:6] - **Hydel** is conventional yet renewable; **hydroelectricity** is the electricity source suited to **sustainable development** (Rocket Environment).
[64:0:7] - **Gobar gas** = mainly **methane**; **gasohol** = **petrol + alcohol** (ethanol), not benzene + alcohol.
[64:0:8] # Not derived from the Sun
[64:0:9] - Wind, hydro, biomass and fossil fuels = stored solar energy.
[64:0:10] - NOT from the Sun: **nuclear** (fission), **geothermal** (Earth's internal heat), **tidal** (Moon's pull).
[64:0:11] > Statement angle: "fossil fuels = coal, oil, gas" ✓; "gasohol = benzene + alcohol" ✗; "geothermal is non-conventional" ✓; "gobar gas mainly methane" ✓ → 1, 3 and 4.
[64:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.60-61; PMF Environment Part 7 p.69 (natural gas a fossil fuel); app notes 5:64 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Solar – India's Most Important Alternative Source
[64:1:0] - **Most important non-conventional source** for India and **greatest renewable potential** (APPSC G2 Mains 2017; UPPSC 2011).
[64:1:1] - **Largest storehouse of alternative energy** = solar; used most in **organic form** (photosynthesis).
[64:1:2] - **No atmospheric pollution** in converting sunlight to electricity; a **solar cell** is the most **eco-friendly** option among petroleum, forest products and nuclear fission.
[64:1:3] - **Photovoltaic cells** relate to **solar energy** (RAS 2016).
[64:1:4] - **A/R angle:** "wind and solar are cleaner, greener" and "India depends heavily on thermal and hydro, which harm the environment" – both true, but R does not explain A.
[64:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.61 (solar → electricity = photovoltaic); Shankar Environment 17 (OCR) p.2 (5,000 trillion kWh); app notes 5:64 sub 0
[64:1:6] - **Source:** solar energy is radiant energy from the **Sun**, not the Moon, ocean or wind.
## SUB 2 | Installed Capacity – Then and Now
[64:2:0] # Source-wise capacity
[64:2:1] TABLE head: Source | Aug 2024 | Jan 2026 (PMF) | Aug 2026
  [64:2:1.0] Solar | 89.43 GW | ~141 GW | 164.59 GW (largest RE)
  [64:2:1.1] Wind | 47.19 GW | ~55 GW | 58.14 GW (second)
  [64:2:1.2] Large hydro | 46.92 GW | ~51 GW | about 52 GW
  [64:2:1.3] Bio-power / co-generation | 10.35 GW | ~11.6 GW | about 11.75 GW
  [64:2:1.4] Small hydro | 5.07 GW | ~5.2 GW | –
  [64:2:1.5] Waste to energy | 0.60 GW | – | –
[64:2:2] - **2014:** **wind** was the largest RE source (**21 GW**; 23.44 GW = 58.54% of 40.04 GW RE in 2014-15), **bio-power** next (8.55 GW); solar only **2.8 GW**. Solar has led since then.
[64:2:3] - **31 Dec 2022:** solar **63.30 GW**. **March 2025:** wind crossed **50 GW**.
[64:2:4] - **Capacity is not generation:** non-fossil is >50% of capacity (521 GW total, Jan 2026), but coal still gives ~69-75% of power and RE ~22% of generation (2024-25).
[64:2:5] - **BPSC 2005 angle:** non-conventional sources gave **less than 1%** of commercial energy then (printed key).
[64:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.65-67 (Jan 2026 capacity, generation share); app notes 5:64 sub 1-2 (Aug 2024 MNRE figures as in APPSC NTRUHS papers; Aug 2026)
## SUB 3 | Targets Ladder
[64:3:0] TABLE head: Target | Status
  [64:3:0.0] 175 GW RE by 2022 = 100 solar + 60 wind + 10 bio-power + 5 small hydro | Missed; replaced
  [64:3:0.1] NDC 2015: 40% non-fossil capacity by 2030 | Achieved early
  [64:3:0.2] Updated NDC / Panchamrit (COP26): 50% non-fossil capacity by 2030 | Reached June 2025, five years early (51.93% by Dec 2025)
  [64:3:0.3] 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 | ~272-300 GW in 2026
  [64:3:0.4] Net Zero | 2070
[64:3:1] - Other Panchamrit goals: 50% energy needs from RE, −1 billion t emissions, −45% emission intensity (2005 base) by 2030.
[64:3:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.67-68; app notes 5:64 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Rankings and State Leaders
[64:4:0] - **IRENA 2026:** India **3rd** in RE capacity (China 2,258 GW, USA 468 GW, **India 250.5 GW**).
[64:4:1] - India **4th in wind**, **3rd in solar** (2025-26).
[64:4:2] - **Potential:** solar **748 GW** (~4.5% used); top RE potential **Rajasthan (23.70%)**; AP 9.10%.
[64:4:3] - **Top installed RE:** **Gujarat** (47.18 GW vs Rajasthan 47.02 GW, 31 Mar 2026; 42.58 GW, 16.5%, June 2026 per app data); Gujarat also leads **wind**; **Rajasthan** leads **solar**.
[64:4:4] ~~ Sources: deshgujarat.com 6 May 2026 (MNRE data, 31 Mar 2026); app notes 5:64 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Green Energy Corridors and RPO
[64:5:0] - **Green Energy Corridor (GEC):** purpose = **transmission to evacuate renewable power** – mainly **intra-state transmission systems** for RE projects, plus inter-state lines.
[64:5:1] - **Intra-State GEC-I:** **8 states** – AP, Gujarat, HP, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu (**not Telangana, not Odisha**); funding **MNRE 40% : KfW (Germany) loan 40% : state utility 20%**.
[64:5:2] - **GEC-II** (2022): **7 states**, ~20 GW RE. **Inter-State GEC** lines built by **PGCIL**.
[64:5:3] - **RPO:** DISCOMs and large/designated consumers must buy a share of renewable power; **solar RPO 8% by March 2022**.
[64:5:4] - **Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022:** RPO recast as a duty to **consume** renewable energy.
[64:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.43 (RPO, solar RPO 8%); app notes 5:64 sub 5-6
## SUB 6 | IREDA and the Clean Energy Fund
[64:6:0] - **IREDA:** set up **1987** as a **Non-Banking Financial** institution; **Public Limited Government Company** under the **administrative control of MNRE**; motto "Energy for Ever".
[64:6:1] - **Objective:** **financial support** to schemes generating electricity from **new and renewable sources** and **conserving energy through energy efficiency**.
[64:6:2] - **Status:** **Navratna** from **April 2024** (it was a Mini Ratna when APPSC G1 asked in Jan 2023); listed on NSE and BSE **29 Nov 2023**.
[64:6:3] - Functions: project finance, appraisal, consultancy – **not setting tariffs**.
[64:6:4] - **National Clean Energy Fund (NCEF):** **Budget 2010-11**; **Clean Energy Cess on coal, lignite and peat** (₹50/t, later ₹400/t); funded **research and innovative clean-energy projects**; cess subsumed in **GST (1 July 2017)**.
[64:6:5] > G1 2023 angle: "Navratna" ✗ then (✓ since April 2024); "finances RE and energy efficiency" ✓; "under MNRE" ✓.
[64:6:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.118 (IREDA); PMF Environment Part 6 p.23 (Clean Energy Cess, Budget 2010-11); app notes 5:64 sub 7

  The National Clean Energy Fund (NCEF) was financed by a cess levied on which of the following?
  Petrol and diesel | *Coal, lignite and peat | Natural gas | Electricity bills
  x: The NCEF, announced in the 2010-11 Budget, was financed by the Clean Energy Cess on coal, lignite and peat.
