  *To fund research and innovative projects in clean energy technologies | To subsidise coal-based power plants | To pay compensation for nuclear accidents | To fund rural roads
  x: The NCEF was set up to fund research and innovative projects in clean energy and renewable energy, to cut dependence on fossil fuels.

=== NOTES 5:67 | Other Renewables – Biomass, Biofuels, Small Hydro, Geothermal, Tidal, Waste-to-energy
## SUB 0 | Bioethanol – Feedstocks, Gasohol, Power Alcohol and Global Producers
[67:0:0] # Feedstocks and process
[67:0:1] - **Bioethanol:** made by **fermentation** of sugar or starch by yeast **Saccharomyces cerevisiae** (baker's yeast); can be mixed with petrol to improve combustion and lower emissions.
[67:0:2] TABLE head: Feedstock | Fact
  [67:0:2.0] Sugarcane (juice, molasses) | India's main ethanol source; molasses = excellent raw material for power alcohol
  [67:0:2.1] Maize (corn) | Starch-rich energy crop for ethanol; principal US feedstock
  [67:0:2.2] Damaged grains, cassava, rotten potatoes, sugar beet | Allowed under the National Policy on Biofuels
  [67:0:2.3] Jatropha, Pongamia, sunflower | Oilseeds → biodiesel, not ethanol
[67:0:3] - Potato, rice and wheat are not the classic "ethanol crop" answer; sugarcane (UPSC 2009) and maize (UPSC 2010) are.
[67:0:4] # Terms
[67:0:5] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [67:0:5.0] Gasohol | Petrol (gasoline) + ethanol, typically ~10% ethanol
  [67:0:5.1] Power alcohol | Fuel-grade (anhydrous) ethanol, mainly from molasses (sugar-industry by-product)
  [67:0:5.2] Rectified spirit | Ethanol with about 5% water (~95% ethanol)
  [67:0:5.3] Absolute alcohol | ~100% ethanol
[67:0:6] # Global producers
[67:0:7] - **USA** (maize/corn) = world's **largest producer, consumer and exporter** of fuel ethanol / gasohol; **Brazil** (sugarcane) second; together ~80% of world ethanol – so in UPSC 2025 Statement I (Brazil > USA) is false, Statement II (corn vs sugarcane) is true.
[67:0:8] - **Brazil:** **mandatory ethanol blending since 1976** (~25% since 2007); regarded as the world's first sustainable biofuel economy.
[67:0:9] # Indian technology firsts
[67:0:10] - **CSIR-NIIST, Thiruvananthapuram** (2017): bioethanol from **discarded cotton stalks** using a wild yeast strain.
[67:0:11] - **IIT Kharagpur "Soil to Soil"** (May 2017): enzyme-based (no chemical pre-treatment) process giving **biofuel** from crop residues; leftover biomass returns to the soil as bio-fertiliser.
[67:0:12] - **TVS Apache RTR 200 Fi E100** (2019) = India's first **ethanol-powered motorcycle** (TVS Motor).
[67:0:13] > Most-asked: ethanol crop (sugarcane / maize), gasohol = petrol + ethanol, largest producer USA, Brazil mandate.
[67:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.32; Rocket Environment p.61-62; web: biospectrumindia.com (IIT-KGP, 31 May 2017); app notes 5:67 sub 3, sub 5
## SUB 1 | Biogas and Biomass Energy
[67:1:0] # Biomass energy
[67:1:1] - **Biomass energy** = solar energy stored by plants through **photosynthesis**; burned directly or converted to biogas/biofuels; renewable (unlike coal, natural gas, petroleum).
[67:1:2] - **Gobar gas = biomass energy** (from cattle dung) – not nuclear, geothermal or hydro.
[67:1:3] - Biomass from waste: agricultural waste (stubble, husk, manure, dairy waste), **food-processing residues, human sewage, biogenic municipal solid waste** (all three are biomass).
[67:1:4] - Burning biomass releases CO2 largely balanced by the CO2 it absorbed while growing (near carbon-neutral).
[67:1:5] # Biogas
[67:1:6] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [67:1:6.0] Composition | Methane ~50–75% + CO2 ~25–50% + traces (H2S, moisture); piped natural gas is 85–95% methane
  [67:1:6.1] Fuel gas | Methane – the burning component (cooking gas / gobar gas); not butane, propane, ethane
  [67:1:6.2] Process | Anaerobic digestion (biomethanation) / fermentation – in the absence of oxygen
  [67:1:6.3] Microbes | Methanogens (archaebacteria) produce methane
  [67:1:6.4] By-product | Slurry = good organic manure
[67:1:7] - **Composting** is **aerobic** decomposition, unlike biogas.
[67:1:8] - Pioneer: floating-drum **"Gramalakshmi"** plant of **Jashbhai Patel (1950s)**, spread by **KVIC**.
[67:1:9] - **CBG (Compressed Biogas)** = purified, compressed biogas, chemically identical to **CNG**.
[67:1:10] - **India's first Bio-CNG plant from agricultural residue: Pirangut, Pune** (Primove Engineering), inaugurated **2016** by Nitin Gadkari and Manohar Parrikar.
[67:1:11] - **Bagasse cogeneration:** sugar mills burn bagasse → **steam and power together**.
[67:1:12] # Gasification and microbial fuel cells
[67:1:13] - **Biomass gasification:** heating with **limited (controlled) oxygen** → syngas (**CO, H2, CO2**).
[67:1:14] - **Producer gas** = CO + H2 + CO2 + **methane**.
[67:1:15] - **Microbial Fuel Cell (MFC):** microbes act as **catalysts**, oxidise organic matter and pass electrons to an electrode; cleans wastewater and makes electricity together (no burning).
[67:1:16] > Biogas = methane + CO2, anaerobic, methanogens – asked about 10 times.
[67:1:17] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.350-351 (Ch22.6); Rocket Environment p.60-62; NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.32; web: gktoday.in (first Bio-CNG plant, Pune); app notes 5:67 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Geothermal Energy
[67:2:0] - **Source:** heat stored in the **Earth's interior**, produced mostly by **decay of radioactive** elements (uranium, potassium) and original planetary heat; surface signs: **hot springs, geysers, volcanoes**.
[67:2:1] - Not ultimately solar: **geothermal and nuclear** energy (biomass, wind, fossil fuels are stored solar energy).
[67:2:2] - Gives **24x7 baseload** power – independent of sunlight or wind.
[67:2:3] - **India's potential:** about **10,600 MW**; GSI identified ~340–381 hot springs.
[67:2:4] - **Provinces:** Himalaya, Naga-Lushai, Andaman-Nicobar; **Cambay**, **Son-Narmada-Tapi (SONATA)**, **West Coast**, Damodar, **Mahanadi**, **Godavari valley** – none in the **Ganga Delta / Indo-Gangetic Plain**.
[67:2:5] TABLE head: Field | State / UT
  [67:2:5.0] Puga Valley, Chumathang | Ladakh – most promising / highest potential (GSI)
  [67:2:5.1] Tattapani | Chhattisgarh
  [67:2:5.2] Manikaran | Himachal Pradesh
  [67:2:5.3] Tapovan | Uttarakhand
  [67:2:5.4] Surajkund | Jharkhand
  [67:2:5.5] Manuguru (old Khammam district), Godavari valley | Telangana (earlier Andhra Pradesh)
[67:2:6] - **India's first geothermal power project: Puga, Ladakh** (**ONGC**); described as the world's highest geothermal project.
[67:2:7] - **World:** first successful tapping of underground heat **Boise, Idaho, USA (1890)** – hot-water pipe network for heating; first geothermal **power** at **Larderello, Italy (1904)**.
[67:2:8] - **National Policy on Geothermal Energy** – India's first, **MNRE, September 2025**; **five pilot projects**.
[67:2:9] - **EGS** (Enhanced Geothermal Systems) = artificially stimulated reservoirs. Challenges: high drilling and exploration cost, remote sites, transmission, gas leakage, subsidence.
[67:2:10] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.353-354 (Ch22.9); OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography Part 10 p.13; PMF S&T Part 7 p.136; app notes 5:67 sub 9
## SUB 3 | Biodiesel – Jatropha, Pongamia and RUCO
[67:3:0] TABLE head: Crop | Fact
  [67:3:0.0] Jatropha curcas (ratanjyot) | The biodiesel plant; non-edible seeds ~40% oil; grows on wasteland, little water
  [67:3:0.1] Pongamia pinnata (Karanja) | Alternative biodiesel plant; oil rich in oleic acid
  [67:3:0.2] Mahua, neem, simarouba | Other non-edible biodiesel sources
[67:3:1] - Not biodiesel plants: guggal, rosha grass, java grass, isabgol, belladonna, senna, cotton, sugarcane, potato.
[67:3:2] - **Biodiesel** = methyl/ethyl esters of fatty acids by **transesterification** of vegetable oils/animal fats with methanol or ethanol.
[67:3:3] - **India's first biodiesel plant: Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh** (early 2000s).
[67:3:4] - **Palm stearin oil** = feedstock of about **94%** of India's biodiesel (mostly imported), not jatropha.
[67:3:5] - **RUCO** (Repurpose Used Cooking Oil, **FSSAI**) = collection and conversion of **used cooking oil into biodiesel**.
[67:3:6] - Blend still **below 0.5%**; target **5% (B5) by 2030**.
[67:3:7] - **April 2023:** Belgian firm **VITO** launched a 2-year biodiesel project at **Ayodhya**.
[67:3:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.61-62; NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.32; Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.352; app notes 5:67 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Tidal, Wave, OTEC and Desalination
[67:4:0] TABLE head: Site | State | Fact
  [67:4:0.0] Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) | Gujarat | Tidal range 5–10 m; ~7,000 MW – largest / best tidal site
  [67:4:0.1] Gulf of Kutch (Hanthal Creek) | Gujarat | Tidal range 5–8 m; major project proposed
  [67:4:0.2] Sundarbans – Durgaduani Creek | West Bengal | ~5 m; 3 MW pilot
[67:4:1] - Criterion: tidal range ~**5 m or more** in a narrow gulf/estuary. **Gulf of Mannar** is not a tidal site (offshore wind zone); Gulf of Aden / Panay are not Indian.
[67:4:2] - **Ocean energy potential (MNRE):** tidal about **12,455 MW** (mainly Khambhat and Kutch); wave about **40,000 MW**.
[67:4:3] - **First wave plant: Vizhinjam, Kerala (1991)**. **Sindhuja-I** ocean wave energy converter – **IIT Madras** (tested off Tuticorin).
[67:4:4] - **OTEC = Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion:** warm surface vs cold deep water (~1,000 m), ~**20°C** gap, tropics; sites **Lakshadweep, A&N**.
[67:4:5] - **NIOT, Chennai (Ministry of Earth Sciences)** = lead ocean-energy body; India's first desalination plant **Kavaratti, Lakshadweep (2005)**, LTTD, **1 lakh L/day**.
[67:4:6] - **Desalination** (removing salts from seawater) prepares large quantities of drinking water.
[67:4:7] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.350 (Ch22.5); PMF Physical Geography Part 7 p.92; app notes 5:67 sub 10
## SUB 5 | Aviation Biofuels and Sustainable Aviation Fuel
[67:5:0] - **First biofuel flight in India:** **SpiceJet**, **Dehradun–Delhi, 27 August 2018**, Bombardier Q-400; one engine 25% bio-jet + 75% ATF; jatropha bio-jet from **CSIR-IIP, Dehradun**.
[67:5:1] - **SAF** = **drop-in** synthesised hydrocarbons (not direct ethanol), blendable up to **50%** with jet fuel.
[67:5:2] - **SAF feedstocks:** **agricultural residues, corn grain, wastewater treatment sludge, wood-mill waste** – all four (UPSC 2024); also oilseeds, algae, MSW.
[67:5:3] - **SAF targets** (international flights): **1% by 2027, 2% by 2028, 5% by 2030**.
[67:5:4] - **IOCL Panipat** = first Indian ISCC CORSIA-certified SAF producer (Aug 2025). **BioE3 Policy 2024** backs bio-jet fuel.
[67:5:5] - **Global Biofuels Alliance:** launched **9 September 2023**, **G20 Summit, New Delhi**; core founders **India, USA, Brazil**; Secretariat **New Delhi**.
[67:5:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.62; app notes 5:67 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Biofuel Generations and Algal Fuels
[67:6:0] TABLE head: Generation | Feedstock | Example
  [67:6:0.0] 1G | Food crops: sugarcane, molasses, corn, vegetable oils | Bioethanol, biodiesel
  [67:6:0.1] 2G | Non-food lignocellulosic residue: rice straw, husk, wood chips, cotton stalks | Cellulosic ethanol
  [67:6:0.2] 3G | Algae / algal biomass | Algal biodiesel, biobutanol
  [67:6:0.3] 4G | Genetically modified algae, yeast, cyanobacteria; carbon-capturing crops | Carbon-negative fuels
[67:6:1] - **Biobutanol** (Clostridium acetobutylicum): higher energy content than ethanol.
[67:6:2] - **Algal biofuel:** grows in seas **and on land** (ponds, tanks, wastewater) – "seas only" is false.
[67:6:3] - **Limitations:** needs **high expertise/technology** and **large-scale facilities** that may raise ecological/social concerns (UPSC 2017: statements 2 and 3); energy-intensive lipid extraction; not cost-effective.
[67:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.31-32; Rocket Environment p.62; PMF S&T Part 8 p.2; app notes 5:67 sub 2
## SUB 7 | National Policy on Biofuels and Ethanol Blending
[67:7:0] - **NPB 2018** – aim: cut import dependence; targets **E20 + B5 by 2030**; categories: **basic** (1G bioethanol, biodiesel) and **advanced** (2G ethanol, drop-in fuels from MSW, 3G, **bio-CNG**); does not discourage advanced biofuels.
[67:7:1] - **Ethanol feedstock widened beyond molasses:** sugarcane juice, B-molasses, **cassava, damaged wheat, rotten potatoes, sugar beet**, maize, surplus FCI rice, agri residues – **not groundnut seeds or horse gram** (UPSC 2020: 1, 2, 5, 6).
[67:7:2] - **Surplus food grains** need **National Biofuel Coordination Committee (NBCC)** approval; NBCC chaired by the **Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas** (approved surplus FCI rice Apr 2020, maize Nov 2020).
[67:7:3] - **NPB 2022 amendment:** E20 advanced to **ESY 2025-26**; more feedstocks; SEZ/EOU production; new NBCC members may be added.
[67:7:4] - Enablers: **Motor Vehicles Act Section 52** (engine conversion); **100% FDI automatic** for biofuel technology (domestic use).
[67:7:5] TABLE head: Ethanol Blending Programme (MoPNG) | Date
  [67:7:5.0] E5 in 9 States + 4 UTs | 1 January 2003
  [67:7:5.1] E10 achieved | June 2022
  [67:7:5.2] PM's World Environment Day pledge: E20 by 2025 | 5 June 2021
  [67:7:5.3] E20 petrol mandatory (min RON 95) | 1 April 2026
  [67:7:5.4] BIS IS 19850:2026 (E22–E30) | May 2026
  [67:7:5.5] Next goal E30 | 2030
[67:7:6] - EBP is run by **MoPNG**; OMC ethanol prices: **maize > molasses > rice**; maize expansion pulled area from **pulses** and oilseeds.
[67:7:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.30-33; app notes 5:67 sub 4, sub 5
## SUB 8 | Bioenergy Schemes and the Andhra Pradesh Angle
[67:8:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Year / Body | Feature
  [67:8:0.0] SATAT | 2018, MoPNG | CBG from agri residue and MSW; CBG obligation 5% from 2028-29
  [67:8:0.1] GOBARdhan | 2018 | Cattle dung, farm waste → compost, biogas, bio-CNG
  [67:8:0.2] PM JI-VAN Yojana | 2019 | 2G / advanced biofuels; extended to 2028-29

## SUB 9 | Waste-to-energy and Small Hydro
[67:9:0] - **India's first waste-to-energy plant: Timarpur, Delhi (1987)**; later Okhla, Ghazipur, Narela-Bawana (Delhi).
[67:9:1] TABLE head: Route | Principle
  [67:9:1.0] Incineration | Direct burning of MSW in excess air
  [67:9:1.1] Pyrolysis | Heating without oxygen → char, bio-oil, syngas
  [67:9:1.2] Gasification | Partial oxidation (controlled oxygen) → syngas
  [67:9:1.3] Biomethanation | Microbes convert wet waste → biogas
  [67:9:1.4] RDF | Refuse-derived fuel = dry combustible part of MSW
[67:9:2] # Small hydro
[67:9:3] TABLE head: Small hydro class | Capacity
  [67:9:3.0] Micro | up to 100 kW
  [67:9:3.1] Mini | 101 kW – 2 MW
  [67:9:3.2] Small | 2 – 25 MW (upper limit)
[67:9:4] - Small hydro sites: hill streams (run-of-river), **canal falls, toes of dams**; ~half the potential in **Arunachal, Himachal, J&K, Uttarakhand**; installed ~5 GW (~**25%** of potential).
[67:9:5] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.350, 352 (Ch22.4.2, 22.8); app notes 5:67 sub 8
## SUB 10 | Renewable Classification – What Counts as Renewable
[67:10:0] - **MNRE renewables:** solar, wind, **bio-power**, **small hydro** and **large hydro** (renewable **since 2019**); geothermal, tidal, OTEC under development.
[67:10:1] - **Nuclear** = non-fossil but **not renewable** (uranium is exhaustible).
[67:10:2] - **Renewable resource:** biomass, solar, wind, hydro, tidal; **coal, natural gas, petroleum** are non-renewable.
[67:10:3] - **Not derived from the Sun:** **nuclear** and **geothermal** (UPPCS 2022 – both are correct; the key gives nuclear); biomass and wind are stored solar energy.
[67:10:4] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.60-61; Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.353; app notes 5:67 sub 0

=== NOTES 5:68 | Green Hydrogen – National Green Hydrogen Mission, Electrolysers, Applications
## SUB 0 | Hydrogen as a Fuel – Basic Facts
[68:0:0] - **Cleanest fuel:** burning hydrogen gives **only water** – least / minimum air pollution (coal, kerosene, diesel, petrol give CO2 and harmful gases; CNG and power alcohol still give CO2).
[68:0:1] - **Highest fuel (calorific) value:** about **150,000 kJ/kg** – above natural gas, gasoline, charcoal.
[68:0:2] - Burns in air at about **4% to 75%** by volume.
[68:0:3] - **Rocket fuel:** liquid hydrogen (**dihydrogen**, H2) with liquid oxygen in cryogenic stages – not hydrogen peroxide, heavy water or CFCs.
[68:0:4] - **Storage for vehicles:** hydrogen absorbed at low temperature by a **metal hydride** (e.g. palladium hydride) and released by exhaust heat.
[68:0:5] - Hydrogen is also the **most abundant element in the Universe** (~3/4 of matter) and the fuel of the Sun's fusion reactions.
[68:0:6] > Least pollution / highest fuel value / burning gives water – the classic hydrogen-fuel PYQ.
[68:0:7] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.354 (Ch22.10 fuel cells); app notes 5:68 sub 0, sub 6
## SUB 1 | Applications of Green Hydrogen
[68:1:0] - **Uses of green hydrogen (UPSC 2023 – all three correct):** **directly as a fuel in internal combustion** engines (H2-ICE), **blended with natural gas** for heat or power, and in **hydrogen fuel cells** to run vehicles.
[68:1:1] - **Decarbonises fertiliser plants (ammonia), oil refineries and steel plants** (UPSC 2023 – all three) – **hard-to-abate** sectors where direct electrification is difficult.
[68:1:2] - **Industry:** refining (**desulphurisation**), **ammonia for fertilisers**, methanol, **steel by DRI** (hydrogen replaces **coking coal**).
[68:1:3] - **Fuel uses:** fuel-cell vehicles (buses, trucks, trains, ships), rocket fuel, **H-CNG** (hydrogen blended with CNG).
[68:1:4] - **Green ammonia** = nitrogen + green hydrogen; fertiliser, fuel, marine fuel.
[68:1:5] - **India's first green hydrogen blending project:** **NTPC + Gujarat Gas Ltd**, **Kawas, Surat** (Jan 2023), blending into the PNG network; PNGRB allowed 5% blending at start, scaling to 20%.
[68:1:6] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.355 (Ch22.10.1); PMF Environment Part 7 p.101 (UPSC 2023 solved); web: pib.gov.in PRID=1888334 (NTPC–Gujarat Gas blending, 3 Jan 2023); app notes 5:68 sub 7
## SUB 2 | Colours of Hydrogen
[68:2:0] TABLE head: Colour | Production route | CO2
  [68:2:0.0] Green | Electrolysis of water with renewable power | Zero – only zero-carbon colour
  [68:2:0.1] Grey | Steam methane reforming (SMR) of natural gas | High; ~95% of production; cheapest
  [68:2:0.2] Blue | SMR + carbon capture and storage (CCS) | Low
  [68:2:0.3] Pink / purple | Electrolysis with nuclear power | Near-zero
  [68:2:0.4] Turquoise | Methane pyrolysis → solid carbon | Near-zero
  [68:2:0.5] Brown / black | Coal gasification without CCS | Very high
  [68:2:0.6] White | Naturally occurring geological hydrogen | –
[68:2:1] - **SMR:** methane + steam at **700–1000°C**, **nickel catalyst** → hydrogen + CO.
[68:2:2] - Cost (Jul 2026): grey **$1.5–2/kg** vs green **~$4/kg**.
[68:2:3] - "Green" means the **production route (renewable energy)** – not sea water, not coal, not a green-coloured gas.
[68:2:4] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.356 (Ch22.10.2); app notes 5:68 sub 1
## SUB 3 | Fuel Cells
[68:3:0] - **Fuel cell** = electrochemical device: **H2 + O2 → electricity (DC) + water + heat**; no combustion; efficiency up to ~55%.
[68:3:1] - With pure hydrogen the only by-products are **heat and water**; FCEV exhaust = **water vapour** (and warm air) – not ammonia, nitrogen, oxygen or hydrogen peroxide.
[68:3:2] - Fuel cells power buildings **and** small devices (laptops); they give **DC, not AC** (UPSC 2015: only statement 1 correct).
[68:3:3] - A fuel cell combines hydrogen with **oxygen**, not carbon dioxide.
[68:3:4] # PEM fuel cell steps
[68:3:5] - 1. **Anode:** H2 → 2H+ + 2e-; electrons flow through the external circuit.
[68:3:6] - 2. **Protons cross the membrane**; **cathode:** 1/2 O2 + 2H+ + 2e- → H2O + heat.
[68:3:7] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.354 (Ch22.10); app notes 5:68 sub 5
## SUB 4 | Hydrogen Mobility Firsts
[68:4:0] TABLE head: First | Builder / Site
  [68:4:0.0] Hydrogen-powered train coach tested | ICF, Chennai (2025)
  [68:4:0.1] Hydrogen train in service | Jind–Sonipat, Haryana, 10 coaches, from July 2026
  [68:4:0.2] Indigenous fuel-cell ferry | Cochin Shipyard Ltd
  [68:4:0.3] Indigenous fuel-cell bus (2022) | KPIT + CSIR-NCL, Pune ("Veera Vahana" is wrong)
  [68:4:0.4] H-CNG buses | Delhi, IOCL (2020)
[68:4:1] - **World's first fuel-cell car to cross a continent to Sydney (27 Dec 2003): "Apollondine"**, built and driven by **Tamagawa University** (Tokyo) students; ~4,084 km run.
[68:4:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:68 sub 8
## SUB 5 | National Green Hydrogen Mission
[68:5:0] - Approved by **Union Cabinet, 4 January 2023**; nodal ministry **MNRE**; outlay **₹19,744 crore** up to **2029-30**.
[68:5:1] TABLE head: Component | Role | Outlay
  [68:5:1.0] SIGHT | Incentives for electrolyser manufacturing + green H2 production | ₹17,490 cr
  [68:5:1.1] Pilot projects | Steel, mobility, shipping, storage, biomass hydrogen | ₹1,466 cr
  [68:5:1.2] SHIP (Strategic Hydrogen Innovation Partnership) | PPP for R&D | ₹400 cr
  [68:5:1.3] Green Hydrogen Hubs | Production-use-export clusters; 4 Hydrogen Valley Innovation Clusters | –
[68:5:2] - **2030 targets:** **5 MMT/year** green hydrogen; **125 GW** added RE; **60–100 GW electrolysers** (not 200 GW); **6 lakh jobs**; ₹8 lakh crore investment; **50 MMT/yr GHG** cut.
[68:5:3] - Goals: **energy independence 2047**, **net zero 2070**.
[68:5:4] - Progress: **15 companies**, 3,000 MW electrolyser manufacturing; green ammonia 7,24,000 TPA at **₹53.27/kg** (SECI); **Japanese** firms signed green ammonia/methanol export deals (Jul 2026).
[68:5:5] - **Hub ports:** **Deendayal (Kandla), Gujarat**; **V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin), Tamil Nadu** (₹35 crore bunkering pilot); Paradip, Odisha.
[68:5:6] - Chronology: rooftop solar programme (2014) → **NGHM (Jan 2023)** → PM Internship Scheme (Oct 2024).
[68:5:7] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. p.355-356 (Ch22.10.1); NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.50; app notes 5:68 sub 2, sub 9
## SUB 6 | Electrolysers, Standard, Certification and Storage
[68:6:0] - **Electrolyser** = uses **electricity to split water** into hydrogen and oxygen.
[68:6:1] TABLE head: Type | Feature
  [68:6:1.0] Alkaline | Liquid KOH/NaOH electrolyte; oldest, mature
  [68:6:1.1] PEM | Solid polymer membrane; compact; quick response suits variable RE
  [68:6:1.2] Solid oxide | High-temperature steam; most efficient
  [68:6:1.3] AEM | Can use non-platinum catalysts (nickel, cobalt, iron)
[68:6:2] - Concern: **Chinese dominance** of electrolyser supply; dependence on imported electrolysers.
[68:6:3] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [68:6:3.0] Green Hydrogen Standard (MNRE, Aug 2023) | Well-to-gate ≤ 2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2 (12-month average)
  [68:6:3.1] GHCI certification scheme | April 2025
  [68:6:3.2] Certification nodal authority | Bureau of Energy Efficiency
[68:6:4] # Storage and transport
[68:6:5] TABLE head: Storage method | Fact
  [68:6:5.0] Compression | High-pressure composite cylinders
  [68:6:5.1] Liquefaction | −253°C (cryogenic)
  [68:6:5.2] Metal hydrides | Solid-state storage; absorbed in alloys, released on heating
  [68:6:5.3] Chemical carriers | Ammonia, methanol, LOHC (not CO2)
[68:6:6] - Water need: **~9 litres** purified water per kg hydrogen.
[68:6:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:68 sub 3, sub 4, sub 6
## SUB 7 | Andhra Pradesh – Green Hydrogen Policy and Valley
[68:7:0] - **AP Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy (2023):** target **0.5 MTPA green hydrogen or 2.0 MTPA green ammonia** in five years (not 1 MTPA); nodal agency **NREDCAP**; RE may be sourced via open access, captive, **third-party sale and power exchange** (allowed, not prohibited); 100% SGST reimbursement for 5 years.
[68:7:1] - **AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024**: green hydrogen export; net zero 2047.
[68:7:2] - **Green Hydrogen Valley Declaration, Amaravati, 19 July 2025:** AP as India's green hydrogen capital; goal **1.5 MMTPA by 2030** + 5 GW electrolyser manufacturing; nodal **SRM University-AP**; valley cluster at Kakinada.
[68:7:3] TABLE head: Project | Place
  [68:7:3.0] NTPC Green Energy hub | Pudimadaka (Anakapalli)
  [68:7:3.1] AM Green green ammonia | Kakinada
  [68:7:3.2] NTPC Simhadri | Seawater-to-hydrogen blending trials (Jan 2026)
[68:7:4] - Amaravati is not a Paradip green ammonia export terminal.
[68:7:5] ~~ Sources: web: iamrenew.com (AP policy notified, 0.5 MTPA, NREDCAP, third-party and power exchange routes); CARE APPSC Feb 2026 p.20; app notes 5:68 sub 10

=== NOTES 5:70 | Energy Efficiency – Bee, Energy Conservation Act, Pat, Star Labelling, Ujala
## SUB 0 | Lighting Technologies – LED, CFL, Fluorescent, Sodium, Filament
[70:0:0] TABLE head: Lamp | Features
  [70:0:0.0] LED | Highest efficacy, longest life, no mercury; semiconductor emitter (gallium arsenide family) – the most energy-saving lamp
  [70:0:0.1] CFL (Compact Fluorescent Lamp) | Mercury vapour + phosphor; ~75% less energy than bulbs; shorter life and less efficient than LED
  [70:0:0.2] Fluorescent tube | Low-pressure mercury vapour + argon (sometimes neon, krypton, xenon)
  [70:0:0.3] Incandescent / GLS filament | Cheapest for the same wattage; only ~10–15% of input radiated as light, rest heat; power factor = unity (purely resistive)
  [70:0:0.4] Sodium vapour | Yellow, monochromatic light that does not split in fog/water droplets → street lights
  [70:0:0.5] Mercury vapour | White light
[70:0:1] - **Why mercury in fluorescent lamps (UPSC 2010):** when switched on, **mercury vapour emits ultraviolet**; the **phosphor coating** converts UV to visible light (mercury itself does not convert UV).
[70:0:2] - **CFL vs LED (IAS 2011):** CFL uses mercury vapour + phosphor, LED a semiconductor ✓; CFL less efficient than LED ✓; "CFL lasts longer" ✗ → **I and III**.
[70:0:3] - **Vacuum filament lamps:** contain **no gas** (gas-filled lamps use argon/nitrogen) → "none of the above".
[70:0:4] - **A–R (APPSC 2021 ×2):** government urges replacing bright and CFL bulbs with **LEDs** because LEDs light with **great energy efficiency** → **A and R true, R explains A**.
[70:0:5] - **A–R (RAS 2013):** LED life longer than CFL ✓; LED more efficient than CFL ✓; books key "R explains A" (LEDs run cooler); strictly the long life comes from solid-state design (no filament or electrodes to wear).
[70:0:6] > Lighting is the heaviest PYQ block of this row (16 PYQs: UPSC 2010, IAS 2011, UPPCS 2000/2006/2007/2015, SSC 2017 ×2, RAS 2013, APPSC 2021, APPSC AEE flashcards).
[70:0:7] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:70 sub 6; general knowledge (filament lamp data), not checked
## SUB 1 | Energy Conservation Act, BEE and Organisations
[70:1:0] # Energy Conservation Act, 2001
[70:1:1] - Set up the **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)**; BEE operational from **1 March 2002**; statutory body under the **Ministry of Power**.
[70:1:2] - **Designated consumers:** mandatory **energy audits** and norms; **penalties** for non-compliance.
[70:1:3] - EE norms for buildings with connected load **>100 kW** or contract demand **>120 kVA**.
[70:1:4] # Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022
[70:1:5] - **Lok Sabha August 2022 → Rajya Sabha December 2022** – passed by Parliament in **December 2022** (APPSC EO 2023).
[70:1:6] TABLE head: Provision | Detail
  [70:1:6.0] Carbon Credit Trading Scheme | Legal basis for a national carbon market – Section 14AA
  [70:1:6.1] Non-fossil obligation | Designated consumers to use a minimum share of non-fossil energy
  [70:1:6.2] Building codes | Extended to large residential buildings (ECSBC)
  [70:1:6.3] Vehicles and vessels | Efficiency norms can be set
[70:1:7] # Organisations
[70:1:8] TABLE head: Body | Status / Role
  [70:1:8.0] BEE | Statutory (EC Act 2001), Ministry of Power; runs PAT, S&L, ECBC, SEEI, CAFE, NECA
  [70:1:8.1] EESL | JV of Ministry of Power PSUs; runs UJALA, SLNP, National Efficient Cooking Programme
  [70:1:8.2] PCRA | Petroleum Conservation Research Association (MoPNG); runs SAKSHAM (not BEE)
[70:1:9] - **NMEEE** = one of the **8 missions of NAPCC (2008)**. India imports ~**80%** of its oil → efficiency = energy security.
[70:1:10] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:70 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Standards and Labelling and Building Codes
[70:2:0] - **S&L programme:** launched **2006**; **BEE under Ministry of Power**; **1–5 star**; each extra star saves **~10–15%**.
[70:2:1] TABLE head: Mandatory | Voluntary
  [70:2:1.0] Refrigerators, ACs, ceiling fans, TVs, washing machines, geysers (storage water heaters), LED lamps, tubular fluorescent lamps, LPG stove, distribution transformers | Industrial motors, computers, microwave ovens
[70:2:2] - **UPSC 2016:** the star label is found on ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps → **1, 2 and 3**.
[70:2:3] - **From 1 January 2026:** labels mandatory for fridges, TVs, LPG stoves; makers **penalised if actual use deviates** from the label.
[70:2:4] TABLE head: Code | Year | Covers
  [70:2:4.0] ECBC | 2007 | New commercial buildings; 25–40% less energy
  [70:2:4.1] ECO Niwas Samhita | 2018 | Residential buildings
  [70:2:4.2] ECSBC | 2024 | Adds sustainability after the 2022 amendment

## SUB 4 | Days, Awards and AP Initiatives
[70:4:0] - **National Energy Conservation Day: 14 December**; Week **14–20 December**.
[70:4:1] - **NECA** (instituted **1991**): given by **BEE / Ministry of Power, not MNRE**; NECA 2025: **Chandigarh** first.
[70:4:2] - **ANGAN 2022** (BEE): **NEERMAN Awards** (National Energy Efficiency Roadmap for Movement towards Affordable & Natural Habitat) announced for the first time.
[70:4:3] - **Rural LED street lighting via EESL:** **Andhra Pradesh** = first State (programme first implemented in the country in AP).
[70:4:4] - **NEC Week 2024 in AP (APPSC FRO 2025):** School Education Department + Special Chief Secretary (Energy) involved students; short-video contest **'Bright Ideas and Brighter Future'** for classes 8–10; focus on climate mitigation, GHG cuts, local efficiency → **all three correct**.
[70:4:5] - **APSECM** (2012): India's **first standalone State Designated Agency** of BEE; won NECA First Prize.
[70:4:6] - AP: **ECBC in 123 ULBs**; **PAT – 59 industries**, ~1.16 Mtoe saved; first **IoT energy pilot at an MSME, East Godavari**; **Super ECBC building, Sagar Nagar, Visakhapatnam**.

## SUB 5 | Everyday Conservation and PCRA
[70:5:0] - Efficiency **reduces the need for new energy sources** → sustainable development (APPSC FBO 2025).
[70:5:1] - Saving practices: **LED lights**, star-rated appliances, switching off idle loads, avoiding AC overuse; **bicycles save fuel** (and cut pollution, noise).
[70:5:2] - **Pressure cooker** saves about **20%** cooking gas for rice (PCRA tip).
[70:5:3] - **PCRA SAKSHAM** (Sanrakshan Kshamata Mahotsav): annual one-month **fuel conservation mega campaign**, launched **January 2020** edition (APPSC PL 2020); SAKSHAM 2026 at Chandigarh.
[70:5:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:70 sub 4, 7
## SUB 6 | UJALA, SLNP and Other Schemes
[70:6:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Year / Body | Feature
  [70:6:0.0] UJALA (Unnat Jyoti by Affordable LEDs for All) | January 2015, EESL | 36.86 crore LED bulbs, 72.18 lakh tube lights, 23.59 lakh fans
  [70:6:0.1] SLNP (Street Lighting National Programme) | January 2015, EESL | LED street lights replace sodium vapour
  [70:6:0.2] ADEETIE | July 2025, ₹1,000 crore | MSME efficiency; interest subvention 5% micro/small, 3% medium; 60 clusters, 14 sectors
  [70:6:0.3] CAFE norms | 2017, BEE | Fuel efficiency for cars
  [70:6:0.4] National Efficient Cooking Programme | EESL | 20 lakh induction stoves
[70:6:1] - 9.5 crore = PMUY LPG connections (do not confuse with UJALA).
[70:6:2] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:70 sub 4
## SUB 7 | PAT and the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
[70:7:0] - **PAT:** market mechanism under **NMEEE** – energy-reduction targets for **Designated Consumers**; over-achievers earn **ESCerts**, under-achievers buy them; traded on **power exchanges**.
[70:7:1] - **PAT Cycle I (2012-15): 478 units in 8 sectors** – thermal power, iron & steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper, textiles; **railways** added later.
[70:7:2] - After CCTS, PAT keeps 4 sectors: **thermal power, railways, DISCOMs, commercial buildings** (Jun 2026).
[70:7:3] TABLE head: Feature | PAT | CCTS
  [70:7:3.0] Certificate | ESCerts (energy intensity) | CCCs (emission intensity)
  [70:7:3.1] Start | 2012 | Notified 2023 – first mandatory carbon market
  [70:7:3.2] Coverage | 478 units, 8 sectors (Cycle I) | 9 heavy industries, 208 units
  [70:7:3.3] Administrator / Regulator | BEE | BEE / CERC
[70:7:4] - CCTS supports **45% cut in GDP emission intensity by 2030** (vs 2005); UK **CBAM** recognised CCTS (from **1 January 2027**).

=== NOTES 5:71 | Energy Access and Distribution Programmes – Saubhagya, Ddugjy, Uday, Pm-kusum, Pm Surya Ghar
## SUB 0 | PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana and Net Metering
[71:0:0] - **Launched Feb 2024; MNRE**; Central Sector scheme; outlay **₹75,021 crore**; goal = **rooftop solar on 1 crore residential houses** by **March 2027** – rural and urban (not urban-only).
[71:0:1] - **Up to 300 units/month free**; households become **prosumers**.
[71:0:2] - **CFA: 60% for the first 2 kW; 40% for extra capacity up to 3 kW** (not a flat 30%); collateral-free loans at about **7%** (repo-linked, not 4%); **100% online** national portal.
[71:0:3] - **Capacity building:** MNRE trains people at the grassroots in installation, operation, maintenance and repair; **more than 3 lakh skilled manpower** through fresh skilling and upskilling.
[71:0:4] - 30 GW rooftop; **one Model Solar Village per district**; **world's largest domestic rooftop solar scheme**; subsumed Rooftop Solar Phase II.
[71:0:5] - Progress (2025): 14.43 lakh systems, 18.14 lakh households.
[71:0:6] - **Net metering (UPSC 2016 ×2):** promotes **production and use of solar energy by households/consumers** – surplus fed to the grid; household pays only the difference.
[71:0:7] > Statements angle: UPSC/IAS 2025 – all three statements correct; RAS 2024 – only "1 crore houses / 300 units" and "100% online" correct.
[71:0:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:71 sub 4; CARE APPSC Apr 2026 p.46; general knowledge (CFA, loan rate), not checked
## SUB 1 | UDAY and RDSS – Discom Finances
[71:1:0] - **UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana), Nov 2015, Ministry of Power:** **financial turnaround and revival of DISCOMs** (UPSC 2016).
[71:1:1] - States took over **75%** of discom debt (**50% in 2015-16 + 25% in 2016-17**) via **UDAY bonds**; discoms bonded the other 25%.
[71:1:2] - UDAY states account for **97%** of total outstanding discom debt (Power Ministry; APPSC G2); bonds actually issued covered ~86% of debt to be taken over (2017).
[71:1:3] - **Rajasthan** had the **largest discom debt exposure** under UDAY (~₹70,000+ crore bonded).
[71:1:4] TABLE head: Feature | UDAY | RDSS (2021)
  [71:1:4.0] Aim | Discom debt takeover | Smart prepaid metering, loss cut
  [71:1:4.1] Outlay | – | ₹3,03,758 crore
  [71:1:4.2] AT&C target | 15% by 2018-19 | 12–15%
  [71:1:4.3] ACS-ARR gap | Zero | Zero
[71:1:5] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (Part 5) "UDAY Scheme"; gktoday.in "UDAY covers 97% of discom debt: Centre" (via search); app notes 5:71 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Saubhagya, DDUGJY and IPDS – Electrification
[71:2:0] - **Saubhagya** (Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana), **Sept/Oct 2017:** **universal household electrification** – last-mile connections to all un-electrified households in **rural and urban** areas (CDS 2020; APPSC FSO).
[71:2:1]   - Not clean cooking fuel (that is **PMUY**), not LPG subsidy.
[71:2:2]   - **2.86 crore** willing households electrified (2.82 crore = older figure).
[71:2:3] - **DDUGJY (Dec 2014):** rural distribution; **feeder separation** (agri vs non-agri); subsumed **RGGVY**.
[71:2:4] - **IPDS (Dec 2014):** **urban** sub-transmission and distribution, metering, IT; subsumed **R-APDRP**.
[71:2:5] - Last village electrified: **Leisang (Manipur), 28 April 2018**.
[71:2:6] TABLE head: Scheme | Year | Ministry
  [71:2:6.0] UDAY | 2015 | Power
  [71:2:6.1] PMUY | 2016 | MoPNG
  [71:2:6.2] Saubhagya | 2017 | Power
  [71:2:6.3] PM-KUSUM | 2019 | MNRE (not Power)
  [71:2:6.4] Surya Nutan | 2022 | IOCL indoor solar stove (not EESL)
  [71:2:6.5] PM Surya Ghar | 2024 | MNRE
[71:2:7] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy (Part 7) "Saubhagya"; app notes 5:71 sub 0-1
## SUB 3 | PM-KUSUM – Farm Solar
[71:3:0] - **PM-KUSUM (2019, MNRE):** primary aim = **subsidies for solar irrigation pumps** and farm solar (APPSC FBO 2025).
[71:3:1] TABLE head: Component | Covers
  [71:3:1.0] A | Grid-connected solar/RE plants on farm/barren land
  [71:3:1.1] B | Standalone solar pumps
  [71:3:1.2] C | Solarisation of grid-connected pumps
[71:3:2] - B and C subsidy: **30% Centre, 30% State, 40% farmer** (bank loan possible).
[71:3:3] - Urban household rooftop solar = PM Surya Ghar, not PM-KUSUM.
[71:3:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:71 sub 3; NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.55
## SUB 4 | Andhra Pradesh – Free Power and Rooftop Solar
[71:4:0] - **Free power for SC/ST households:** the Social Welfare Department paid bills up to **75 units** (APPSC question) → **100 units** (Dec 2018, Jagjeevan Jyothi) → **200 units** for BPL SC/ST since 2019 (now **20.26 lakh** households; ₹10,449.92 crore subsidy, FY 2024-25).
[71:4:1] - **SC/ST:** free rooftop solar via **Virtual Net Metering**.
[71:4:2] - PM Surya Ghar target in AP: **6 lakh** (6,000 per constituency).
[71:4:3] - PM-KUSUM in AP: **2.93 lakh** pumps solarised; RDSS ₹15,083.14 crore.
[71:4:4] ~~ Sources: thehansindia.com 'Free power up to 100 units to SC, ST households' (6 Dec 2018, via search); app notes 5:71 sub 6
## SUB 5 | Clean Cooking – PMUY
[71:5:0] - **PMUY (2016, MoPNG):** deposit-free LPG to poor women; Phase I **8 crore** by **2019**; now **9.5 crore+**.
[71:5:1] - **Ujjwala 2.0:** free first refill and stove; migrants by **self-declaration**; **₹1,600** per connection.
[71:5:2] - Refill subsidy since **Oct 2023: ₹300 × 9 refills/year**.
[71:5:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:71 sub 5

=== NOTES 5:73 | Environment, Ecology and Ecosystem – Components, Food Chains, Energy Flow and Ecological Pyramids
## SUB 0 | Ecosystem – Concept, Biotic and Abiotic Components, Producers and Decomposers
[73:0:0] # Concept
[73:0:1] - **Ecosystem:** a community of organisms **together with the non-living environment** in which they live, interacting as one functional unit (pond, ocean, forest, even an **aquarium**). Term coined by the British botanist **Sir Arthur G. Tansley in 1935**.
[73:0:2] - **Two components:** **biotic** (producers, consumers, decomposers) and **abiotic** (energy, water, air, soil, nutrients, climate). "Evolution" is a process, not a component.
[73:0:3] - An ecosystem is a **natural, open system**: energy and matter enter and leave; it has its own **productivity**; it is **not a closed system with fixed boundaries** (UPSC/APPSC "NOT correct" item).
[73:0:4] - The **biosphere** (narrow zone where **lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere** meet) is treated in most books as an **open system** – energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat (UPPSC RO/ARO 2017 key: A true, R false). Strictly, the Earth is open for energy but nearly **closed for matter**.
[73:0:5] - All components are **interdependent**: a change in one population affects the rest – so "components are not interdependent" is false, while "human activities affect the environment" is true.
[73:0:6] - **Functions:** energy flow (one-way), nutrient cycling, production, **self-regulation (homeostasis)**; the **food chain** is the **dynamic part** of an ecosystem (APPSC G1 2008), while producers, consumers and decomposers form its structure.
[73:0:7] - **Biogeochemical (nutrient) cycle:** movement of **chemical elements** (C, N, P) through **biotic and abiotic** components – energy does not cycle; **photosynthesis removes CO₂**; the **phosphorus cycle begins with rock weathering**.
[73:0:8] # Abiotic components
[73:0:9] TABLE head: Type | Factors
  [73:0:9.0] Energy | Sunlight – primary source and driving force
  [73:0:9.1] Climatic | Light, temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind
  [73:0:9.2] Edaphic | Soil – texture, pH, minerals, drainage
  [73:0:9.3] Topographic | Altitude, slope, aspect
  [73:0:9.4] Materials | CO₂, water, nitrates, phosphates; humus and other organic compounds
[73:0:10] - **Abiotic factor:** any **non-living** component that affects organisms or their environment – air, water, light are abiotic; plants, bacteria and animals are biotic.
[73:0:11] - **Liebig's Law of the Minimum:** growth limited by the nutrient in shortest supply. **Shelford's Law of Tolerance:** both too little and too much limit.
[73:0:12] - **Stenothermal** organisms tolerate only a **narrow** temperature range; **eurythermal** a wide range (likewise stenohaline / euryhaline for salinity).
[73:0:13] - **Cold-blooded (poikilothermic)** animals – **frogs**, snakes, lizards, fish, crocodiles – take the temperature of their surroundings.
[73:0:14] # Producers (autotrophs) – trophic level I
[73:0:15] - **Autotrophs** make their own food; their **carbon and energy needs are met by photosynthesis** (NCERT X): they take in **CO₂ and water** (not oxygen) and, with **sunlight and chlorophyll**, convert them into **carbohydrates**, which give the plant energy.
[73:0:16] - **Photosynthesis** turns **light energy into chemical energy**; it needs light – normally daytime sunlight, but it also runs under moonlight or artificial light, so it is not tied to clock time (State PSC key "day or night").
[73:0:17] - On land the major producers are **herbaceous and woody plants**; in water, **phytoplankton** / microscopic **algae** and seaweeds.
[73:0:18] - **Chemoautotrophs:** bacteria of deep-sea vents / active volcanoes oxidise **hydrogen sulphide**; many **archaea** (methanogens) use energy from chemical compounds – they too are producers.
[73:0:19] - Some **bacteria** (green sulphur bacteria) photosynthesise with **invisible infrared** light.
[73:0:20] - **Producers act as intermediaries between the biotic and abiotic components** (official UPPSC key; many books also call **decomposers** the link, because they return nutrients to the abiotic pool).
[73:0:21] - **Chlorella** (a green alga) has the highest efficiency of converting solar energy into chemical energy among the usual options.
[73:0:22] - **Oxygen:** most of Earth's oxygen comes from **algae** / marine phytoplankton – ocean phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria give **about 50%** of the world's oxygen, more than rainforests; oxygen-rich surface water holds far **less** oxygen than air (UPSC 2025: only statement II correct).
[73:0:23] - **Cactus** photosynthesises in its green **stem** (leaves reduced to spines).
[73:0:24] # Consumers and decomposers
[73:0:25] TABLE head: Component | Examples
  [73:0:25.0] Primary consumers (herbivores) | Cow, deer, goat, rabbit, caterpillar, zooplankton
  [73:0:25.1] Secondary consumers | Wolves, frog, fox
  [73:0:25.2] Tertiary / top carnivores | Lion, tiger, hawk, eagle
  [73:0:25.3] Omnivores | Man (primary and secondary consumer), bear
  [73:0:25.4] Decomposers (saprotrophs) | Bacteria and fungi – not viruses
  [73:0:25.5] Detritivores | Earthworms, millipedes, woodlice, nematodes – not jellyfish or seahorses
[73:0:26] - **Fungi are heterotrophs** (mostly saprotrophs that absorb food from dead matter; some parasitic or symbiotic).
[73:0:27] - **Parasitic nutrition:** obtaining food from another living organism **without killing it**.
[73:0:28] - **Decomposition:** breakdown of dead organic matter by **microorganisms (bacteria, fungi)** into simple inorganic nutrients; biodegradable waste is converted into useful compost by **bacteria**.
[73:0:29] - Steps: **fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation**; fully decomposed litter = **humus**. Fast when detritus is rich in nitrogen and sugars and climate warm and moist; slow with lignin, chitin, cold or anaerobic conditions.
[73:0:30] - If **decomposers are removed**, **mineral (nutrient) movement is blocked** – energy flow would continue for a while, but nutrients are not recycled.
[73:0:31] - Macroconsumers = phagotrophs; microconsumers = saprotrophs (osmotrophs). Free-living **Azotobacter** fixes nitrogen.
[73:0:32] - **Protists** are unicellular **eukaryotes**, not prokaryotes; cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes.
[73:0:33] # Types of ecosystem
[73:0:34] TABLE head: Type | Examples
  [73:0:34.0] Natural terrestrial | Forest, grassland, desert, tundra, mountain
  [73:0:34.1] Natural aquatic | Pond, lake, river, wetland, estuary, ocean
  [73:0:34.2] Artificial (man-modified) | Crop field, aquarium, park, village; city = extreme example
[73:0:35] - A **lake / pond** is the classic **self-sufficient (complete, self-regulating) natural ecosystem**; an aquarium, farmland or polyhouse depends on human inputs.
[73:0:36] > Exam angle: about 40 PYQs – definition of ecosystem, Tansley 1935, biotic vs abiotic, producers (green plants, algae, archaea), decomposers (bacteria and fungi), detritivores (UPSC 2021), "producers = intermediaries" (UPPSC), "most oxygen from algae".
[73:0:37] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.5-7 (Tansley 1935, components, producers on land/water, natural vs artificial); Rocket Environment p.59 (sheet #34: open system, components, bacteria + fungi); Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.13-16; PMF Environment Part 1 p.34, 36-37; PMF Environment Part 2 p.1-2 (UPSC 2013 decomposers, UPSC 2021 detritivores); OnlyIAS NCERT Geography Part 9 p.2-4 (decomposition steps)
[73:0:38] - **Frost** is an **abiotic** stressor of forests (freezes soil moisture, injures tissue); oomycetes, parasites and pathogens are biotic.
[73:0:39] - **Water balance:** organisms must maintain body water to live; **terrestrial** life needs **fresh water** because it cannot tolerate the high salt of saline water.
## SUB 1 | Food Chains, Trophic Levels, Food Webs and Biomagnification
[73:1:0] # Food chain
[73:1:1] - **Food chain:** the order in which organisms **feed upon each other** – producer → herbivore → carnivore; energy passes along it. It runs **across species**, not within one species' population, and it does **not** show the **numbers** eaten (that is a pyramid / food web) – UPSC 2013: only statement 1 correct.
[73:1:2] TABLE head: Chain | Starts with | Example
  [73:1:2.0] Grazing | Living green plants (autotrophs pass energy to herbivores) | Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake (→ eagle); grass → goat → human
  [73:1:2.1] Detritus (DFC) | Dead organic matter | Leaf litter → earthworm → chicken → hawk
  [73:1:2.2] Pond / aquatic | Phytoplankton | → zooplankton → small fish → large fish
  [73:1:2.3] Marine | Diatoms | → crustaceans → herrings (UPSC 2014)
  [73:1:2.4] Grassland | Grass | → grasshopper or rabbit → snake or hawk
[73:1:3] - "Grazing food chain begins with **dead leaves**" is **false** (that is the detritus chain); "autotrophs capture energy and transfer it to herbivores" is true (APPSC G2 Mains 2025: A false, R true).
[73:1:4] - In water the grazing chain is the main energy conduit; on land more energy flows through the detritus chain.
[73:1:5] # Trophic levels
[73:1:6] TABLE head: Level | Organisms
  [73:1:6.0] I | Producers – green plants, phytoplankton, seaweeds, chemosynthetic bacteria (vents, active volcanoes), algae
  [73:1:6.1] II | Primary consumers / herbivores – deer, ants, caterpillar, goat, zooplankton
  [73:1:6.2] III | Secondary consumers – frog, fox; a man eating goat flesh
  [73:1:6.3] IV | Tertiary / top carnivores – snake (in grass → grasshopper → frog → snake), hawk, lion
  [73:1:6.4] None single | Decomposers and detritivores recycle all levels
[73:1:7] - The **highest trophic level** is held by **carnivores** (top carnivores), not herbivores or decomposers.
[73:1:8] - **Man** is an omnivore – **primary as well as secondary consumer**; eating goat flesh makes him a **secondary consumer**.
[73:1:9] - **Producers outnumber primary consumers** (energy and numbers fall at each level).
[73:1:10] - A species can occupy more than one level; chains rarely exceed **4–5 levels**.
[73:1:11] - Missing-level question: "tiger, grass, snake, frog" has **no herbivore – second level missing**.
[73:1:12] # Food web and stability
[73:1:13] - **Food web:** network of interlinked food chains; **more complex → more stable** (alternative feeding paths).
[73:1:14] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [73:1:14.0] Resistance | Withstand a disturbance
  [73:1:14.1] Resilience | Recover after a disturbance
  [73:1:14.2] Homeostasis | Self-regulation up to a limit through feedback
[73:1:15] - Diverse systems (rainforest, coral reef) are more stable than tundra, desert or monoculture; overall the **ocean (marine ecosystem) is the most stable ecosystem** – it stays unchanged over long periods.
[73:1:16] - Warming and ocean acidification weaken calcifying plankton and corals, disrupting marine food webs.
[73:1:17] # Bioaccumulation vs biomagnification
[73:1:18] TABLE head: Bioaccumulation | Biomagnification (biological magnification)
  [73:1:18.0] Build-up of a pollutant inside one organism over its life | Rising concentration of toxicants at each higher trophic level – maximum in the topmost level
[73:1:19] - Only **persistent, fat-soluble, non-biodegradable** pollutants (DDT, mercury, PCBs) biomagnify – an increase in **toxicants**, not in algae, insects or weeds.
[73:1:20] - DDT (a **chlorinated hydrocarbon**): food crop → rat → snake → **hawk** – highest in the hawk; grasshopper → toad → **snake** – highest in the snake; causes **eggshell thinning** and seabird crashes.
[73:1:21] - **Methylmercury** – Minamata disease (Japan).
[73:1:22] - Pollutant types: biodegradable = sewage; non-biodegradable = DDT, plastic, asbestos; primary = CO, SO₂, NOx; secondary = O₃, **PAN**, smog.
[73:1:23] - **Trophic level:** the functional position (feeding step) an organism occupies in a food chain.
[73:1:24] > Exam angle: about 30 PYQs – food-chain order (UPPSC 2010, UPSC 2014), UPSC 2013 statements (×3), trophic level I = green plants (×4), man as consumer, biomagnification (UPSC 1997, 2010, 2018; APPSC ×2), most stable = ocean (×3).
[73:1:25] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 1 p.62-63 (trophic levels, food chains); PMF Environment Part 2 p.1-14 (UPSC 2013/2014/2021 PYQs, biomagnification, DDT); Rocket Environment p.55, 59, 63 (trophic levels, DDT highest at top level); Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.20-22, 24-25; NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.8
## SUB 2 | Environment, Ecology and Levels of Organisation
[73:2:0] # Environment
[73:2:1] - **Environment:** the sum total of living and non-living components, influences and events surrounding an organism; **biotic and abiotic factors interact**; it is never static. Composite: **physical** (land, water, air, nutrients), **biological** (organisms) and **cultural** elements – "all of the above" definitions hold.
[73:2:2] - Term "environment" first used in English by **Thomas Carlyle (1828)**.
[73:2:3] TABLE head: Category | Includes
  [73:2:3.0] Physical | Lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere; nutrients, water, air
  [73:2:3.1] Biotic | Plants, animals, microbes
  [73:2:3.2] Cultural | Man-made – social, economic, political institutions
[73:2:4] - Renewable resources come from **both** biotic and abiotic parts (sunlight, wind, water) – "only biotic elements give renewable resources" is false.
[73:2:5] - **Primary functions:** provide resources, **assimilate wastes**, habitat for biodiversity – "generating synthetic chemicals" is NOT a function.
[73:2:6] - Every **habitat is an environment**, but an environment may exist without life.
[73:2:7] # Ecology
[73:2:8] - **Ecology** (Greek *oikos* = home + *logos* = study): study of the **relationship between organisms (plants, animals) and their environment**; term coined by **Ernst Haeckel in 1866** ("Ökologie"); also called **bionomics** – synonymous with ecology, stressing natural systems that influence human systems.
[73:2:9] TABLE head: Branch / term | Meaning
  [73:2:9.0] Autecology | Ecology of a single species in relation to its environment
  [73:2:9.1] Synecology | Ecology of communities
  [73:2:9.2] Deep ecology | Term of the Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess (1973)
  [73:2:9.3] Ecological transition | Concept of John W. Bennett (*The Ecological Transition*, 1976)
  [73:2:9.4] Ecad | An organism (plant) modified by its environment – a habitat form without genetic change
  [73:2:9.5] Variation | Differences among individuals of the same species
  [73:2:9.6] Bionomics | = ecology ("management / laws of life")
[73:2:10] # Levels of organisation
[73:2:11] - Order from smallest to largest: **organism → population → community → ecosystem → (landscape) → biome → biosphere** (UPPSC 2017: population – community – ecosystem – landscape).
[73:2:12] TABLE head: Level | Meaning
  [73:2:12.0] Population | Individuals of one species in an area
  [73:2:12.1] Community | All populations of different species in an area
  [73:2:12.2] Ecosystem | Community + its non-living environment; basic functional unit of ecology
  [73:2:12.3] Biome | Large region defined by climate + dominant vegetation (rainforest, tundra, desert)
  [73:2:12.4] Biosphere | Narrow zone of contact of lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere where life exists; all ecosystems together
[73:2:13] - **Biodiversity** measured as **alpha, beta, gamma**; "biological diversity" coined by **Raymond F. Dasmann**; hotspot concept – **Norman Myers** (≥1,500 endemic vascular plants, ≥70% habitat lost).
[73:2:14] - **Sere** = whole sequence of communities in succession; **habitat fragmentation** = continuous habitat broken into isolated patches; **anthrome** = human-altered terrestrial biome.
[73:2:15] # Ecologists and contributions
[73:2:16] TABLE head: Ecologist | Contribution
  [73:2:16.0] Ernst Haeckel | Coined "ecology" (1866)
  [73:2:16.1] Eduard Suess | Coined "biosphere" (1875)
  [73:2:16.2] A.G. Tansley | Coined "ecosystem" (1935)
  [73:2:16.3] Joseph Grinnell | Ecological niche concept (habitat niche, 1917)
  [73:2:16.4] Charles Elton | *Animal Ecology* (1927); food chains; pyramid of numbers
  [73:2:16.5] G.E. Hutchinson | n-dimensional niche (1957)
  [73:2:16.6] Raymond Lindeman | Ten percent law (1942)
  [73:2:16.7] E.P. Odum | *Fundamentals of Ecology* (1953) – not E. Lucy Braun
  [73:2:16.8] H.C. Cowles | Ecological succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes
  [73:2:16.9] F.E. Clements | Phases of succession (1916)
  [73:2:16.10] Ramdeo Misra | Father of Indian ecology
[73:2:17] - Other pairs often mixed in: **Robert Brown** discovered the **cell nucleus**; **Leeuwenhoek** – father of microbiology; Newton – universal law of gravitation.
[73:2:18] > Exam angle: about 25 PYQs – who coined ecology (×5) / ecosystem (×3) / environment / deep ecology, ecologist matches (APPSC AEE, TSPSC), order of organisation (×2), definitions of environment (×3).
[73:2:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.1 p.2-3 (Haeckel, Elton, Tansley, autecology/synecology, components); Rocket Environment p.43-44 (sheet #25 terms; ecology – Haeckel, ecosystem – Tansley, biodiversity – Dasmann); Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.12-14 (environment, six levels of organisation); general knowledge, not checked (Carlyle, Naess, Bennett, ecad)
## SUB 3 | Energy Flow, Productivity and the Ten Percent Law
[73:3:0] # Energy flow
[73:3:1] - **Unidirectional**: **sunlight → producers → herbivores → carnivores**; energy is not cycled. **Solar energy** is the primary source and **driving force** of an ecosystem.
[73:3:2] - **Law of conservation of energy** (first law of thermodynamics): energy can be neither created nor destroyed but **can be transformed** from one form to another – light → chemical energy in photosynthesis. Second law: each transfer loses energy as **heat**.
[73:3:3] - Under 50% of sunlight is **PAR**; plants fix about **2–10% of PAR**; green plants capture only about **1% of the sunlight** falling on their leaves (UPPSC 2025, SSC 2011).
[73:3:4] - **Total primary production efficiency** = share of incoming **solar energy captured and used in photosynthesis** – about **1–2%**.
[73:3:5] # Ten percent law
[73:3:6] - **Raymond Lindeman (1942)**: only about **10%** of the energy (as food) passes to the next trophic level; about **90%** is lost (respiration, excretion, locomotion, heat) – energy **decreases** at each transfer, hence 4–5 levels.
[73:3:7] - 1% = solar energy captured by plants; 10% = energy passed between trophic levels.
[73:3:8] # Productivity
[73:3:9] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [73:3:9.0] GPP (Gross Primary Production) | Total rate of organic matter (solar energy) fixed by producers in photosynthesis
  [73:3:9.1] NPP | GPP − producer respiration; available to consumers
  [73:3:9.2] Primary productivity | Rate at which solar energy is stored in green plants as food (autotroph level)
  [73:3:9.3] Secondary productivity | Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers (heterotroph level)
[73:3:10] - Primary production in an **aquatic ecosystem** depends on **light penetration, nutrients and temperature** (all of these), with phytoplankton as producers.
[73:3:11] - Highest NPP per unit area: **tropical rainforest**; estuaries, coral reefs, swamps, mangroves also high. Lowest: **deserts and open ocean** (ocean total still large by area).
[73:3:12] - Decreasing productivity: **mangroves > grasslands > lakes > oceans** (UPSC 2013); ecotones (mangroves, estuaries) beat their surroundings.
[73:3:13] > Exam angle: about 17 PYQs – energy-flow sequence (APPSC 2019 ×2), 10% law (×2), 1% capture (×2), GPP / secondary productivity / primary productivity definitions (APPSC 2023, FRO, FSO), UPSC 2013 productivity order.
[73:3:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.7 (unidirectional flow, Lindeman 10% law); Rocket Environment p.55, 59 (10% law – Lindeman; primary productivity autotroph level, secondary heterotroph level; mangroves highest, oceans lowest); OnlyIAS NCERT Geography Part 9 p.3, 5-6 (GPP, NPP, secondary productivity, PAR 2-10%, 10% law); PMF Environment Part 2 p.12
[73:3:15] - **Upwelling** brings **nutrient-rich** deep water to the surface – high phytoplankton productivity (UPSC 2011).
[73:3:16] - NPP (Whittaker & Likens 1975, g/m²/yr): algal beds and reefs ~2,500, **tropical rainforest ~2,200**, swamps and marshes ~2,000, estuaries ~1,500; books usually give tropical forests as highest.
## SUB 4 | Habitat, Niche and Population
[73:4:0] # Habitat vs niche
[73:4:1] TABLE head: Habitat | Niche
  [73:4:1.0] Physical place where an organism lives – its "address" | Functional role of a species in its habitat – its "profession"
  [73:4:1.1] One habitat holds many species | Unique to each species – no two species have identical niches
[73:4:2] - **Ecological niche** describes not only the physical space occupied but also the **functional role** in the community (UPSC 2013); it covers the range of conditions tolerated, resources used and role played. Concept enunciated by **Grinnell**.
[73:4:3] - **Fundamental niche:** full range of biotic and abiotic conditions and resources a species could use **free from interference of other species**; **realised niche**: actual range used under competition.
[73:4:4] - **Niche breadth:** specialists (**koala** – only eucalyptus) vs generalists.
[73:4:5] - **Resource partitioning:** competing species coexist by using different parts of a shared resource.
[73:4:6] - **Terrestrial** organisms live on land; **hydrophytes** are aquatic plants (not necessarily rootless).
[73:4:7] # Population attributes
[73:4:8] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [73:4:8.0] Natality | Birth of individuals; rate expressed per unit population per unit time, or as individuals produced per female per unit time
  [73:4:8.1] Mortality | Deaths per unit time
  [73:4:8.2] Density | Individuals per unit area (or volume)
  [73:4:8.3] Others | Age structure, sex ratio, dispersal (NOT dominant vegetation)
  [73:4:8.4] J-curve | Exponential growth, unlimited resources
  [73:4:8.5] S-curve | Logistic growth levelling at carrying capacity K
[73:4:9] - Age pyramids: **triangular = expanding; bell = stable; urn = declining**.
[73:4:10] - **Carrying capacity:** the **maximum population an environment can sustain** for ever **without being degraded**. It is **dynamic** – it changes with resources, climate and technology. Conditions: resource extraction must stay **below** regeneration, and **waste within the absorption capacity** (UPPSC 2025: only 2 correct).
[73:4:11] TABLE head: r-selected | K-selected
  [73:4:11.0] Many small offspring, little care, short life, unstable habitats – insects, weeds | Few large offspring, much care, long life, near K – elephants, humans
[73:4:12] > Exam angle: about 15 PYQs – niche (UPSC 2013, APPSC 2021/2022, UPPSC 2005/2022), carrying capacity (APPSC AEE ×2, UPPSC 2025), natality and density (APPSC G2 2025).
[73:4:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.1 p.4, 7-8 (habitat; density, natality); NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.2-3 (niche, koala); Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.17 (niche unique to a species); Rocket Environment p.59 (niche – Grinnell; maximum sustainable population = carrying capacity); PMF Environment Part 6 p.13-14 (carrying capacity)
## SUB 5 | Ecological Pyramids
[73:5:0] - Show trophic levels; **base = producers**, apex = top consumers; **three types** – numbers, biomass, energy.
[73:5:1] TABLE head: Pyramid | Upright | Inverted
  [73:5:1.0] Numbers | Grassland, pond | Tree ecosystem; parasitic chain
  [73:5:1.1] Biomass | Forest, grassland | Pond, marine (small, fast-turning phytoplankton crop)
  [73:5:1.2] Energy | Always | Never
[73:5:2] - **Biomass** = total (dry) weight of organisms per unit area; **standing crop** = living biomass in a trophic level per unit area **at a given time** – a quantity, not a rate.
[73:5:3] - Limitations: assume a simple chain, ignore food webs; a species cannot be shown at two levels; **saprophytes and decomposers get no place**.
[73:5:4] - Energy decreases upward mainly through **heat loss**.
[73:5:5] > Exam angle: own MCQs and APPSC G2 Mains 2025 – energy pyramid never inverted; biomass inverted in pond/sea; numbers inverted in a tree.
[73:5:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.55 (sheet #31 pyramids); NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.3-4, 8; PMF Environment Part 2 p.8-13 (standing crop, limitations)
[73:5:7] - **Ecological pyramids** were first put forward by **Charles Elton (1927)** (pyramid of numbers).
## SUB 6 | Biotic Interactions and Species Roles
[73:6:0] TABLE head: Interaction | Sign | Example
  [73:6:0.0] Mutualism | +/+ | Lichen, fig–fig wasp, mycorrhiza
  [73:6:0.1] Commensalism | +/0 | Epiphytic orchid on a tree; cattle egret near cattle; suckerfish on shark
  [73:6:0.2] Parasitism | +/− | Cuscuta, ticks, lice, tapeworm
  [73:6:0.3] Predation | +/− | Tiger–deer; Pisaster eating mussels
  [73:6:0.4] Competition | −/− | Same limited resource; Gause's exclusion principle
  [73:6:0.5] Amensalism | −/0 | Large tree shading small plant; Penicillium (antibiosis)
  [73:6:0.6] Neutralism | 0/0 | Neither affected
[73:6:1] - **Mycorrhiza** = fungi + roots (mutualism); **lichen** = fungus + alga; coevolved pollinators: fig–fig wasp, **yucca–yucca moth**, **Ophrys orchid–bee** (sexual deceit).
[73:6:2] TABLE head: Role | Meaning | Example
  [73:6:2.0] Keystone | Effect far larger than its numbers | Pisaster sea star (controls mussels), sea otter
  [73:6:2.1] Foundation | Creates or shapes habitat | Corals, kelp
  [73:6:2.2] Flagship | Charismatic, draws support | Tiger, giant panda
  [73:6:2.3] Indicator | Signals environmental health | Lichens (SO₂)
  [73:6:2.4] Umbrella | Wide-ranging; protecting it protects many | Tiger, snow leopard
[73:6:3] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.25 and Part 4 p.1 (biotic interactions); PMF Environment Part 2 p.3-5 (amensalism, Penicillium, commensalism); app notes 5:73 sub 6
[73:6:4] - **Epiphytes** use the host only for **mechanical support**; they take moisture and nutrients from air and rain.
[73:6:5] - **Community structure** is shaped by foundation and keystone species; **succession** = predictable appearance of species after a disturbance.
[73:6:6] - **Litmus** is a dye extracted from **lichens** (e.g. Roccella).
[73:6:7] - **Mistletoe** is a **partial (hemi-) parasite** – green and photosynthetic, but it draws water and minerals from the host; green plants are **autotrophs**.
## SUB 7 | Ecotones, Ecogeographic Rules and Plant Adaptations
[73:7:0] - **Ecotone:** transition zone where two communities meet – mangroves (marine–terrestrial), estuary, **grassland (forest–desert)**, river bank; a uniform forest stand is NOT an ecotone.
[73:7:1] - **Edge effect:** more species and higher density of some species in the ecotone; they are **edge species**.
[73:7:2] TABLE head: Rule | Trait
  [73:7:2.0] Bergmann | Body size – colder = larger
  [73:7:2.1] Allen | Colder = shorter ears and limbs
  [73:7:2.2] Jordan | Fish vertebrae – colder = more
  [73:7:2.3] Gloger | Colouration – warm-humid = darker
[73:7:3] - **Plant groups by water and substrate:**
[73:7:4] TABLE head: Group | Habitat | Adaptation – example
  [73:7:4.0] Xerophytes | Dry | Thick cuticle, sunken stomata, spines, CAM, green photosynthetic stem – Opuntia (cactus)
  [73:7:4.1] Hydrophytes | Water | Aerenchyma, reduced roots – Hydrilla, lotus
  [73:7:4.2] Halophytes | Saline | Pneumatophores, vivipary – Rhizophora
  [73:7:4.3] Phreatophytes | Groundwater | Deep roots
  [73:7:4.4] Lithophytes | Rocks | –
[73:7:5] - **Cuscuta (dodder)**: stem parasite with haustoria. Desert flora do NOT have broad thin leaves.
[73:7:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.43 (ecotone); NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.1 p.11-12 (edge effect); Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.17 (ecotone examples); PMF Environment Part 1 p.61 (xerophytes, hydrophytes); app notes 5:73 sub 7
[73:7:7] - **Cryophytes:** plants (mostly algae, mosses, lichens) growing on **snow and ice** – e.g. red snow (Chlamydomonas nivalis); **cryptophytes** are Raunkiaer's life form with buds below ground or water.
[73:7:8] - **Mesophytes:** land plants of **moderate** water supply – neither very dry nor very wet.
[73:7:9] - Desert plants are generally **succulent** – fleshy, water-storing stems or leaves.
[73:7:10] - **Rensch's rule:** sexual size dimorphism increases with body size (tested in shorebirds).
[73:7:11] - **Cuscuta** is a **parasitic angiosperm**: leafless, without chlorophyll; its haustoria tap the host's **stem** (xylem and phloem), not its leaves.
[73:7:12] - Halophytes cope with salt by **filtering it out at the roots** (ultrafiltration, e.g. Rhizophora), salt glands and succulence.
[73:7:13] - **Utricularia (bladderwort)** is an aquatic insectivorous plant; Sequoia is a giant conifer, Nostoc a cyanobacterium.
[73:7:14] - **Insectivorous plants:** **Nepenthes** (pitcher plant), **Utricularia** (bladderwort), Drosera (sundew) – they trap insects for nitrogen.
[73:7:15] - **Mangroves** have aerial roots – **pneumatophores** (breathing roots) and **stilt roots**; epiphytic **orchids** also have aerial (velamen) roots.
[73:7:16] - Desert plants have **long, deep roots** to search for **water**; hot soil does not promote root growth.
## SUB 8 | Terrestrial Ecosystems and Biomes
[73:8:0] - **Natural**: forests, grasslands, oceans, lakes, deserts. **Artificial**: crop fields, parks; **city** = extreme example. Estuary, marine, wetlands are aquatic, not terrestrial.
[73:8:1] - **Rainforest**: highest land species richness; fast decay → poor soil. **Taiga**: slow decay, thick litter, acidic soil. **Mature forests** give little net oxygen (respiration balances photosynthesis).
[73:8:2] - Hot desert: **Thar**, Sahara. Cold desert: Ladakh, **Gobi**.
[73:8:3] TABLE head: Grassland | Region
  [73:8:3.0] Prairie | North America
  [73:8:3.1] Pampas | Argentina
  [73:8:3.2] Steppe | Eurasia
  [73:8:3.3] Veld | South Africa
  [73:8:3.4] Downs | Australia
  [73:8:3.5] Shola | Western Ghats – Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu
  [73:8:3.6] Banni | Kutch – threat Prosopis juliflora
[73:8:4] - India's first guide to **Open Natural Ecosystems** launched at **UNCCD COP17, Ulaanbaatar** (Aug 2026): over 10% of India, **under 5%** protected.
[73:8:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.6-7, 9; Shankar Environment 10th ed. Part 3 p.18 (biomes); app notes 5:73 sub 8
[73:8:6] - **Grassland:** rainfall too low for forest, so **low water availability** is its defining feature.
## SUB 9 | Aquatic Ecosystems, Wetlands and Andhra Pradesh
[73:9:0] TABLE head: Class | Salinity | Examples
  [73:9:0.0] Freshwater | < 5 ppt | Lotic: rivers; Lentic: ponds, lakes, swamps
  [73:9:0.1] Brackish | 5–35 ppt | Estuaries (≈35 ppt at the mouth), mangroves
  [73:9:0.2] Marine | ≥ 35 ppt | Open ocean, coral reefs, hydrothermal vents (not rivers)
[73:9:1] - **Zones of lakes and oceans:**
[73:9:2] TABLE head: Zone | Feature
  [73:9:2.0] Littoral (lake) | Shallow; light reaches bottom; rooted plants
  [73:9:2.1] Profundal (lake) | Deep, dark; decomposers
  [73:9:2.2] Pelagic / Benthic (ocean) | Open water column / sea floor
  [73:9:2.3] Aphotic (ocean) | Below ~1,000 m, dark
[73:9:3] - Lakes: **oligotrophic** = low nutrients, clear; **eutrophic** = nutrient-rich, algal blooms.
[73:9:4] - **Ocean** = largest ecosystem (~71% of the surface). **Coral reefs** = "rainforests of the sea"; they also break storm waves (A-R: both true, R not the explanation). Mangroves buffer cyclones; estuaries on the west coast: **Narmada, Tapi**.
[73:9:5] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [73:9:5.0] Ramsar Convention | 2 Feb 1971, Ramsar, Iran; not punitive; Montreux Record
  [73:9:5.1] India | Party since 1982; 103 Ramsar sites (Oct 2026)
  [73:9:5.2] Indian law | Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017
  [73:9:5.3] World Wetlands Day | 2 February
  [73:9:5.4] Largest wetland area | Gujarat
[73:9:6] - Wetland functions: flood moderation, purification, biodiversity, carbon storage; **lagoons** are coastal wetlands.
[73:9:7] TABLE head: AP site | Type
  [73:9:7.0] Kolleru | Freshwater lake between Godavari and Krishna deltas
  [73:9:7.1] Pulicat | Brackish lagoon, AP–TN border
  [73:9:7.2] Coringa | Mangrove estuary, Godavari delta
  [73:9:7.3] Nallamala, Seshachalam | Eastern Ghats forests
[73:9:8] - AP coastline **1,053.07 km** (3rd in India after Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, revised figures, PIB Dec 2025).
[73:9:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.9 (marine 71%, freshwater 0.8%); Rocket Environment p.43 (lentic, lotic); RUNBOOK settled facts (Ramsar 103, AP coastline 1,053.07 km); app notes 5:73 sub 9
[73:9:10] - **OECMs:** the **AP State Biodiversity Board** plans Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures – conserved areas **outside protected areas**.
[73:9:11] - Wetlands as **kidneys**: aquatic plants absorb **heavy metals and excess nutrients** (UPSC 2022).
[73:9:12] - Ramsar imposes no duty to protect every wetland; the **Wetlands Rules 2010** (India's own, not on Ramsar's advice; now replaced by the **2017 Rules**) covered the wetland's **drainage / catchment area**.
[73:9:13] - AP's coastal plain is fringed by **mangrove swamps** (Coringa, Krishna delta) and palm trees.
[73:9:14] - **Mangroves:** specialised tropical/subtropical coastal forests that stabilise the shoreline – but that is a function, not why they exist (UPSC 1996: both true, R not the explanation).
[73:9:15] - **Coral reefs** – the usual answer for the **oldest ecosystem** (reefs from ~485 million years ago, Ordovician).
[73:9:16] - **Limnetic zone:** open, sunlit surface water of a lake away from the shore – phytoplankton abound there.
[73:9:17] - India: **inland wetlands ≈ 69%**, coastal ≈ 27% of wetland area (SAC National Wetland Atlas 2011).
[73:9:18] - Mangroves are a bio-shield against **tsunamis** and storm surges (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami).
