=== NOTES 5:74 | Biogeochemical Cycles, Ecological Succession and Ecosystem Services
## SUB 0 | Nitrogen Cycle
[74:0:0] # Reservoir and Processes
[74:0:1] - Main reservoir = **atmosphere (N₂ about 78% of air)**, NOT soil (APPSC G2 2025).
[74:0:2] - Plants take nitrogen as **nitrate**; atmospheric N₂ is not directly usable.
[74:0:3] TABLE head: Process | What happens | Agents
  [74:0:3.0] Fixation | N₂ → ammonia/nitrate (enzyme nitrogenase) | Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc), lightning, industrial Haber process
  [74:0:3.1] Ammonification | Organic N in dead matter → ammonia | Decomposer bacteria and fungi
  [74:0:3.2] Nitrification | Ammonia → nitrite → nitrate | Nitrosomonas (to nitrite), Nitrobacter (to nitrate)
  [74:0:3.3] Denitrification | Nitrate → N₂ gas, returned to air | Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus
[74:0:4] - Fixation, ammonification and nitrification **add** usable N to soil; denitrification **removes** it.
[74:0:5] # Legumes and Root Nodules
[74:0:6] - **Rhizobium** – symbiotic, in **legume root nodules** (pulses, pea); **Rhizobium japonicum** – soybean.
[74:0:7] - **Leghaemoglobin**: **pink/red** pigment in nodules (alfalfa, soybean); binds oxygen to keep it low, since **nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen**.
[74:0:8] - **Boron** is necessary for nodule formation.
[74:0:9] - Pea family (Fabaceae/Leguminosae): groundnut, horse-gram, soybean; N-fixing plants: alfalfa, chickpea, clover.
[74:0:10] # Biofertilisers
[74:0:11] TABLE head: Organism | Nature | Crop / role
  [74:0:11.0] Rhizobium | Symbiotic, legume nodules | Pulses, pea
  [74:0:11.1] Azotobacter, Azospirillum | Free-living N fixers | Cereals, millets, non-leguminous upland crops
  [74:0:11.2] Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) | Photosynthetic N fixers; heterocysts | Rice / paddy
  [74:0:11.3] Azolla–Anabaena | Water fern Azolla + Anabaena in its leaves | Water-logged rice fields (Azolla pinnata)
  [74:0:11.4] Frankia | Actinomycete, non-legumes | Alnus, Casuarina
  [74:0:11.5] VAM (mycorrhiza) | Fungus–root association | Phosphorus and water uptake
  [74:0:11.6] PSB | Bacillus megaterium, Pseudomonas striata | Solubilise phosphate
[74:0:12] Azotobacter is NOT partnered with Anabaena; symbiotic fixation in legume nodules is by Rhizobium, not cyanobacteria; VAM does not denitrify.
[74:0:13] - **Insectivorous plants** grow in **nitrogen-deficient** (often waterlogged) soils and trap insects for nitrogen.
[74:0:14] - **Uptake forms:** plants take nitrogen as **inorganic nitrates/nitrites** (also ammonium) and some **organic** compounds – **never directly from the air**.
[74:0:15] - **Rain** raises soil **nitrogen**: lightning fixes N₂ into nitrogen oxides that rain carries down as nitrates.
[74:0:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 2 p.18-21; NextGen Rocket Biology p.98-104, 129; app notes 5:74 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Carbon Cycle
[74:1:0] TABLE head: Adds CO₂ | Removes CO₂
  [74:1:0.0] Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion, volcanic activity, deforestation | Photosynthesis (plants, algae, some bacteria), dissolving in oceans, carbonate sedimentation, silicate weathering
[74:1:1] - Reservoirs and sinks: atmosphere, oceans, forests, soils; long-term – carbonate rocks and fossil fuels. Forests = vital carbon sinks.
[74:1:2] Photosynthesis does NOT add CO₂ – it removes it.
[74:1:3] - **Where the extra CO₂ goes:** much is removed by ocean uptake and **photosynthesis by phytoplankton**; it does not escape to the outer stratosphere, and polar ice only archives old air (UPSC 2011: 2 only).
[74:1:4] - **Deep Carbon Observatory (DCO, 2009-2019):** global research programme on the role of carbon in Earth, including field studies of **deep microbial life** (both statements correct, UPPSC 2019).
[74:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.52; PMF Environment Part 2 p.17-18; superkalam.com UPSC 2011 key
## SUB 2 | Biogeochemical Cycles – Basics and Types
[74:2:0] - Nutrients are recycled indefinitely between organisms, air and the Earth's crust; driven by energy flow; **all cycles are linked to the water cycle**.
[74:2:1] - Organisms need at least **27 elements** (15 metals). Macronutrients: potassium, sodium, magnesium, calcium, sulphur, phosphorus, chlorine.
[74:2:2] TABLE head: Type | Cycles | Main reservoir
  [74:2:2.0] Gaseous | Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, water | Atmosphere / ocean
  [74:2:2.1] Sedimentary | Phosphorus, sulphur, calcium, potassium, iron | Earth's crust – soil and rocks
[74:2:3] Hydrogen (H₂) is NOT a gaseous cycle in exam lists.
[74:2:4] APPSC 2025: Removing decomposers blocks mineral movement – nutrients locked in dead matter never return to the soil.
[74:2:5] # Phosphorus Cycle
[74:2:6] - **No atmospheric phase**; natural reservoir = **rock (phosphates)**; weathering of rocks is the main source; much ends in **ocean sediments**.
[74:2:7] - P is used in membranes, nucleic acids, energy transfer, shells, bones, teeth.
[74:2:8] - **Definition:** movement of nutrient elements through the biotic and abiotic components = **biogeochemical (nutritional) cycle**.
[74:2:9] - **Soil's major nutrients** for cultivation: **nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium (NPK)**.
[74:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.52; NextGen Environment Part 1.2 p.8; PMF Environment Part 2 p.16, 27-28
## SUB 3 | Ecological Succession – Terms and Types
[74:3:0] # Terms
[74:3:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [74:3:1.0] Succession | Gradual, orderly replacement of one community by another in an area over time
  [74:3:1.1] Pioneer species | First hardy colonisers – lichens, mosses
  [74:3:1.2] Sere / seral stage | Whole sequence = sere; each step = seral stage (seral communities in between)
  [74:3:1.3] Climax community | Final stable community in balance with climate (forest, grassland, coral reef)
  [74:3:1.4] Seasonal succession | Cyclic, driven by environmental rhythms; NOT caused by disturbance
[74:3:2] # Primary vs Secondary
[74:3:3] TABLE head: Primary | Secondary
  [74:3:3.0] Area that never had life – lava, bare rock, volcanic island; no soil | After fire, flood, logging; soil, seeds, roots remain
  [74:3:3.1] Pioneers: lichens and mosses | Faster than primary
[74:3:4] - On a surface without soil, **lichens and mosses** survive; **ferns need soil**.
[74:3:5] - Grasslands do not turn into forest because of **water limits and dry-season fire**.
[74:3:6] # Seres by Starting Medium
[74:3:7] TABLE head: Sere | Starts on
  [74:3:7.0] Hydrosere | Water (pond, lake)
  [74:3:7.1] Xerosere | Dry land
  [74:3:7.2] Lithosere | Bare rock (sub-type of xerosere)
  [74:3:7.3] Psammosere | Sand (sub-type of xerosere)
  [74:3:7.4] Halosere | Saline soil or water
[74:3:8] - **Sub-climax:** a disturbance that holds a sere at an intermediate stage gives a **sub-climax** community.
[74:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 1.1 p.14 and Part 1.2 p.1-2; PMF Environment Part 1 p.56-61
## SUB 4 | Succession – Phases, Sequences and Theories
[74:4:0] # Clements' Phases (1916)
[74:4:1] TABLE head: Phase | What happens
  [74:4:1.0] 1. Nudation | Bare area forms (erosion, landslide, volcano, fire)
  [74:4:1.1] 2. Invasion | Seeds/spores arrive; ecesis (successful establishment), aggregation
  [74:4:1.2] 3. Competition and co-action | Unfit species eliminated
  [74:4:1.3] 4. Reaction | Organisms modify soil, water, light, temperature – most important phase
  [74:4:1.4] 5. Stabilisation | Climax community
[74:4:2] Invasion comes right after nudation; ecesis belongs to the invasion phase.
[74:4:3] # Sequences
[74:4:4] - **Xerosere**: crustose lichens → foliose lichens → mosses → herbs and grasses → shrubs → forest. **Lichens** (algae + fungi) start succession on bare rock.
[74:4:5] - Pioneer trees (birch, oak) need high light; shade-tolerant species form the climax.
[74:4:6] - **Hydrosere**: **small phytoplankton** (pioneers in water) → submerged rooted (Chara) → floating (Lemna, Pistia, water lilies) → reed-swamp → sedge-meadow → woodland → forest; ends in wet woodland (**fen carr**).
[74:4:7] - Hydroseres are better studied – **lake sediments keep a permanent record**.
[74:4:8] # Ecologists and Climax Theories
[74:4:9] TABLE head: Person | Contribution
  [74:4:9.0] F.E. Clements | Phases of succession (1916); monoclimax – one climax per region, set by climate
  [74:4:9.1] Tansley | Polyclimax; coined "ecosystem"
  [74:4:9.2] Whittaker | Climax-pattern
  [74:4:9.3] E.P. Odum (1971) | Succession = orderly community change within a unit area
  [74:4:9.4] H.C. Cowles | Succession on sand dunes
  [74:4:9.5] Elton / Lindeman | Food chains, pyramid of numbers / 10% law
[74:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 1.1 p.12-14 and Part 1.2 p.1-2; PMF Environment Part 1 p.58-61
## SUB 5 | Functions of the Environment
[74:5:0] # Four Functions
[74:5:1] TABLE head: Function | Meaning
  [74:5:1.0] Supplies resources | Both renewable AND non-renewable raw materials (first function)
  [74:5:1.1] Assimilates waste | Biodegradation – microorganisms break organic waste into nutrients for reuse
  [74:5:1.2] Sustains life | Genetic diversity, biodiversity, ozone layer UV protection
  [74:5:1.3] Aesthetic services | Scenery, recreation
[74:5:2] APPSC 2022: "Environment provides renewable resources only" is the INCORRECT statement.
[74:5:3] "Assimilating wealth" is NOT a vital function of the environment.
[74:5:4] # Function → Description (APPSC 2023 match)
[74:5:5] TABLE head: Function | Description
  [74:5:5.0] Waste decomposition | Breakdown of organic waste into simpler compounds
  [74:5:5.1] Cultural heritage | Source of traditional practices, knowledge and identity
  [74:5:5.2] Recreation and aesthetics | Scenic and leisure value
  [74:5:5.3] Medicinal resources | Supply of drugs and herbal remedies
[74:5:6] - **Ecosystem functions**: ecological succession, nutrient cycling, energy flow through food chains, **homeostasis** (maintenance of ecological balance).
[74:5:7] - Nutrients are recycled; **energy flows through and is not recycled**.
[74:5:8] - **NOT a function:** "recycling" is not one of the four listed functions (APPSC ACF 2022); "disorganises waste" and "helps get rid of water pollution" are wrong wordings too.
[74:5:9] - **Order:** the **first** function is **production / supply of raw materials (resources)**; waste recycling by microbes = **biodegradation function**.
[74:5:10] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:74 sub 0; NextGen Environment Part 1.1 p.3
## SUB 6 | Ecosystem Services and Valuation
[74:6:0] # Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (MEA, 2005, UN)
[74:6:1] TABLE head: MEA category | Examples
  [74:6:1.0] Provisioning | Tangible goods – food, fresh water, timber, fibre, medicinal resources
  [74:6:1.1] Regulating | Climate, flood, disease regulation, water purification, pollination, waste decomposition
  [74:6:1.2] Cultural | Recreation, aesthetics, cultural heritage, spiritual value
  [74:6:1.3] Supporting | Basis of all other services – soil formation, nutrient cycling, primary production
[74:6:2] Pollination and waste decomposition = regulating; nutrient cycling and soil formation = supporting. UPSC 2012 official key grouped **nutrient cycling and crop pollination** as the supporting option (pollination is strictly regulating).
[74:6:3] - **Cultural services** are hardest to price in money, so their value is underestimated.
[74:6:4] # Forest Services
[74:6:5] TABLE head: Economic products | Ecological services
  [74:6:5.0] Timber, bamboo, fuelwood, fodder, NTFPs | Carbon sequestration, soil and water conservation, groundwater recharge, flood moderation, air purification
[74:6:6] - **AP angle**: AP forests give intangible services – carbon sink, water-flow regulation, soil and moisture conservation. AP has the **second-largest mangrove ecosystem** in India (Godavari and Krishna estuaries).
[74:6:7] # Valuation Frameworks
[74:6:8] TABLE head: Report / framework | By / year | Role
  [74:6:8.0] MEA | 2005, UN | Four service categories
  [74:6:8.1] Costanza et al. | 1997 | First valued global services at about US$33 trillion a year
  [74:6:8.2] TEEB | Launched 2007, Potsdam (G8+5); hosted by UNEP | "Making nature's values visible" in decision-making
  [74:6:8.3] EnviStats India | MoSPI, annual | Natural capital accounting under the UN SEEA framework
[74:6:9] - Later values: coral reefs US$375 billion–9.9 trillion a year; Amazon US$2.2–3.4 trillion a year.
[74:6:10] - Debate: pricing nature aids decisions but undervalues cultural and spiritual services.
[74:6:11] - **TEEB:** global initiative hosted by **UNEP** (not IMF / WEF) – draws attention to the **economic benefits of biodiversity** and helps decision-makers **recognise, demonstrate and capture** the value of ecosystems (UPSC 2016: 2 and 3 only).
[74:6:12] - **Trees:** planting trees helps **maintain ecological balance**; trees reduce air pollution – causing it is not a function of a tree.
[74:6:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 2 p.46-47 (TEEB); app notes 5:74 sub 1
## SUB 7 | Human Disruption of Cycles
[74:7:0] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [74:7:0.0] Fossil fuels + deforestation | Raise atmospheric CO₂ → climate change
  [74:7:0.1] Chemical pesticides | Alter soils and microbial networks; may weaken resilience (not always increase it)
  [74:7:0.2] Nitrogen overload | Human activity has at least doubled nitrogen available to plants
  [74:7:0.3] Fertiliser runoff | Algal blooms; decay uses up dissolved oxygen → dead zones
  [74:7:0.4] N fertiliser in soil | Microbes release nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas
[74:7:1] - **Prosopis juliflora** (invasive) called an "ecological first responder" – a pioneer spreading where hydrology and soil chemistry have changed (7 May 2026).
[74:7:2] - **Reactive nitrogen sources (UPSC 2019):** agricultural soils release **nitrogen oxides**, cattle release **ammonia**, the poultry industry releases reactive nitrogen compounds – all three correct.
[74:7:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 2 p.19; app notes 5:74 sub 6
## SUB 8 | Water Cycle Regulation – Wetlands and Forests
[74:8:0] - Water carries elements through the ecosystem; cycles would stop if water did not cycle.
[74:8:1] - **Wetlands as sponges**: store floodwater, recharge aquifers, keep dry-season flow; also control erosion, retain sediment, support nutrient cycling and biodiversity.
[74:8:2] - **Wetlands as "kidneys" of the Earth**: aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess substances.
[74:8:3] - **Microclimate regulators**: stored water evaporates and holds heat, steadying local temperature and humidity.
[74:8:4] - **Forests**: regulate water flow, conserve soil and moisture, recharge groundwater, moderate floods.
[74:8:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:74 sub 5; NextGen Environment Part 2.1 p.1

  x: Nitrogen overload: human activity has at least doubled nitrogen available to plants.
[f2684a430a46e] sub7
  Nitrogen fertiliser in soil leads microbes to release which greenhouse gas?
  *Nitrous oxide | Methane | Carbon monoxide | Ozone
  x: Microbes release nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, from nitrogen fertiliser in soil.
[g53dc275f67e1] sub7
  The decay of algal blooms caused by fertiliser runoff uses up dissolved oxygen and creates which of the following?
  *Dead zones | Heat islands | Ozone holes | Ecotones
  x: Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms; their decay uses up dissolved oxygen, creating dead zones.
[nenvironment-22-4] sub8
  Why do wetlands act as microclimate regulators?
  *Evaporates and moderates local temperature and humidity | Blocks sunlight from reaching the ground | Removes humidity from the air | Raises local temperature
  x: The water stored in wetlands evaporates and holds heat, moderating nearby temperature and humidity.
[n96a9b984503] sub8
  Which ecosystem acts as a sponge by storing floodwater, recharging aquifers and sustaining lean-season flow?
  Tundra | Grasslands | Deserts | *Wetlands
  x: Wetlands store floodwater, recharge aquifers and sustain lean-season flow.
[nenvironment-22-7] sub8
  Which one of the following is a function of wetlands?
  Increasing soil erosion | Blocking nutrient cycling | Reducing biodiversity | *Retaining sediment
  x: Wetlands control erosion, retain sediment, support nutrient cycling and support biodiversity.

=== NOTES 5:75 | Land Degradation, Desertification, Deforestation, Soil Erosion and Urban Heat Islands
## SUB 0 | Processes and Causes of Land Degradation
[75:0:0] - Main cause of desertification in semi-arid regions: **overgrazing and deforestation** (APPSC 2025).
[75:0:1] TABLE head: Process | How it degrades land
  [75:0:1.0] Overgrazing | Strips vegetation cover
  [75:0:1.1] Deforestation | Exposes soil to wind and water erosion
  [75:0:1.2] Water erosion | Removes topsoil; silts rivers and reservoirs
  [75:0:1.3] Wind erosion | Blows topsoil away in dry areas (Anantapur)
  [75:0:1.4] Salinisation, waterlogging | Poor drainage and over-irrigation (AP delta areas); by 2050, 50% of world arable land could be affected
[75:0:2] # Agriculture-driven Degradation
[75:0:3] - Effects of **modern (intensive) agriculture**: soil degradation, pollution, ecological imbalance – **all of these** (APPSC 2018).
[75:0:4] - Fertilisers and pesticides contaminate soil and water; **excess urea** upset the NPK ratio in **Punjab and Haryana**.
[75:0:5] - Resource depletion → cause: groundwater – over-irrigation; topsoil – erosion from overgrazing and deforestation; habitats – deforestation; land – salinity and waterlogging.
[75:0:6] - **Punjab, Haryana, western UP:** **over-irrigation** → waterlogging, salinity and alkalinity is the main cause of land degradation (NCERT X); overgrazing = Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Maharashtra; mining = Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, MP, Odisha.
[75:0:7] - **Linked with desertification:** deforestation, drought and loss of vegetation – all of these.
[75:0:8] - **Heavy sand mining in riverbeds (UPSC 2018):** **pollutes groundwater** and **lowers the water table**; it does not decrease river salinity.
[75:0:9] - **Borrow pit:** a pit dug to take earth, sand or gravel for use as fill elsewhere (roads, embankments) – a land-degrading practice.
[75:0:10] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography Part 10 (NCERT X Resources and Development); app notes 5:75 sub 1
## SUB 1 | Key Terms
[75:1:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [75:1:0.0] Desertification (UNCCD) | Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas from climatic variation and human activity – NOT just the spread of existing deserts
  [75:1:0.1] Environmental degradation | Depletion of air, water, soil; destruction of ecosystems; extinction of wildlife
  [75:1:0.2] Tragedy of the Commons | Over-use of a shared pasture lowers land quality – Garrett Hardin, 1968 (APPSC 2018)
  [75:1:0.3] LDN | Land Degradation Neutrality – no net loss of land health by 2030 (SDG 15.3)
  [75:1:0.4] Soil Organic Carbon | Indian soils fell from 1% to 0.3% in 70 years
  [75:1:0.5] Ridge to valley | Watershed approach of the PMKSY Watershed Development Component
[75:1:1] - **Controlled grazing:** regulating the grazing **time and consumption level** of a pasture (rotational grazing is one method).
[75:1:2] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.7 (UNCCD-LDN); PMF Environment Part 5 p.44-47; app notes 5:75 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Conservation Movements
[75:2:0] TABLE head: Movement | State | Leader / year
  [75:2:0.0] Chipko | Chamoli, Uttarakhand | Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna; 1973; Gaura Devi at Reni (1974)
  [75:2:0.1] Appiko | Karnataka | Panduranga Hegde, 1983
  [75:2:0.2] Mitti Bachao | Madhya Pradesh (Tawa dam, Hoshangabad) | 1977, against waterlogging and salinity
[75:2:1] - **Protagonist of Chipko:** **Chandi Prasad Bhatt** (Rocket: "protagonist / key figure"); Sunderlal Bahuguna took it nationwide; Chipko = against **deforestation**, i.e. **plant (tree) conservation**.
[75:2:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.56
## SUB 3 | Desertification Geography and Data
[75:3:0] - **Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas 2021**: by **ISRO's Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad**.
[75:3:1] - **97.85 Mha = 29.77%** of India degraded; main contributors: **water erosion + chemical degradation**.
[75:3:2] - About **one-fourth** of degraded land faces desertification; **Rajasthan** has over **23%** of desertified land.
[75:3:3] - FAO: **one-third** of world soils degraded; Global Land Outlook: degradation costs over 10% of global GDP.
[75:3:4] - Worst-hit continents: **Africa (Sahel) and Asia**.
[75:3:5] - **Sand and dust storms** hit NW India (Rajasthan), West Asia and the Sahel.
[75:3:6] - **Dust storm season:** In north-west India (Rajasthan), dust storms are most common in the hot, dry pre-monsoon summer months (April to June).
[75:3:7] - **Least affected continent:** **Europe** (no large hot desert; smallest dryland share).
[75:3:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 5 p.42-47; app notes 5:75 sub 4
## SUB 4 | UNCCD, Days and Conferences
[75:4:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [75:4:0.0] UNCCD | Adopted 1994, Paris; in force 1996; secretariat Bonn; India ratified 1996
  [75:4:0.1] Status | Only legally binding framework on desertification; one of three Rio conventions
  [75:4:0.2] World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought | 17 June (UNGA 1994); 2026 host Kenya – "Rangelands: Recognise. Respect. Restore."
  [75:4:0.3] UN Decade on Sand and Dust Storms | 2025-2034; day 12 July
  [75:4:0.4] COP14 | New Delhi, 2019: India target 26 Mha by 2030 (from 21 Mha, Paris 2015)
  [75:4:0.5] COP17 | Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, 2026: MoEFCC launched India's first guide to Grasslands and Open Natural Ecosystems
[75:4:1] - Global Land Outlook: UNCCD flagship (2017, 2022).
[75:4:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 5 p.42-47; NextGen Rocket Environment p.7
## SUB 5 | Restoration Initiatives
[75:5:0] TABLE head: Initiative | Aim
  [75:5:0.0] Aravalli Green Wall | Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, Delhi; barrier to the Thar; 41,410 ha planted 2024-25
  [75:5:0.1] Great Green Wall (Africa) | African Union; Sahel belt, Senegal to Djibouti; 100 Mha by 2030
  [75:5:0.2] Bonn Challenge | 2011, Germany + IUCN: 150 Mha by 2020, 350 Mha by 2030
  [75:5:0.3] Great Green Wall of AP | SPSR Nellore: 50% green cover by 2047 (Jul 2026)
  [75:5:0.4] China's Three-North programme | Straw-checkerboard dune fixing
[75:5:1] - **24 Dec 2025**: MoEFCC banned new mining leases in the Aravallis.
[75:5:2] - MoEFCC-IUCN: India restored **21.76 Mha** in 2011-2020; **Telangana** led (4.18 Mha), then MP, Odisha, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh.
[75:5:3] - **Bonn Challenge** aims to **restore degraded and deforested land**; India joined in 2015 (Paris): 13 Mha by 2020 + 8 Mha by 2030 (21 Mha), raised to **26 Mha by 2030** at UNCCD COP14, Delhi 2019.
[75:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 4.2 p.1; app notes 5:75 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Soil Erosion and Conservation
[75:6:0] TABLE head: Erosion type | Feature
  [75:6:0.0] Sheet | Thin even layer of topsoil removed over wide areas
  [75:6:0.1] Rill | Small channels on slopes
  [75:6:0.2] Gully | Deep channels in clayey soil → badlands; called ravines in the Chambal basin
  [75:6:0.3] Wind | Topsoil blown off in dry areas
  [75:6:0.4] Method | How it works
  [75:6:0.5] Contour ploughing | Ploughing along contours slows water down slopes
  [75:6:0.6] Terracing | Steps on slopes; western and central Himalayas
  [75:6:0.7] Strip cropping | Grass strips between crops break wind force
  [75:6:0.8] Shelter belts | Tree rows as windbreaks; stabilised dunes in western India
[75:6:1] - Support: MGNREGA, state watershed projects, participatory forest management.
[75:6:2] - **Soil Health Card**: launched **19 Feb 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan**; card every **2 years**.
[75:6:3] ~~ Sources: OnlyIAS NCERT Human Geography Part 10; OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography Part 4, 6 (Chambal ravines)
## SUB 7 | Deforestation and Global Forest Data
[75:7:0] - Impacts: faster erosion, falling fertility, desertification; **loss of CO₂ sink adds to greenhouse effect**.
[75:7:1] - Highest loss: **tropical forests** – Amazon, Congo Basin, Southeast Asia.
[75:7:2] TABLE head: FAO FRA 2025 (Oct 2025) | Fact
  [75:7:2.0] Forest share of land | About 32%
  [75:7:2.1] Five countries with over 54% of forests | Russia, Brazil, Canada, USA, China
  [75:7:2.2] Net loss | 10.7 Mha/yr (1990s) → 4.12 Mha/yr (2015-2025)
  [75:7:2.3] Only region with net gain | Asia, led by China and India
  [75:7:2.4] India | 9th in forest area (10th in 2020); 3rd in annual gain
[75:7:3] - Older FRA (APPSC 2018): net loss **8.3 Mha/yr (1990s) → 5.2 Mha/yr (2000-2010)**.
[75:7:4] - Forest Declaration Assessment 2025: 8.1 Mha lost in 2024, about **94%** in tropical forests.
[75:7:5] Check which FRA edition the question uses: 8.3 → 5.2 (FRA 2010) vs 10.7 → 4.12 (FRA 2025).
[75:7:6] # India State of Forest Report 2023
[75:7:7] - Forest + tree cover **25.17%** (forest 21.76%, tree 3.41%); up 1,445 sq km since 2021.
[75:7:8] - Top gains: **Chhattisgarh**, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan; largest losses: **Madhya Pradesh**, Karnataka.
[75:7:9] - **Impacts of deforestation:** soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, drying of Himalayan water sources – **urbanisation is a cause, not an impact**.
[75:7:10] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:75 sub 3 (FAO FRA 2025, ISFR 2023)
## SUB 8 | Urban Heat Islands
[75:8:0] - **UHI**: cities markedly hotter than surroundings. Causes: **low-albedo concrete/asphalt** and **loss of vegetation** (separate causes).
[75:8:1] - **Cool roofs**: white/reflective coatings – absorb less heat, lower cooling load.
[75:8:2] - **AP Cool Surface Policy 2023** objectives: affordable urban heat solutions, lower heat and energy demand, reflective materials.
[75:8:3] APPSC 2023: "rural heat" is NOT an objective of the AP Cool Surface Policy.
[75:8:4] - First Heat Action Plan: **Ahmedabad, 2013**; **NDMA** heat action plan guidelines **2016**.
[75:8:5] - **Namo Van–Nagar Van Scheme**: urban forests against UHI (Jul 2026).
[75:8:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:75 sub 8 (AP Cool Surface Policy 2023); NextGen Environment Part 8.2 p.4
## SUB 9 | AP Land Degradation
[75:9:0] TABLE head: Place | Feature
  [75:9:0.0] Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai | Drought-induced degradation, desertification, wind erosion, groundwater depletion
  [75:9:0.1] Uppada (Kakinada) | Coastal erosion
  [75:9:0.2] Delta areas | Salinity and waterlogging
[75:9:1] - SDG India Index 2023-24: AP degraded land **33.81%** (best Punjab **3.15%** – ten times less); desertification area up 3.45% (Rajasthan −1.34%).
[75:9:2] - AP forest cover **18.28%**, tree cover 2.87%; **fallow land 21.26%** (34.65 lakh ha) – more than forest area.
[75:9:3] - Rayalaseema measures: ridge-to-valley watershed works, afforestation and green-wall planting.
[75:9:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:75 sub 9 (SDG India Index 2023-24; ISFR 2021)

=== NOTES 5:76 | Environmental Legislation in India – Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment (protection) Act 1986
## SUB 0 | Environment (Protection) Act 1986
[76:0:0] # Background and Nature
[76:0:1] - Trigger: **Bhopal Gas Tragedy (December 1984)**; gives effect to the **Stockholm Conference, 1972**.
[76:0:2] - Basis: **Article 253**. Purpose: **protect and improve the environment and control pollution** (APPSC 2025).
[76:0:3] - Called **umbrella legislation** – coordinates central and state authorities under the Water and Air Acts; the **Central Government** is the primary authority. Last amendment mentioned: 1991.
[76:0:4] # Key Sections and Powers
[76:0:5] TABLE head: Section | Content
  [76:0:5.0] 3 | Centre's powers – emission/discharge standards, location of industries, hazardous waste, public health; supports EIA and CRZ notifications
  [76:0:5.1] 3(3) | Constitute authorities
  [76:0:5.2] 5 | Directions, including closure
  [76:0:5.3] 15-21 | Penalties
  [76:0:5.4] 16 | Environment Protection Fund
[76:0:6] - Authorities under Section 3(3): **Central Ground Water Authority (January 1997)** – regulates groundwater development; **National Ganga River Basin Authority (2009)**.
[76:0:7] # Environment Protection Fund
[76:0:8] - In the **Public Account**; holds fines under the Air, Water and EP Acts; **75% to States/UTs, 25% to Centre**.
[76:0:9] - **Environmental (Protection) Fund Rules, 2026** notified by MoEFCC.
[76:0:10] Water Cess → Consolidated Fund of India; EP Fund → Public Account.
[76:0:11] # Notifications and Rules under EPA
[76:0:12] TABLE head: Notification | Key point
  [76:0:12.0] Doon Valley (1989) | No industry burning over 24 MT coal/fuel a day
  [76:0:12.1] Revdanda Creek (1989) | No industries around the creek
  [76:0:12.2] CRZ (1991) | Regulates coastal stretches; no ash/waste dumping; CRZ under EPA confirmed (Jul 2026)
  [76:0:12.3] Dhanu Taluka (1991) | Ecologically fragile; no power plants
  [76:0:12.4] EIA (1994, revised 2006) | Prior environmental clearance
  [76:0:12.5] Eco-Sensitive Zones; Plastic Waste Management Rules | Notified under EPA
  [76:0:12.6] Green Credit Rules (2023) | Voluntary tree planting on degraded land earns Green Credits
[76:0:13] - Green Credit afforestation can be swapped for compensatory afforestation under Van (S&S) Rules 2023; guidelines 16 Sep 2025.
[76:0:14] - **UPSC 2019:** EPA empowers the Centre to **lay down emission/discharge standards** – but not to "state the requirement of public participation" (2 only).
[76:0:15] - **CRZ 2011:** Sundarbans and other ecologically sensitive areas identified under the EPA are **Critical Vulnerable Coastal Areas (CVCA)**, managed **with coastal communities incl. fisherfolk** (both statements true).
[76:0:16] - **Recognised labs (Section 12):** EPA lets the Centre establish or recognise environmental laboratories; **EPTRI, Hyderabad** (state-government institute) is on the list of recognised government/semi-government labs.
[76:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 6 p.11-14; NextGen Rocket Environment p.10-12; PMF Environment Part 6 p.63-64; dpcc.delhi.gov.in recognised-lab list
## SUB 1 | Chronology of Environmental Acts
[76:1:0] TABLE head: Year | Act / body | Key point
  [76:1:0.0] 1972 | Wildlife (Protection) Act | Central Zoo Authority set up under it (1992)
  [76:1:0.1] 1974 | Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act | India's first pollution-control law; in force 23 March 1974; created the Boards
  [76:1:0.2] 1977 | Water (P&CP) Cess Act | Cess on water used by industries and local bodies; Cess Rules 1978
  [76:1:0.3] 1980 | Forest (Conservation) Act | Central approval for diverting forest land
  [76:1:0.4] 1981 | Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act | Followed the Water Act framework
  [76:1:0.5] 1986 | Environment (Protection) Act | Umbrella law
  [76:1:0.6] 1991 | Public Liability Insurance Act | Relief for hazardous-substance accidents
  [76:1:0.7] 2002 | Biological Diversity Act | –
  [76:1:0.8] 2010 | National Green Tribunal Act | Specialised tribunal; latest in the chain
[76:1:1] - Amendments: Water Act **1978, 1988, 2024**; Air Act **1987** (noise added).
[76:1:2] Order: Water 1974 → Water Cess 1977 → Forest 1980 → Air 1981 → EPA 1986 → PLI 1991 → NGT 2010.
[76:1:3] The CPCB (1974) came before the Air Act (1981).
[76:1:4] - **Older / other Acts:** Indian Forest Act **1927**; **Indian Fisheries Act 1897**; National Environment Tribunal Act **1995** (never worked; repealed by the NGT Act 2010) → order Fisheries → Water → Air → NET.
[76:1:5] - **Other milestones:** Joint Forest Management **1990**; all Delhi buses on **CNG by 2002** (after the 1998 SC order) → Water Act 1974 → JFM 1990 → CNG 2002.
[76:1:6] - **Acts bearing on biodiversity (UPSC 2011):** Import and Export (Control) Act 1947, MMDR Act 1957, Customs Act 1962, Indian Forest Act 1927 – **all four**.
[76:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.12, 66; PMF Environment Part 6 p.59, 99; indiacode.nic.in (Fisheries Act 1897); v1.wii.gov.in (NET Act 1995)
## SUB 2 | CPCB, SPCBs and MoEFCC
[76:2:0] # CPCB
[76:2:1] - **Statutory body**, constituted **September 1974** under the **Water Act**; under **MoEFCC**; gives technical services to the Ministry under EPA 1986.
[76:2:2] - National level; deals with water (1974 Act) and air (1981 Act) pollution; an **enforcement body under the EPA framework**.
[76:2:3] - Functions: **coordinates SPCBs**, technical assistance, research, training, national monitoring.
[76:2:4] TABLE head: Item | CPCB | SPCB
  [76:2:4.0] Level | National | State
  [76:2:4.1] Chairperson nominated by | Central Government | State Government
  [76:2:4.2] Functions | Coordination, standards, research | Inspection, sample analysis, granting consents
[76:2:5] - Monitoring: **NAMP** – 1,646 stations in 603 cities (March 2026); **National AQI 2015**; **SAMEER app** gives real-time air quality (SAFAR is a separate forecasting system); **AUM Photonic** – indigenous real-time remote air monitoring.
[76:2:6] - **NCAP (2019)**: **40% PM10 cut by 2025-26** over 2019-20 in **130 cities, 24 States/UTs**.
[76:2:7] # MoEF / MoEFCC
[76:2:8] - **Department of Environment 1980 → Ministry of Environment and Forests 1985 → MoEFCC 2014**.
[76:2:9] - Bodies: CPCB (statutory), Central Zoo Authority (1992, under WPA 1972).
[76:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 7 p.2; NextGen Rocket Environment p.11, 37; PMF Environment Part 6 p.59-60
## SUB 3 | Water Act 1974 and Water Cess Act 1977
[76:3:0] # Water Act 1974
[76:3:1] - Purpose: **prevent and control water pollution** and **maintain or restore the wholesomeness of water**.
[76:3:2] - Passed under **Article 252** – applies in States that adopt it by resolution.
[76:3:3] - Created the **Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution (1974)** – renamed **CPCB** by the **1988 amendment** – and the State Boards.
[76:3:4] - Structure: **8 chapters, 64 sections**; standards for **discharge of effluents**; prior consent of the Board needed before discharging effluent.
[76:3:5] - **Section 33A**: directions, including **environmental compensation**.
[76:3:6] - Penalties: **1.5 to 6 years' jail**. Rules: Water Rules 1975.
[76:3:7] # Water Cess Act 1977
[76:3:8] - Cess on water consumed by specified industries and local authorities – funds the Boards.
[76:3:9] - Proceeds go to the **Consolidated Fund of India**; subsumed in **GST in 2017**.
[76:3:10] - **Water (Amendment) Act 2024:** minor offences decriminalised – penalties Rs 10,000 to 15 lakh; Centre may exempt some plants from consent.
[76:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 6 p.8-10; NextGen Rocket Environment p.37; PMF Environment Part 6 p.60-61
## SUB 4 | Air Act 1981
[76:4:0] - Purpose: **prevention, control and abatement of air pollution**; maintain **air quality standards** (APPSC G2 2025); Central and State Boards set and enforce standards.
[76:4:1] - Enacted **29 March 1981**; in force **16 May 1981**; modelled on the Water Act.
[76:4:2] - Structure: **7 chapters, 54 sections**.
[76:4:3] - The existing **CPCB got air functions**; SPCBs enforce in States.
[76:4:4] - **Noise** added to the definition of "air pollutant" by the **1987 amendment** (not 1991).
[76:4:5] - **Air pollution control areas**: declared by the **State Government** – Chapter IV, Sections 19-31; a special power of the Air Act, not the Water Act.
[76:4:6] - Emission standards for industry and automobiles. **Section 31A**: directions; Boards can levy compensation.
[76:4:7] # Water Act vs Air Act
[76:4:8] TABLE head: Feature | Water Act 1974 | Air Act 1981
  [76:4:8.0] Aim | Wholesomeness of water | Prevent, control, abate air pollution
  [76:4:8.1] Structure | 8 chapters, 64 sections | 7 chapters, 54 sections
  [76:4:8.2] Basis | Article 252 | Modelled on Water Act
  [76:4:8.3] Boards | Created CPCB and SPCBs | Same Boards given air functions
  [76:4:8.4] Special power | Effluent discharge standards | Air pollution control areas
  [76:4:8.5] Amended | 1988 (CPCB name) | 1987 (noise added)
  [76:4:8.6] Compensation | Section 33A | Section 31A
[76:4:9] - Common: both require **prior consent** of the Board to establish and operate a polluting unit.
[76:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment Part 6 p.8; NextGen Rocket Environment p.36; PMF Environment Part 6 p.62
## SUB 5 | Constitutional Provisions
[76:5:0] TABLE head: Provision | Covers | Nature
  [76:5:0.0] Article 21 | Right to life – read by courts to include a clean and healthy environment | Fundamental Right
  [76:5:0.1] Article 48A | State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife | DPSP
  [76:5:0.2] Article 51A(g) | Citizens shall protect and improve the natural environment and show compassion for living creatures | Fundamental Duty
  [76:5:0.3] Article 252 | Parliament legislates for States that pass resolutions | Basis of Water Act
  [76:5:0.4] Article 253 | Laws to implement international agreements | Basis of EPA
[76:5:1] - Articles 48A and 51A(g) were inserted by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**.
[76:5:2] Water Act = Article 252; EPA = Article 253.
[76:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.10; PMF Environment Part 6 p.59
## SUB 6 | Consent Mechanism and Industry Categories
[76:6:0] # CTE and CTO
[76:6:1] - Two-stage consent from the **SPCB**: **Consent to Establish (CTE)** before setting up → **Consent to Operate (CTO)** before production.
[76:6:2] - **29 Jan 2026 reform**: single application for Air and Water consents plus waste authorisations; **CTO valid until cancelled** (earlier periodic renewal).
[76:6:3] # Colour Categories
[76:6:4] TABLE head: Category | Pollution Index | Level
  [76:6:4.0] Red | 60 and above | Highly polluting (cement, petrochemicals)
  [76:6:4.1] Orange | 41-59 | Moderate
  [76:6:4.2] Green | 21-40 | Low
  [76:6:4.3] White | 20 or less | Practically non-polluting – no consent/EC needed
  [76:6:4.4] Blue (new) | – | Essential environmental services, e.g. Compressed Biogas
[76:6:5] - Basis: pollution potential from **emissions, effluents and hazardous waste** (CPCB, Jun 2026).
[76:6:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:76 sub 8 (CPCB categorisation); NextGen Environment Part 4.1 p.11
## SUB 7 | Penalties and Jan Vishwas Act 2023
[76:7:0] - EPA original penalty: up to **5 years or Rs 1 lakh**, plus **Rs 5,000 per day** for continuing offence.
[76:7:1] - **Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023** **decriminalised** the EPA penalty regime – monetary penalties fixed by an **adjudicating officer**; appeals go to the **NGT**. The Water and Air Acts were also amended.
[76:7:2] - Minor offences decriminalised by amendment in 2024.
[76:7:3] - **PLI Act 1991** (amended by Jan Vishwas): penalty instead of imprisonment; penalty rates moved to the rules; Environmental Relief Fund money can go to CPCB/SPCBs for restoration; relief for death raised from **Rs 25,000 to Rs 5 lakh**.
[76:7:4] The 5 years / Rs 1 lakh / Rs 5,000 per day figures belong to the EPA; Water Act jail is 1.5-6 years.
[76:7:5] - **Economic instruments:** a **pollution tax** (polluter pays) is considered the most effective instrument of pollution control – better than subsidies, moral persuasion or common law.
[76:7:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 6 p.61-64; app notes 5:76 sub 5
## SUB 8 | AP Pollution Control Board
[76:8:0] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [76:8:0.0] Set up | 1976 under the Water Act as the State Water Board; later renamed APPCB (APPSC 2022)
  [76:8:0.1] Head office | Vijayawada; 3 Zonal and 13 Regional offices
  [76:8:0.2] Laws implemented | Water, Air and EP Acts + hazardous, bio-medical, plastic and solid waste rules
  [76:8:0.3] Other functions | Siting guidelines for industries; SOPs for marine outfall monitoring and hazardous waste
  [76:8:0.4] Online consent | OCMMS (Online Consent Management and Monitoring System) – faster, transparent consents
  [76:8:0.5] Ease of doing business | Computerised inspection allocation – high-risk industries inspected more often
[76:8:1] - Davis Instruments Airlinks is NOT among the APPCB scientific division machines.
[76:8:2] - **Environmental compensation**: SC (Aug 2025) upheld PCB power under **S.33A Water Act / S.31A Air Act**, only where harm is clear or imminent.
[76:8:3] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:76 sub 7
## SUB 9 | Judicial Principles and Cases
[76:9:0] # Principles → Case
[76:9:1] TABLE head: Principle | Meaning | Landmark case
  [76:9:1.0] Absolute liability | Hazardous industry liable for all harm; no exceptions of strict liability | M.C. Mehta v. Union of India – Oleum gas leak (Shriram plant, Delhi, 1985; Bench led by CJ Bhagwati)
  [76:9:1.1] Polluter pays | Polluter bears cost of preventing and remedying damage | Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) – Bichhri, Udaipur, H-acid sludge; first SC application
  [76:9:1.2] Precautionary principle | Act to prevent harm even without full certainty | Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996) – tanneries; both principles part of sustainable development and law of the land
  [76:9:1.3] Public trust doctrine | State holds air, waters, forests in trust for the public | M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath – motel on the Beas; lease quashed
[76:9:2] # Recent Cases and Orders
[76:9:3] TABLE head: Case | Holding
  [76:9:3.0] Vanashakti v. UoI (31 Jul 2026) | SC nullified the 2021 Office Memorandum on ex post facto ECs on paying penalty; ruling prospective; orders cannot override EIA 2006; ex post facto EC only via Article 142 in fit cases
  [76:9:3.1] M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI | CSR inherently includes environmental protection
  [76:9:3.2] NGT suo motu (15 Jan 2026) | Notice to Rajasthan, MP, UP over sewage in drinking water; chairperson Prakash Shrivastava
[76:9:4] - **Bichhri case:** Bichhri village is near Udaipur in **Rajasthan**, where chemical units dumped H-acid sludge (ICELA, 1996).

=== NOTES 5:78 | Environmental Institutions – MoEFCC, Cpcb and SPCBs, National Green Tribunal, National Biodiversity Authority
## SUB 0 | MoEFCC and Its Institutions
[78:0:0] # Evolution
[78:0:1] TABLE head: Year | Step
  [78:0:1.0] 1980 | Department of Environment
  [78:0:1.1] 1985 | Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF)
  [78:0:1.2] 2014 | Renamed MoEFCC
[78:0:2] - MoEFCC is the **nodal agency for UNEP** in India (and for environmental and forestry policy).
[78:0:3] - **ENVIS** (Environmental Information System): central sector scheme **since 1982** (**Sixth Plan**, not Fifth); renamed **EIACP** (2022).
[78:0:4] - **Green Skill Development Programme (GSDP):** pilot **June 2017**, full launch May 2018, under **ENVIS** – trains youth for jobs in the **environment and forest sectors**.
[78:0:5] # Institutes and locations
[78:0:6] TABLE head: Institute | Location
  [78:0:6.0] Botanical Survey of India (1890) and Zoological Survey of India | Kolkata
  [78:0:6.1] Forest Survey of India (1981), WII, FRI, ICFRE | Dehradun
  [78:0:6.2] NEERI | Nagpur
  [78:0:6.3] SACON | Coimbatore
  [78:0:6.4] GBPNIHE | Kosi-Katarmal, Almora
  [78:0:6.5] IITR (toxicology) | Lucknow
  [78:0:6.6] CMLRE ("Bhavasagara") | Kochi
[78:0:7] - **FSI Large Forest Fire Monitoring Programme:** beta launched **16 Jan 2019** with near-real-time **SNPP-VIIRS** data; tracks large fires and sends large-fire alerts; part of **FAST 3.0** (Forest Fire Alert System) – not "FAST 5.0".
[78:0:8] # Other statutory bodies
[78:0:9] TABLE head: Body | Basis
  [78:0:9.0] CAQM (NCR) | CAQM Act 2021; replaced EPCA
  [78:0:9.1] Central Ground Water Authority | 1997, Section 3(3) EP Act
  [78:0:9.2] NMCG | Successor to NGRBA (2009)
  [78:0:9.3] NRCP | 38 rivers in 16 States
[78:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.11, p.39-40; Shankar Environment Part 9 p.18 (ENVIS 1982); moef.gov.in (GSDP); PMF Internal Security & DM Part 2 p.67 (FAST 3.0); PMF Environment Part 3 p.60; app notes 5:78 sub 0, 7, 8
## SUB 1 | SPCBs and the Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board
[78:1:0] # SPCBs
[78:1:1] - Created under the **Water Act 1974** (with the CPCB); chairperson nominated by the **State Government**; inspect, analyse samples, enforce standards, **grant consents**.
[78:1:2] - **Consent to Establish** before setting up; **Consent to Operate** before **starting production or discharge**.
[78:1:3] # APPCB
[78:1:4] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [78:1:4.0] Set up | 1976 by the Government of AP as the State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution (Water Act 1974); later renamed APPCB
  [78:1:4.1] Offices | Head office Vijayawada; 3 Zonal and 13 Regional offices
  [78:1:4.2] Laws enforced | Water, Air and EP Acts + waste rules (not the Water Act alone)
  [78:1:4.3] Lab instruments | UV-Visible spectrometer, specific ion analyser, Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometer (heavy metals such as lead, cadmium) – Davis Instruments Airlinks is NOT listed
  [78:1:4.4] River water quality | APPCB rates AP river water Class 'C' (usable for drinking only after conventional treatment and disinfection; high coliform – e.g. Nagavali, Vamsadhara)
[78:1:5] # Other AP environment bodies
[78:1:6] - **AP Environment Management Corporation (APEMC/APEMCL):** cabinet approval **Nov 2019**; **collection, transport, storage, treatment and disposal of industrial and other waste**, with the APPCB.
[78:1:7] - **AP SEIAA:** clears **Category B** projects under EIA 2006.
[78:1:8] - **AP State Biodiversity Board:** biodiversity parks on flood plains of **5 polluted rivers**.
[78:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.37; thehansindia.com (11 Mar 2019, APPCB 'C' category); app notes 5:78 sub 2, 7
## SUB 2 | National Biodiversity Authority and the Biological Diversity Act 2002
[78:2:0] - **Biological Diversity Act 2002** (follows the **CBD**): conservation, sustainable use, **access and benefit sharing**; amended **2023**; BD Rules 2024.
[78:2:1] - **NBA:** statutory, autonomous body set up in **2003** to implement the Act; HQ **Chennai** (not Bengaluru).
[78:2:2] - **Three tiers:** **NBA** (national) → **State Biodiversity Boards** → **Biodiversity Management Committees** (local).
[78:2:3] - **People's Biodiversity Register (PBR):** a **record of biodiversity and related knowledge at the local level**, prepared by the BMC with local people.
[78:2:4] - **Biopiracy:** foreigners need **NBA approval** to access bio-resources or traditional knowledge; NBA approval **precedes IPR**.
[78:2:5] - NBA handles biodiversity, **not NCAP**.
[78:2:6] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment Part 21 p.16-17; NextGen Rocket Environment p.40, p.66; PMF Environment Part 6 p.94; app notes 5:78 sub 6
## SUB 3 | Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)
[78:3:0] # Set-up and status
[78:3:1] - Constituted in **September 1974** under the **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974** as the Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution; renamed **CPCB** in **1988**; the **oldest national pollution-control body**.
[78:3:2] - **Air functions** came from the **Air Act 1981**; it gives technical services to the MoEFCC under the EP Act 1986.
[78:3:3] - **Statutory body** under the **MoEFCC** (not an executive-order body); HQ **New Delhi**.
[78:3:4] - **Chairman:** a **full-time Chairman nominated by the Central Government** (not the President, PM, Vice-President or Minister); Amandeep Garg (Sep 2026).
[78:3:5] - Role: **enforces environmental standards** under the EP Act framework; sets standards, monitors, advises the Centre; **nodal agency** for standards and monitoring of waste residues with SPCBs.
[78:3:6] # Functions and programmes
[78:3:7] TABLE head: Item | Detail
  [78:3:7.0] Principal functions | Cleanliness of streams and wells (water); improve air quality
  [78:3:7.1] NAMP | National Air Monitoring Programme – 1,646 stations in 603 cities (March 2026)
  [78:3:7.2] National AQI | Launched 2015
  [78:3:7.3] RTWQMS | Real-time water quality of the Ganga and Yamuna
  [78:3:7.4] NCAP | Tracked on the PRANA portal
[78:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.11, p.37, p.39; PMF Environment Part 6 p.56; Praveen CA-360 Sep 2026 p.43, p.90; app notes 5:78 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Major Environmental Laws – Year and Area
[78:4:0] TABLE head: Act | Year | Core area
  [78:4:0.0] Wildlife (Protection) | 1972 | Wild animals
  [78:4:0.1] Water | 1974 | Water pollution; created CPCB and SPCBs
  [78:4:0.2] Forest (Conservation) | 1980 | Forest diversion
  [78:4:0.3] Air | 1981 | Air pollution
  [78:4:0.4] Environment (Protection) | 1986 | Umbrella legislation
  [78:4:0.5] NEAA | 1997 | Appeals on clearances
  [78:4:0.6] Biological Diversity | 2002 | Biodiversity and benefit sharing
  [78:4:0.7] Forest Rights | 2006 | Forest-dweller rights
  [78:4:0.8] NGT | 2010 | Environmental justice
[78:4:1] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.12, p.66; app notes 5:78 sub 5

  In which year was the Forest (Conservation) Act, which regulates forest diversion, enacted?
  1972 | 1974 | *1980 | 1986
  x: The Forest (Conservation) Act is of 1980; the Wildlife Act is 1972 and the EPA 1986.

=== NOTES 5:79 | International Environmental Treaties – Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992, Ramsar, Cites, Cbd and Its Protocols
## SUB 0 | Stockholm 1972, UNEP and World Environment Day
[79:0:0] # Stockholm Conference
[79:0:1] - **UN Conference on the Human Environment (UNCHE)**, **Stockholm, Sweden, 5–16 June 1972** – the **first major world conference on the environment**.
[79:0:2] - Outcomes: **Stockholm Declaration (26 principles)** + Action Plan; **UNEP** set up in **1972**; **5 June = World Environment Day** (first observed **1973**).
[79:0:3] - **Indira Gandhi** was the **only visiting head of government**; she linked poverty and environment.
[79:0:4] - **India's follow-up:** the **National Committee on Environmental Planning and Coordination (NCEPC)** was set up in **1972** (Feb 1972, under the Dept of Science and Technology); the Stockholm decisions were implemented through the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**.
[79:0:5] - **Sustainable development:** Stockholm first put environment and development together on the world agenda; the term was defined by the **Brundtland Report "Our Common Future" (1987)** and spread worldwide by **Rio 1992**.
[79:0:6] # UNEP and UNEA
[79:0:7] - **UNEP:** est. **1972** (Stockholm), HQ **Nairobi, Kenya**.
[79:0:8] - **UN Environment Assembly (UNEA):** created at **Rio+20 (2012)**; meets **biennially in Nairobi**. **UNEA-4: 11–15 March 2019, Nairobi** – theme "Innovative solutions for environmental challenges and sustainable consumption and production"; India's resolutions on single-use plastics and sustainable nitrogen management adopted.
[79:0:9] - **Global 500 awards** (protection of the environment) were launched in **1987 by UNEP**. **Champions of the Earth** (2005) = UNEP's highest honour.
[79:0:10] - **International Nitrogen Initiative (INI):** set up in **2003** under **SCOPE and IGBP** (not UNEP); aim – **optimise nitrogen's beneficial role in sustainable food production** while minimising its harm.
[79:0:11] # World Environment Day – 5 June
[79:0:12] TABLE head: Year | Host | Theme
  [79:0:12.0] 2016 | Angola | Zero tolerance for the illegal wildlife trade ("Go Wild for Life")
  [79:0:12.1] 2017 | Canada | Connecting People to Nature
  [79:0:12.2] 2018 | India | Beat Plastic Pollution
  [79:0:12.3] 2019 | China | Beat Air Pollution
  [79:0:12.4] 2020 | Colombia (in partnership with Germany) | Time for Nature (biodiversity)
  [79:0:12.5] 2022 | Sweden | Only One Earth
  [79:0:12.6] 2023 | Côte d'Ivoire | Beat Plastic Pollution – PM launched MISHTI and Amrit Dharohar that day
[79:0:13] - Older themes used as distractors: 2013 "Think, Eat, Save"; 2014 "Small Islands and Climate Change"; 2015 "Seven Billion Dreams; One Planet; Consume with Care".
[79:0:14] > WED = 5 June (not 22 May, 2 Feb, 3 March). UNEP (1972) and UNEA (2012) are both in Nairobi – do not mix their origins.

## SUB 1 | Ramsar Convention and India's Wetlands
[79:1:0] # Convention basics
[79:1:1] - **Convention on Wetlands of International Importance** ("waterfowl convention"): adopted **2 February 1971** at **Ramsar, Iran** (hence **World Wetlands Day = 2 February**); in force **1975**; secretariat **Gland, Switzerland** (hosted by IUCN); not part of the UN system.
[79:1:2] - Purpose: **conservation and wise use of wetlands** and their resources – the **only global environmental treaty dealing with a particular ecosystem**.
[79:1:3] - **Three pillars:** **wise use** of all wetlands; designating **wetlands of international importance** (Ramsar List); **international cooperation** – never a ban on all human use.
[79:1:4] - **Wise use** = conserve sites through an **ecosystem approach while allowing their sustainable use** (UPSC 2010) – not keeping them inaccessible or allowing only tourism.
[79:1:5] - **Montreux Record** (1990): Ramsar sites whose ecological character is changing from human interference. Indian sites now: **Keoladeo NP + Loktak Lake**; **Chilika removed (2002)** after restoration.
[79:1:6] - **Wetlands International** is a **global NGO** (a Ramsar International Organisation Partner), **not an intergovernmental body**; it works at ground level and uses field experience to advocate better policies (UPSC 2014 → "2 only").
[79:1:7] - **World Wetlands Day 2017 theme:** **Wetlands for Disaster Risk Reduction**.
[79:1:8] - **Ramsar Wetland Conservation Award 2018 (Wise Use):** **Fundación Global Nature, Spain** (presented at CoP13, Dubai).
[79:1:9] - Ramsar **CoP15** (July 2025): India's resolution on **sustainable lifestyles for wise use of wetlands** adopted.
[79:1:10] # India's Ramsar sites
[79:1:11] - India a Party since **1982** (accession; first sites designated **1 October 1981**): **Chilika Lake** (Odisha) and **Keoladeo NP** (Rajasthan) – the first.
[79:1:12] - **103 Ramsar sites** (as of 2026) after **Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh)** and **Sauj Jheel (Mainpuri, UP)** were added in mid-October 2026 (Rocket CA: 15 Oct); India is **3rd in the world** after the UK and Mexico; **Tamil Nadu** has the most (20).
[79:1:13] - **Udaipur and Indore** = India's first accredited **Wetland Cities** (January 2025).
[79:1:14] - **Amrit Dharohar** (wetlands / Ramsar sites) and **MISHTI** (mangroves) – both launched on **World Environment Day, 5 June 2023**.
[79:1:15] TABLE head: Wetland | State
  [79:1:15.0] Chilika | Odisha
  [79:1:15.1] Keoladeo, Sambhar | Rajasthan
  [79:1:15.2] Wular | J&K
  [79:1:15.3] Loktak | Manipur – India's first floating elementary school (Feb 2017)
  [79:1:15.4] Kolleru | Andhra Pradesh – between the Godavari and Krishna deltas; Ramsar site since 2002; AP's only Ramsar site
  [79:1:15.5] Harike | Punjab
  [79:1:15.6] Kabartal (Kanwar Lake) | Begusarai, Bihar
  [79:1:15.7] East Kolkata, Sundarban | West Bengal (Sundarban not Odisha)
[79:1:16] - **Not Ramsar sites:** the Godavari river, **Pulicat Lake** and **Nellapattu** bird sanctuary (APPSC DL 2020 → Kolleru).
[79:1:17] > Ramsar = wetlands (not ozone, tigers, wild trade, arid lands). Ramsar 1971 is older than Stockholm 1972.
[79:1:18] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.7, p.38; Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 02 p.84, p.146-147; NextGen Environment - APPSC Part 1.2 p.10, Part 6 p.14, Part 8.1 p.11; Shankar Environment ch.28 p.454-456; ramsar.org/2018-awards; old app notes 5:79 (sub 3)

## SUB 3 | Cartagena and Nagoya Protocols
[79:3:0] TABLE head: Point | Cartagena Protocol | Nagoya Protocol
  [79:3:0.0] Subject | Biosafety – safe transfer, handling and use of LMOs/GMOs from modern biotechnology | Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) of genetic resources
  [79:3:0.1] Adopted → in force | 29 Jan 2000 → 11 Sep 2003 | 2010 (COP10) → 2014
  [79:3:0.2] Named after | Cartagena, Colombia | Nagoya, Japan
  [79:3:0.3] Parent | CBD | CBD
  [79:3:0.4] India | MoEF(CC) is the nodal ministry; GEAC approves GM organisms | Ratified 2012; implemented through the Biological Diversity Act, 2002
[79:3:1] - **Both protocols are under the CBD** – not UNFCCC, Ramsar, CITES or the Paris Agreement.
[79:3:2] # Cartagena
[79:3:3] - **Advance Informed Agreement (AIA):** the importing country must consent **before the first transboundary movement** of an LMO meant for release; LMO shipments carry documents identifying the LMO.
[79:3:4] - **Biosafety Clearing-House** = an **online information platform** on LMOs, **not a testing laboratory**.
[79:3:5] - First COP/MOP-1: **February 2004, Kuala Lumpur** (not the Philippines). **India is a Party; the USA is not** a Party to the CBD or its Biosafety Protocol.
[79:3:6] - **Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol** on Liability and Redress (2010) – supplementary to **Cartagena**.
[79:3:7] # Nagoya
[79:3:8] - A **legally binding** supplementary agreement to the CBD – **not voluntary** (APPSC JL 2024 statement 2 false).
[79:3:9] - **Utilisation of genetic resources** = **research and development on the genetic and/or biochemical composition** of genetic resources (so "biochemical R&D", not cloning humans, space research or fossil trade).
[79:3:10] - Covers plant, animal and microbial genetic resources + associated **traditional knowledge**; **excludes human genetic material**.
[79:3:11] - Pillars: **access** with **prior informed consent**, **benefit-sharing** on **Mutually Agreed Terms** (monetary/non-monetary), **compliance**.
[79:3:12] - In India the **Biodiversity Management Committees** are key to Nagoya's objectives. India's **1st National Report**: **3,556 IRCCs**, over **60%** of the global total. **Red sanders** is India's single largest ABS earner.
[79:3:13] > Cartagena = biosafety/LMO; Nagoya = ABS. Nagoya: adopted 2010, India ratified 2012, in force 2014.
[79:3:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC Part 4.1 p.13-14; Rocket Environment p.7-8, p.29-30, p.64; Shankar Environment ch.28 p.449-451; old app notes 5:79 (sub 8)
## SUB 4 | CITES – Basics, Appendices and India
[79:4:0] # Basics
[79:4:1] - **Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora** = the **Washington Convention**: drafted after a **1963 IUCN** resolution, signed **3 March 1973, Washington D.C.** (hence **World Wildlife Day = 3 March**); in force **1 July 1975** (not 1985); members are called **Parties**.
[79:4:2] - Aim: ensure that **international trade** in wild animals and plants **does not threaten their survival** – a watchdog on trade in endangered species (not conservation of migratory species = CMS, nor heritage = WHC).
[79:4:3] - **Legally binding** on Parties, but it **does not take the place of national laws**. Secretariat **Geneva**, administered by **UNEP**.
[79:4:4] - Coverage: about **40,900 species – ~6,610 animals and ~34,310 plants** (2026; older books: ~5,000 animals and ~29,000 plants).
[79:4:5] - CoP meets **every 2-3 years**; species move between Appendices **only by a vote of the CoP**.
[79:4:6] # Appendices
[79:4:7] TABLE head: Appendix | Listing criterion | Trade | Examples
  [79:4:7.0] I | Threatened with extinction | Commercial trade prohibited; exceptional non-commercial trade with import + export permits | Tiger, rhino, clouded leopard, Indian pangolin, Indian star tortoise (CoP18, 2019)
  [79:4:7.1] II | Not necessarily threatened, but may become so without trade control | Allowed with export permits | Corals, most sharks and rays, red sanders, rosewood (Dalbergia), striped hyena, golden gecko
  [79:4:7.2] III | Protected in one Party that asks others' help | Permits / certificates of origin | Walrus (Canada)
[79:4:8] - **Dalbergia** = the **rosewood** genus (legume family; D. latifolia, D. sissoo) – not cashew, coffee or tea.
[79:4:9] # CITES CoPs
[79:4:10] TABLE head: CoP | Venue / year | Highlight
  [79:4:10.0] CoP3 | New Delhi, 1981 | Only CITES CoP hosted by India
  [79:4:10.1] CoP19 | Panama, 2022 | 54 sharks and rays to App II
  [79:4:10.2] CoP20 | Samarkand, Uzbekistan, 2025 | First CITES CoP in Central Asia; 50 years of CITES; whale shark, oceanic whitetip and manta rays → App I; India defeated an EU proposal on Guggul (Commiphora wightii)
[79:4:11] - India's proposals at CoPs include rosewood, otters, tortoises, **Tokay gecko**, wedgefish.
[79:4:12] # India and CITES
[79:4:13] - India a Party since **1976**; implementing law **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** – the 2022 amendment added a CITES chapter and **Schedule IV for CITES-listed specimens**.
[79:4:14] - **Wildlife Crime Control Bureau** (statutory, **2007**, under **MoEFCC**) helps Customs enforce CITES. **ZSI** hosts a CITES Cell. **CITES Trade Database** = **UNEP-WCMC**; **MIKE** monitors elephant poaching.
[79:4:15] - **Red sanders** (Pterocarpus santalinus): endemic to **Seshachalam** / southern Eastern Ghats (AP); IUCN **Endangered**; CITES **App II**; India removed from the CITES **Review of Significant Trade** in **November 2023**.
[79:4:16] > CITES 1973, in force 1975 (not 1963/1985); Washington = CITES, Bonn = CMS. CITES is binding – a statement "not legally binding" is the incorrect one.
[79:4:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC Part 1.2 p.10, Part 2.2 p.12 (UPSC 2015 PYQ), Part 8.1 p.11; Shankar Environment ch.28 p.456; CRS report RL32751 (Jan 2026) for species counts; old app notes 5:79 (sub 4-5)
## SUB 5 | IUCN, TRAFFIC and the Bonn Convention (CMS)
[79:5:0] TABLE head: Body | Year / HQ | Mandate | Status
  [79:5:0.0] IUCN – International Union for Conservation of Nature (formally "... and Natural Resources") | 1948; HQ Gland, Switzerland | Red List; runs field projects worldwide | Union of States and NGOs – not a UN organ
  [79:5:0.1] TRAFFIC | 1976; Cambridge, UK | Ensure that trade in wild plants and animals is not a threat to conservation | Network of WWF and IUCN – not a UNEP bureau
  [79:5:0.2] CMS (Bonn Convention) | 1979; secretariat Bonn | Conservation of migratory species of wild animals | Binding treaty under UNEP; India a Party since 1983
[79:5:1] - **IUCN Luc Hoffmann Award:** first Indian = **Dhrubajyoti Ghosh** (2016), for the **East Kolkata Wetlands**.
[79:5:2] - **CMS Appendices:** I = endangered migratory species (strict protection); II = species needing cooperation agreements.

## SUB 6 | Rio Earth Summit 1992 and Follow-ups
[79:6:0] - **UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED)** = "**Earth Summit**", **Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, June 1992** – the **first international Earth Summit**.
[79:6:1] - Outputs: **Agenda 21** (action plan for sustainable development), **Rio Declaration** (27 principles), **Forest Principles** (non-binding), and two binding treaties opened for signature – **UNFCCC** and **CBD**. **UNCCD** followed in **1994**.
[79:6:2] - **UNFCCC** was drawn up at Rio 1992 (not Stockholm 1972, Johannesburg 2002 or Copenhagen 2009); in force **21 March 1994**.
[79:6:3] - **UN Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD):** set up by the UNGA in **December 1992** to follow up Rio/Agenda 21 (replaced by the HLPF in 2013).
[79:6:4] TABLE head: Summit | Year / venue | Outcome
  [79:6:4.0] Rio+5 (Earth Summit +5) | 1997, UNGA special session, New York | Reviewed Agenda 21
  [79:6:4.1] Rio+10 (WSSD) | 2002, Johannesburg | Johannesburg Plan of Implementation
  [79:6:4.2] Rio+20 (UNCSD) | 2012, Rio | "The Future We Want"; launched the SDG process; created UNEA
[79:6:5] # Global Environment Facility (GEF)
[79:6:6] - Pilot GEF agreed **1990**, set up on the eve of Rio 1992; first partners **UNDP, UNEP, World Bank**.
[79:6:7] - **Financial mechanism** for the **CBD, UNFCCC**, UNCCD, Stockholm (POPs) and Minamata conventions (UPSC 2014 → option a); it is not an OECD agency and does not itself do research.
[79:6:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.2, p.6, p.8, p.16, p.71; Shankar Environment ch.28 p.447-448; NextGen Environment - APPSC Part 8.1 p.11; old app notes 5:79 (sub 0, 2); CSD 1992: general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 7 | CBD – Objectives, COPs, Aichi Targets and the Kunming-Montreal GBF
[79:7:0] # Convention on Biological Diversity (1992)
[79:7:1] - **Opened for signature at Rio 1992** (Earth Summit), not Stockholm 1972; text adopted **22 May 1992** (hence **International Day for Biological Diversity = 22 May**); **legally binding**; in force **29 December 1993**; secretariat **Montreal, Canada**; India ratified **1994**.
[79:7:2] - **Three objectives:** **conservation** of biodiversity, **sustainable use** of its components, **fair and equitable sharing of benefits** from genetic resources (not compulsory technology transfer).
[79:7:3] - One of the **three Rio Conventions** (UNFCCC, CBD, UNCCD); financial mechanism = **GEF**. In-situ = conservation in the natural habitat; **ex-situ = outside the natural habitat** (zoos, gene banks).
[79:7:4] - India implements it through the **Biological Diversity Act, 2002** (amended **2023**; criticised for diluting ABS and the role of local communities): three tiers – **National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai)**, **State Biodiversity Boards**, **Biodiversity Management Committees** (prepare **People's Biodiversity Registers**; may **levy collection fees**).
[79:7:5] - **AP State Biodiversity Board:** aims at **zero loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services by 2050**; portal **BIOMIS**.
[79:7:6] # CBD COPs (every two years)
[79:7:7] TABLE head: COP | Year | Venue | Outcome
  [79:7:7.0] COP1 | 1994 | Nassau, Bahamas | First COP
  [79:7:7.1] COP10 | 2010 | Nagoya, Japan | Nagoya Protocol; Aichi Targets (Strategic Plan 2011-2020)
  [79:7:7.2] COP11 | 2012 | Hyderabad, India | Hosted by India
  [79:7:7.3] COP12 | 2014 | Pyeongchang, Korea | Mid-term review of Aichi
  [79:7:7.4] COP13 | Dec 2016 | Cancun, Mexico | –
  [79:7:7.5] COP14 | 2018 | Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt | Began the post-2020 framework
  [79:7:7.6] COP15 | 2021 (Kunming) + Dec 2022 (Montreal) | China + Canada | Kunming-Montreal GBF; 30x30; GBF Fund
  [79:7:7.7] COP16 | Oct 2024 | Cali, Colombia | Cali Fund on DSI; India's updated NBSAP
[79:7:8] - Sequence: **Nagoya 2010 → Kunming 2021 → Montreal Dec 2022 → Cali Oct 2024**. COP15 also served as the 10th MOP of Cartagena and 4th MOP of Nagoya.
[79:7:9] # Aichi Biodiversity Targets
[79:7:10] - **20 targets** under **5 strategic goals**, Strategic Plan **2011-2020**, adopted at **COP10, Nagoya (Aichi Prefecture), 2010** (not COP12 2014 as one NextGen line says). Deadline 2020; **none fully met** (Global Biodiversity Outlook 5).
[79:7:11] # Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (Dec 2022)
[79:7:12] - Adopted at **COP15, Montreal, December 2022** – not Kunming 2021, not COP16 Cali. **4 goals for 2050, 23 targets for 2030**.
[79:7:13] TABLE head: Item | Content
  [79:7:13.0] Goal A | Halt human-induced extinction; cut extinction rate tenfold
  [79:7:13.1] Goal B / C / D | Sustainable use / fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources / finance and technology (close the US$700 bn gap)
  [79:7:13.2] Target 1 | Loss of high-biodiversity areas close to zero
  [79:7:13.3] Target 2 | Restore 30% of degraded land and water ecosystems
  [79:7:13.4] Target 3 (30x30) | Conserve 30% of land and 30% of oceans by 2030
  [79:7:13.5] Target 6 | Cut invasive alien species introduction by at least 50%
  [79:7:13.6] Target 7 | Halve excess nutrients and pesticide risk
  [79:7:13.7] Target 16 | Halve food waste
  [79:7:13.8] Target 18 | Cut harmful subsidies by US$500 bn a year
  [79:7:13.9] Target 19 | Mobilise US$200 bn a year by 2030 from all sources
  [79:7:13.10] Target 22 | Full participation and rights of indigenous peoples and local communities
[79:7:14] - **30x30 is a biodiversity (area-protection) target, NOT a renewable-energy target** (APPSC G1 2024). It is championed by the **High Ambition Coalition (HAC) for Nature and People**, co-chaired by **Costa Rica, France and the UK**; **India joined in Oct 2021 – the first BRICS country** to do so.
[79:7:15] - Money: **GBF Fund under the GEF**; **Cali Fund** – large DSI users pay **1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue**. National reports under **Article 26**.
[79:7:16] - **India's updated NBSAP 2024-2030:** **23 national targets**, released at **COP16 Cali**. India's **7th National Report** = first full review against the 23 KMGBF targets.
[79:7:17] > US$200 bn = mobilise (T19); US$500 bn = subsidy cut (T18); US$700 bn = finance gap (Goal D). 30% conserve = T3; 30% restore = T2.
[79:7:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment - APPSC Part 4.1 p.14, Part 4.2 p.2, Part 8.1 p.11; Rocket Environment p.7, p.16, p.29; Shankar Environment ch.28 p.448-452; old app notes 5:79 (sub 7, 9-11)
