=== NOTES 5:80 | Sustainable Development – Meaning, Nature, Scope and Components
## SUB 0 | Meaning and the Brundtland Definition
[80:0:0] # Brundtland Commission (1987)
[80:0:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [80:0:1.0] Formal name | World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) – UN-mandated, set up in the early 1980s
  [80:0:1.1] Chair | Gro Harlem Brundtland, then Prime Minister of Norway ("Mother of Sustainable Development")
  [80:0:1.2] Report | "Our Common Future" = the Brundtland Report
  [80:0:1.3] Year | 1987
  [80:0:1.4] Contribution | First widely accepted (official) definition; popularised the term and linked economic development with environmental stability
[80:0:2] - **Definition:** development that "**meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**" – given by the **WCED (1987)**, not UNEP, the World Bank, the IMF, UNCED 1992 or the Tbilisi Declaration (1977).
[80:0:3] - **Our Common Future on poverty:** "**Poverty is a major cause and effect of global environmental problems**" – so environment cannot be tackled without tackling poverty and inequality.
[80:0:4] - **Concepts in one line:** sustainable development = the definition above; Our Common Future = the 1987 report; **intergenerational equity** = fair sharing of resources between present and future generations.
[80:0:5] - Exam shorthand: "**improving the conditions of the present generation without affecting the needs of future generations**" = sustainable development exactly.
[80:0:6] > Most-asked (×20): who defined it / which report / which year → **Brundtland, Our Common Future, 1987**. Rio 1992 and Stockholm 1972 are the tempting wrong options.
[80:0:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 6 p.6 (21.4.1 Brundtland Commission); NextGen Society Group 2 Part 2 p.10-11; NextGen Rocket Environment p.71; PMF Human & Economic Geography Part 2 p.45; en.wikisource.org Brundtland Report ch.1 (poverty sentence)
## SUB 1 | Rio Earth Summit 1992 and Agenda 21
[80:1:0] # UNCED – the first Earth Summit
[80:1:1] - **UNCED = United Nations Conference on Environment and Development** ("Earth Summit"), **Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 3-14 June 1992**; 20th anniversary of Stockholm 1972; about **178-179 countries**.
[80:1:2] - **Outcomes:** **Agenda 21**, **Rio Declaration** (**27 principles**), **Forest Principles** (non-binding); legally binding conventions opened for signature: **UNFCCC** and **CBD** (UNCCD followed in 1994).
[80:1:3] - **UNFCCC** was negotiated in New York and **drawn/opened for signature at UNCED, Rio 1992** – not at Stockholm 1972, WSSD 2002 or Copenhagen 2009.
[80:1:4] # Agenda 21
[80:1:5] TABLE head: Point | Fact
  [80:1:5.0] What | Comprehensive (non-binding) global action plan for sustainable development – globally, nationally, locally, wherever humans affect the environment
  [80:1:5.1] Origin | UNCED, Rio 1992 – NOT the Johannesburg WSSD 2002 (UPSC 2016: statement 1 only)
  [80:1:5.2] "21" | 21st century
  [80:1:5.3] Key objective | Every local government should draw its own Local Agenda 21 (LA21)
  [80:1:5.4] Sample programme area | Ch.2: "Promoting sustainable development through trade"; Ch.4 is *changing* (not maintaining) consumption patterns
  [80:1:5.5] Aim | Combat environmental damage, poverty and disease through global co-operation
[80:1:6] - Agenda 21 is not a law that each country must enact, and not a "20th-century only" target.
[80:1:7] > Rio 1992 is the "first Earth Summit" (not Washington, Geneva or Buenos Aires); MPPSC 1992 printed "UN Conference on Sustainable Development" for Rio – formally the 1992 meeting was UNCED.
[80:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.2, p.6, p.16, p.71; NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.11; Shankar Environment 21 (OCR) p.23-24; PMF Environment Part 6 p.3, p.6-7, p.14; NCERT Human Geography (OnlyIAS) Part 10 p.25; static.un.org Agenda 21 ch.2
## SUB 2 | Follow-up Summits – Rio+5, WSSD, Rio+20, 2030 Agenda
[80:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Formal name (popular name) | Venue | Outcome
  [80:2:0.0] 1972 | UN Conference on the Human Environment (UNCHE) | Stockholm | First world environment conference; UNEP (HQ Nairobi)
  [80:2:0.1] 1992 | UNCED – Earth Summit | Rio de Janeiro | Agenda 21, Rio Declaration, UNFCCC, CBD
  [80:2:0.2] 1997 | Earth Summit +5 (Rio+5), UNGA special session | New York | Reviewed Agenda 21
  [80:2:0.3] 1997 | Kyoto COP3 | Kyoto | Kyoto Protocol (climate)
  [80:2:0.4] 2000 | Millennium Summit | New York | MDGs (2000-2015)
  [80:2:0.5] 2002 | World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) – Rio+10 | Johannesburg | Johannesburg Declaration; Johannesburg Plan of Implementation (JPOI)
  [80:2:0.6] June 2012 | UN Conference on Sustainable Development (UNCSD) – Rio+20 | Rio de Janeiro | "The Future We Want"; green economy; SDGs born here; PAGE
  [80:2:0.7] 25 Sept 2015 | UN Sustainable Development Summit (UNGA 70) | New York | "Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda" – 17 SDGs
[80:2:1] - **JPOI:** states to formulate **national strategies for sustainable development** and **begin their implementation by 2005**.
[80:2:2] - **Rio+20:** 20-year follow-up to 1992, 10-year follow-up to 2002; third SD conference, hosted by Brazil. The SDGs were **born at Rio+20, 2012** (not 2010).
[80:2:3] - **PAGE (Partnership for Action on Green Economy):** **emerged at Rio+20 (2012)** as a response to The Future We Want (launched 2013); agencies **UNEP, UNDP, ILO, UNIDO, UNITAR**.
[80:2:4] - **2015** also saw the **COP21 Paris Agreement** – the SDGs coincided with it.
[80:2:5] # UN Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD)
[80:2:6] - **Established by the UN General Assembly in December 1992** (Res. 47/191) to **review implementation of Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration**.
[80:2:7] - **Replaced in 2013** by the **High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development (HLPF)** (under ECOSOC/UNGA), as decided at Rio+20.
[80:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.6, p.16, p.20, p.71; PMF Environment Part 6 p.4, p.7-9; Shankar Environment 21 (OCR) p.24; un.org/esa/sustdev JPOI ch.11 para 162(b); press.un.org GA/11393 (HLPF replaces CSD, 2013)
## SUB 3 | 2030 Agenda and SDGs – Basics
[80:3:0] - **17 SDGs, 169 targets, 232 indicators**; adopted by **all 193 UN member states** in **September 2015**; in force **1 Jan 2016**; target year **2030**.
[80:3:1] - **Not legally binding** and not a single development model; they **replaced the MDGs (2000-2015)**.
[80:3:2] - **Five Ps:** **People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership** (not Patriotism).
[80:3:3] - **Dimensions:** **economic, social, environmental**.
[80:3:4] - **Goal 1:** "**End poverty in all its forms everywhere**" – no 50%/75% target.
[80:3:5] - Aim: get rid of poverty, protect the environment and ensure peace and prosperity for all; scope covers goals like life below water, decent work and cultural diversity (target 4.7) – **not political alliances**.
[80:3:6] - Biggest hurdle for poverty eradication: **economic inequality and unequal distribution of resources**.
[80:3:7] - **UNDP** is the UN development agency that leads SDG support work in countries; in India **NITI Aayog** coordinates.
[80:3:8] - **Andhra Pradesh** adopted **all 17 SDGs** with **212 indicators** to monitor progress to 2030; SDG targets are built into **Swarna Andhra @2047**.
[80:3:9] # Sustainable Development Report (UN SDSN)
[80:3:10] - **SDR 2025:** India **99th of 167** – first time in the top 100.
[80:3:11] - **SDR 2026:** India **94th of 169** (best ever); **Finland** first, Sweden and Denmark next.
[80:3:12] > Detail on each goal and the SDG India Index: see row 81.
[80:3:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.20; PMF Environment Part 6 p.8-10; NextGen Society Group 2 Part 2 p.11; NextGen Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 01 p.26, Part 02 p.166; app notes 5:80 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Three Pillars and Types of Sustainability
[80:4:0] TABLE head: Pillar | Aim
  [80:4:0.0] Economic | Growth that lasts – NOT profit maximisation that ignores social or environmental impact
  [80:4:0.1] Social | Social equity / equality, inclusion, community development
  [80:4:0.2] Environmental | Reduce waste, conserve natural resources, protect ecosystems
[80:4:1] - UN wording: **economic growth, environmental protection, social equity** – interlinked; SD's key goal is to ensure all three together.
[80:4:2] - **Triple bottom line:** **People, Planet, Profit**.
[80:4:3] - **NOT a pillar:** political, military, cultural, technological, legal or financial.
[80:4:4] - "Social sustainability focuses exclusively on growth and jobs" ✗; "economic sustainability = maximising profits" ✗ (A false, R true).
[80:4:5] - **Sustainability** broadly = programmes and actions to preserve a particular resource; SD is achieved by social and economic improvement that protects the environment and supports equality (A/R: both true, R not the explanation).
[80:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society Group 2 Part 2 p.10 (parameters of SD); PMF Environment Part 6 p.6; app notes 5:80 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Principles, Nature and Scope
[80:5:0] TABLE head: Principle | Meaning
  [80:5:0.0] Intergenerational equity | Present must not deplete (natural) resources at the cost of future generations – "inter-generational sensibility" in the use of natural resources
  [80:5:0.1] Carrying capacity | Human use within what ecosystems can support – the Brundtland idea is intertwined with carrying capacity (UPSC 2010)
  [80:5:0.2] Precautionary principle | Lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone measures against harm
  [80:5:0.3] Polluter pays | The polluter (person or company) bears the cost of preventing or remedying the damage – not the government or public
  [80:5:0.4] CBDR | Shared duty; developed nations carry more
  [80:5:0.5] Integration | Environment and economy are integrated, not opposites
[80:5:1] - **NOT a principle:** over-exploitation of resources, growth at the cost of environment, more pollution for industry.
[80:5:2] - **NCERT principles:** respect all life, improve quality of life, **conserve the earth's vitality and diversity**, **minimise depletion of natural resources**, change attitudes, let communities care for their own environment.
[80:5:3] - **Measures:** renewables, recycling, lower and more efficient energy use; all pollution minimised; consumption must **not exceed** the rate of regeneration.
[80:5:4] - **Challenges:** **over-consumption**; **increased use of fossil fuels** is a negative impact of technology.
[80:5:5] - **Education** helps by **promoting environmental awareness**; communication for SD aims at **transformative learning**.
[80:5:6] - **Environmental sustainability needs participatory, open and democratic decision-making**; **environmental protection** maintains (and restores) a healthy natural environment and **is not a luxury** at today's level of development.
[80:5:7] - SD includes a **constant or rising stock of capital assets**; natural **climatic change over time** is not part of the concept.
[80:5:8] - **Scope includes** meeting present needs, **equity within and across generations**, inclusion ("leave no one behind"); **excludes** growth that runs down natural capital and treating environment and development as opposites.
[80:5:9] - **Poverty alleviation** is printed as "not related to environmental protection" (UP 2013 key).
[80:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 6 p.13-14 (carrying capacity); PMF Environment Part 4 p.48 (polluter pays); NCERT Human Geography (OnlyIAS) Part 10 p.25; NextGen Society Group 2 Part 2 p.10; app notes 5:80 sub 5-6
## SUB 6 | Precursors and Thinkers
[80:6:0] TABLE head: Year | Milestone | Point
  [80:6:0.0] 1962 | Silent Spring – Rachel Carson | Set off the modern environmental movement
  [80:6:0.1] 1972 | The Limits to Growth – Club of Rome (MIT team, Donella and Dennis Meadows) | Computer model: growth cannot go on forever on finite resources
  [80:6:0.2] 1980 | World Conservation Strategy – IUCN with UNEP and WWF | Subtitle "Living Resource Conservation for Sustainable Development" – first prominent use of the term
  [80:6:0.3] 1987 | Our Common Future | First accepted definition
[80:6:1] - **Green Development** (1990; "Environment and Sustainability in the Third World/Developing World") – **W.M. (Bill) Adams**, Cambridge geographer.
[80:6:2] - **When did the term come in?** Printed key **1980** (World Conservation Strategy); many books say **1987** (Brundtland) because the report popularised and defined it.
[80:6:3] - The Club of Rome did NOT propose the SDGs (UPSC 2016).
[80:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Society Group 2 Part 2 p.11 (Limits to Growth, Club of Rome); PMF Environment Part 6 p.9; environmentandsociety.org (WCS 1980); routledge.com (Green Development, W.M. Adams); app notes 5:80 sub 1
## SUB 7 | Measuring Sustainability – Natural Capital and Footprints
[80:7:0] TABLE head: Measure | Meaning
  [80:7:0.0] Natural capital | Resources created by nature – air, water, land, minerals, forests; roads are NOT (man-made)
  [80:7:0.1] Ecological footprint | Biologically productive land and sea area needed to supply a person's/population's consumption and absorb its wastes; unit global hectare
  [80:7:0.2] Earth Overshoot Day | Date when humanity's yearly demand exceeds what Earth can regenerate – a sign of environmental degradation; calculated by Global Footprint Network; conceived by Andrew Simms (New Economics Foundation), first campaign 2006
  [80:7:0.3] Green GDP | GDP – net natural capital consumption (depletion + degradation)
  [80:7:0.4] Genuine Progress Indicator | Adds unpaid work; subtracts pollution, crime, resource loss
[80:7:1] - Humanity's footprint ≈ **1.5 Earths**; India ≈ 0.9 (sustainable lifestyle).
[80:7:2] - Biota, biome and niche are not area measures.
[80:7:3] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 3 (OCR) p.16-17; Shankar Environment 19 (OCR) p.20; NextGen Rocket Environment p.43; PMF Environment Part 2 p.47-48; app notes 5:80 sub 7

## SUB 9 | Indian Law – Courts and the NGT
[80:9:0] TABLE head: Case / body | Principle
  [80:9:0.0] Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. UoI (1996) | Made sustainable development, precautionary principle and polluter pays part of Indian law
  [80:9:0.1] M.C. Mehta v. UoI | Polluter pays
[80:9:1] - **NGT** must apply **sustainable development, precautionary and polluter-pays** principles; HQ **New Delhi**; benches **Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai** – **no Hyderabad bench**.
[80:9:2] - **National Environment Policy 2006:** conservation and livelihood security are **linked**; its Expert Panel led to the **Wetlands Rules 2010**.

=== NOTES 5:81 | Goals of Sustainable Development – the 17 SDGs, Targets and India's Sdg Index Performance
## SUB 0 | The 17 SDGs – Number, Goal Numbers and Themes
[81:0:0] # The 17 goals (most-asked angle)
[81:0:1] TABLE head: SDG | Goal | Key words in the stem
  [81:0:1.0] 1 | No Poverty | end poverty in all its forms everywhere
  [81:0:1.1] 2 | Zero Hunger | end hunger, food security, improved nutrition, sustainable agriculture
  [81:0:1.2] 3 | Good Health and Well-being | healthy lives, well-being for all ages
  [81:0:1.3] 4 | Quality Education | inclusive, equitable quality education, lifelong learning
  [81:0:1.4] 5 | Gender Equality | empower all women and girls
  [81:0:1.5] 6 | Clean Water and Sanitation | availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation
  [81:0:1.6] 7 | Affordable and Clean Energy | affordable, reliable, sustainable, modern energy
  [81:0:1.7] 8 | Decent Work and Economic Growth | jobs, youth employment
  [81:0:1.8] 9 | Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure | (internet access only a target, 9.c)
  [81:0:1.9] 10 | Reduced Inequalities | within and among countries; safe, orderly migration
  [81:0:1.10] 11 | Sustainable Cities and Communities | urbanisation
  [81:0:1.11] 12 | Responsible Consumption and Production | 
  [81:0:1.12] 13 | Climate Action | urgent action to combat climate change
  [81:0:1.13] 14 | Life Below Water | oceans, seas, marine resources (Blue Economy)
  [81:0:1.14] 15 | Life on Land | forests, desertification, land degradation, biodiversity
  [81:0:1.15] 16 | Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions | 
  [81:0:1.16] 17 | Partnerships for the Goals | finance, technology, capacity-building, trade (means of implementation)
[81:0:2] - **Count:** **17 goals, 169 targets** (232 indicators) – asked in some 15 APPSC papers as "how many SDGs" (11 / 13 / 15 / 21 are distractors).
[81:0:3] - **Grouping:** Goals **1–7** extend the MDG concerns; **8–10** inclusiveness, jobs, infrastructure, distribution; the last seven (**11–17**) sustainability, peace and partnership.
[81:0:4] # Problem → goal
[81:0:5] TABLE head: Problem or theme | SDG
  [81:0:5.0] Food insecurity, malnutrition | 2
  [81:0:5.1] Inadequate healthcare | 3
  [81:0:5.2] Literacy, vocational skills | 4
  [81:0:5.3] Gender inequality; child marriage, violence against women | 5
  [81:0:5.4] Unsafe drinking water, open defecation | 6
  [81:0:5.5] Lack of electricity, cooking fuel; subsidy for solar panels | 7
  [81:0:5.6] Youth unemployment | 8
  [81:0:5.7] Remittance costs (below 3%), migration | 10
[81:0:6] - **Goal 4 targets:** free primary and secondary education; early-childhood care; **affordable technical, vocational and tertiary** education; **Target 4.7** – knowledge for sustainable development, **global citizenship**, **culture of peace** and cultural diversity.
[81:0:7] - **Goal 5 targets:** end **all discrimination and violence** against women and girls; end **child marriage** and **FGM**; **recognise unpaid care work**; women's **full participation in leadership**.
[81:0:8] # NOT an SDG (NOT-type questions)
[81:0:9] - **Not goals:** "Conflict-free outer space", "Life in sky", "Stop migration", "**Internet for all**", "**End racism**", "**Organising international sports tournaments**", **Blue Economy**, **Green Economy**, Digital Inclusion.
[81:0:10] - **"Reducing poverty"** is the odd one out when Gender Equality, Zero Hunger and Peace–Justice are listed verbatim: SDG 1 seeks to **end** poverty ("No Poverty").
[81:0:11] > ⚠ Trap: the two "life" goals are **Life Below Water (14)** and **Life on Land (15)**; SDG 2 is "Zero Hunger", not "No Hunger".
[81:0:12] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment sheet #10 p.20 (SDG table); NextGen Indian Economy P1 p.35-36; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy ch.19 p.37-38; app notes 5:81 sub 2-3
## SUB 1 | Agenda 2030 – Origin, Adoption and the MDGs
[81:1:0] # Adoption
[81:1:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [81:1:1.0] Proposed at | Rio+20 (UN Conference on Sustainable Development), Rio de Janeiro, 2012; idea from Colombia and Guatemala
  [81:1:1.1] Rio+20 outcome | "The Future We Want" – called for goals to follow the MDGs
  [81:1:1.2] Framework | "Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (not 2035)
  [81:1:1.3] Adopted | 25 September 2015, UN Sustainable Development Summit, UNGA 70th session, by all 193 member states (not 198)
  [81:1:1.4] Period | 2016–2030, a 15-year plan; in force 1 January 2016; target year 2030
  [81:1:1.5] Motto | "Leave no one behind" – a universal call to action to end poverty and protect the planet
[81:1:2] - **Universal:** binds all countries (MDGs were mainly for developing countries); three dimensions – **economic, social, environmental**.
[81:1:3] - **Human-rights basis:** guided by the **UDHR (1948)** and human-rights treaties.
[81:1:4] - **USDG vision:** universal access to **clean water, sanitation and healthcare** is essential for **human dignity**.
[81:1:5] - **"A Million Voices: The World We Want"** (Sept 2013): post-2015 consultation report of the **UN Development Group (UNDG)**.
[81:1:6] # MDGs (Millennium Summit 2000)
[81:1:7] TABLE head: Feature | MDGs | SDGs
  [81:1:7.0] Goals / targets | 8 / 21 | 17 / 169
  [81:1:7.1] Period / deadline | 2000–2015 | 2016–2030
  [81:1:7.2] Scope | Mainly developing countries | Universal
[81:1:8] - **The 8 MDGs:** extreme poverty and hunger; universal primary education; gender equality; child mortality; maternal health; HIV/AIDS, malaria; environmental sustainability; global partnership.
[81:1:9] - **Results:** under-5 mortality **90 → 43** per 1,000; India **halved extreme poverty** (MDG target) before 2015.
[81:1:10] # Chronology
[81:1:11] TABLE head: Year | Milestone
  [81:1:11.0] 1951 | India's First Five Year Plan
  [81:1:11.1] 2000 | Millennium Declaration – 8 MDGs
  [81:1:11.2] 2002 | UNGA res. 57/254 → UN Decade of Education for Sustainable Development 2005–2014 (lead agency UNESCO)
  [81:1:11.3] 2012 | Rio+20 – SDG idea
  [81:1:11.4] 2015 | Agenda 2030 adopted
  [81:1:11.5] 2016 | SDGs in force; first SDSN SDG Index
  [81:1:11.6] 2018 | First SDG India Index (NITI Aayog)
  [81:1:11.7] 2021 | NER District SDG Index, 1st edition (August)
[81:1:12] > Order: **Rio+20 2012 → Agenda 2030 2015 → in force 2016 → SDG India Index 2018**.
[81:1:13] ~~ Sources: Ramesh Singh Indian Economy ch.19 p.37; PMF Environment p.8 (MDGs, Rio+20); AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.314; Rocket Environment p.20, p.71; UN A/RES/57/254; news.un.org (UNDG report, 2013); app notes 5:81 sub 0-1, 5-6
## SUB 2 | NITI Aayog SDG India Index – Editions, Scores and Ranks
[81:2:0] # Editions
[81:2:1] TABLE head: Edition | Coverage | India | Top State / UT
  [81:2:1.0] 2018 Baseline (1st) | 13 goals, 39 targets, 62 indicators | 57 | Kerala, Himachal Pradesh
  [81:2:1.1] 2019-20 (2nd, 30 Dec 2019) | 16 goals | 60 | Kerala 70, Himachal 69; AP, Tamil Nadu, Telangana 67 (3rd)
  [81:2:1.2] 2020-21 (3rd, 3 June 2021) | 16 goals, 115 indicators | 66 (+6) | Kerala 75; UT Chandigarh 79
  [81:2:1.3] 2023-24 (4th, 12 July 2024) | 16 goals, 113 indicators | 71 | Kerala and Uttarakhand 79; Bihar last (57)
[81:2:2] - **Prepared by NITI Aayog** (not CSO, NHRC or NIC); aligned with **MoSPI's National Indicator Framework**.
[81:2:3] - **2018 Baseline left out** SDG **12 (Sustainable Consumption and Production)**, 13, 14 and 17 – it scored only 13 goals (question keys still say "based on 17 goals").
[81:2:4] - **Categories:** **Achiever = 100**; **Front Runner 65–99**; Performer 50–64; Aspirant 0–49.
[81:2:5] - **Kerala** has topped every edition (2023-24 jointly with Uttarakhand).
[81:2:6] # 2020-21 highlights
[81:2:7] - India **66**, up **6 points** from 60, driven by **Goal 6 (Clean Water, 83)** and **Goal 7 (Clean Energy, 92)** – India's best goal in that edition.
[81:2:8] - **Below 50:** **Goal 2 (Zero Hunger)** and **Goal 5 (Gender Equality)** demand special attention.
[81:2:9] - **Goal 2 top performers:** **Kerala** (States) and Chandigarh (UTs).
[81:2:10] # 2023-24 highlights
[81:2:11] - **32** States/UTs Front Runners (10 new, incl. Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Uttar Pradesh); **no State is an Achiever**; UP is below the national 71.
[81:2:12] > ⚠ Trap: 60 is **India's** 2019-20 score, not AP's (AP 67).
[81:2:13] ~~ Sources: NITI Aayog SDG India Index & Dashboard 2020-21 report p.4, p.44, p.46, p.52; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.315-316; drishtiias.com (SDG India Index 2019-20; 2023-24); app notes 5:81 sub 7

## SUB 4 | SDG Monitoring in India – NITI Aayog, MoSPI and Localisation
[81:4:0] # Who does what
[81:4:1] TABLE head: Body | Role
  [81:4:1.0] NITI Aayog | Nodal agency to oversee and monitor SDGs; SDG India Index (ranks States)
  [81:4:1.1] MoSPI | Develops the National Indicator Framework (NIF); SDG-NIF Progress Report 2026: 277 indicators
  [81:4:1.2] UN SDSN | Sustainable Development Report (ranks countries)
[81:4:2] - **NIF is MoSPI's, not NITI Aayog's.** India's **Voluntary National Review (VNR)** goes to the UN HLPF.
[81:4:3] - **Multidimensional poverty (NIF):** **24.85% (2015-16) → 14.96% (2019-21)**.
[81:4:4] # Localisation
[81:4:5] - **Localised SDGs in Gram Panchayats** (**Ministry of Panchayati Raj**): **nine themes** – poverty-free, healthy, child-friendly, water-sufficient, clean and green, self-sufficient infrastructure, socially just and secure, good governance, **women-friendly village**; "industrially advanced village" is **not** one.
[81:4:6] - **NER District SDG Index:** 1st edition **August 2021**.
[81:4:7] - **SDG Conclave 2020** ("Partnerships, Cooperation and Development of North Eastern States", Guwahati, 24-26 Feb 2020): **NITI Aayog** with **North Eastern Council, Government of Assam, Tata Trusts, RIS, UNDP** – **not the World Bank**.
[81:4:8] > Easy rule: **NITI ranks States, SDSN ranks countries, MoSPI counts indicators.**
[81:4:9] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.314; Ramesh Singh Indian Economy ch.19 p.38 (MoSPI indicators); Rocket Environment p.20; india.un.org/en/node/163196 (SDG Conclave 2020); app notes 5:81 sub 9-10

=== NOTES 5:82 | Sustainable Development in Practice – Green Economy, Circular Economy and Esg
## SUB 0 | Green Economy, Green Technology and Green Skills
[82:0:0] # Green economy
[82:0:1] - **Green economy:** reduces environmental risks and ecological scarcities; **decouples growth from resource use and pollution**; **central theme of Rio+20 (2012)**.
[82:0:2] - **Green jobs:** work in agriculture, industry, services or administration that **preserves or restores environmental quality**.
[82:0:3] - **UNEP Green Economy Initiative:** **2008**. **PAGE** (Partnership for Action on Green Economy): **2013**, a response to the **Rio+20** call ("The Future We Want"); UNEP, ILO, UNIDO, UNDP, UNITAR.
[82:0:4] # Green technology
[82:0:5] - **Green technology** pollutes less, uses resources sustainably and recycles more of its waste.
[82:0:6] - **NOT correct:** "green technology is not expensive for developing countries" – **high cost is its main barrier**.
[82:0:7] - **CII–Sohrabji Godrej Green Business Centre:** India's first platinum-rated green building – **Hyderabad**.
[82:0:8] - **ISO 14001** = **Environmental Management System** (9001 quality, 22000 food safety, 27001 information security).
[82:0:9] # Green chemistry and cleaner production
[82:0:10] - **12 Principles of Green Chemistry:** **1998**, **Paul Anastas and John Warner**; core idea – **waste prevention rather than cleanup**; **Green Pharmacy** = green chemistry for medicines.
[82:0:11] - **Green chemistry + cleaner production** reduce waste and pollution across the **whole product life cycle** – hence they serve **EIA** and **Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA)**.
[82:0:12] # Green Skill Development Programme
[82:0:13] - Launched **2017** by **MoEFCC** on the **ENVIS** network; trains youth in **biodiversity conservation, pollution monitoring, waste management, forestry and wildlife** (not semiconductors).
[82:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 p.43 (green economy, green jobs); PMF Environment p.8 (PAGE 2013, Rio+20); Shankar Environment 10th ed. ch.29 (ISO 14000 series); app notes 5:82 sub 0, 2-4; CII-GBC: general knowledge
## SUB 1 | Circular Economy and the 3 Rs
[82:1:0] - **Circular economy:** **reuse, recycling and repair** of materials to reduce waste; waste becomes a resource; replaces the linear **take–make–dispose** ("use and dispose") model.
[82:1:1] - **3 Rs (environment-friendly):** **Reduce, Reuse, Recycle**.
[82:1:2] TABLE head: Linear model | Circular model
  [82:1:2.0] Take, make, dispose | Reduce, reuse, repair, recycle; keep materials in use
  [82:1:2.1] Waste = end point | Waste = resource; growth decoupled from resource use
[82:1:3] - **Why it cuts GHG emissions (UPSC 2025):** it **reduces raw-material inputs** and **reduces production waste** – both true and both explain the emission cut.
[82:1:4] - **Not** exclusively about carbon or fossil fuels; **not** linear growth.
[82:1:5] - **India:** NITI Aayog + MoEFCC committees drew up action plans for priority waste streams – **plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres, metals**.
[82:1:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment p.34 (circular economy of reduce, reuse, recycle); app notes 5:82 sub 1
## SUB 2 | European Green Deal
[82:2:0] - **December 2019**: make the EU **climate-neutral (net-zero GHG) by 2050**; at least **55% cut by 2030 vs 1990** – package **"Fit for 55"**.
[82:2:1] - **Poland** did not commit to the 2050 climate-neutrality target at the December 2019 summit.
[82:2:2] TABLE head: Component | Content
  [82:2:2.0] Farm to Fork | Sustainable food system
  [82:2:2.1] Circular Economy Action Plan | Resource efficiency, recycling
  [82:2:2.2] Biodiversity Strategy | Protect and restore ecosystems (so the Deal is NOT only about carbon)
  [82:2:2.3] Just Transition Fund | Support for affected regions
  [82:2:2.4] Renovation Wave | Energy-efficient buildings
[82:2:3] > Order: GEI 2008 → Rio+20 2012 → PAGE 2013 → GSDP 2017 → Green Deal 2019 → Green Credit 2023.
[82:2:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:82 sub 2; Poland 2019: general knowledge
## SUB 3 | Greenwashing, Green Finance and ESG
[82:3:0] # Greenwashing
[82:3:1] - **Greenwashing** ("green sheen"): **false or exaggerated claims / promises** that a product, firm or country is environment-friendly.
[82:3:2] - A **clear taxonomy** helps regulators curb **greenwashing and "transition washing"**.
[82:3:3] # Green finance
[82:3:4] TABLE head: Instrument | Fact
  [82:3:4.0] Green bond | Pioneer EIB 2007, World Bank 2008
  [82:3:4.1] Sovereign Green Bonds (India) | Announced Budget 2022-23; first issue 2023, Rs 8,000 crore
  [82:3:4.2] Blue bond | Ocean and water projects; first sovereign – Seychelles 2018
  [82:3:4.3] India's first blue bond | Sagarmala Finance Corporation (planned)
  [82:3:4.4] RBI Green Deposit Framework | 2023 – deposits earmarked for green lending
  [82:3:4.5] Social bond / Sustainability bond (ICMA) | Positive social outcomes / a mix of green and social projects
[82:3:5] - **Climate finance taxonomy:** Budget 2024-25; **no final all-sector taxonomy** yet; **Ministry of Steel – Green Steel Taxonomy**; **MSE-GIFT** – green finance for MSMEs.
[82:3:6] # ESG and BRSR
[82:3:7] - **ESG** = **Environmental, Social, Governance**.
[82:3:8] - **BRSR** set by **SEBI**: **top 1,000 listed companies** report audited ESG metrics yearly; **SEBI regulates ESG Rating Providers**.
[82:3:9] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment 10th ed. 29.3.4 (greenwashing); NextGen Indian Economy P1 p.43 (blue bonds, Seychelles); app notes 5:82 sub 5-7
## SUB 4 | Resource Efficiency, EPR and Green Credit
[82:4:0] - **Draft National Resource Efficiency Policy, 2019** (**MoEFCC**): secondary raw materials; a **National Resource Efficiency Authority**.
[82:4:1] - **EPR regimes:** **plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries, tyres**.
[82:4:2] - **Green Credit Programme:** notified by **MoEFCC, October 2023**; **market-based incentive** for voluntary actions (tree plantation, water conservation); tightened August 2025.
[82:4:3] - **National Green Hydrogen Mission:** Rs **19,744 crore**; **5 MMT a year** by 2030; linked to **net zero 2070**.
[82:4:4] - **AMRUT 2.0:** treated used water for **20% of city** and **40% of industrial** demand.
[82:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment p.40, p.88-89 (Green Credit Programme); app notes 5:82 sub 8

=== NOTES 5:83 | International Treaties on Chemicals and Waste – Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm POPs, Minamata; Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment
## SUB 0 | Ozone Depletion – CFCs, Chlorine and Bromine
[83:0:0] # Cause
[83:0:1] - **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons)** are the **main cause** of ozone depletion and of the "ozone hole" – not CO2, CO, methane, N2 or SO2.
[83:0:2] - **Full form:** CFC = **Chlorofluorocarbon** – carbon + chlorine + fluorine; entirely **man-made**, non-toxic, non-flammable.
[83:0:3] - **Mechanism:** under UV in the stratosphere CFCs release **chlorine**; **chlorine and bromine atoms destroy ozone catalytically** (one Cl atom breaks thousands of O3 molecules before it is locked up again) → more UV reaches the Earth.
[83:0:4] - **Bromine** comes from **halons** (fire extinguishers) – about **100 times more potent** than CFCs; **carbon tetrachloride** and **methyl chloroform** also release chlorine.
[83:0:5] - Depletion happens in the **stratosphere** (not in the lower atmosphere where humans live, not in the mesosphere).
[83:0:6] - **CFCs are also greenhouse gases** – they cause both warming and ozone loss (A-R: both true, but "CFCs are used in fridges, ACs, aerosols" is **not the explanation** of that).
[83:0:7] - **A–R (APPSC EO):** "ozone depletion = reduction of stratospheric ozone" ✓; "caused by high chlorine and bromine from CFCs and halons" ✓ → **R explains A**.
[83:0:8] - **Wrong statements trap (TSPSC JL):** ozone is in the **stratosphere, not mesosphere**; it is the **chlorine**, not the carbon, of CFCs that splits O3.
[83:0:9] # Sources of CFCs and related gases
[83:0:10] TABLE head: Gas | Main source
  [83:0:10.0] CFCs | Freon refrigerant, ACs, aerosol propellants, plastic foams, cleaning electronic parts
  [83:0:10.1] Halons | Fire extinguishers
  [83:0:10.2] Nitrogen oxides | Fertiliser plants, vehicles, combustion
  [83:0:10.3] Methane | Bacterial decomposition (wetlands, paddy, livestock)
[83:0:11] - **CFC uses (UPSC 2012):** **plastic foams, cleaning electronic components, aerosol pressurising agents** – **not tubeless tyres** → **1, 3 and 4**.
[83:0:12] > Recall angle (asked ~20 times: UPSC, UPPCS, UKPSC, MPPSC, APPSC G2, Forest, TSPSC): gas most responsible for ozone depletion = **CFC**.
[83:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.5-6; Rocket Environment p.48-49; Shankar Environment Part 16 (Ch19 Ozone depletion); app notes 5:83 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Ozone Layer, Dobson Unit and the Ozone Hole
[83:1:0] # Ozone layer
[83:1:1] - **Ozone = O3** (three oxygen atoms); formed when **UV radiation splits O2** (UV + O2 → O3).
[83:1:2] - About **90%** of ozone is in the **stratosphere** (**10–50 km**; main layer ~15–30 km) – **protective**, absorbs harmful **UV (UV-B)**; ~10% is in the troposphere, where it is a **pollutant**.
[83:1:3] - Ozone protects the biosphere from **ultraviolet rays** – not infra-red, X-rays or gamma rays.
[83:1:4] - **Natural regulation:** stratospheric ozone is naturally regulated by **nitrogen oxides – "nitrogen dioxide"** in books and keys (the NO/NO2 cycle; N2O from soils is the source gas).
[83:1:5] # Dobson Unit
[83:1:6] - **Dobson Unit (DU)** measures the **thickness/concentration of ozone in a column of air from the ground to the top of the atmosphere** – not decibel (sound), angstrom (length), knot, poise or Maxwell.
[83:1:7] - **1 DU = 0.01 mm** of pure ozone at **0°C and 1 atm**; an **"ozone hole"** = total column ozone **below 220 DU**.
[83:1:8] # Ozone hole
[83:1:9] - Most affected region: **Antarctica**; seasonal thinning in the **Southern Hemisphere spring (Aug–Nov)**.
[83:1:10] - **Polar stratospheric clouds** in extreme cold turn stable chlorine compounds into **active chlorine**, which destroys ozone when sunlight returns.
[83:1:11] - Ozone began to **drop sharply in the 1980s**; the Antarctic hole was **reported in 1985 by the British Antarctic Survey** (NextGen: first noticed 1983).
[83:1:12] - **Tibetan ozone low ("halo") 2005:** discovered by **G.W. Kent Moore**, University of Toronto.
[83:1:13] - **Recovery:** NASA/WMO report healing of the Antarctic hole, mainly due to the **ban on CFCs** under Montreal.
[83:1:14] TABLE head: Region | Back to 1980 levels
  [83:1:14.0] Most of the world | 2040
  [83:1:14.1] Arctic | 2045
  [83:1:14.2] Antarctic | 2066
[83:1:15] > Dobson Unit asked 7 times (APPSC, UKPSC 2005/2010/2025, UP RO 2021, Chhattisgarh 2023).
[83:1:16] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.47-49; NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.5; Shankar Environment Part 16 (Ch19); app notes 5:83 sub 0-1
## SUB 2 | Vienna Convention and Montreal Protocol
[83:2:0] - **Vienna Convention (1985):** framework treaty for **protection of the ozone layer** – research, monitoring, reporting.
[83:2:1] - **Montreal Protocol:** the action treaty under Vienna to **phase out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances (ODS)** – not GHGs/global warming, acid rain, smog, DDT, petrol or marine life.
[83:2:2] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [83:2:2.0] Signed | 16 September 1987, Montreal, Canada
  [83:2:2.1] In force | 1 January 1989 ("the 1989 treaty to protect the ozone layer")
  [83:2:2.2] Nature | Legally binding; adjustments/amendments: London, Copenhagen, Montreal, Beijing, Quito Adjustment, Kigali (2016)
  [83:2:2.3] Coverage | ~100 chemicals: CFCs, halons, CTC, methyl chloroform, HCFCs, methyl bromide
  [83:2:2.4] Parties | 198 – first and only UN treaties universally ratified (Vienna + Montreal)
  [83:2:2.5] Secretariat | Ozone Secretariat, Nairobi (UNEP)
[83:2:3] - Montreal is **not part of the Kyoto Protocol** (Kyoto belongs to UNFCCC) → statements "signed 1987", "phases out ODS", "universally ratified" are correct.
[83:2:4] - **UNEP's role:** **monitors and implements** international agreements like the Montreal Protocol (Ozone Secretariat).
[83:2:5] - **Results:** **~99% of ODS phased out** (2024); avoids **0.5–1°C** warming by 2050; widely called the most **successful** environmental treaty.
[83:2:6] - **Multilateral Fund (1991):** technical and financial aid to developing countries. **MOP37** focused on implementing **Kigali**.
[83:2:7] TABLE head: Treaty | Concern
  [83:2:7.0] Montreal Protocol | Ozone / ODS
  [83:2:7.1] Kyoto Protocol (1997, UNFCCC) | Binding GHG cuts by developed countries
  [83:2:7.2] Basel (1989) | Hazardous waste
  [83:2:7.3] Cartagena (2000, CBD) | Biosafety
  [83:2:7.4] Nagoya (2010, CBD) | Access and benefit sharing
  [83:2:7.5] Bretton Woods (1944) | IMF/World Bank – economic, not ozone
[83:2:8] > Montreal "related to / focussed on" asked 15 times; signing year **1987** (JL 2020 ×2).
[83:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.6; Rocket Environment p.29, p.64; app notes 5:83 sub 5
## SUB 3 | ODS vs HFCs – Refrigerants, Foams and Fire Extinguishers
[83:3:0] TABLE head: Substance | ODS? | Main uses
  [83:3:0.0] CFCs (CFC-12 in refrigerators) | Yes – main culprit | Refrigerators, ACs, aerosols, foams, solvents
  [83:3:0.1] Halons (Halon-1211, 1301) | Yes – ~100× CFC | Portable fire extinguishers
  [83:3:0.2] HCFCs (HCFC-141b) | Yes, weaker – interim substitute | Foam blowing (HCFC-141b), ACs
  [83:3:0.3] CTC, methyl chloroform | Yes | Solvents, feedstock
  [83:3:0.4] Methyl bromide | Yes | Agricultural fumigation and quarantine
  [83:3:0.5] Nitrous oxide (N2O) | Not controlled under Montreal (books: "not responsible") | Fertilisers, laughing gas; a GHG
  [83:3:0.6] HFCs | No (non-ODS) – but very high GWP | ODS substitutes in ACs, refrigeration → Kigali
[83:3:1] - **HFCs** are entirely **man-made**; used as **aerosol propellants, foam-blowing agents and fire retardants/suppressants (clean agents)** – **not lubricants** → UPSC 2023: **only three**.
[83:3:2] # Refrigerants and extinguishers
[83:3:3] TABLE head: Item | Use
  [83:3:3.0] Freon (CFC; DuPont trade name, stable halocarbon) | Domestic refrigerators
  [83:3:3.1] Mafron (halogenated hydrocarbon, trade name) | Refrigerator gas (UKPSC 2010 key)
  [83:3:3.2] Liquid ammonia | Large cold-storage plants
  [83:3:3.3] Carbon dioxide | Best extinguisher for electrical fires (non-conducting)
  [83:3:3.4] Soda-acid extinguisher | NaHCO3 + dilute H2SO4 → CO2
[83:3:4] - **Ammonia** liquefies at ambient temperature only at **high pressure** (not low) → A true, R false (IAS 2000).
[83:3:5] - Radon, sodium, fluorine, neon, oxygen are not refrigerants.
[83:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.6; Rocket Environment p.48; Shankar Environment Part 16 (Ch19); app notes 5:83 sub 3
## SUB 4 | World Ozone Day
[83:4:0] - **16 September** = **International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer** (World Ozone Day) – declared by **UNGA on 19 December 1994**; marks the **signing of the Montreal Protocol (16 Sep 1987)**.
[83:4:1] - Wrong options: 5 June (World Environment Day), 22 May (Biodiversity), 22 April (Earth Day), 21 Sept, 26 Sept.
[83:4:2] - **2026 theme: "Global Action for a Cooler Planet"** – marks **10 years of the Kigali Amendment**.

## SUB 5 | Kigali Amendment and India's Ozone Action
[83:5:0] # Kigali Amendment (2016)
[83:5:1] - Adopted **2016, Kigali, Rwanda** (197 nations); **amends the Montreal Protocol** (not Kyoto, Bali or Paris); legally binding; in force **1 January 2019**.
[83:5:2] - Phases down **HFCs** – not ODS but potent GHGs (ACs, refrigeration); expected to avoid up to **0.5°C** warming by 2100; Parties cut HFCs **80–85%** from baselines by the late 2040s.
[83:5:3] TABLE head: Group | Baseline | Freeze | Final cut
  [83:5:3.0] Developed | 2011–13 | Reductions from 2019 | 85% by 2036
  [83:5:3.1] Group 1 (incl. China) | 2020–22 | 2024 | 80% by 2045
  [83:5:3.2] India (Group 2, with Gulf states, Iran, Iraq, Pakistan) | 2024–26 | 2028 | 85% by 2047
[83:5:4] - India **ratified Kigali in 2021**; MoEFCC: **no environmental clearance** for new/additional HFC production **after 31 December 2027**.
[83:5:5] # India's ozone action
[83:5:6] - **Ozone Cell (MoEFCC)** = India's **National Ozone Unit**; **ODS (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000** under the **Environment (Protection) Act**.
[83:5:7] TABLE head: Substance | Phased out in India by
  [83:5:7.0] Halons (except essential use) | 1 Jan 2001
  [83:5:7.1] CFCs in manufacturing (except MDIs) | 1 Jan 2003
  [83:5:7.2] CTC, methyl chloroform, CFCs in MDIs | 1 Jan 2010
  [83:5:7.3] Methyl bromide | 1 Jan 2015
  [83:5:7.4] HCFCs | Allowed up to 1 Jan 2040
[83:5:8] - **HPMP Stage-II:** India **first developing country** to fully phase out **HCFC-141b**, used by **foam manufacturing enterprises** (rigid foam) – the most potent ODS after CFCs.
[83:5:9] - **India Cooling Action Plan (MoEFCC, March 2019):** 20-year horizon to **2037–38**; cut **cooling demand 20–25%** and **refrigerant demand 25–30%**; six themes – space cooling in buildings, cold chain, servicing, domestic production, R&D, transport – **not coal-based power**.
[83:5:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.6-7; Rocket Environment p.48, p.64; app notes 5:83 sub 7-8
## SUB 6 | UV Radiation – Effects of Ozone Loss
[83:6:0] TABLE head: Target | Effect of more UV-B
  [83:6:0.0] Humans | Skin cancer, eye cataracts, sunburn, immune suppression, DNA damage; 1% ozone loss raises harmful UV ~2%
  [83:6:0.1] Crops | Reduced growth and photosynthesis
  [83:6:0.2] Phytoplankton / marine | Damage to plankton and fish larvae (not more phytoplankton)
  [83:6:0.3] Materials | Degrades plastic, rubber, wood
[83:6:1] - UV bands: UV-A 315–400 nm, **UV-B 280–315 nm**, UV-C 100–280 nm.
[83:6:2] TABLE head: Term | Meaning (match, NTRUHS)
  [83:6:2.0] Stratospheric ozone | Protective layer against UV
  [83:6:2.1] Ozone depletion | Allows harmful UV rays to reach Earth
  [83:6:2.2] UV-B increase | Eye damage, skin cancer, sunburn
  [83:6:2.3] Tropospheric ozone | Air pollutant harmful to health, plants, materials
[83:6:3] - Not effects of UV: respiratory infections, hearing loss, digestive disorders.
[83:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.5; Rocket Environment p.47; app notes 5:83 sub 4
## SUB 7 | Chemicals and Waste Conventions – Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Minamata
[83:7:0] TABLE head: Convention | Year (in force) | Focus
  [83:7:0.0] Basel | 1989 (1992) | Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes and their disposal
  [83:7:0.1] Rotterdam | 1998 (2004) | Prior Informed Consent (PIC) for hazardous chemicals and pesticides in trade
  [83:7:0.2] Stockholm | 2001 (2004) | Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)
  [83:7:0.3] Minamata | 2013 (2017) | Mercury
[83:7:1] # Basel
[83:7:2] - India ratified **1992**; Basel's PIC operates in India under the **Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016**.
[83:7:3] - **Ban Amendment:** bans hazardous-waste exports from **OECD/EU + Liechtenstein** to other countries; in force **5 December 2019**. Wrong options: carbon emissions, wetlands, deforestation, biodiversity.
[83:7:4] # Rotterdam and Stockholm
[83:7:5] - **PIC:** the **importing country must agree** before a listed chemical is exported; Annex III lists **pesticides and industrial chemicals banned or severely restricted**. India **acceded 2005**; DNAs: **Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilisers + Ministry of Agriculture**.
[83:7:6] - **BRS:** Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm share **one joint secretariat** under UNEP; India – MoEFCC **Hazardous Substances Management Division**.
[83:7:7] - **POPs:** **toxic, persistent, bioaccumulate, travel long distances**; **POPs Review Committee** assesses candidates. India ratified Stockholm **2006**; **7 more POPs ratified 2020**.
[83:7:8] - Initial **12 "dirty dozen"** (DDT, PCBs, dioxins, furans, aldrin…); now **37** listed.
[83:7:9] TABLE head: Annex | Meaning | Example
  [83:7:9.0] A | Elimination | Aldrin
  [83:7:9.1] B | Restriction | DDT (malaria control)
  [83:7:9.2] C | Unintentional by-products | Dioxins, furans
[83:7:10] - **2025 Annex A additions:** **chlorpyrifos** (neurotoxic insecticide – not in the dirty dozen), **long-chain PFCAs** ("**forever chemicals**"), medium-chain chlorinated paraffins.
[83:7:11] # Minamata (mercury)
[83:7:12] - Protects from **man-made emissions of mercury**; named after **Minamata, Japan** (factory wastewater mercury poisoned fish-eaters, 1950s).
[83:7:13] - **Mercury pollution (UPSC 2023):** **gold mining** ✓, **coal-based thermal power plants** ✓, **no known safe level of exposure** (WHO) ✓ → **all three**. Solar PV panels in normal operation are not a source.
[83:7:14] - **Dental amalgam** phase-out by **2034**. "Mercury – Rotterdam" is a wrong pair.
[83:7:15] # Chronology
[83:7:16] - **Vienna 1985 → Montreal 1987 → Basel 1989 → Kyoto 1997 → Cartagena 2000 → Stockholm 2001 → Minamata 2013 → Kigali 2016.**
[83:7:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 5.1 p.9-10; Rocket Environment p.8, p.30, p.65, p.71; app notes 5:83 sub 9-11
